title: The Escape
text: The film opens with a prologue on eugenics that contrasts the careful breeding of animals with the way humans reproduce, and then tells the story of the Joyce family. The abusive father, Jim Joyce, corrupts his naturally sensitive son Larry into cruelty. Larry contracts syphilis and is treated by Dr. Von Eiden, who becomes involved with Larry's sister May and encourages her to leave the family. Unable to find stable work, May becomes the companion of a wealthy senator but refuses to marry him. Her sister Jennie marries the brutal "Bull" McGee, who kills their baby while drunk; Jennie loses her mind, rocking a doll in the empty cradle, and McGee sells her into prostitution. May rescues her, but Jennie dies soon afterwards. Von Eiden performs an operation that restores Larry's original sensitivity, and May leaves the senator and agrees to marry the doctor. The film, directed by D. W. Griffith, is now lost. Eugenics frames the whole film: its prologue compares the selective breeding of animals with human reproduction, and the misfortunes of the Joyce family are presented as the story that follows from that comparison, placing the film within the eugenics movement of the 1910s. The scientist figure is a physician, Dr. Von Eiden, who treats Larry's syphilis, cures his cruelty with an operation and ends up marrying May, so medicine is portrayed as a source of rescue rather than harm. The family's troubles, however, are shown as coming from a mix of causes, including the father's abuse, venereal disease, alcohol and poverty, not only from inheritance. Because no copy of the film is known to survive, its plot is known only from written accounts, and how strongly it argued the eugenic case on screen cannot be checked today.

title: Where Are My Children?
text: District attorney Richard Walton prosecutes Dr. Homer, a physician arrested for distributing birth-control literature deemed obscene. On the stand, Homer argues for legal contraception, recalling cases from his practice: children abused in an alcoholic household, a poor family unable to care for sick children, and an abandoned mother who kills herself and her baby. Meanwhile, Walton's wife Edith has for years secretly used the services of Dr. Malfit, an abortionist, so that pregnancy will not interrupt her social life, and she sends friends to him too. When her brother seduces the young daughter of the Waltons' maid, the girl dies after a botched abortion by Malfit. After Malfit's trial, Walton finds his wife's name in the doctor's ledger, expels her friends from the house and confronts her with the question "Where are my children?". The couple grow old in a childless, lonely home. Genetics appears here through eugenics, the early-twentieth-century movement to improve the population by controlling who reproduces. Written partly as a response to Margaret Sanger's 1914 prosecution for promoting birth control, the film argues didactically for contraception and against abortion, and it presents examples of desirable and undesirable children as the products of good or bad breeding; a married couple in the cast are credited simply as the "eugenic" husband and wife. Critics have noted that its condemnation of abortion is framed in moral and eugenic terms, aimed at wealthy women who are seen as failing to produce the "right" children. There are no geneticists and no science on screen: heredity is a background ideology rather than a plot device. The film is mainly of historical interest as evidence of how readily American popular culture of the 1910s absorbed eugenic ideas, ideas that also underpinned compulsory sterilisation laws in the United States.

title: The Black Stork
text: The Black Stork, also released as Are You Fit To Marry?, is a silent eugenics propaganda film written by and starring the Chicago surgeon Harry J. Haiselden, who plays himself. It opens with a warning that social problems such as crime and poverty result from careless management of human breeding. A newborn baby is born with severe malformations, and the doctor refuses the surgery that could save its life, telling the mother that "God does not want this child to live." The medical profession is outraged, but the mother has a vision of her son's future: disabled, unhappy and violent, and the father of five disabled children of his own. Convinced, she lets the baby die, and the film ends with Jesus receiving the infant's soul as the doctor looks on. The story dramatises Haiselden's real refusal to operate on the newborn Allan Bollinger in 1915. Heredity and eugenics are the whole point of the film. It argues that "defective" traits pass inevitably from parents to children, so that letting a malformed newborn die protects future generations, a view it supports with the mother's vision of her son fathering disabled children. The doctor is not a geneticist but a real surgeon who used the film to defend his practice of withholding treatment from disabled infants; he presented this as a scientific and humane choice. In the real Bollinger case, Chicago's health commissioner testified that the baby's condition was treatable, and a coroner's jury rejected Haiselden's claim that the child would have grown up mentally or morally defective. Haiselden was expelled from the Chicago Medical Society over his publicity, yet the film circulated in the United States for years, in the era of American eugenic sterilisation laws. It is a historical document of how eugenic ideas were sold to the public, not a portrayal of genetic science.

title: Tomorrow's Children
text: Alice Mason wants to marry her fiancé Jim Baker and raise a family, but her plans collapse when the authorities order her parents to undergo sterilization or lose their welfare payments. The Masons are presented as a "defective" family: the parents are idle alcoholics and Alice's siblings have physical and mental disabilities or criminal ties. Because the family's bloodline is judged to be corrupt, the court rules that Alice, the only capable member of the household, must be sterilized too. She runs away but is caught by the police. Jim persuades Dr. Brooks to testify on her behalf, yet the court does not change its decision. Father O'Brien pleads with Mrs. Mason, who, drunk, reveals that Alice was a foundling the family took in and is not related to them by blood. The priest races to the hospital, and Dr. Brooks stops the operation in time. Eugenics is the subject of the film. It portrays the compulsory sterilization of people deemed hereditarily unfit, a practice endorsed in the United States in 1927, when Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that society could "prevent those who are manifestly unfit from continuing their kind". The film assumes, as eugenicists did, that alcoholism, disability and criminality run in families, and the state applies that belief through courts and doctors. Its plot twist exposes the weakness of judging people by their "bloodline": Alice is condemned for a heredity she does not have. The physicians are divided, with Dr. Brooks siding with Alice against the order. The film was openly critical of these policies; its themes of sterilization and hereditary defect led several state censorship boards to ban it, and it was approved in only a few states.

title: Bedtime for Bonzo
text: Psychology professor Peter Boyd is engaged to Valerie, daughter of his college's dean, Tillinghast. When the dean learns that Peter's father was a criminal, he forbids the marriage, declaring that Peter's blood is tainted. Peter, who believes environment matters more than heredity, sets out to prove it by raising a chimpanzee, Bonzo, as a child in a law-abiding home. He hires a young woman, Jane, as nanny, and the two act as Bonzo's parents, teaching him good habits. After a misunderstanding Valerie breaks off the engagement, and Peter learns that Bonzo is to be sold to Yale for medical research. Bonzo escapes and takes a necklace from a jewellery store, and Peter is arrested trying to return it, but Bonzo, as he has been taught, puts the necklace back himself. The experiment is judged a success, Bonzo is kept, and Peter and Jane are to marry. The film is a light comedy built on the nature versus nurture debate. The dean stands for a crude hereditarian view in which criminality runs in the blood, the kind of thinking that fed the eugenics movement of the early twentieth century; the professor stands for the opposite, that upbringing shapes character. Genetics as a science never appears: there is no geneticist, no laboratory work and no mention of genes, only "blood" and "heredity". The chimpanzee experiment is played for laughs and settles the question in favour of environment, which is also the romantic resolution. It has a real precedent: in 1931–32 the psychologist Winthrop Kellogg raised an infant chimpanzee, Gua, alongside his own son for nine months to see how human a chimpanzee could become; Gua learned many everyday behaviours but never human language. Today nature and nurture are understood to interact, and neither a chimpanzee's upbringing nor a father's record decides character on its own.

title: Picnic on the Grass
text: Étienne Alexis, a celebrated French biologist, is the favourite to become the first president of a united Europe. His programme calls for compulsory artificial insemination to improve humanity and make it worthy of modern science. To celebrate his engagement to his German cousin Marie-Charlotte, he holds a picnic near his estate in Provence, beside the ruins of a temple of Diana. Among the servants is Nénette, a farmer's daughter who wants a child without a husband and has volunteered for his insemination experiments. When the goatherd Gaspard plays his flute, a sudden wind scatters the party, a bacchanal breaks out, and Étienne, separated from the others, falls for Nénette. After a few days at her father's house he is dragged back to his old life, but on his wedding day he finds Nénette pregnant with his child and decides to marry her instead. Jean Renoir's comedy is a satire of scientific rationalism, and its target is eugenics. Étienne Alexis wants to replace sexual reproduction with state-run artificial insemination, selecting donors to breed a better population and, he hopes, to do away with passion altogether. Genetics as such is never discussed in technical terms; what the film mocks is the idea that reproduction can be planned rationally from above. The scientist is a respected public figure and a presidential candidate, presented as stiff and well-meaning rather than evil, and the film's answer to him is nature itself: a wind, a flute and a summer afternoon are enough to make him abandon his programme and father a child the old-fashioned way. Made in 1959, the film treats eugenic ambitions as absurd rather than menacing, and links them to a technocratic vision of the new united Europe.

title: Space Seed
alt: Semilla espacial Star Trek: The Original Series, season 1, episode 22
text: The USS Enterprise finds the SS Botany Bay, a derelict 20th-century ship carrying dozens of people in suspended animation. Their leader, brought aboard for medical care, is identified by Spock as Khan Noonien Singh, a 20th-century dictator and one of a group of genetically altered "superpeople" who once ruled much of Earth. Khan persuades Lieutenant Marla McGivers to help him, revives his followers and seizes the ship, threatening to suffocate Captain Kirk in a decompression chamber until the crew submits. McGivers frees Kirk, who regains control of the Enterprise and overpowers Khan in a fistfight in Engineering. At a hearing, Kirk exiles Khan and his people to the harsh planet Ceti Alpha V; Khan accepts, saying it is better to reign in hell than serve in heaven, and McGivers chooses to go with him. The story continues in the film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982). The episode introduces one of Star Trek's most lasting ideas: humans deliberately improved by science who become tyrants. In its backstory, Khan and his followers were produced by selective breeding to create perfect humans; they took power over more than a third of the planet in the Eugenics Wars, which the franchise's own chronology dates to 1992–1996. The scientists who created them never appear; the story focuses on the creation, whose physical and mental superiority goes hand in hand with a will to rule. Sociologist William Sims Bainbridge argued that selective breeding could not produce supermen so quickly and that direct genetic engineering would be more plausible. Later Star Trek productions adopted that view, recasting the "augments" as genetically engineered, and established that human genetic enhancement is illegal in the Federation, as in the Deep Space Nine episode "Doctor Bashir, I Presume?".

title: Blood of the Condor
text: A Quechua community in the Bolivian Andes receives medical care from the "Cuerpo del Progreso" (Progress Corps), a fictional US-backed aid agency modelled on the Peace Corps. The villagers do not suspect that the foreigners are secretly sterilising the community's women. When the truth comes out, the villagers attack the foreigners, and the attackers are rounded up and shot by the authorities. Ignacio Mallku, the community's leader, is wounded, and his brother Sixto takes him to the city and desperately looks for medical care, but without money for proper treatment Ignacio dies. At the end Sixto returns to the countryside with Ignacio's widow, and the final image suggests an uprising of the indigenous people. Directed by Jorge Sanjinés, the film tells its story largely through flashbacks and is spoken in Quechua, Spanish and English. The film does not deal with genetics as such but with forced sterilisation, a practice historically linked to eugenics and to population control. The Spanish Wikipedia article describes the sterilisations in the film as a eugenic practice meant to stop indigenous people from reproducing. The perpetrators are foreign doctors and aid workers who present themselves as bringing health and progress, and the film portrays them as agents of a racist, imperialist policy. The story was based on accounts that Sanjinés collected from indigenous people, and its release contributed to a government investigation and to the expulsion of the Peace Corps from Bolivia in 1971. Historians note, however, that no documentary evidence has emerged that the Peace Corps sterilised women in Bolivia. Forced sterilisation of indigenous women did happen elsewhere, notably in Peru in the 1990s. Because its subject is coercive birth control rather than heredity, the title is only loosely connected to genetics.

title: The Resurrection of Zachary Wheeler
text: Reporter Harry Walsh witnesses a car crash and recognises the badly injured survivor as Senator Zachary Wheeler, a likely presidential candidate. When the hospital denies that Wheeler was ever admitted and his editor fires him for refusing to retract the story, Walsh follows the trail to New Mexico. Wheeler, meanwhile, wakes up in a secret clinic run by Dr. Redding and Dr. Layle Johnson, where he has been rebuilt with organs taken from "somas", bodies grown artificially from his own DNA. The price of his recovery is political: a shadowy Committee expects him to serve its interests as senator and threatens to reveal his transplant if he refuses. Walsh reaches the base at Los Alamos, finds a spare Wheeler soma and, mistaking it for the senator, escapes with it. Eventually Walsh and Wheeler meet and agree to expose the Committee, while its members look forward to their next "client". The film is one of the earliest to show cloning used to supply spare body parts, even though the word "clone" is never spoken. The "somas" (Greek for "body") are mindless copies of the senator grown from his DNA and kept at a secret facility so that their organs can be transplanted without rejection. The doctors who run the programme are not mad scientists but employees of a powerful Committee that uses the technology as a means of blackmail, offering survival to influential patients in return for political obedience; the film treats medicine as "a new type of money". In reality a clone would have to develop from an embryo and grow for years, so ready-made adult copies are fiction, but the premise anticipates a real concern: the harvesting of organs and tissues from cloned humans is one of the abuses most often cited by opponents of reproductive cloning.

title: Blackenstein
text: Eddie Turner, an African American soldier, has lost his arms and legs to a land mine in Vietnam. His fiancée, the physicist Dr. Winifred Walker, turns to her former teacher Dr. Stein, recently awarded a Nobel Prize for "solving the DNA genetic code", whose "DNA solution" and "laser beam fusion" have already reattached a patient's legs and kept a 90-year-old woman looking 50. Stein gives Eddie new arms, but his assistant Malcomb, rejected by Winifred, sabotages the DNA injections for Eddie's leg surgery with contaminated RNA. Eddie regresses into a brutish, Neanderthal-like creature who leaves the house each night to kill and dismember victims, beginning with an orderly who abused him at the veterans' hospital. After he stops Malcomb from raping Winifred, Eddie kills him, Stein's other patients and, in a struggle, Stein himself. He is finally cornered by police Dobermans, which tear him to pieces. The film updates the Frankenstein story for the age of molecular biology: instead of bringing a corpse to life with electricity, the scientist rebuilds a body with an injectable "DNA solution", and an unexplained "RNA problem" accounts both for a patient's tiger-striped leg and for Eddie's transformation into a monster. Genetics is the pretext for the horror rather than its subject, and the terms are used loosely. Dr. Stein is a celebrated, well-meaning surgeon who wants to help a maimed veteran; although his treatments already show odd side effects, the catastrophe is caused by his jealous assistant's sabotage, and Stein dies at the hands of his creation. Eddie's "regression" to a primitive, ape-like state reflects the popular idea of genetic damage as a step back in evolution, not any real mechanism. The film's Nobel Prize nods to recent history: the deciphering of the genetic code earned Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and Robert Holley the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: Flesh for Frankenstein
text: In 19th-century Serbia, Baron Frankenstein neglects his wife and sister, Katrin, while assembling a "perfect" man and woman from parts of corpses. He means to mate them and found a new Serbian race that will obey his every command. Obsessed with the male creature's appearance and libido, he checks that its nose has the proper Serbian shape and looks for a more sexually driven head to replace its own. With his assistant Otto, he kills a young man on his way to a monastery, mistaking him for a lusty farmhand, Nicholas, and grafts his head onto the creature. Nicholas, who has become Katrin's lover, discovers the laboratory and is captured. The experiment collapses in carnage: Katrin and the female creature die, the Baron kills Otto, and the male creature, recovering memories of its former life, kills the Baron and then itself. Genetics in the strict sense plays almost no part. The Baron builds his creatures by surgery, stitching together parts of corpses, and nothing in the story involves genes, heredity mechanisms or laboratory genetics. The link to the theme is eugenic: his stated goal is to breed a new, obedient Serbian race from an ideal couple, choosing body parts for "racial" features such as the shape of the nose and for sexual drive, and treating people as raw material for that project. The film, produced by Andy Warhol and directed by Paul Morrissey, plays this as gory, deliberately camp satire of the mad scientist and his fantasies of a master race, and the experiment ends in the deaths of everyone involved. It is of interest here mainly as a parody of eugenic ambitions rather than as a story about genetics.

title: The Infinite Vulcan
alt: El vulcano infinito Star Trek: The Animated Series, season 1, episode 7
text: While surveying the planet Phylos for possible colonization, the Enterprise landing party meets its plant-like inhabitants, who save Sulu from a poisonous walking plant. The Phylosians explain that they were nearly wiped out by a disease brought to their world by Dr. Stavos Keniclius, a human scientist who survived Earth's Eugenics Wars. A giant clone of Keniclius, Keniclius 5, kidnaps Spock. Keniclius has lived for centuries by moving his consciousness into successive, more advanced clone bodies, and he believes the galaxy is still as ravaged by war as Earth was. To impose peace, he creates a giant clone of Spock and transfers Spock's mind into it, leaving the original body an empty shell. The new Spock mind-melds with the original to save his life, and the two Spocks and Kirk convince Keniclius that his plan is unnecessary. Spock Two and Keniclius 5 stay behind to help rebuild Phylosian civilization. Cloning drives the episode. Keniclius, a scientist linked to the franchise's fictional Eugenics Wars, prolongs his own life through a series of clones and plans to build a peacekeeping force from a cloned, enlarged Spock. He is portrayed less as a villain than as a misguided idealist acting alone, whose experiments have already devastated a native population by accident. The episode treats a clone as receiving a full mind and memories through a transfer of consciousness, and makes clones giant, which has no basis in real cloning: a clone is a genetic copy that develops normally and does not inherit memories. Writer Walter Koenig, who played Chekov in the original series, said the cloning plot was inspired by newspaper articles on the subject at the time.

title: Zardoz
text: In 2293, humanity is divided between the immortal Eternals, who lead a luxurious but aimless life inside the Vortex, a community guarded by an artificial intelligence called the Tabernacle, and the mortal Brutals, who farm an irradiated wasteland to feed them. A flying stone head, Zardoz, arms a caste of Brutal Exterminators to keep the others in line. One of them, Zed, stows away aboard Zardoz and reaches the Vortex, where he is held captive and studied. He discovers that the Eternals, unable to die, have grown bored, impotent and corrupt, and that Zardoz is a fraud run by the Eternal Arthur Frayn. Helped by May and the rebel Friend, Zed absorbs the Eternals' knowledge and shuts down the Tabernacle, letting the Exterminators in to kill the Eternals, who welcome death. Zed and Consuella then have a son and grow old together. Genetics appears as a late twist rather than as the main subject. A genetic analysis of Zed reveals that he is the end product of a long eugenic breeding programme secretly devised by Arthur Frayn, who used his control over the Exterminators to breed a superior man capable of entering the Vortex and breaking the Eternals' stagnation. Frayn also guided Zed's education, leading him to read The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the source of the name Zardoz. Frayn is a manipulator rather than a laboratory scientist, and his creation turns out more thoughtful and humane than the Eternals expect. The film touches on related ideas: the Eternals no longer need to reproduce and, when they die by accident, are reborn into identical, synthetically produced bodies. The breeding programme is closer to selective animal breeding than to modern genetics, and the film treats it allegorically, as part of a fable about immortality, power and the value of mortality.

title: Mission of the Darians
text: Moonbase Alpha picks up a distress call from Daria, a colossal ship drifting past the Moon. Commander Koenig leads a rescue team aboard and the group splits up. Dr Russell is captured by the Survivors, a tribe of savages who send anyone with a deformity, even security officer Lowry with a missing finger joint, into a vaporisation chamber, and offer healthy people as sacrifices to their god, Neman. Koenig and Professor Bergman learn the ship's history from the elegant Kara: nine hundred years ago a reactor accident irradiated most of the 50,000 crew, and only fourteen people in the command area escaped mutation. Neman, the ship's captain, reveals that the sacrifices are harvested for organs to keep the fourteen alive while they guard a gene bank meant to recreate a pure Darian race. The Alphans fight back, a Survivor smashes Neman into the gene bank, and Koenig persuades both groups to cooperate. Heredity and racial purity drive this episode. The ship's elite preserve a gene bank of unmutated Darian genetic material, intending to use it to create a new race once they reach their destination, and they treat the radiation-damaged descendants of the crew as raw material: the deformed are recycled as food and the healthy are harvested for organs. The Survivors' ritual killing of anyone with a birth defect is a crude form of eugenic selection taught to them by the rulers. According to the episode's production history, writer Johnny Byrne combined the 1972 Andes plane-crash cannibalism case with a spin on racial purity, the "Darians" standing for "Aryans". The leaders are not scientists but an aristocracy using science to prolong their own lives, and the destruction of the gene bank symbolises the end of their scheme. The idea that radiation produces heritable mutations is grounded in real science; the rest is allegory.

title: My Daughter Hildegart
text: Madrid, 9 June 1933: Aurora Rodríguez goes to the home of a lawyer and tells him she has just shot dead her 18-year-old daughter, Hildegart. Framed by the recollections of the journalist Eduardo de Guzmán and by Aurora's interrogations, psychiatric examinations and trial, the film reconstructs in flashbacks how she conceived Hildegart as a project: after raising her nephew, the child pianist Pepito Arriola, until his mother took him back, she chose a man to father a child and educated her daughter under iron discipline to be the woman of the future. Hildegart becomes a prodigy, a lawyer, a socialist activist and a writer on sexual reform who corresponds with figures such as Havelock Ellis. When she begins to escape her mother's control, falls in love and plans to leave, the paranoid Aurora, convinced of a conspiracy to take her away, kills her. Based on a real case, the film portrays a private eugenic experiment. Aurora Rodríguez Carballeira believed that a child could be shaped from conception to serve human progress; she chose a "physiological collaborator", a former priest and navy chaplain, to father her daughter, and then subjected Hildegart to a rigorous education. The film blends heredity and upbringing: Aurora's faith in the father she selected is shaken when he confesses that sex has ruined his life, and her plan rests at least as much on training as on biology. There are no scientists in the story, but its backdrop is the eugenics and sex-reform movement of the Second Spanish Republic, in which the real Hildegart took part as secretary of the League for Sexual Reform and a speaker at the First Spanish Eugenics Conference in 1933. The film does not judge Aurora's ideas directly; it presents her as a possessive, paranoid mother who treats her daughter as a work she has the right to destroy.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering animal experimentation human experimentation
text: In 1911, after the wreck of the ship Lady Vain, the engineer Braddock is the only survivor to reach a Pacific island, where he is nursed back to health in the compound of the scientist Dr. Moreau. Also living there are Moreau's mercenary associate Montgomery, his misshapen mute servant M'Ling, and a young woman, Maria. Braddock discovers that the island is populated by "Humanimals", creatures Moreau has made from wild animals by injecting them with a serum containing human genetic material. The creatures live by laws Moreau has given them and fear his laboratory, the "House of Pain". When Braddock tries to leave with Maria, Moreau injects him with a serum to turn him into an animal and record the experience. After Moreau kills Montgomery, the creatures revolt; Moreau dies and the compound burns. Braddock, slowly returning to his human state, escapes by boat with Maria. This adaptation of H. G. Wells's 1896 novel updates Moreau's methods. In the novel he shapes animals into people by vivisection; here he injects a serum containing human genetic material, so the creation of human-animal hybrids becomes a matter of transferring heredity rather than surgery. The film also reverses the process when Moreau injects Braddock to make him regress towards an animal. Moreau is the classic mad scientist: working alone and beyond any oversight, he seeks to "perfect life", treats his creatures with cruelty, regards compassion as a weakness and kills his own associate. His experiments end in revolt and destruction. The idea that a serum could reshape an adult body into another species is pure fantasy, but the story anticipates later concerns about human-animal hybrids and about scientists who place their curiosity above the suffering of their subjects.

title: The Boys from Brazil
themes: nazi cloning nature nurture human experimentation
text: In Paraguay, young Barry Kohler spies on a meeting of fugitive Nazis at which Dr. Josef Mengele orders the murder, over two years, of 94 civil servants aged around 65 in Western Europe and North America. Kohler is killed while telephoning Ezra Lieberman, a veteran Nazi hunter in Vienna. Lieberman investigates the deaths and finds that each victim had an adopted 13-year-old son and that the boys look identical. After consulting a biologist, he concludes that they are clones of Adolf Hitler, created by Mengele from a single sample and placed with families resembling Hitler's own. Mengele's backers abandon the project, but he travels to Pennsylvania and kills one more father, Henry Wheelock. When Lieberman arrives, Mengele wounds him but is killed by the family's Dobermans, set on him by the boy, Bobby. Lieberman then burns Mengele's list of the 94 boys, refusing to let innocent children be hunted down. The film is built on cloning, but its real subject is nature versus nurture. Mengele knows that identical genes are not enough to make another Hitler, so he places the boys in families like Hitler's own: an older civil-servant father and a younger, doting mother, echoing Alois Hitler, a customs official over twenty years older than his wife Klara. He then arranges for each father to be killed at 65, the age at which Alois died, when Adolf was 13. The plot is therefore an explicit, if fictional, experiment on the relative weight of heredity and environment, and Lieberman's refusal to have the boys killed rests on the same idea: they are not condemned by their genes. Gregory Peck's Mengele is a fanatical Nazi scientist working in exile. The real Mengele, a physician with a doctorate in anthropology who assisted the geneticist Otmar von Verschuer, experimented on twins at Auschwitz and lived in hiding in South America until his death in 1979. Cloning from an adult cell was first achieved in a mammal with Dolly the sheep, born in 1996.

title: Parts: The Clonus Horror
text: In an isolated desert compound called Clonus, clones are raised as a source of replacement organs for wealthy and powerful people, among them the soon-to-be president-elect Jeffrey Knight. The clones are kept ignorant of the outside world and train in the hope of being "accepted" to go to "America"; the chosen ones are given a farewell party, then sedated, sealed in plastic bags and frozen so their organs can be harvested. Many have been lobotomised to keep them docile. Richard, a clone with normal intelligence, begins to question his existence, discovers the truth and escapes. He is taken in by a retired journalist, Jake Noble, who brings him to Richard Knight, the man he was cloned from and Jeffrey's brother. Richard returns to the colony for Lena, whom he loves, but finds she has been lobotomised, and he is captured and killed. Before his own murder, Noble manages to send Richard's tape exposing the project to the press. Human cloning is the premise of the film: copies of the elite are bred and kept in a closed community as living stores of spare organs. The film presents the clones as full human beings with feelings and curiosity, and its horror comes from the way they are deceived, mutilated to keep them docile and finally killed. The scientists and staff of Clonus are not driven by research but serve a political conspiracy that reaches the future president and a senator, and they kill outsiders to protect the secret. Released in 1979, the film anticipated by decades the debate on cloning for "spare parts"; its premise was later echoed closely by The Island (2005), and the makers of Clonus sued DreamWorks for copyright infringement, reaching a settlement. In reality, cloning a mammal from an adult cell was first achieved with Dolly the sheep in 1996, and a clone starts life as an embryo, so it could not provide matched adult organs without being raised for years, as the film imagines.

title: The Clones of Bruce Lee
text: On 20 July 1973, right after Bruce Lee's death in Hong Kong, Colonel Colin of the Special Branch of Investigations asks the scientist Professor Lucas to take samples of the star's brain tissue. From them Lucas creates three clones of Lee, who are trained in martial arts and sent to fight crime in Southeast Asia. Bruce Lee #1 goes undercover as an actor for a corrupt, gold-smuggling film producer who plans to have him killed on camera. The other two travel to Thailand to stop Dr. Ngai, a mad scientist who injects men with a formula that turns their skin to bronze and plans to conquer the world with them. After the clones return, Lucas, resentful that he was not properly rewarded, turns them against each other and then sends his henchmen after them. One clone is killed, but the others defeat Lucas's men and the professor is arrested. Cloning provides the premise but is treated as a pretext for the fights. The film never explains how the clones are made beyond taking brain tissue from Lee's body, and they appear as fully grown adult fighters soon afterwards, played by different Bruce Lee imitators. The scientist Professor Lucas works for a state security agency, and when he feels insufficiently rewarded he turns his creations against one another, a cheap version of the mad scientist who sees his clones as his property. The film belongs to the "Bruceploitation" cycle that cashed in on Lee's death. In reality, cloning by nuclear transfer yields an embryo that must develop like any other, so a clone would be a much younger genetic twin rather than a ready-made copy; no primate had been cloned from adult cells, let alone a human.

title: The Henderson Monster
text: Dr. Tom Henderson, a Nobel Prize-winning scientist, carries out genetic engineering experiments at a college in a small American town, assisted by Dr. Louise Casimir, his former girlfriend, whose husband Pete is a hard-drinking writer. Henderson is close to a major breakthrough and shows little concern for ethics. As questions arise about the safety of the work, the town's new mayor, Frank Bellona, bans the experiments and calls a public hearing, and Professor Leo Tedeschi, a former Manhattan Project scientist, arrives to bring some oversight to the research. Alongside the public dispute, the film follows the strained relationships between Henderson, Louise and Pete. Despite the title, reviewers note that no creature ever appears: the "monster" remains a theoretical possibility, and this CBS television film, directed by Waris Hussein from a script by Ernest Kinoy, is a talk-driven drama rather than a horror story. The film is a social-issue drama about the risks and regulation of recombinant DNA research. Henderson is the ambitious scientist absorbed by the prospect of a breakthrough and dismissive of possible hazards, while the mayor, the townspeople and the visiting Tedeschi stand for public oversight; bringing in a veteran of the Manhattan Project frames genetic engineering as a technology whose consequences could escape its creators. One reviewer singles out the still unsettling idea of an engineered sample being flushed into the water supply. The premise closely echoes real events: in 1976 the mayor of Cambridge, Massachusetts, Alfred Vellucci, tried to ban genetic engineering at Harvard and MIT for fear that researchers could accidentally produce hazardous organisms, which led to months of public hearings with scientists before a panel of residents rejected the ban. As reviewers point out, the techniques that alarmed the public in 1980 have since become routine laboratory tools.

title: Per Aspera Ad Astra
text: In the 23rd century, the Earth starship Pushkin finds a derelict alien ship whose crew are identical humanoids produced by cloning. Most are dead, but one young woman survives. Professor Sergei Lebedev takes her into his home on Earth and names her Neeya. She has no memory of her past and shows telekinetic powers. A scientist, Professor Nadezhda Ivanova, discovers a neural centre in her brain that can be triggered remotely, and flashbacks reveal that Neeya comes from the planet Dessa, where a scientist named Glan created clones he could control. Neeya stows away on the Astra, which is taking a Dessan delegation home. Dessa's air and water have been poisoned by the exhaustion of its resources, and the profiteer Turanchoks, who sells gas masks from Glan's former institute, sabotages the Earth crew's clean-up and uses Glan's control device to force Neeya to plant a bomb. Neeya breaks free, helps defeat Glan's last experiment, and stays to help restore Dessa. Cloning is part of the film's premise. Neeya is one of a series of identical humanoids grown in the laboratory of the Dessan scientist Glan, who was building an army of clones fitted with a remotely triggered neural control system so they would obey orders. The story uses the cloned woman to ask whether a manufactured being can develop a free will and a human identity, and Neeya's choice to resist her programming is the moral centre of the film. Glan is portrayed as a scientist serving a plan to seize power, and his last experiment, a deadly blob-like creature, turns on the people of his own institute. The film combines this with an ecological theme, the destruction of a planet by exploitation. As in most science fiction of its time, cloning here produces adult copies with built-in control mechanisms, which goes far beyond what cloning can do.

title: Blade Runner
text: In the Los Angeles of 2019, the Tyrell Corporation manufactures replicants, bioengineered humanoids used as slave labour on off-world colonies and banned from Earth. Former police officer Rick Deckard, a "blade runner", is forced back into service to track down and "retire" four Nexus-6 replicants led by Roy Batty, who have returned to Earth illegally. Visiting Eldon Tyrell, Deckard discovers that Tyrell's assistant Rachael is an experimental replicant who believes she is human because she has been implanted with memories. Roy and his companions trace the eye designer Hannibal Chew and the genetic designer J. F. Sebastian, who suffers from a premature-ageing disorder, and through him reach Tyrell to demand a longer life. When Tyrell says it is impossible, Roy kills him. Deckard kills the remaining replicants except Roy, who, dying as his four-year lifespan ends, spares Deckard's life. Deckard then leaves with Rachael. Genetic engineering underlies the whole premise. Replicants are not robots but bioengineered beings, designed by a corporation as disposable labour (Pris is a "basic pleasure model"), and given a built-in four-year lifespan as a safeguard. The film shows biotechnology as an industry: Tyrell, the creator, is a remote corporate magnate, while the designers who make eyes and bodies are craftsmen working to order, with no say over how their products are used. The question of what separates a manufactured being from a human, and whether it may be owned and killed, drives the story; Roy's confrontation with Tyrell, a creature demanding more life from its maker, has been linked by critics to Frankenstein, and the film is described as exploring the moral implications of human mastery of genetic engineering. Nothing close to designing a complete human-like organism is possible today. The film is a founding work of cyberpunk and influenced biopunk, the subgenre built around biotechnology and genetic engineering.

title: Forbidden World
text: On Xarbia, a remote desert planet, scientists at a genetic research station have created an experimental life form, Subject 20, from a synthetic DNA strain called Proto B, intended to end a galaxy-wide food crisis. The organism mutates rapidly, kills the laboratory animals and encloses itself in a cocoon. Troubleshooter Mike Colby arrives with his robot SAM-104 and wants to destroy it, but the research staff resist. Once hatched, the creature kills most of the crew one by one, and the scientists' secret comes out: Subject 20 incorporates human DNA, and it kills by injecting Proto B into its victims, turning their bodies into a mass of pure protein that it eats. In its final form, a large insect-like monster, it is destroyed when it eats the cancer-ridden liver of the station's doctor, Cal, and its body breaks down from within. Colby and lab assistant Tracy are the only survivors. Forbidden World is a low-budget Roger Corman production in the vein of Alien, and genetic engineering supplies its monster. Subject 20 is a designed organism made from a synthetic DNA strain and, it turns out, human DNA, created by a research team with the benevolent aim of solving a food shortage. The scientists are shown as secretive and reckless: they hide the creature's human origin and resist destroying it, and their creation kills almost everyone on the station. The film's genetics is pure invention, with DNA working as a kind of acid or contagion: Proto B erases the genetic differences between cells in its victims' cells and reduces them to edible protein, and cancer cells act as a poison that makes the creature self-destruct. As in many films of the period, the story mainly serves as a warning about creating new life forms without controls rather than as an exploration of real science.

title: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan
alt: Star Trek II, la ira de Khan
text: In 2285, Admiral James T. Kirk is restless behind a desk. The starship Reliant, searching for a lifeless planet on which to test the Genesis Device, a technology that turns dead matter into habitable worlds, lands by mistake on Ceti Alpha V. There Captain Terrell and Chekov are captured by Khan Noonien Singh, a genetically engineered tyrant whom Kirk exiled fifteen years earlier and whose followers, including his wife, died when the planet became a wasteland. Using mind-controlling eels, Khan seizes Reliant, attacks the Regula I station where Kirk's former lover Carol Marcus and their son David developed Genesis, and steals the device. Kirk lures him into the Mutara Nebula, where his inexperience in three-dimensional combat costs him the battle. Mortally wounded, Khan activates Genesis. To save the crippled Enterprise from the blast, Spock repairs the warp drive in the irradiated engine room and dies of radiation poisoning; his coffin lands on the newly formed Genesis planet. Genetics defines the villain rather than the plot. Khan, introduced in the 1967 episode "Space Seed" to which the film is a sequel, is one of a group of genetically engineered superhumans bred to be free of ordinary mental and physical limitations, who in Star Trek's history controlled more than a quarter of the Earth during the "Eugenics Wars" of the 1990s before being overthrown. The film relies on that backstory: Khan's strength, intellect and arrogance are presented as products of his design, and his pride and obsession with revenge are his downfall, as Kirk exploits his lack of experience. Behind the space opera lies a warning about eugenics: engineered superiority produces not better people but would-be rulers. The scientists in the film, Carol and David Marcus, work on the Genesis Device, not on genetics. The history imagined by the franchise did not come true: there was no genetic enhancement of humans in the 1990s, and the first gene-edited babies, born in China in 2018, led to the scientist responsible being sentenced to prison.

title: Swamp Thing
text: In the Louisiana swamps, government agent Alice Cable joins a secret bioengineering project led by Dr. Alec Holland and his sister Linda, who are developing a plant-animal hybrid able to survive in hostile environments. When Linda's formula proves to trigger explosive plant growth, the lab is raided by the paramilitary forces of Anton Arcane, who wants the formula for himself. Linda is shot, and Alec, doused in the chemicals and set on fire, plunges into the swamp. He re-emerges as the Swamp Thing, a powerful plant creature that protects Alice from Arcane's men. Arcane recovers Alec's notebooks, recreates the formula and tests it on his henchman Bruno, who shrinks into a small, misshapen man, because the formula only amplifies what a person already is. Arcane takes it himself, turns into a beast, and is killed by the Swamp Thing in the swamp. Genetics is present as the scientific premise of a comic-book horror story. The Hollands' research aims to combine plant and animal traits in a hybrid organism able to withstand extreme conditions, and Alec becomes, accidentally, the subject of his own experiment, fused with the swamp's vegetation. The film's notion of the formula is vague: it regenerates tissue, makes plants grow explosively and, on people, "amplifies what is already there", turning the timid Bruno into a dwarf and the cruel Arcane into a monster. Alec and Linda are idealistic researchers working for the government, while the villain is a wealthy outsider who seeks the formula for power and immortality, a familiar contrast between well-meaning science and its misuse. There is no attempt at scientific realism: the transformations are instant and the mechanism is never explained. Real transgenic organisms combining genes from distant species exist, but they gain specific traits, not wholesale changes in body form.

title: Anna to the Infinite Power
themes: cloning nature nurture human experimentation nazi
text: Anna Hart, a twelve-year-old genius at a school for gifted children in New Jersey, is also a kleptomaniac who suffers headaches and strange prophetic dreams. When she sees her exact double, Anna Smithson, on the television news, she starts investigating and discovers that she is one of several clones of Anna Zimmerman, a scientist who died twenty years earlier. Her dreams turn out to be Zimmerman's memories of growing up as a Jewish child prodigy in Nazi Germany. Taken to a facility on Albacore Island for "re-evaluation", Anna finds other Annas kept there and learns that the project's director, Dr. Jelliff, plans to eliminate the failed clones while grooming another girl to become the new Zimmerman. Her neighbour and piano teacher, Michaela, reveals herself as Anna Parkhurst, the first clone, and forces Jelliff to spare all the Annas in exchange for the plans of Zimmerman's "replicator". Human cloning is the core of this television film, based on Mildred Ames's 1981 novel. A dead scientist's genome is reproduced in several girls who are placed with chosen families, each a scientist married to a musician, to recreate the conditions of her childhood and see whether she will turn into the same person. The story is therefore an experiment in nature versus nurture: Anna discovers she is expected to become Zimmerman, but chooses to be herself. The scientists who continue the project see the girls as experimental material and are prepared to kill the ones who do not turn out as planned, and the backstory links the research to Nazi plans for human genetic engineering. The film shares the 1970s and 1980s fascination with cloning seen in The Boys from Brazil. Real clones are genetically identical but develop differently, and inherited memories, as suggested by Anna's dreams, have no basis in biology.

title: Trading Places
text: In Philadelphia, the elderly brothers Randolph and Mortimer Duke own the commodities brokerage Duke & Duke. Holding opposing views on nature versus nurture, they make a bet: they will swap the lives of their refined managing director, Louis Winthorpe III, and a poor street hustler, Billy Ray Valentine. Winthorpe is framed as a thief and drug dealer, loses his job, home and fiancée, and is helped only by a prostitute, Ophelia. Valentine, meanwhile, is installed in Winthorpe's job and house and proves a natural at the business. When Valentine overhears the Dukes settling their wager for one dollar and planning to throw him back onto the street, he joins Winthorpe, Ophelia and the butler Coleman. Learning that the Dukes plan to corner the frozen orange juice market with a stolen crop report, the four swap the report for a forgery and, on the trading floor, ruin the brothers while making a fortune. Genetics appears only as an idea, but it drives the plot. The Dukes' wager is an informal experiment on nature versus nurture: one brother believes that a person's character and abilities are inherited, the other that environment determines how anyone behaves. Swapping the lives of a privileged white broker and a poor Black hustler turns this old argument, which has long been used to justify class and racial hierarchies, into comedy. The outcome favours nurture: Valentine thrives once given opportunity, and Winthorpe quickly falls apart when he loses his status. There are no scientists in the film; the experimenters are two wealthy, cynical businessmen who treat people as subjects for a one-dollar bet, and who end up ruined by their own subjects. Research on twins and adoptees has found that heredity and environment both contribute substantially to most behavioural traits, often inextricably, a far subtler answer than the Dukes' all-or-nothing wager.

title: Bagi, the Monster of Mighty Nature
text: In the South American jungle, the Japanese hunter Ryosuke "Ryo" Ishigami tracks a monster with the help of a local boy, Chico, and recalls how he knows it. As a child he rescued a kitten and raised it as a pet, until the animal, Bagi, grew into an intelligent cat-woman and had to flee. Nine years later Bagi reappears and saves the teenage Ryo from his motorcycle gang. Together they discover that she was created at the SuperLife Center by Ryo's mother, the geneticist Professor Yoko Ishigami. They follow her to the republic of Monica, where a laboratory is developing a genetically engineered rice capable of destroying humanity, which the country's president wants to use against his opponents. The professor refuses to cooperate and is killed, and Ryo wrongly blames Bagi. In the end he stabs Bagi, then finds his mother's remorseful letter in her locket; Bagi's body disappears, and her silhouette is last seen running towards distant mountains. Genetic engineering drives the whole story. Bagi is a human–mountain lion hybrid created at the SuperLife Center by combining human and puma cells, part of a programme in which Professor Ishigami and the centre's ambitious chief had produced other similar creatures. A second thread involves an engineered rice that a dictator plans to use as a weapon, turning agricultural biotechnology into an instrument of political repression. The geneticist mother is a conflicted figure: she refuses to help build the weapon and dies for it, and her last letter expresses remorse for her failures both as a scientist and as a mother. Bagi, intelligent but rejected by humans and increasingly feral, is a Frankenstein-like creation abandoned by its makers, and the film sides with her rather than with the institutions that produced her. Written and directed by Osamu Tezuka for Nippon TV, the film combines environmental themes with a warning about biotechnology placed at the service of profit and power.

title: Dune
text: In the year 10,191, the emperor Shaddam IV hands control of the desert planet Arrakis, the only source of the life-extending spice melange, to House Atreides, while secretly plotting with the rival House Harkonnen to destroy it. Lady Jessica, concubine of Duke Leto Atreides, belongs to the Bene Gesserit, a sisterhood with extraordinary powers that has spent centuries on a breeding programme to produce the Kwisatz Haderach, a male "superbeing". Ordered to bear a daughter, Jessica instead bore a son, Paul. After the Harkonnens attack and Leto dies, Paul and Jessica take refuge with the desert people, the Fremen, who see Paul as their prophesied messiah. Paul leads them in raids that halt spice production, drinks the poisonous Water of Life and gains psychic powers. He defeats the emperor's troops, kills the Harkonnen heir Feyd-Rautha in a duel and is declared the Kwisatz Haderach. Genetics enters Dune through the Bene Gesserit breeding programme, a long-term scheme of selective breeding in which the sisterhood arranges unions between noble bloodlines to produce a being with superhuman mental powers. Paul is the product of that programme, and he exists only because Jessica disobeyed the order to bear a daughter. The programme is a form of eugenics carried out over many generations by a secretive religious and political order, not by scientists, and it is presented as a tool of power. The film does not use the vocabulary of genes or DNA, and much of Paul's transformation comes from the spice and the Water of Life rather than from heredity alone. Genetics is therefore an important background element of the story rather than its main subject.

title: Creator
text: Dr. Harry Wolper, an eccentric medical professor at a Southern California college, has spent thirty years trying to clone his wife Lucy, who died in childbirth, from cells he has kept. He hires Boris Lafkin, a struggling pre-med student, as his lab assistant and in exchange coaches him in his courtship of a fellow student, Barbara. To obtain eggs for the experiment, Harry recruits Meli, an uninhibited young woman who moves in with him and gradually falls in love with him. A rival professor, Sid Kuhlenbeck, tries to have Harry sidelined and take over his lab, but the plan backfires when Harry wins a large research grant. When Barbara suffers an aneurysm and falls into a coma, Harry helps Boris keep her alive until she wakes. Having found new love, Harry pours Lucy's cells into the sea and marries Meli. Cloning is the central scientific idea of this romantic comedy, though it is handled lightly. Harry wants to recreate his dead wife from her preserved cells, using an egg donated by Meli, and the film treats this as an expression of grief and devotion rather than as a menace. The portrait of the scientist is affectionate: Harry is brilliant, irreverent and humane, contrasted with an ambitious, petty rival who is more interested in his lab space than in research. The story ultimately rejects the cloning project, not on ethical grounds but because Harry realises that he must love the living instead of trying to recover the past, and he discards Lucy's cells. The film predates the cloning of Dolly the sheep by more than a decade. Even a successful reproductive clone would be a new individual who merely shares the donor's genome and must be born and grow up, so cloning could not truly bring a person back.

title: Alex: The Life of a Child
text: This ABC television film, based on sportswriter Frank Deford's 1983 memoir, follows the short life of his daughter Alexandra, who has cystic fibrosis and dies in 1980 at the age of eight. Craig T. Nelson plays Frank, Bonnie Bedelia his wife Carol and Gennie James Alex. The family's routine is shaped by the disease: daily medication, painful chest percussion to clear mucus from her lungs and repeated hospital stays. Alex is portrayed as funny, precocious and protective of her family, worried that her older brother Christian is overshadowed by her illness, and she asks increasingly direct questions about death. Lung haemorrhages and collapsed lungs mark her decline, and the film shows the harsh physical reality of the illness, such as a romp with her father that leaves her coughing blood. The film is about the experience of a genetic disease rather than about genetics as a science. Cystic fibrosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: it is caused by mutations in both copies of the CFTR gene, so that two healthy carrier parents can have an affected child. The disorder makes mucus thick, damaging the lungs above all. No scientists or geneticists play a significant role; the focus is on the child, her parents and the medical routine. Frank Deford's book and the film were credited with raising public awareness of the disease and of the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, which he served as a trustee. Treatment has changed greatly since then: CFTR modulator drugs that target the defective protein now substantially improve survival for many patients, though there is still no cure.

title: The Fly
text: Seth Brundle, a brilliant and eccentric scientist, shows science journalist Veronica "Ronnie" Quaife his invention: a pair of "telepods" that teleport objects from one to the other. Living tissue comes out mutilated until Seth reprograms the computer to understand flesh, and a baboon is transported successfully. Jealous and drunk, Seth teleports himself without noticing that a housefly has entered the pod with him. At first he feels stronger and more energetic, but he grows arrogant and violent, and his body begins to fall apart. Reviewing the computer's records, he discovers that it fused him with the fly at the molecular-genetic level. As he turns into the creature he calls "Brundlefly", Ronnie learns that she is pregnant by him and fears the child. Seth tries to fuse himself with Ronnie and their unborn child to recover his humanity, but the attempt merges him with the telepod instead, and Ronnie ends his suffering with a shotgun. Genetics enters the story through an accident rather than a design: the teleporter, unable to handle two organisms at once, splices the genes of a man and a fly, producing a gradual hybrid whose transformation is the film's body horror. Seth Brundle is an independent researcher, funded by a company but working alone, driven by curiosity, ambition and pride; he refuses to heed the warning signs and tries to repair his body with the same machine that ruined it. The film also raises fears about heredity, as Ronnie does not know whether her child was conceived before or after Seth's genes were altered and dreams of giving birth to a giant maggot. The science is fantasy: teleportation of matter does not exist, and combining two genomes would not gradually turn an adult animal into a mixture of both. The interest of the film lies in its portrait of a scientist's hubris and of the anxiety about losing one's humanity, which Cronenberg intended as a metaphor for disease and ageing and some critics read as a metaphor for AIDS.

title: American Ninja 2: The Confrontation
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation
text: US Army Rangers Joe Armstrong and Curtis Jackson are sent to a remote Caribbean island to investigate the disappearance of several Marines. They find that the kidnappings are the work of a drug lord known as "The Lion", who has also abducted a local scientist and is using his research to create a private army of "super-ninjas" from the genetic material of the captured Marines, turning them into brainwashed killing machines. Joe and Curtis team up with Alicia Sanborn, the kidnapped scientist's daughter, and infiltrate the Lion's base on Blackbeard Island. While Joe fights the Lion's chief ninja, Curtis leads an assault with the local Marines. Genetics plays a small role in this martial-arts action film. The villain's plan is to breed an army of genetically engineered "super-ninjas" from the genetic material of kidnapped soldiers, using research forced out of an abducted scientist. The genetic engineering is never explained and serves only as a pretext for the fight scenes; the scientist is a victim coerced by a drug lord rather than a central character. The idea that soldiers' genes could be harvested to produce obedient super-fighters has no scientific basis. The film is a minor example of the "genetically engineered super-soldier" motif common in 1980s and 1990s action and science fiction.

title: Life Story
text: This BBC drama, made for the Horizon science series, follows the race to determine the structure of DNA in the early 1950s. In Cambridge, the young American James Watson and the British physicist Francis Crick try to guess the structure by building models, reasoning from what the molecule must do. At King's College London, Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin work with X-ray diffraction, but their partnership is soured by mutual mistrust, and Franklin insists on patient measurement before theorising. Both teams also fear being beaten by the American chemist Linus Pauling. The film portrays the rivalries, the institutional turf wars and the sexism that Franklin faces, and ends with Watson and Crick building the double-helix model. It was written by William Nicholson, based on Watson's memoir The Double Helix, and stars Jeff Goldblum, Tim Pigott-Smith, Juliet Stevenson and Alan Howard. Life Story is a historical drama about the founding discovery of molecular genetics, the 1953 double-helix model of DNA, and its scientists are real people. It contrasts two styles of research: Watson and Crick's intuitive leaps and model building, and Franklin's careful experimental work, against a background of competition, personal friction and the marginalisation of a woman scientist. It shows how Watson and Crick won partly by reasoning from DNA's genetic function to predict its chemical structure. The film follows the record closely; Crick wrote that it had a few inaccuracies, such as making Watson too manic, but called it a success overall. Historically, Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray image known as Photo 51 was shown to Watson by Wilkins without their knowledge and was key evidence for the helix. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize; Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not awarded posthumously.

title: Light Years
text: The peaceful land of Gandahar is attacked by the Men of Metal, an army of automata that turn villagers to stone and carry them away. The Council of Women sends the young Sylvain to investigate. On his way he meets the Deformed, a community of mutant beings created by accident in genetic experiments by Gandahar's scientists and then abandoned. With Airelle, a woman he rescues, he finds the robots' base and is taken to Metamorphis, a giant brain living in the ocean, another failed creation of the same scientists. Metamorphis reveals that the Men of Metal come from the future through a portal and asks Sylvain to kill him a thousand years later. When Sylvain wakes from stasis, he learns that the aged Metamorphis has sent his robots back in time to absorb the Gandaharians' cells and prolong his life. With the Deformed's help, Sylvain kills him with a special syringe. Genetic engineering appears as the original sin of a seemingly idyllic society. Gandahar's scientists created both the Deformed, mutants born of failed experiments and pushed out of sight, and Metamorphis, a giant brain they abandoned in the sea when it grew too fast and became violent. The threat that falls on Gandahar is therefore the delayed consequence of its own research. The scientists themselves are seen only through these results: they act for the state, experiment without responsibility and discard what does not please them. The film is sympathetic to the outcasts, since the Deformed, despised as undesirable, end up saving the population. Metamorphis's need to absorb other people's cells because his own can no longer regenerate is pure fantasy, but René Laloux's animated film, based on a 1969 novel by Jean-Pierre Andrevon, uses it as a fable about scientific hubris and the treatment of those judged imperfect.

title: First Born
text: A three-part BBC serial adapted from Maureen Duffy's novel Gor Saga. Edward Forester works at a government institute officially trying to cross orangutans and gorillas; secretly, he is attempting a human-gorilla hybrid, using his own sperm. A gorilla named Mary gives birth to a seemingly human boy, Gor. When the government orders all hybrid research stopped and the embryos destroyed, Forester falsifies the records and has Gor fostered, later adopting him after surgery in Switzerland allows the boy, whose vocal cords are fused like a gorilla's, to speak. As a young man, Gor falls in love with Forester's daughter Nell, unaware she is his half-sister. Digging into his past, he learns the truth about his origins and his father. He enters Mary's cage and is killed by her. Months later, Nell's newborn son makes the same sounds Gor made as a baby. The serial is built entirely around a genetic experiment: the creation of a human-gorilla hybrid by artificial insemination and its consequences. Forester is a classic overreaching scientist in the Frankenstein mould. He works for a state institute under military oversight, hides his true goal from his superiors, uses his own sperm, and falsifies records when ordered to destroy the child. Yet he also loves Gor and protects him, and the story weighs ambition, secrecy and paternal feeling. Gor looks entirely human and shows few gorilla traits beyond his strength and his fused vocal cords, which keeps the drama grounded until the ending, in which the hybrid is killed and his son reveals that the gorilla inheritance continues. Science fiction historian Brian Stableford dismissed it as a "knee-jerk hymn of hate against scientists". No human-ape hybrid has ever been verified; humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes and the other great apes 24, and Soviet attempts in the 1920s to cross humans with chimpanzees failed to produce a pregnancy.

title: Twins
themes: eugenics genetic engineering nature nurture human experimentation
text: A secret genetic experiment tries to create the perfect child by combining the DNA of several distinguished individuals, but the embryo splits into twins. The mother, Mary Ann Benedict, is told that her baby died. Julius is raised by one of the scientists on a remote island and grows into a strong, highly educated but naïve man, while Vincent is left in a Los Angeles orphanage and becomes a short, cynical small-time crook. On his 35th birthday Julius learns of his brother and finds him in Los Angeles. Vincent, deep in debt, steals a car carrying a prototype fuel injector worth five million dollars, and the brothers set off to deliver it while searching for their mother, pursued by a hitman. In the end the twins defeat the hitman, reunite with their mother and marry two sisters, each later having twins of his own. Genetics provides the comedy's premise. Scientists in a secret programme try to engineer an ideal human by mixing the DNA of several exceptional donors; when the embryo splits, the joke is that one twin received all the desirable traits and the other the "leftovers", so that Arnold Schwarzenegger and Danny DeVito can play identical twins. The scientists are cold experimenters who deceive the mother about her children and abandon one of them, and one of them still calls Vincent a genetic failure decades later; the film sides with the brothers and suggests that loyalty and family matter more than pedigree. It also adds an element of nurture, as the twins grow up in opposite circumstances. Biologically the premise is impossible: identical (monozygotic) twins form when a single zygote splits into two embryos, so they carry essentially the same genome, and a split cannot sort good and bad genes between them.

title: Godzilla vs. Biollante
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras engineered pathogens gmo
text: After Godzilla's attack on Tokyo, samples of its cells are smuggled to a research institute in the fictional Middle Eastern country of Saradia, to be merged with genetically modified plants that could turn the desert into farmland. A terrorist bombing destroys the laboratory and kills Erika, the daughter of the geneticist Genshiro Shiragami. Five years later, in Japan, Shiragami has merged Erika's cells with those of a rose to preserve her soul, while the scientist Kazuhito Kirishima and the army are using Godzilla cells to develop an "anti-nuclear energy bacteria" as a weapon against the monster. Saradian agents and the American company Bio-Major fight over the cells. Shiragami secretly adds Godzilla cells to one of his roses, which grows into the giant plant monster Biollante. When Godzilla is freed, it fights Biollante twice; the bacteria and an artificial lightning storm weaken Godzilla, and Biollante dissolves into spores that rise to the sky in the image of Erika. Genetic engineering is at the heart of the film. Godzilla's cells are treated as a valuable biological resource, and governments, a company and spies compete for them, foreshadowing later stories about corporate control of genetic material. Biollante is a hybrid of plant, human and Godzilla cells, created by a grieving geneticist who wants to keep his dead daughter's soul alive; his motive is personal rather than commercial, but his experiment produces a monster that he cannot control. Other scientists work for the army on a bacterial weapon derived from Godzilla's cells. The story came from a public contest won by a dentist whose entry focused on the dilemmas of biotechnology, and director Kazuki Ōmori drew on his own background in biology to make the genetic engineering plot more plausible. Scholars of kaiju cinema have noted that the film criticised genetic engineering and biotechnology several years before Jurassic Park brought the subject to mainstream Hollywood. Merging whole cells of different species to transfer a person's identity is, of course, fantasy.

title: The Fly II
themes: heredity hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation animal experimentation
text: Months after scientist Seth Brundle became a human-fly hybrid, Veronica Quaife dies giving birth to a larval sac from which a seemingly normal boy emerges. Anton Bartok, owner of the company that financed Brundle's teleportation experiments, adopts the child, Martin, and raises him in a laboratory. Martin ages very fast, has a genius intellect and needs no sleep. At five, with the body of a 25-year-old, he is asked to repair his father's Telepods, which have failed to teleport living creatures. He succeeds, falls in love with an employee, Beth Logan, and begins to show signs of becoming a hybrid himself. He discovers that Bartok knew his fate and plans to exploit his body and the Telepods' power of genetic manipulation for profit. Fully transformed, Martin forces Bartok into a Telepod and uses it to swap his insect genes for Bartok's healthy human genes, regaining human form while Bartok becomes a deformed creature. The film turns the first film's teleportation accident into a story about inheritance. Martin carries the fly genes his father acquired in the Telepod, and his accelerated growth and eventual metamorphosis are presented as a hereditary condition waiting to "awaken". The cure he devises is a crude form of gene therapy: the Telepods exchange his mutated genes for healthy human ones taken from another person, who then suffers the disfigurement. The scientist figure is a corporate one: Bartok raises Martin as an experimental subject, spies on him and wants to use his body and the machines' capacity for genetic manipulation for profit. Laboratory animal experimentation, shown through a deformed dog kept alive for study, is another theme. Scientifically, acquired changes in an adult's body are not passed to children in this way, and genes cannot be swapped between whole organisms like parts, but the film uses these ideas as body horror.

title: Unnatural Selection
alt: Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 2, episode 7
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement evolution gene therapy
text: The Enterprise finds the supply ship USS Lantree adrift, its entire crew dead of old age although many were young. The ship's last stop was the Darwin Genetic Research Station on Gagarin IV, whose scientists are now ageing rapidly too and beg Captain Picard to evacuate the station's genetically engineered children, who have been kept in isolation. Dr. Pulaski examines one of the children, a telepathic teenager, aboard a shuttle piloted by Data, and catches the disease. She discovers that the children were engineered with aggressive immune systems that fight pathogens by genetically altering them, even outside their bodies; reacting to a harmless flu carried by a Lantree officer, they produced airborne antibodies that rewrite the DNA of ordinary humans and make them age. Using a strand of Pulaski's hair as a genetic template, the crew restores her through the transporter, then treats the station's staff. The children must remain isolated. Genetic engineering is the core of the episode. Scientists at a Federation research station have designed children with enhanced abilities, including telepathy and a super-immune system, and Dr. Pulaski first greets them as "the next step in human evolution". The improvement backfires: the children's immune defence, which alters pathogens genetically, becomes a weapon that rewrites the DNA of everyone around them and kills by accelerated ageing. The researchers are well-meaning but have failed to foresee the consequences of their designs, and the children end up condemned to permanent isolation, unintended victims of the experiment. The episode is a cautionary tale about human enhancement. Scientifically, antibodies are proteins that bind targets but do not alter DNA, and restoring someone's genome from a hair sample through a "transporter" is pure fiction; the link between DNA damage and ageing, however, is a real field of research.

title: Up the Long Ladder
alt: Que entren los clones Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 2, episode 18
text: The Enterprise answers a distress call from Bringloid V, a colony threatened by solar flares and founded centuries earlier by the crew of the SS Mariposa. Its inhabitants, led by Danilo Odell and his daughter Brenna, live a pre-industrial Irish rural life and are evacuated aboard the ship. Odell mentions a second Mariposa colony, and Riker, Worf and Dr. Pulaski visit it. Pulaski discovers that all its people are clones: only five scientists survived the original landing, too few for a viable population, so they reproduced by cloning alone. After almost three centuries, accumulated copying errors are about to make further clones nonviable. Prime Minister Granger asks for the crew's DNA, and when Riker refuses, the Mariposans abduct him and Pulaski and grow copies of them, which Riker destroys. Pulaski proposes instead that the two colonies merge to create a viable gene pool. Cloning and population genetics are central. A colony founded by only five people chooses cloning over sexual reproduction, and after generations of copies faces "replicative fading", an accumulation of small errors in the genetic code that will soon make new clones nonviable. The solution is not more technology but genetic diversity: Dr. Pulaski persuades the Mariposans to mix with the Bringloidi so that a varied gene pool can sustain the colony. The Mariposan scientists are polite but willing to take DNA without consent, and the episode frames bodily integrity and individual uniqueness as reasons to refuse being copied. The idea loosely echoes a real concern: very small founding populations suffer from inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity, although "replicative fading" itself is a fictional device. The episode drew criticism because Riker's destruction of his clones was read as a stance on abortion.

title: Gremlins 2: The New Batch
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: After the death of his owner, Mr. Wing, the mogwai Gizmo is captured by scientists from Splice O' Life, a genetic engineering laboratory in the Clamp Centre, a Manhattan skyscraper owned by the eccentric billionaire Daniel Clamp. Billy Peltzer and Kate Beringer, who now work in the building, rescue him, but Gizmo gets wet and spawns new mogwai, which eat after midnight and turn into gremlins. The gremlins overrun the tower, and in the laboratory they drink Dr. Catheter's experimental serums: one becomes a talking, intelligent Brain Gremlin, others turn into a spider-like creature, a bat, a vegetable gremlin, a female gremlin and an electric gremlin, which kills Catheter. As the gremlins prepare to break out into the city, Billy traps the electric gremlin and uses it, together with the building's sprinklers and fire hoses, to destroy the rest, while Gizmo kills the spider gremlin with a flaming arrow. Genetic engineering is the film's main satirical target. Splice O' Life is a corporate laboratory inside Clamp's tower, a building that parodies late-1980s commercial excess (Clamp was modelled on Donald Trump and Ted Turner), and its head, Dr. Catheter, is played by Christopher Lee as an openly sinister scientist, at director Joe Dante's request. His shelves of gene-altering serums give the second half of the film its set pieces: each gremlin that drinks one instantly takes on new traits, such as a bat's wings, a spider's body, plant tissue, pure electricity or human-level intelligence, producing comic hybrids of gremlin with animal, vegetable or even a female identity. The science is deliberately cartoonish: real genetic modification acts on cells or embryos and takes effect over generations or long treatments, not as a drink that transforms an adult animal in seconds. The film uses the idea to mock both corporate biotechnology and the monster-movie trope of the mad scientist.

title: Chimera
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation animal experimentation
text: Nurse Tracy Pickford leaves London for a job at the Jenner Clinic, a private fertility clinic in rural Cumbria, where a locked outbuilding and secret meetings make her suspicious. One night an unseen creature kills the clinic's staff, including its founder Dr. Jenner, and Tracy too. Her boyfriend, the journalist Peter Carson, arrives to find the police sidelined by a government official, Hennessey, who hands the manhunt to the army. With Alison Wells, a researcher who survived, Peter learns from Jenner's former colleague Dr. Liawski that Jenner, funded by Hennessey, created a human-chimpanzee hybrid as the first of a new species for slave labour, military use and medical experiments. The hybrid, Chad, had been kept caged for years and killed the staff when Jenner ordered him dissected. Hiding on a farm, Chad befriends two children. Peter and Alison try to expose him to the public, but he is shot dead. In the final scene, a facility holds dozens of infant hybrids. Genetic engineering is the core of this ITV miniseries, adapted by Stephen Gallagher from his 1982 novel.
