A fertility clinic serves as cover for a secret, state-funded project to create human-chimpanzee hybrids, using patients as surrogate mothers, with the aim of producing a slave species for labour, war and medical research. Dr. Jenner is a scientist serving government interests with no regard for his creation, whom he keeps caged, mutilates and finally orders to be dissected; his colleague Liawski is ashamed but silenced, and another colleague is fascinated and carries on the work. Chad, the hybrid, is the tragic figure of the story, and the drama focuses on the cruelty and the official cover-up rather than the science. Human-chimpanzee hybrids have never been produced, and such experiments are banned on ethical grounds. In the United States the series was re-edited and released as Monkey Boy.

title: DNA
text: The crew of Red Dwarf board a drifting spacecraft. Rimmer and Kryten find the remains of a mutated human with three heads, while Cat accidentally activates a machine that turns Lister into a chicken. Kryten works out that the ship's crew were researching DNA modification and that the machine can rewrite the DNA of anything organic. Lister is turned into a hamster before Cat repeats his steps and restores him, but Kryten, whose brain is partly organic, is transformed into a human. Back on Red Dwarf, Kryten is delighted at first, but finds he cannot do what he did as a mechanoid and soon wants to change back. As a test, Lister has the machine modify the meat in his vindaloo, which becomes an indestructible curry monster. Lister turns himself into a one-foot-tall cyborg "Man Plus" and kills the creature by exploiting its weakness for lager. The episode is built around a DNA-rewriting machine, and its official full title is "Do Not Alter". The machine can reshape any organic being by rewriting its DNA, turning Lister into a chicken, a hamster and a tiny super-human, a robot with an organic brain into a man, and a curry into a monster. The premise draws on the popular idea of DNA as a code that defines what an organism is, and the story plays it entirely for comedy, raising light questions about identity and what it means to be human through Kryten's brief life as a person. The scientists who built the machine never appear; the three-headed corpse aboard their ship hints that their experiments went wrong. Real genetic modification works on cells and embryos and cannot transform a living adult into another species, still less convert machinery or cooked meat, so the episode is a farce on genetic engineering rather than a portrayal of it.

title: The Guyver
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation mutants
text: Dr. Tetsu Segawa, a researcher for the Chronos corporation, steals an alien device called the Guyver unit and is killed by Lisker, a Chronos henchman who can transform into a monstrous Zoanoid. Before dying, Segawa hides the unit, and it is found by Sean Barker, the boyfriend of Segawa's daughter Mizuki. The unit fuses with Sean and covers him in a powerful biomechanical armour. With the help of CIA agent Max Reed, Sean fights the Zoanoids, who kidnap Mizuki to recover the device. In one battle the armour's control metal is ripped off and Sean dies, but the metal regenerates in Chronos's laboratories and, after it is accidentally swallowed by Dr. East, the head of genetics research, it brings Sean back to life. Sean defeats Lisker and the Chronos president, Fulton Balcus, who reveals himself as the Zoalord. Genetic engineering is the business of the villains. The Chronos corporation turns human beings into Zoanoids, genetically engineered monsters that look human but can transform into combat creatures, and its laboratories, run by a head of genetics research, keep a gallery of these forms and experiment on captives; the CIA agent Max Reed is forcibly mutated into a cockroach-like Zoanoid and dies when his body rejects the new form. The Guyver itself is alien biotechnology that bonds permanently with its host, regenerating both itself and the person wearing it. The scientists are portrayed as corporate servants of a hidden, non-human leader seeking power, and their work is shown only as a source of weapons and suffering. The film is a low-budget adaptation of a Japanese manga and does not attempt any scientific realism; genetics serves as a pretext for transformations, monsters and fights.

title: The Unborn
text: Virginia Marshall, a children's book author, and her husband Brad have been unable to conceive. They join an experimental in vitro fertilisation programme run by Dr. Richard Meyerling, and Virginia quickly becomes pregnant. The pregnancy goes badly: the regimen Meyerling prescribes makes her ill, and she becomes increasingly unstable and paranoid. She learns that other women treated at the clinic had terrible outcomes, including children who grew up cold and psychopathic, and she comes to believe that Meyerling is secretly carrying out unauthorised genetic experiments on the embryos he implants, aiming to create superior children. Her fears prove justified, and the pregnancy ends with the birth of a monstrous baby. The film was directed by Rodman Flender. The Unborn is a horror film in the tradition of Rosemary's Baby and It's Alive, with genetic engineering in place of the devil. Its fear is of reproductive medicine: in vitro fertilisation, still relatively new when the film was made, becomes the route by which a doctor secretly manipulates embryos in the hope of creating superior children, and the results are psychopathic or monstrous offspring. Dr. Meyerling is a classic mad scientist, running a private fertility clinic and deceiving his patients for his own eugenic project. Reviewers have noted that the film draws on the Human Genome Project, launched in 1990 and much in the news at the time, and a montage pairs a headline about cracking the DNA code with tabloid stories. The film's genetics is vague and never explained. In reality, in vitro fertilisation and genetic modification of embryos are very different things. Editing human embryos for reproduction became a real controversy only in 2018, when He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited twins, work widely condemned as a breach of accepted ethical norms.

title: Killer Tomatoes Eat France
alt: Los tomates asesinos se comen Francia
text: In the fourth and last film of the Killer Tomatoes series, released direct to video, the mad scientist Dr. Mortimer Gangreen escapes from prison and sets up base in his assistant Igor's castle outside Paris, still bent on world domination. An old prophecy foretells that the king of France, Louis XVII, will return to claim the throne, and since Igor closely resembles the only known image of the lost king, Gangreen plans to use his army of killer tomatoes to stage a second French Revolution and crown Igor as a puppet monarch. To build his army, he kidnaps FT, a friendly, intelligent tomato. Michael, an American has-been actor, and Marie, a French woman he falls in love with, try to stop him while the tomatoes, including a giant fire-breathing one, attack France. The real Louis returns and triumphs over Igor, and Gangreen flees in a tomato-shaped hot-air balloon, swearing revenge. Genetics is little more than a running gag in this parody. Earlier films in the series established that the killer tomatoes were the product of Professor Gangreen's experiments, and here he wants the DNA of FT, a benign tomato, to build a new tomato army; one review summarises his plan in exactly those terms. Gangreen is the classic cartoon mad scientist: an escaped convict who uses his creations for a ludicrous political scheme, with no interest in science for its own sake. The film is inconsistent even with its own franchise, as it shows fruit and vegetables that are sentient without his intervention, and the tomatoes now speak English. Its jokes are aimed at horror clichés and French stereotypes rather than at biology, and the "genetic" element makes no statement about real plant breeding or genetic modification.

title: Lorenzo's Oil
text: Based on a true story, the film follows Augusto and Michaela Odone, whose young son Lorenzo begins to show neurological problems after the family moves from the Comoro Islands to the United States. He is diagnosed with adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), a degenerative disease expected to kill him within two years. Finding that doctors can offer no treatment, the parents, who have no scientific training, study medical libraries and animal research, badger researchers, clash with a sceptical support group and organise an international symposium on the disease. They learn that oleic acid lowers the very long chain fatty acids that accumulate in ALD, and later add erucic acid, eventually persuading an elderly British chemist to produce a purified mixture of the two. The oil normalises Lorenzo's blood levels and halts the progression of his disease, although the damage already done recovers only very slowly. The film ends with boys treated early with the oil. The film is a medical drama about an inherited disease. ALD is an X-linked disorder: women who carry the faulty gene often develop milder symptoms later in life, while their sons can develop the severe childhood form. The film shows Michaela learning that she passed the disease on to Lorenzo, and her guilt is part of the drama. The genetics is in the background, however; the story is about biochemistry and about lay parents confronting a slow and cautious medical establishment, represented by a well-meaning but hesitant specialist, Professor Nikolais. Hugo Moser, the real researcher on whom Nikolais was based, called the portrayal "an abomination", and the film was criticised for suggesting a miracle cure. Later research has not clearly shown that Lorenzo's oil helps once neurological symptoms have started, although it appeared to prevent onset in many boys treated before symptoms appeared. Lorenzo Odone died in 2008 at the age of 30, two decades longer than doctors had predicted.

title: The Hand That Rocks the Cradle
alt: La mano que mece la cuna
text: Claire Bartel, a Seattle housewife pregnant with her second child, is sexually assaulted by her new obstetrician, Dr. Victor Mott, during a check-up. Encouraged by her husband Michael, she reports him, other women come forward, and Mott kills himself. His pregnant widow loses her home and her baby, and has to have a hysterectomy; she blames Claire. Six months later, under the name Peyton Flanders, she is hired as the Bartels' nanny and sets out to destroy the family from within. She secretly breastfeeds the baby, turns the daughter against her mother, gets the loyal handyman Solomon fired, sabotages Michael's work, and plants evidence of an affair. When a family friend discovers her identity, Peyton kills her with a trap in Claire's greenhouse and empties Claire's asthma inhalers. Once unmasked, Peyton attacks the family to take the children, but Claire, helped by Solomon, defeats her, and Peyton dies in a fall. Genetics plays no real part in this psychological thriller. Its only link to the field is Michael Bartel, Claire's husband, whom Spanish- and German-language plot summaries describe as a biotechnology engineer or genetic engineer; English-language sources do not state his profession. His work appears only as background: Peyton's destruction of a funding proposal he has to submit is one of her many attacks on the Bartels. The film shows nothing of his research and does not use genetics as a theme; no scientific work is seen on screen, and nothing in the plot depends on his field. He is portrayed as a decent, supportive husband, and it is he who encourages Claire to report the abuse. If those summaries are right, the title is an example of a scientist appearing in a mainstream film in a purely incidental role, as an ordinary professional whose occupation signals the family's social standing. The story's real concerns are motherhood, trust and revenge.

title: The Masterpiece Society
alt: La obra de arte social Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 5, episode 13
text: The Enterprise tracks a stellar core fragment from a disintegrated neutron star that will pass close to Moab IV, home of a human colony founded about two centuries earlier. Its leader, Aaron Conor, refuses evacuation, because the colonists were genetically engineered and selectively bred so that each person fits a role in a perfectly balanced society, and leaving would destroy it. The colony's scientist, Hannah Bates, works with Geordi La Forge on a tractor beam to deflect the fragment, and La Forge adapts the technology of his VISOR to make it work, noting that the colony's planners would never have allowed someone born blind like him to exist. Meanwhile Troi and Conor become attracted to each other. The colony is saved, but Bates and 22 other colonists ask to leave with the Enterprise. Picard accepts their request as a matter of free will, and reflects that the Federation's contact may have harmed the society as much as the fragment would have. The episode is an extended argument about genetic perfectionism. The colony of Moab IV is a planned society built through genetic engineering and selective breeding, in which every person is designed from conception for a particular function, and its leaders see any outside contact as a threat to a carefully tuned order. The script undercuts this ideal from two directions. Geordi La Forge, blind from birth, points out that such a society would have screened him out, yet it is the technology built around his disability that saves the colony. And the colonists who leave show that being engineered for a role does not mean accepting it: their departure, framed by Picard as a matter of free will, suggests that a society fixed in advance by design leaves no room for individual choice. Bates, the colony's own scientist, is portrayed sympathetically. The themes anticipate later debates on embryo selection and on whether choosing traits before birth narrows a person's future, as explored in films such as GATTACA.

title: Carnosaur
themes: genetic engineering engineered pathogens de extinction hybrids chimeras
text: Dr. Jane Tiptree carries out secret research for the Eunice Corporation in a laboratory near the small town of Climax, Nevada, where she works with genetically modified chickens. One of her eggs hatches a Deinonychus, which escapes and begins killing people, while the townspeople fall ill with a mysterious flu-like disease. Doc Smith, the night watchman at a nearby quarry, and Ann Thrush, an environmental activist, survive the creature's attacks and trace it back to the laboratory. There Tiptree reveals her plan: infected chicken eggs spread an airborne virus that makes women pregnant with dinosaur embryos, so that dinosaurs can replace the human race. The government quarantines the town and orders civilians shot on sight. Tiptree herself dies giving birth to a dinosaur, and Doc kills her Tyrannosaurus rex and injects Thrush with a cure, but soldiers kill them both and burn their bodies, destroying the serum. Genetic engineering is the engine of the plot. Tiptree recreates dinosaurs by modifying chickens, the living relatives of dinosaurs, and engineers a virus that makes human women carry dinosaur embryos, so genetics becomes a weapon for exterminating humanity. She is a pure mad-scientist figure, working in secret for a corporation that funds her research while the defence agency DARPA watches but cannot legally intervene; her motive is misanthropic, a wish to give the Earth back to the dinosaurs. The authorities respond with quarantine, killing and, in a satirical subplot, plans for a new social order based on controlled fertilisation and artificial wombs. The premise is not plausible: birds descend from dinosaurs, but genuine dinosaur DNA has never been recovered, and early reports of it were later traced to contamination. The oldest DNA known is around two million years old, while non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The film, produced by Roger Corman, was released just before Jurassic Park.

title: Eve
themes: cloning eugenics human enhancement human experimentation nature nurture
text: Two men are killed at the same moment on opposite sides of the United States, one in Connecticut and one in California, each drained of blood through incisions in the neck. FBI agents Mulder and Scully find that each victim had a young daughter, Teena and Cindy, who look identical. Both girls were conceived by in vitro fertilization at a San Francisco clinic, where Dr. Sally Kendrick had been fired for eugenics experiments with patients' eggs. Deep Throat tells Mulder about a Cold War programme that produced genetically engineered clones called "Adams" and "Eves". In a psychiatric hospital the agents meet Eve 6, who looks exactly like Kendrick and explains that the clones had extra chromosomes that gave them superhuman intelligence and strength but also homicidal psychosis. Kendrick, really Eve 7, cloned the girls from herself. The girls poison her, then try to poison the agents. They are locked up alongside Eve 6, where Eve 8 comes to visit them. Cloning and genetic engineering are central to the episode. A secret government programme created clones with enhanced abilities, and one of them, posing as a fertility doctor, secretly uses patients' IVF treatment to produce new copies of herself, so the parents unknowingly raise her clones. The episode links the scientists to eugenics and military research and shows the results as monstrous: the clones are brilliant and strong but psychopathic, and the girls kill their fathers. The idea that "extra chromosomes" produce superhuman traits has no basis; in reality, an extra chromosome is a cause of genetic disorders such as Down syndrome, and most extra autosomes are lethal to the embryo. The episode also plays on the fear, common in the 1990s, that reproductive technology could be secretly misused, and uses identical twins separated at birth as the hook of the mystery.

title: Jurassic Park
text: Industrialist John Hammond has built a theme park of cloned dinosaurs on Isla Nublar, off Costa Rica. After a worker is killed, his investors demand a safety review, and Hammond invites palaeontologist Alan Grant, palaeobotanist Ellie Sattler and mathematician Ian Malcolm, along with the investors' lawyer and his own grandchildren, Lex and Tim. The visitors learn how the animals were made and debate the ethics of the park. During a tropical storm, the computer programmer Dennis Nedry shuts down the security system to steal frozen embryos for a rival company, and the electric fences fail. A Tyrannosaurus escapes and attacks the tour, Nedry is killed, and Grant and the children must cross the park on foot, discovering on the way that the dinosaurs are breeding. Attempts to restart the power release the Velociraptors, which kill several staff. The survivors are rescued by helicopter after Grant and Hammond agree not to endorse the park. Genetic engineering is the premise of the film. Hammond's scientists, led by chief geneticist Henry Wu, recovered dinosaur DNA from the blood in mosquitoes preserved in amber, filled the gaps in the genomes with frog DNA and made all the animals female to prevent breeding. The plan fails because of that frog DNA: like some amphibians, the dinosaurs change sex in a single-sex population, so life finds a way. Through Malcolm the film argues that genetic power was obtained without discipline or humility, and the geneticists serve a commercial project, although Hammond himself is a sympathetic showman rather than a villain. Real ancient DNA cannot do this. DNA breaks down over time, and even under the best conditions the upper limit for sequencing is thought to be roughly one to two million years, while the last non-avian dinosaurs died about 66 million years ago.

title: Man's Best Friend
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: Television reporter and animal activist Lori Tanner breaks into the laboratories of EMAX, a genetic research company run by the scientist Dr. Jarret, and frees a Tibetan Mastiff named Max. She adopts him without knowing that he is the product of genetic engineering, spliced with DNA from big cats, snakes, chameleons and birds of prey, and that he needs a drug to keep his violent rages in check. Max is loyal and affectionate with Lori and can understand human speech, but when she is away he kills a mugger, a cat, a parakeet and a mailman, and sabotages the car of her boyfriend, Perry. When Lori gives him away, he kills the junkyard owner who abuses him and returns home to find he has been replaced by a puppy. The police hunt him, and Jarret kidnaps Lori to lure Max back to the lab, where the scientist shoots him and is himself electrocuted. Months later, a neighbour's collie gives birth to a puppy that looks like Max. Genetic engineering is the source of the threat. Max is a transgenic animal combining the DNA of several species, and each borrowed trait gives him a new ability, such as his strength, speed, senses and acidic urine, in the style of a monster film rather than real biology. His violent instability is the side effect the company tries to manage with drugs, and the final shot of a puppy he has fathered suggests that his engineered traits may now spread through breeding. The scientist, Dr. Jarret, is presented as an animal experimenter whose laboratory is exposed as a place of cruelty; he reports Max stolen instead of warning about the danger, and dies in his own facility. The film reflects early-1990s public unease about genetic engineering and animal experimentation. Real transgenic animals carry one or a few added genes, and nothing like a mixture of mammal, reptile and bird traits has been produced.

title: Rightful Heir
alt: Heredero legítimo Star Trek: The Next Generation, season 6, episode 23
text: Going through a crisis of faith, Worf travels to the Klingon monastery on Boreth, where the faithful await the return of Kahless, the legendary warrior who founded the Klingon Empire. After days of ritual, a man appearing to be Kahless materialises before him, and Worf brings him aboard the Enterprise, though he is troubled by gaps in Kahless's memory. Chancellor Gowron, suspecting an impostor planted by the priests to gain power, brings an ancient dagger stained with Kahless's blood and asks for a genetic comparison; the DNA matches. Gowron then defeats Kahless in a duel, and the high priest Koroth admits that this Kahless is a clone of the original. Worf persuades Gowron to install the clone as a ceremonial emperor who can unite the Klingon people while real power stays with the council. Cloning and DNA identification drive the plot, but the episode's real subject is faith and political legitimacy. The priests of Boreth use ancient blood preserved on a dagger to clone their messiah, and the deception survives a genetic test precisely because a clone carries the same DNA as the original: the test proves genetic identity, not that the man is the historical Kahless. The scientists here are religious leaders who use the technology to revive belief and strengthen their own influence, and the episode leaves open whether their manipulation is harmful or beneficial for the Klingon people. It also makes the point, familiar from real discussions of cloning, that a clone is a new individual who shares a genome with the donor but not his memories or experience; this Kahless lacks the memories the real one would have had. Recovering an intact genome from centuries-old blood and cloning from it remains well beyond current science.

title: Tomcat: Dangerous Desires
themes: gene therapy hybrids chimeras genetic disease human experimentation
text: Tom, a young modern dancer, suffers from a rare degenerative condition of the nervous system. Jacki, a scientist in genetic research who becomes his lover, treats him with an experimental therapy based on genetic material from a cat. The treatment restores his health, but it has side effects: Tom gradually takes on feline traits and becomes devious and dangerous. As he grows attached to Imogen, a fellow dancer, Jacki becomes jealous, fearing she will lose both her patient and her lover. Tom turns on the people around him, killing Jacki and then those who stand between him and Imogen, until a final pursuit in a lumberyard. The premise is an inter-species genetic treatment: a geneticist cures a man's degenerative disease with feline DNA, and the cure slowly turns him into a predatory, cat-like killer. The film combines this idea with an erotic thriller in the style of Basic Instinct, and the scientist's motives are personal as much as professional, since her patient is also her lover. Sources differ slightly on the treatment itself, which Wikipedia describes as injections of feline brain material and other summaries as a genetic implant of cat DNA. According to the Moria review, the genetic angle is barely explored and its main visible effect is Tom's sudden fear of water, a trait the reviewer notes is not genetically determined in cats. As science, the idea that animal genes would transfer behaviour and personality to a human is fantasy; it belongs to a long line of "hybrid monster" stories rather than to real gene therapy.

title: Dragon Ball Z: Bio-Broly
alt: Doragon Bōru Zetto: Chō Senshi Gekiha!! Katsu no wa Ore da Dragon Ball Z: Los guerreros de plástico
text: Mr. Jaguar, a rich man who was Mr. Satan's rival at summer camp, invites the martial arts champion to his island laboratory to fight his "bio-warriors", humanoids created by the scientist Dr. Collie, threatening otherwise to expose an embarrassing secret. Android 18 goes along to make sure Mr. Satan pays her a debt, and the boys Goten and Trunks stow away. During the tournament the boys discover a tank holding what looks like Broly, the Legendary Super Saiyan they had killed. A shaman explains that he took a sample of Broly's blood to Jaguar, who had a clone created. The clone breaks out, and the fight ruptures tanks of a bio-fluid that devours matter. Drenched in it, the clone becomes the deformed Bio-Broly and later merges with the fluid. The heroes discover that seawater turns the fluid to stone, flood the island and destroy the petrified giant. Cloning drives the plot. Jaguar and his scientist, Dr. Collie, grow artificial bio-warriors in tanks and create a clone of the dead Broly from a blood sample, intending to use these fighters to humiliate Mr. Satan. Their motives are petty and personal rather than scientific, and the experiment escapes their control: the culture fluid used in the laboratory proves more dangerous than the clone itself, kills the bio-warriors and most of the scientists and threatens to cover the whole Earth. The film treats cloning as a way of bringing back a dead fighter with his powers intact, a common idea in fiction that does not match real cloning, which produces a genetically identical individual who must still develop from an embryo and would not share the original's memories or abilities. The genetics is a premise for a martial arts adventure and is not explored further.

title: Felidae
text: In the late 1980s, Francis, an intelligent house cat, moves with his owner into a run-down house and finds a cat killed by a bite to the neck. With the help of the one-eyed Bluebeard, he investigates a series of feline murders and discovers a sect of cats that worships a figure called Claudandus. A video recording reveals that the top floor of his house was once a laboratory where stray cats were used to test a tissue glue, until the only survivor, Claudandus, killed the deranged lead researcher, Dr. Preterius. Haunted by nightmares of the geneticist Gregor Mendel, Francis finally learns that the killer is Pascal, the elderly, computer-literate cat who is Claudandus himself. Pascal has spent years breeding a new race of cats and killing those who refused to cooperate. Francis deletes his records, and in the fight that follows Claudandus dies as the house burns. The film is an animated adaptation of Akif Pirinçci's 1989 novel. Genetics enters through classical heredity rather than genetic engineering. Claudandus, the survivor of cruel animal experiments, was taken in by a former laboratory assistant and learned Mendel's laws of inheritance. He uses them to run a eugenic breeding programme, selecting mates over generations to bring back the traits of an imagined ancestor of all domestic cats, a superior breed meant eventually to wipe out humanity. Cats who refuse to take part are murdered. The villain is thus both a victim of science and a self-taught geneticist who turns its methods into a racial project, with clear echoes of human eugenics; Mendel himself appears in Francis's nightmares. The scientists of the original laboratory are portrayed as cruel and, in Preterius's case, unhinged. The approach Claudandus uses is real in principle: domestic animal breeds are produced by selective breeding, and Mendel's experiments on pea plants established how traits are passed on. Recreating an ancestral species this way, however, is far beyond what breeding can achieve.

title: Junior
text: Austrian research geneticist Dr. Alex Hesse and obstetrician Dr. Larry Arbogast have developed Expectane, a drug to reduce the risk of miscarriage, but the FDA will not let them test it on humans. With a pharmaceutical company willing to fund the trial if they find a volunteer, Larry persuades Alex to test it on himself: an egg codenamed "Junior" is fertilised and implanted in his abdomen. Alex suffers morning sickness and mood swings, and when the trial should end he decides to carry the pregnancy to term. He falls for Dr. Diana Reddin, a scientist from the egg-freezing department, who is furious to learn the egg was hers but comes to accept that she is the mother and he the father. Alex hides in a retreat for expectant mothers disguised as a woman, the lab director tries to claim credit, and Alex finally gives birth by caesarean to a healthy girl. Genetics plays a modest role in this comedy; its real subject is reproduction and gender roles. The protagonist is a research geneticist and the heroine a scientist who works on egg freezing, but the science involves a fertility drug, in vitro fertilisation and the implantation of an embryo in a man's abdomen. The scientists are ambitious and break the rules: they bypass the FDA, keep the trial secret and use an egg without its donor's consent, which the film treats as a romantic complication rather than an ethical breach. A greedy lab director who tries to take the credit serves as the villain. The film's interest lies in Alex learning empathy and the emotional side of parenthood. Male pregnancy by implanting an embryo in the abdomen has never been attempted; specialists consider it theoretically conceivable but so dangerous for parent and child that it is unlikely ever to be studied in humans. The title fits the database mainly through its geneticist protagonist.

title: The Erlenmeyer Flask
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering human experimentation
text: After a car chase in Maryland, a fugitive, Dr. William Secare, is shot and escapes into the water; the police find that his blood is green. Deep Throat steers Mulder to the case, which leads to Dr. Terrance Berube, a geneticist who worked on the Human Genome Project and who is soon murdered by a government operative. In Berube's laboratory Mulder finds a flask labelled "Purity Control", whose contents a Georgetown microbiologist identifies as containing DNA of extraterrestrial origin; she and her family are then killed. Mulder discovers a storage facility with men suspended in tanks. Deep Throat explains that Berube had been experimenting on six terminally ill volunteers with alien material and had created alien–human hybrids, and that the project worked better than expected. To rescue the captured Mulder, Scully obtains an alien foetus from a high-security facility; Deep Throat exchanges it and is shot dead. The X-Files are closed. This season-one finale introduces one of the central ideas of The X-Files mythology: secret government experiments that combine human and alien DNA to create hybrids. The scientist at its centre, Dr. Berube, is presented as a genome researcher working covertly for the government; the experiments on terminally ill volunteers appear to cure them, and he is killed when he tries to protect one of his subjects. Genetics provides both the evidence (DNA in the flask that cannot come from any earthly organism) and the conspiracy itself, and later episodes develop the themes of hybrids, toxic alien blood and alien foetuses introduced here. Genome sequencing and experimental gene transfer were real and topical when the episode aired in 1994, during the Human Genome Project, but alien–human hybridisation and the "extraterrestrial" DNA signature are fiction.

title: Carnosaur 2
text: At the Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository in the Nevada desert, unseen creatures kill the night staff, leaving only Jesse, a teenage hacker and the nephew of one of the workers. A team of civilian technicians, led by Major Tom McQuade of the Department of Defense, is sent to fix the site's power and communications. As they explore the lower, classified levels, they are picked off by Velociraptors. McQuade finally admits that a biotech firm had recreated dinosaurs from fossil DNA, and that dozens of eggs seized by the government were stored in the facility, where they hatched. Radiation is leaking from damaged containers holding nuclear warheads, and the survivors fight their way to the surface using dynamite. McQuade and an injured technician blow themselves up to kill the remaining raptors, and Jesse defeats a Tyrannosaurus rex before destroying the facility. Genetics provides only the backstory. The dinosaurs come from a biotech company's experiments with fossilised DNA, events of the first Carnosaur film, and the sequel concerns the military's attempt to hide the results rather than the science itself. No geneticist appears on screen; the relevant figure is a Defense Department officer who conceals the danger from the team he leads, so the film's suspicion is directed at government secrecy around biotechnology. The rest is a monster-siege action film, often compared with Aliens, produced on a small budget by Roger Corman, who had launched the first film after learning that Jurassic Park was entering production. Recreating dinosaurs from fossil DNA is not possible: DNA breaks down over time, and the dinosaur DNA sequences reported in the 1990s turned out to be contamination.

title: Colony
text: In the Beaufort Sea, the crew of a ship recovers a body from a crashed object: an alien bounty hunter. He soon begins killing identical-looking doctors who work at abortion clinics, stabbing them in the back of the neck and burning their clinics. Mulder and Scully trace further copies of the same man, but the bounty hunter keeps reaching them first, at one point disguised as an FBI agent. A man introducing himself as CIA official Ambrose Chapel tells them the doctors are clones from a Soviet genetics programme being eliminated by both governments; "Chapel" is in fact the shapeshifting bounty hunter. Scully discovers a laboratory and four more clones, who are killed after she puts them in custody. Meanwhile Mulder's father summons him home, where his sister Samantha, abducted as a child, has apparently returned and tells him that the clones and the bounty hunter are aliens. The story continues in "End Game". Human cloning is at the centre of this mythology episode. The victims are a group of genetically identical men, first explained as products of a Soviet genetics programme and then revealed to be alien clones living among humans, and the episode builds the series' mythology around them. No geneticist appears on screen: the clones are hunted, a laboratory linked to them is destroyed, and the governments and the bounty hunter are presented as hiding the evidence. The episode also uses forensic biology: Scully's autopsy finds that a victim's blood has coagulated abnormally. Real cloning can produce genetically identical animals but not adult copies with shared appearance and occupations, so the episode uses cloning as conspiracy-thriller material rather than as a realistic depiction.

title: End Game
alt: Fin de juego The X-Files, season 2, episode 17
text: An American submarine finds a craft under the Arctic ice and is disabled by it. Continuing from "Colony", an alien bounty hunter disguised as Mulder kidnaps Scully and offers to exchange her for Mulder's sister Samantha, who has reappeared. Samantha explains that she and a group of identical doctors are clones descended from two original aliens, who worked in abortion clinics to obtain foetal tissue for experiments aimed at establishing a colony on Earth; because their hybrid experiments were considered to taint their race, the bounty hunter was sent to kill them. The exchange goes wrong and Samantha's body later dissolves into green liquid. In a clinic, Mulder finds several more Samantha clones, who admit that the woman he protected was one of them, before the bounty hunter kills them and burns the building. Mulder pursues him to the stranded submarine, is infected by his toxic blood and is saved by Scully, who learns that it contains a retrovirus inactivated by cold. Cloning and hybridisation drive this two-part story. The alien colonists exist as many identical clones, including several women who look exactly like Mulder's missing sister, and they work in clinics using human foetal tissue for a programme to create alien–human hybrids. The episode thus links real reproductive medicine settings with a secret project of genetic manipulation, a recurring theme of The X-Files mythology. The scientists here are the clones themselves, working for an alien agenda and hunted by their own kind for contaminating their race. Scully's contribution is more grounded: she identifies a retrovirus in the alien blood and works out that cold inactivates it, which saves Mulder, and her report credits science for the cure. Retroviruses that insert their genetic material into host cells are real, but the clones, their alien origin and the hybrid programme are fiction.

title: Faces
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation hybrids chimeras heredity
text: Tom Paris, B'Elanna Torres and Peter Durst are captured by the Vidiians, a species ravaged by a disease called the Phage. Their chief surgeon, Sulan, splits Torres, who is half human and half Klingon, into two separate individuals: a full-blooded Klingon and a full-blooded human. Because Klingons are naturally immune to the Phage, he infects the Klingon Torres to study her genetics in search of a cure. The Klingon Torres is fierce and proud of the heritage she hid as a child, while the human Torres, kept in a labour camp with Paris and Durst, is timid and frail. Sulan, attracted to the Klingon Torres, kills Durst and wears his face. The two halves of Torres join forces to escape and lower the shields so that Voyager can rescue them. The Klingon Torres dies protecting the others, and the Doctor restores Torres by reintegrating the Klingon DNA. The episode treats genetic ancestry as identity. Sulan separates Torres's human and Klingon genomes into two bodies, and each half is shown with a distinct personality: the Klingon aggressive and proud, the human cautious and fragile. The story uses this split to explore Torres's conflict about her mixed heritage, and it ends with her accepting that she needs both. The scientist is a Vidiian doctor driven by a real emergency, the Phage that is destroying his people, but his methods include forced experimentation on prisoners and wearing a murdered man's face. Behind the procedure lies a plausible idea, studying a naturally immune individual to find a cure, but splitting a hybrid into two complete beings is impossible: a person's two parental genomes are combined in every cell, and personality is not divided by ancestry. The notion that behaviour follows species or racial heritage is a Star Trek convention rather than science.

title: Judge Dredd
themes: cloning genetic engineering eugenics dna forensics
text: In 2139, Mega-City One is policed by Judges who act as police, jury and executioner. Judge Dredd is framed for the murder of a journalist by Rico, his former best friend, whose execution Dredd had ordered years earlier but who has been secretly kept alive in a penal colony. Dredd is convicted when DNA on the bullets matches his own. On the way to prison, his dying mentor, former Chief Justice Fargo, reveals the truth: Dredd and Rico are clones created by the Janus Project, a secret genetic engineering programme designed to produce perfect Judges from DNA combining the best traits of the Council members. Judge Griffin, who concealed Rico's survival, uses Rico's killing spree to persuade the Council to reopen Janus and grow a clone army. Rico replaces the DNA sample with his own to create clones loyal to him. Dredd, the hacker Fergie and Judge Hershey destroy the lab, and Dredd kills Rico. Genetic engineering and cloning drive the film's plot. The secret Janus Project, run by the Judges' own Council, tried to engineer ideal law enforcers from a DNA blend of its best members, creating the hero and the villain as brothers with the same origin; one became a model Judge and the other a killer, an implicit point about the limits of genetic design. The project is then revived by a power-hungry Judge to produce a clone army, and Rico hijacks it with his own DNA. DNA forensics also matter: Dredd is convicted because the bullets carry his DNA, which is possible only because Rico shares his genes. The clones are adults grown rapidly in tanks, which is unscientific, and real clones would not be identical copies of someone's character. The science is not explored, but the film presents state-run genetic engineering as a dangerous tool of authoritarian power.

title: Mighty Aphrodite
text: Narrated by a Greek chorus in an ancient theatre, the film follows Lenny Weinrib, a Manhattan sportswriter married to Amanda, an ambitious art curator. The couple adopt a baby boy, Max, who turns out to be remarkably gifted. Lenny becomes obsessed with finding out who Max's biological mother is, and eventually discovers that she is Linda Ash, a good-natured but not very bright prostitute and part-time porn actress. Rather than revealing who he is, he befriends her and tries to change her life, helping her escape her pimp and trying to match her with a young boxer, Kevin, who leaves her when he learns about her past. Meanwhile, Lenny's marriage falters as Amanda begins an affair. Lenny and Linda sleep together once before he reconciles with Amanda. A year later they meet by chance in a toy store, each with a child: Linda, now married, is raising Lenny's daughter without telling him, just as he is raising her son. The film turns on a popular assumption about heredity. Lenny is convinced that Max's intelligence must come from his biological parents, and he sets out to find the brilliant mother he imagines, only to find a woman he considers anything but brilliant. The joke undermines his simple view that talent is passed directly from parent to child, while the story leaves open where Max's gifts come from. The final twist mirrors the opening: each of them unknowingly ends up raising the other's biological child, an ironic reversal of the nature and nurture roles that Lenny was so preoccupied with. There are no scientists or genetic tests in the film; genetics is a matter of the characters' beliefs. In reality, intelligence is influenced by many genes and by the environment, and a child's abilities cannot be predicted from those of one parent, so the gap between Max and Linda is not as paradoxical as Lenny thinks.

title: Outbreak
text: In 1967, in Zaire, US Army officers Donald McClintock and Billy Ford discover a deadly virus, Motaba, and destroy the infected camp to keep it secret. Twenty-eight years later, Army virologist Sam Daniels investigates a new Motaba outbreak in Zaire and warns of its spread, but Ford, now his superior, dismisses him. An infected capuchin monkey is smuggled into California and spreads the virus; in the town of Cedar Creek it mutates into an airborne strain, and the Army quarantines the town under martial law. Daniels learns that his superiors knew of the virus and had kept the original strain as a biological weapon, and that McClintock plans to firebomb Cedar Creek to hide the mutation. He escapes arrest, tracks down the host monkey, and uses its antibodies, combined with Ford's experimental serum, to produce an antiserum that saves his ex-wife, CDC scientist Roberta Keough, and the town. With Ford's help he stops the bombing. Outbreak is mainly about virology and epidemiology rather than genetics, but viral mutation is the turning point of the story: a virus spread by contact becomes airborne after a superspreading event, and only the original host animal holds the antibodies needed for a cure. Scientists appear on both sides. Daniels and his civilian and military colleagues are dedicated investigators who risk infection, while McClintock represents military biological weapons research, willing to sacrifice a town to keep a weapon secret. Ford sits in between, complicit in the cover-up but finally siding with Daniels. Motaba is fictional but modelled on Ebola, and the film was released in March 1995, while a real Ebola outbreak was under way in Zaire. Its science has often been criticised, especially in comparison with Contagion (2011): the virus multiplies within hours instead of days, and an effective cure is produced in minutes and works almost immediately, whereas developing and testing real antivirals or antisera takes months or years.

title: Species
text: Scientists working with the SETI programme receive radio transmissions from an alien source containing a DNA sequence and instructions for combining it with human DNA. Assuming the senders are friendly, a government team led by Xavier Fitch creates a female human–alien hybrid, Sil, who looks like a normal girl but grows at an extraordinary rate. When the scientists decide to kill her with cyanide gas, she escapes from the laboratory. Fearing that she will mate with human men and produce offspring that could wipe out humanity, the government assembles a team: anthropologist Stephen Arden, molecular biologist Laura Baker, the empath Dan Smithson and the mercenary Press Lennox. Sil, now an adult woman, travels to Los Angeles looking for a mate, killing anyone who stands in her way. She eventually conceives a child with Arden, kills him and Fitch, and gives birth in the sewers, where Press and Smithson destroy both her and her offspring. The film is built around the creation of a hybrid. Scientists follow genetic instructions received from space and splice alien DNA with human DNA, hoping for a docile, controllable organism; instead they obtain Sil, a being with superhuman strength, rapid growth and regeneration, driven by an instinct to reproduce. Genetics thus becomes the route by which an alien species could invade Earth from within. The scientists are government researchers who act recklessly and then try to destroy what they made: Fitch, the project leader, is portrayed as cold and responsible for the danger, while the molecular biologist Laura Baker helps hunt Sil down. The film draws on the fear of an uncontrolled creation breeding with humans. Its starting point is real: SETI exists, and screenwriter Dennis Feldman, who considered messages such as the Arecibo transmission unwise, researched the script with SETI scientists and with Human Genome Project researchers at the Salk Institute. The human–alien hybrid itself is pure fiction.

title: The City of Lost Children
alt: La Cité des enfants perdus La ciudad de los niños perdidos
text: On an abandoned oil rig off a port city lives Krank, a malevolent being created by a vanished scientist. Krank cannot dream and is ageing prematurely, so he steals the dreams of children kidnapped for him by the Cyclops, a cult of men with mechanical eyes. He shares the rig with the scientist's other creations: six identical, childlike clones, a dwarf named Martha and Irvin, a talking brain in a tank. When the Cyclops kidnap Denrée, the adopted little brother of the carnival strongman One, One sets out to find him with Miette, a sharp orphan girl from a gang of child thieves. A bottled message from Irvin reveals the truth to an amnesiac diver living under the harbour, who turns out to be the scientist himself, thrown off the rig by Krank and Martha. Miette defeats Krank inside a dream, the children are freed and the rig explodes. Genetics is not explained in detail, but the story depends on artificial creation. The absent scientist has made a whole household of beings on the rig: a set of identical clones, the dwarf Martha, the disembodied brain Irvin and Krank himself. Each creation is flawed in some way, and Krank's inability to dream, which makes him age prematurely, drives his cruelty towards the city's children. The scientist is a lonely, Frankenstein-like figure who wanted to build a family of companions, and his creations betray and abandon him; he ends the film half mad, trying to destroy what he made. The film is a dark fairy tale rather than science fiction in any technical sense, and cloning is shown as a way to produce adult copies at will, which bears no relation to the real technique. Its interest lies in its portrait of a creator who cannot make his creatures whole, and in the moral damage that flows from them.

title: Twelve Monkeys
text: In 2035, after a virus has killed most of humanity, scientists send a prisoner, James Cole, back in time to find the source of the plague, believed to be a group called the Army of the Twelve Monkeys, so that they can obtain a pure sample and develop a cure. Sent by mistake to 1990, Cole is committed to a psychiatric hospital, where he meets psychiatrist Kathryn Railly and a patient, Jeffrey Goines. In 1996, he kidnaps Railly, who gradually comes to believe him, and they trace Jeffrey, now leader of the Army and son of the eminent virologist Leland Goines. The Army proves to be a false lead, an animal rights group that frees the animals from a zoo. At the airport, Railly realises that the real culprit is Dr. Peters, the elder Goines' assistant, who is boarding a plane with the virus. Cole is shot dead trying to stop him, watched by his own younger self. Genetics plays a limited role in 12 Monkeys: the catastrophe is a deadly virus created in a laboratory, and the future scientists want a sample of it in its original form so that they can study it and develop a cure. The film's sympathy lies with the virus's victims, but its central twist concerns who releases it. Suspicion falls on the Army of the Twelve Monkeys, a group of animal rights activists led by the virologist's unstable son, but the real culprit is the virologist's own assistant, Dr. Peters, an apocalyptic who has spoken publicly about humanity's damage to the planet. The scientist who creates the pathogen, Leland Goines, is respected and mainstream; it is an insider with access to his laboratory who turns his work into a weapon. The film thus reflects anxieties about biosecurity and access to dangerous pathogens rather than any detailed science, and the virus itself is never described.

title: Afterlife
alt: Vida futura The Outer Limits, season 2, episode 15
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation
text: Sergeant Linden Stiles, wrongly convicted of murdering eleven people, is offered a choice by a secret government unit led by Maculhaney: execution or taking part in an experiment. His Christian faith forbids him to choose death, so he agrees. Scientists splice his genes with extraterrestrial DNA recovered from a downed alien craft, hoping to learn about the aliens and how to fight them. Stiles gradually turns into a nonhuman creature with heightened senses and intelligence. He escapes, but his flight has been allowed so that a military unit can hunt and kill him, even though he refuses to fight back. Dr. Ellen Kersaw, who is responsible for him, objects in vain. As the hunters close in, aliens resembling the transformed Stiles appear, stop them and take him away with them. The humans realise that they themselves were being tested, and failed. Genetic engineering is the instrument of the plot. A secret military programme splices a prisoner's genes with alien DNA and turns him, step by step, into an alien, a fantasy version of transgenesis in which foreign DNA rewrites an adult's entire body and mind. The scientists and officials work for the government on a defence project and treat their subject as expendable: he is coerced into consenting, then hunted for sport and data. One scientist, Dr. Kersaw, recognises that he is still a person and opposes the hunt, and she takes over when her superior is discredited. The episode's twist turns the experiment into a moral test of the experimenters, who judge Stiles by his appearance rather than his conduct. In reality, genes from an unrelated organism could not transform a grown human in this way, but the story is a parable about consent and dehumanisation in research.

title: Herrenvolk
text: In rural Alberta, a telephone lineman dies after a bee sting while five identical boys silently watch. Mulder escapes the Alien Bounty Hunter with Jeremiah Smith, who promises to show him his missing sister, Samantha. In Canada, Smith leads him to fields tended by identical children, the girls all resembling Samantha at the age she was abducted. Smith explains that the clones are mute drones used as workers to tend the fields. Meanwhile, Scully and Agent Pendrell decode the files the Smiths were compiling and find that they catalogue human beings, linked through X to the government's smallpox eradication programme. The Syndicate sets a trap for X, who is shot and dies after writing the initials of a United Nations official in his own blood. Mulder fails to bring back a clone, the fields are abandoned, and the Smoking Man has the Bounty Hunter heal Mulder's dying mother. Cloning and the cataloguing of human beings are central to this season opener of The X-Files, whose title is the German word for "master race". The cloned children, identical boys and girls who copy Samantha Mulder, are shown as speechless drones bred for labour, a vision of human reproduction turned into the production of workers, as in a beehive. The episode also suggests that a public health programme, smallpox vaccination, has been used to record the population. The scientists remain unseen; the programme is run by a secret group of powerful men, the Syndicate, working with alien forces, in keeping with the series' mistrust of government. Reproductive cloning of humans has never been achieved, and clones would be ordinary individuals, not drones; the episode's interest lies in its picture of genetics placed at the service of a hidden elite.

title: Home
text: In the small town of Home, Pennsylvania, children playing baseball find the body of a severely deformed newborn buried in a field. Mulder and Scully learn from the local sheriff that the nearby farmhouse belongs to the Peacock brothers, three deformed men whose family has lived there without electricity or running water and is rumoured to have been inbreeding since the Civil War. The autopsy shows the baby was buried alive, and laboratory tests show its parents were Peacocks. Believing the brothers have abducted and raped a woman, the agents investigate; the brothers murder the sheriff and his wife and kill a deputy with a booby trap. Searching the house, Mulder and Scully find Mrs. Peacock, the brothers' mother, a quadruple amputee hidden under a bed, who has continued to bear children with her sons. Two brothers die in the confrontation, but the mother and her eldest son escape to start a new family elsewhere. Inbreeding is the core of the episode. The baby's malformations are explained by generations of incest within the Peacock family, and laboratory tests establish that both of the baby's parents were Peacocks, which points the investigation towards the incest. Scully raises inbreeding as the medical explanation for the defects, while Mulder at first rejects it because the household seems to be all male. There are no scientists in the story; the genetic theme is presented as a horror of rural isolation and of a family determined to perpetuate itself at any cost. Real inbreeding does increase the risk of birth defects, because children of closely related parents are more likely to inherit two copies of a harmful recessive allele, but the episode exaggerates the effects for horror, and the family's claim that none of them can feel pain is not explained. The episode was inspired partly by the documentary Brother's Keeper and was controversial for its graphic content.

title: Multiplicity
alt: Mis dobles, mi mujer y yo
text: Doug Kinney, an overworked Los Angeles construction foreman, never has time for his wife Laura and their children. While working on a new wing of a scientific institute he meets Dr. Leeds, a scientist who has developed a method of cloning humans and offers to help. Leeds creates a copy of Doug who shares all his memories but exaggerates his masculine, work-focused side; this clone takes over Doug's job. A second clone, sensitive and domestic, takes over at home. The two clones then copy themselves, producing a fourth Doug who, as a copy of a copy, is noticeably dim. The clones' different behaviour confuses Laura and costs Doug his job, and she leaves with the children. With the clones' help, Doug finally fixes up the family house, wins Laura back and starts his own business, while the three clones move to Florida to run a pizzeria. Cloning is the comic engine of the film. Dr. Leeds's process produces instant adult copies that keep the original's memories, and each copy develops a distinct personality, exaggerating one side of Doug's character. The film's main genetic joke is that a clone of a clone is degraded, "like a copy of a copy", and the fourth Doug is less intelligent than the others. The scientist is benign and plays only a small part; he helps Doug out of sympathy, and the consequences are domestic rather than catastrophic. The film was released in July 1996, the same month that Dolly the sheep was born, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Real cloning bears little resemblance to the film's: it produces an embryo that grows like any other, effectively a delayed identical twin with none of the original's memories. The idea that copies of copies deteriorate is a photocopier metaphor rather than biology, although the reprogramming of the donor cell in real cloning is imperfect and many cloned embryos develop abnormally.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering animal experimentation religion
text: United Nations negotiator Edward Douglas survives a plane crash in the Java Sea and is taken by Montgomery to an island ruled by Dr. Moreau, a scientist who fled the United States after a backlash against his experiments on animals. In the laboratory, Douglas sees a human-animal hybrid give birth and finds Moreau's daughter Aissa, who takes him to the village of the "Beast-Folk". Moreau, worshipped as a father by his creatures, controls them with drugs and with electrical implants that inflict pain. When the hyena-swine hybrid discovers his implant and removes it, the creatures rebel and kill Moreau. Montgomery destroys the serum that stops the hybrids from reverting to animals, and Aissa, also a hybrid, begins to regress before she is killed. As the island descends into violence, Douglas turns the new leader against his followers and escapes on a raft, seen off by the peaceful hybrids. The film is the third major adaptation of H. G. Wells's 1896 novel. In Wells's novel, Moreau makes his beast-men by vivisection; this 1996 version recasts him as a genetic engineer who introduces human DNA into animals in search of a higher being incapable of harm. The hybrids are unstable: they need regular drugs to stop them from "retrogressing", and Moreau plans to use Douglas's DNA to stabilise his daughter Aissa permanently. The film keeps the novel's questions about cruelty, moral responsibility and human interference with nature. Moreau is an exiled, god-like scientist who believes his aims are benevolent but rules his creations through pain and fear, and whose work ends in rebellion and bloodshed. Genetics here is central but entirely speculative: animal-human hybrids of this kind, with human speech and intelligence, have no counterpart in real science, and the idea of creatures sliding back towards their animal origins owes more to nineteenth-century anxieties about evolution than to how genes work.

title: The Twilight of the Golds
text: Adapted by Jonathan Tolins from his own stage play, this television film is set in the near future. Suzanne Gold, from a well-off Jewish family, is married to Rob, a doctor working on the human genome project who tests fetuses for diseases and abnormalities. When Suzanne becomes pregnant, Rob's boss persuades them to have the baby tested, and the result indicates a high probability that their son will be gay. Suzanne considers an abortion, which deeply hurts her gay brother David, whose sexuality the family has never fully accepted, and the crisis exposes what her parents, Walter and Phyllis, really feel about him. Unlike the play, in which Suzanne has the abortion and the family is broken, in the film she decides to keep the baby, although this leads to the end of her marriage, since Rob does not want to raise a gay son. The whole drama depends on a fictional prenatal genetic test that predicts a fetus's sexual orientation, and it uses this to raise questions about selective abortion, eugenics and what parents may choose about their children. The genetic test is presented as an extension of real prenatal screening for disease, and the scientist involved, Rob, works within the medical system: he is not a villain, but his professional confidence in the test and his rejection of a gay son put the problem at the centre of the family. The play premiered in 1993, the year Dean Hamer's study linking male homosexuality to a region of the X chromosome was dubbed the "gay gene" by the media; later studies failed to replicate that link. A 2019 study of nearly half a million people found that hundreds or thousands of genetic variants are involved, together accounting for only a modest part of the variation in same-sex behaviour, so a predictive test like the one in the film does not exist.

title: Unnatural Selection
text: Howard and Joanne Sharp are expecting their first child and live in a world where genetic enhancement of unborn babies is illegal but widely bought on the black market. The procedure promises a "perfect" child, but carries a small risk, about 1 in 10,000, of genetic rejection syndrome, which turns the child into a monster. The couple weigh whether to give their baby the advantages of enhancement. They then discover that their neighbours' son, said to have died years earlier, is alive and hidden in the basement, transformed by the syndrome. Horrified, Howard and Joanne try to reverse the enhancement they have already begun on their unborn child, and the episode asks whether they have acted in time. Genetic enhancement of embryos is the subject of the episode. It imagines a society where parents feel pressure to buy genetic upgrades for their children on the black market, despite the procedure being illegal and risky, and it uses the hidden, disfigured son next door to show the price of failure. The story is a cautionary tale about "designer babies", parental ambition and the gap between the promise of a perfect child and the reality of unpredictable biological risk; the scientists who sell enhancements stay in the background as an illicit industry. The invented "genetic rejection syndrome" has no real counterpart, but the episode anticipates later debates: germline editing of embryos is prohibited or tightly restricted in many countries, in part because changes would be passed on to future generations.

title: Alien: Resurrection
text: Two hundred years after Ellen Ripley's death, military scientists aboard the spaceship USM Auriga clone her from blood samples. Because her DNA had become mixed with that of the alien queen she carried, the eighth clone, Ripley 8, carries an alien queen embryo, which the scientists remove and raise to breed Xenomorphs, using humans abducted by a crew of mercenaries as hosts. Ripley 8 has enhanced strength, acidic blood, some of Ripley's memories and a psychic link to the creatures. When the aliens escape and kill most of the crew, Ripley 8 joins the mercenaries, including the android Call, to reach their ship and destroy the Auriga before it reaches Earth. On the way she finds the deformed results of the seven failed cloning attempts, and burns the laboratory after one begs to be killed. The queen, contaminated by Ripley's genes, gives birth to a human-like hybrid that sees Ripley as its mother; she kills it, and the survivors escape as the Auriga crashes into Earth. Cloning and genetic hybridisation are at the centre of the film. Ripley 8 is the product of human cloning in which human and alien DNA have become intermixed, and the hybridisation runs both ways: she gains alien traits, while the queen develops a womb and produces a human-like newborn. The scientists, led by Dr. Wren and Dr. Gediman, work for the military and treat both the aliens and the abducted human hosts as material for research, and most of them are killed by what they create. The scene in which Ripley finds the failed clones, kept as specimens, is the film's strongest comment on the human cost of the experiment. Its science is loose: inheritance of memories through "genetic memory" has no basis, since memories are not stored in DNA, and DNA from different species cannot blend in a single body in this way. The film appeared shortly after the birth of Dolly the sheep in 1996, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell and the only lamb to survive to adulthood out of 277 attempts.

title: An Elephant Makes Love to a Pig
alt: Ingeniería genética South Park, season 1, episode 5
text: Kyle's mother will not let him keep his new pet elephant in the house, so after a class on genetic engineering he decides to cross it with Cartman's pot-bellied pig to create a small "pot-bellied elephant". His rival Terrance bets that he can clone a whole person first. The boys visit Dr. Alphonse Mephesto at the South Park Genetic Engineering Ranch, home to animals with four pairs of buttocks, who tells them that pig and elephant DNA "just won't splice" and secretly takes a blood sample from Stan. Chef suggests they let the animals breed naturally instead. Meanwhile, Mephesto creates a giant clone of Stan that escapes and rampages through town, until Mephesto shoots it. At the science fair, Terrance presents a monkey with five pairs of buttocks, but Kyle's pig gives birth to a piglet that looks like Mr. Garrison, and Garrison awards it first prize. Genetic engineering is the subject of this early South Park episode, broadcast in Spain as "Ingeniería genética". It mixes the main public worries of the late 1990s: crossing species, creating grotesque animals and cloning a human. Dr. Mephesto, modelled on Marlon Brando's Dr. Moreau in the 1996 film The Island of Dr. Moreau, is the mad scientist who builds absurd creatures for no clear purpose and clones a child from a stolen blood sample. A Baltimore Sun reviewer read the episode as a parody of genetic engineering and a statement on its possible evils, notably through the monstrous clone of Stan. Its scientific jokes are partly accurate: an elephant and a pig cannot interbreed or simply have their DNA "spliced", and a clone would be born as a baby, not appear as a fully grown giant.

title: Cloned
text: A year after the death of their young son, Skye Weston and her husband Rick are thinking of having another child when Skye sees a boy in a shopping district who looks exactly like her dead son. Investigating, she finds evidence of several women raising identical boys and gathers more information by asking for help online. The trail leads to a fertility expert, Dr. Kozak, and to the company behind him, which has been using cloning without the parents' knowledge, partly as preparation for growing replacement organs. Skye confronts Kozak, who argues that the ends justify the means, while the company's security men try to stop her from exposing the operation. Human cloning carried out in secret within reproductive medicine is the premise of this television film. A mother discovers that her dead son exists in several copies, created without the parents' consent, and the drama follows her attempt to uncover who made them and why. The scientist, a fertility specialist, is portrayed as a man who has sold out, justifying unethical methods by their supposed benefits, but the main antagonists are the business interests financing the work, which see cloning as a step towards producing replacement organs. The film thus plays on two real fears raised by cloning: the misuse of patients' biological material and the idea of humans as a source of spare parts. It aired in 1997, the year the cloning of Dolly the sheep was announced. Information on the film is limited, so this summary relies on brief synopses and one review.

title: DNA
text: In the jungles of Borneo, Ash Mattley, a doctor running a village clinic, helps the scientist Carl Wessinger collect a rare beetle whose enzyme he is studying, but Wessinger betrays the team and abandons them in a cave. He later uncovers the fossil of a creature that the local people fear as "Balacau". Two years later, gruesome killings begin in the jungle, and CIA agent Claire Sommers asks Mattley to help her find Wessinger, whose research the agency had funded. At Wessinger's abandoned compound they learn that he used the beetle enzyme to bring the fossil back to life; the creature was an alien that had terrorised the region centuries earlier, and Wessinger planned to clone it and sell it to the highest bidder before it escaped. Pursued by the creature, which can turn invisible, and by Wessinger's mercenaries, Mattley and Sommers survive with the help of the local tribe, and Mattley finally kills Balacau with a rocket launcher. Despite its title, genetics plays a limited role. The science consists of reviving an ancient creature from a fossil using an enzyme taken from a beetle, with the aim of cloning it; the film's interest lies in the hunt for the monster rather than in the science. The scientist Wessinger fits the classic profile of the unscrupulous researcher: he betrays his colleagues, works with secret funding from the CIA and private mercenaries, and intends to sell clones of a dangerous creature to the highest bidder, which ends with his own death. The doctor Mattley, by contrast, is a physician committed to the local community. Neither reviving an organism from a fossil nor cloning it is possible with real techniques, since cloning requires living cells or at least well-preserved DNA. The film is a low-budget action film made in the Philippines and openly influenced by Alien, Predator and Jurassic Park.

title: Doctor Bashir, I Presume?
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 5, episode 16
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: Holographic engineer Lewis Zimmerman comes to Deep Space Nine to use Dr. Julian Bashir as the template for a new long-term medical hologram. Against Julian's wishes, he invites Bashir's estranged parents, Richard and Amsha, to be interviewed. Speaking to what they think is their son but is in fact the hologram, the parents mention that they had him illegally genetically modified as a child, and Zimmerman and Chief O'Brien overhear. Julian explains that as a young boy he was a poor learner and small for his age, and that before his seventh birthday his parents took him to Adigeon Prime for treatments that enhanced his mental and physical abilities. Because Federation law bars genetically enhanced people from Starfleet and from practising medicine, he prepares to resign. His parents instead make a deal with Starfleet's Judge Advocate General: Richard pleads guilty and accepts two years in prison, and Julian keeps his commission and his licence. Human genetic enhancement is the centre of the episode. In the Star Trek universe it is outlawed because of the Eugenics Wars, in which genetically engineered "supermen" such as Khan seized power on Earth; in the episode, a Starfleet admiral cites them to justify the ban. The episode presents the issue through a family drama. Bashir's parents acted out of love and anxiety, wanting a son who could keep up, while Julian feels that his original self was erased and that he is a fraud. The geneticists themselves remain off screen, in an alien clinic beyond Federation law. The story raises questions that remain central to debates on germline editing and enhancement: the distinction between therapy and enhancement, a child's consent, and the risk of discrimination against enhanced people. The writers decided at the last minute to make Bashir genetically engineered, and later episodes developed the idea further. Enhancing intelligence by gene editing is not possible today, because intelligence depends on thousands of genetic variants with small effects.

title: Double Helix
alt: Doble Hélice The Outer Limits, season 3, episode 12
text: Dr. Martin Nodel, a university geneticist, studies introns, stretches of DNA that do not code for proteins and that he believes hold the secret of future evolution. He develops a formula to activate them and tests it on himself. He starts to develop strange marks: a map grows on his back and a pattern of symbols appears on his hand. He then screens students for an "advanced seminar", selecting those with a high IQ, no surgery, no imperfections such as tattoos or glasses, and specific age, height and weight. The map leads the group, joined by his son and the son's girlfriend, to a cave in a secret military installation, where soldiers capture them. Behind a sealed door is an alien spacecraft bearing Nodel's symbols. When he touches it, an alien message is transmitted through him, and Nodel, the students and the young couple board the ship, which takes off. Genetics is central. A geneticist experimenting on himself discovers that the so-called "junk" parts of human DNA contain a hidden programme, apparently left by aliens, which activates when triggered and summons a selected group of humans. His selection of students by IQ, physical perfection and body measurements has a clearly eugenic flavour, although the episode presents it as the aliens' design and treats the departure as a hopeful step in human evolution. Nodel is portrayed as a driven but sympathetic researcher, opposed by a secretive military. The story plays on a real scientific debate of the 1990s about the function of introns and other non-coding DNA, much of which was then dismissed as junk. Introns are removed from RNA by splicing and are not "junk" in a simple sense, but there is no evidence that they store dormant instructions, and the episode's ideas are pure science fiction. The story continues in the season 4 episode "The Origin of Species".

title: GATTACA
themes: eugenics genetic discrimination genetic testing nature nurture dna forensics
text: In a near future where most children are genetically selected, Vincent Freeman, conceived naturally, is classed at birth as an "in-valid": a blood test predicts a heart condition and a life expectancy of about 30 years. Barred from his dream of space travel, he works as a cleaner at the Gattaca Aerospace Corporation until he assumes the identity of Jerome Eugene Morrow, a genetically selected former swimming star left paralysed after being hit by a car. Using Jerome's blood, urine, hair and skin, Vincent passes the company's constant DNA checks and is chosen as navigator for a mission to Titan. A week before launch, an administrator is murdered, and one of Vincent's eyelashes found at the scene puts the police on the trail of an unregistered in-valid. While he falls in love with his colleague Irene, he must face the detective on the case: his genetically selected younger brother, Anton. Genetics is the core of the film. Its society practises eugenics through embryo selection, and a single blood or hair sample is enough to read a person's predicted health, lifespan and prospects. Genetic discrimination is illegal but routine, enforced through DNA checks at work and in police investigations. The scientists who appear are clinicians serving this system, although Dr. Lamar, who runs Gattaca's tests, turns out to know Vincent's secret and lets him fly, remarking that his own genetically selected son is "not all that they promised". The film argues against genetic determinism: the in-valid succeeds through effort, while the genetically privileged Jerome is crushed by the expectation to be the best. Embryo screening for single-gene disorders is real today, but predictions for complex traits from DNA remain modest, far from the certainty shown here. The film is widely cited in bioethics debates; reviewing it in Nature Genetics, molecular biologist Lee Silver said geneticists should see it to understand how the public views their field.

title: Mimic
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras evolution pandemic
text: In New York, cockroaches are spreading Strickler's disease, which is killing hundreds of children. Entomologist Dr. Susan Tyler, recruited by CDC deputy director Dr. Peter Mann, uses genetic engineering to create the "Judas breed", a hybrid of mantis and termite that releases an enzyme which makes the roaches starve to death. The epidemic ends, and Susan and Peter marry. Three years later, people start disappearing in the subway, and two boys sell Susan a strange insect that resembles her creation. The Judas insects were all female and designed to die within six months, but they have survived, bred and evolved into a human-sized species that hunts people in the tunnels, folding its body to look like a man in a coat. Trapped underground with a few companions, Susan and Peter realise they must kill the colony's single fertile male. Peter blows up the nest with a gas leak, Susan lures the male in front of a train, and both survive. Genetic engineering is the central idea. Susan Tyler creates the Judas breed for a humanitarian purpose, to stop an epidemic killing children, and builds in safeguards: the insects are all female and live only six months, so the breed should die out after one generation. The film's point is that these controls fail, and an accelerated metabolism lets the breed pass through tens of thousands of generations in three years, evolve lungs and grow large enough to mimic its human prey. Tyler is a sympathetic scientist who must face the unintended consequences of her work, rather than a villain. The premise echoes real methods of insect control.
