In the sterile insect technique, used against pests such as the screw-worm fly, mass releases of irradiated sterile males make populations collapse; approaches based on genetically modified insects are still under development. The film's evolutionary leap, however, is impossible on such a timescale and works as a cautionary fable about releasing engineered organisms.

title: Re-generation
text: Graham, a powerful public figure, uses his influence to offer his wife Rebecca the chance to clone their son Justin, who died in an accident. Rebecca is at first repulsed but agrees to carry the clone. Six months into the pregnancy, she begins to see things through her son's eyes, and she and Dr. Cole conclude that the unborn child is not only a clone but carries Justin's memories. Rebecca notices that the baby reacts strangely to Graham, and through the fetus's memories she relives Justin's death: Graham, impatient, had pulled a toy from the boy's hands and knocked him down, causing the fatal head injury. When she decides to leave, she comes to believe that Graham will kill her to protect his secret, and she shoots him. Three months later she brings her newborn son in for a check-up, and Dr. Cole, now pregnant, calms her own unborn child by calling it Graham. Human reproductive cloning is the premise of the episode. A grieving mother carries a clone of her dead son, made possible through her husband's power and connections, and the story explores the hope that cloning can bring back a lost child. It then adds a supernatural element: the clone inherits the dead boy's memories, which reveal the father's guilt. The doctor who performs the procedure is portrayed as sympathetic, although the final twist suggests she has cloned the dead husband in turn. Scientifically, a clone is a genetic copy, a delayed identical twin, and does not inherit the memories or personality of the original; the episode uses that misconception as a deliberate fantasy device. The episode aired in January 1997, a month before the announcement of Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, which brought human cloning into public debate.

title: Statistical Probabilities
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 6, episode 9
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: Dr. Julian Bashir, whose own genetic enhancement as a child has recently come to light, volunteers to help four genetically enhanced patients whose augmentation left them unable to function in society: the hyperactive, paranoid Jack, the hypersexual Lauren, the childlike Patrick and the silent Sarina. Bashir concludes that they are mostly bored, because the law bars them from any profession that would use their abilities. With Captain Sisko's permission, the group analyses peace talks with the Dominion and correctly deduces the Dominion's real aim. Given more intelligence, they build a statistical model predicting that the Federation will lose the war with hundreds of billions of casualties, and recommend surrender. When Starfleet refuses, they decide to pass Starfleet's plans to the Dominion. Bashir objects, is tied up, and is freed by Sarina, which lets him stop the others. He realises that one person's unpredictable choice has proved their model wrong. The episode explores the consequences of human genetic enhancement in the Star Trek universe, where the Federation bans genetic augmentation partly because of its fictional Eugenics Wars. Jack, Lauren, Patrick and Sarina were enhanced as children, and their brilliance comes with severe psychiatric and social difficulties, presented as unintended neurological side effects of the procedure. Their situation also shows the discrimination enhanced people face: they are kept in an institution and barred from careers where their talents could be used. Bashir, enhanced himself but able to pass as normal, serves as their bridge to society, and the episode questions whether superior intelligence makes people right; their confidence in their statistical predictions almost leads them to treason. No geneticist appears on screen. The episode raises recognisable questions about enhancement, disability and the limits of prediction.

title: The Lost World: Jurassic Park
text: Four years after the disaster at Jurassic Park, a girl is attacked by small dinosaurs on Isla Sorna, InGen's "Site B", where the animals were bred before being moved to the park and which was abandoned after a hurricane. Peter Ludlow, Hammond's nephew, takes control of InGen and plans to capture the dinosaurs for a new park in San Diego. Hammond sends mathematician Ian Malcolm and a small team to document the animals living in the wild and argue for leaving them alone; Malcolm goes mainly to rescue his girlfriend, palaeontologist Sarah Harding. The two groups clash on the island, and after a pair of Tyrannosaurus attack them in search of their injured infant, survivors of both teams cross the island under attack from Velociraptors. Ludlow ships a male Tyrannosaurus to San Diego, where it escapes and rampages through the city before Malcolm and Harding lure it back to the ship. The island is then declared a nature reserve. Genetics is the background rather than the subject of this sequel. The dinosaurs are the genetically engineered animals of the first film, and Isla Sorna is where InGen produced them, but the story is about what happens once created animals live and breed on their own: a self-sustaining population of cloned dinosaurs, complete with family groups and parental care. The conflict is between exploitation and conservation. Ludlow treats the animals as company property to be captured and displayed, while Hammond, now remorseful, wants them protected from human interference, and the ending turns the island into a reserve. No geneticist plays a significant role, and the cloning process itself is not revisited. The same scientific objection as for Jurassic Park applies: DNA does not survive for tens of millions of years, so dinosaur cloning is not possible with real ancient DNA.

title: The Post-Modern Prometheus
themes: genetic engineering mutants hybrids chimeras human experimentation
text: Presented as a comic book in black and white, the episode sends Mulder and Scully to rural Albion, Indiana, where Shaineh Berkowitz says she was impregnated while unconscious 18 years ago and has just been attacked again. Locals describe a creature with a lumpy head and two mouths, which her son Izzy has turned into a comic character, "The Great Mutato". The agents meet geneticist Francis Pollidori, who shows them fruit flies with legs growing from their mouths produced by manipulating Hox genes and says such experiments could in theory be done on humans. After Pollidori's wife is attacked, suspicion falls on his father, whom Pollidori then murders. Hunted by a mob, Mutato explains that he is a failed genetic experiment by Pollidori, rescued and raised by the old man, who tried to create a mate for him using farm animals. Pollidori refuses to make him a companion and is arrested; the agents take Mutato to a Cher concert. The episode is a comic retelling of Frankenstein in which the creator is a geneticist. Dr. Pollidori's research on Hox genes in Drosophila is based on real developmental biology: mutations in these genes, which control the body plan, can make flies grow the wrong appendages, such as legs where antennae should be. The episode extrapolates from this to a deformed human created in the laboratory, and Pollidori, like Victor Frankenstein, rejects his creation as "a mistake" and refuses to give him a mate. The scientist is the real villain, vain and violent, while the "monster" turns out to be gentle and is finally accepted by the town. His surrogate father's attempts to imitate the experiments with farm animals, and the women impregnated while unconscious, add a darker strand to the comedy. Producing a viable human with such radical body-plan changes is far beyond any real technique, but the fly images reflect genuine experiments from the history of genetics.

title: Chrysalis
alt: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, season 7, episode 5
text: Jack, Lauren and Patrick, three genetically enhanced savants, arrive on Deep Space Nine posing as an admiral and his staff and bring with them Sarina, who has been catatonic for most of her life. They want Dr. Julian Bashir, himself genetically enhanced, to cure her. With their help Bashir refines a medical instrument and operates on her, and for the first time Sarina is able to speak and connect with her surroundings; within minutes of her reunion with her friends she masters singing and joins them in an improvised fugue. Bashir introduces her to the station's crew and falls in love with her, handing her care to another doctor so that he can court her. Overwhelmed, Sarina withdraws into her catatonic state again, and later explains that she felt pressured to become the woman of his dreams to thank him for curing her. She leaves the station for a scientific internship. The episode deals with the consequences of human genetic enhancement in the Star Trek universe. The four savants, introduced in "Statistical Probabilities", were engineered as children to have extraordinary intelligence, but their modifications left them with behavioural problems that make it hard for them to live in society: Jack is aggressive and hyperactive, Lauren hypersexual, Patrick childlike and Sarina catatonic. Bashir, who was enhanced without side effects, cures Sarina's catalepsy, which Memory Alpha describes as a side effect of her genetic modification, by correcting the neural connections it left incomplete. The episode presents genetic enhancement as a gamble with lasting human costs. Its main subject, though, is consent and autonomy: Sarina must decide who she is rather than repay the man who cured her. Real genetic enhancement of intelligence is not possible today, and intelligence depends on many genes of small effect.

title: Cowboy Bebop
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement engineered pathogens human experimentation animal experimentation
text: In 2071, after an accident with a hyperspace gateway has made Earth nearly uninhabitable, humanity lives across the Solar System, and registered bounty hunters, known as "cowboys", pursue criminals for rewards. The series follows the crew of the spaceship Bebop: Spike Spiegel, a former hitman of the Red Dragon crime syndicate; Jet Black, a former police officer; Faye Valentine, an amnesiac con artist; the child hacker Edward; and Ein, a genetically engineered Welsh corgi. Most of its 26 episodes are self-contained cases, while an overarching arc follows Spike's rivalry with his former partner Vicious and his love for Julia, ending in a final confrontation in which Spike kills Vicious and is himself gravely wounded. Several episodes touch on biological experimentation: Ein is stolen from a laboratory that illegally experimented on him, a virus that turns humans into apes appears in another case, and the assassin Mad Pierrot is the product of brutal experiments meant to create a super soldier. Genetics is a background element rather than a central theme. Its clearest example is Ein, a "data dog" whose intellect has been genetically enhanced and who is introduced in "Stray Dog Strut" as the stolen subject of illegal laboratory experiments; the scientists who made him appear on screen as bumbling villains chasing the dog and end up arrested. Other episodes treat the body as raw material for research: in "Gateway Shuffle" eco-terrorists threaten to release "Monkey Business", a virus said to act on the small difference between human and ape DNA, and are turned into monkeys by it, and in "Pierrot le Fou" the near-invulnerable assassin Mad Pierrot turns out to be the survivor of a secret police experiment in enhancing assassination skills, described as altering him genetically and physically, which left him childlike and murderous. The engineers are criminals or secret government agents, and the series treats their subjects as victims shaped by others' ambitions. The enhanced dog is a playful idea; the more serious note is the recurring image of people experimented on and left damaged.

title: Criminal Nature
alt: Naturaleza criminal The Outer Limits, season 4, episode 1
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering mutants nature nurture genetic discrimination
text: Years after the events of "Unnatural Selection", genetic enhancement of babies is common but flawed, and children affected by Genetic Rejection Syndrome (GRS) have grown into deformed, violent adults who commit murders. Detective Ray Venable leads a team hunting them. He and his wife Marie once had a son with GRS, Dylan, whom they paid an agency to take away; its director now admits that such children are sent to labour camps abroad. Now Dylan is harassing the family. Ray injects himself with a serum that temporarily gives him the heightened senses of GRS sufferers so that he can track his son, only to discover that Dylan planted the serum for him to find. Dylan forcibly injects him with more, making the change irreversible, and claims that the gene behind his own violence was not altered but inherited from Ray. Ray kills Dylan, but his family now fears him. The episode is about the consequences of human genetic enhancement. It continues "Unnatural Selection", in which parents buy black-market genetic improvements for their unborn children at the risk of Genetic Rejection Syndrome, a fictional condition that causes deformities, violence and psychosis. Here the generation of failed enhancements has grown up, and society deals with it by shipping the children off to labour camps and hunting the adults. The story questions both the enhancement industry and the parents who abandoned their children, and adds a twist on nature versus nurture: Dylan claims that the gene behind his rage was inherited from his father rather than created by the enhancement, a claim the episode leaves unconfirmed, while its closing narration suggests that what parents pass on may lie in the soul rather than the genes; Ray, once transformed, becomes a monster in his family's eyes. No scientist appears prominently. GRS is invented, but the episode reflects a real concern about heritable genetic modification: early experiments editing human embryos produced unintended mutations, and safety is central to the debate.

title: Go Fish
alt: Buffy the Vampire Slayer, season 2, episode 20
themes: human enhancement human experimentation hybrids chimeras
text: Members of the Sunnydale High School swim team, the Razorbacks, are being killed one by one: all that is left of each victim is his skin, next to a creature resembling the Creature from the Black Lagoon. Buffy and her friends suspect that the team's best swimmers are the targets and that they are taking steroids. Xander joins the team as an undercover investigator and discovers that a substance is being pumped into the sauna steam, which he is inhaling too. The truth is that the swimmers are not being eaten but transformed: Coach Marin, with the help of school nurse Greenliegh, has been experimenting on them with fish DNA to improve their performance, and the creatures are the swimmers themselves, shedding their human skin. When the nurse wants to stop the experiments, Marin pushes her into the sewer, where the creatures kill her. Marin later dies the same way, and Xander and the surviving swimmers are treated in time. The episode uses genetic manipulation as a twisted form of doping. A coach obsessed with winning the state championship, assisted by the school nurse, exposes his swimmers to fish DNA hidden in the sauna steam, supposedly to make them faster in the water; instead they turn into fish–human hybrids that kill and eat their teammates. The experimenters are not professional scientists but school staff, and the episode connects the experiment with its main satirical theme: the privileges granted to star athletes and the willingness of adults to cover up anything in the name of victory. Both experimenters end up killed by their own creations. The premise is pure fantasy: exposure to another species' DNA does not transform an organism, and the episode makes no attempt at a scientific explanation.

title: Mr. Murder
text: Drew Oslett Sr. and his son, Drew Oslett Jr., are shadowy operatives who supply assassins and plan to use genetic engineering and cloning to create a perfect, untraceable killer. After killing their chosen candidate to obtain his DNA, they discover that the tissue samples have been contaminated and replaced by those of Marty Stillwater, a successful mystery novelist. Seven years later the clone, Alfie, has been engineered as a perfect soldier and conditioned into a remorseless killing machine. Unknown to his creators, he has developed a telepathic bond with Marty and the ability to see remotely. Jealous of Marty's life and family, Alfie sets out to take his place, and the Osletts order a hit on the whole Stillwater family. The two-part television miniseries, starring Stephen Baldwin in both roles, is based on the 1993 novel by Dean Koontz. Cloning is the premise. A secret organisation uses genetic engineering to grow an assassin from a donor's DNA, but a lab mix-up means the clone is made from the cells of an unsuspecting writer, so the killer is genetically identical to an ordinary family man. The story is about identity: the clone wants the life of the man he was copied from, and the relationship between them is presented as a mystical, telepathic bond rather than a biological one. The scientists and handlers are cynical figures working for covert interests who treat the clone as a weapon and are willing to murder a whole family to protect their secret. The plot greatly exaggerates what cloning can do: a real clone is a genetic copy that develops from an embryo and ages normally, and it would have no special connection to its donor's mind.

title: Pokémon: The First Movie
text: Giovanni, leader of the criminal Team Rocket, recruits the scientist Dr. Fuji to create a cloned super-soldier from an eyelash of the rare Pokémon Mew; Fuji accepts because he hopes the research will let him clone his dead daughter, Amber. The result, Mewtwo, gains consciousness in the laboratory, where the other clones, including Amber's, fail and die. Learning that his creators see him only as an experiment, Mewtwo destroys the lab and kills Fuji and the scientists, then breaks with Giovanni when he realises he is meant to be a weapon. Resolving to take revenge on humans and Pokémon alike, he lures trainers to New Island, including Ash, Misty and Brock, and uses cloning to build an army of copies of their Pokémon. Originals and clones fight until Ash is turned to stone stepping between Mewtwo and Mew. Moved by his sacrifice, Mewtwo accepts that living beings should be judged by their choices, not their origins, and erases everyone's memories. Cloning and genetic modification are the core of the story. Mewtwo is a clone of Mew, created from an eyelash and enhanced to be more powerful, and much of the film is an existential reflection on whether a being made in a laboratory, and copies in general, have the same worth as the originals. The scientist who creates him is not simply a villain: Dr. Fuji works for a criminal organisation, but his own motive is grief, the wish to bring back his daughter. The experiment ends in disaster, as the creature turns on its makers. The original Japanese version was praised for its treatment of cloning, genetic engineering and existentialism, while the English dub was criticised for removing most of these ethical themes, including part of Mewtwo's origin story. In reality, a clone shares its donor's genome but is a separate individual: the first cloned cat, CC (2001), even had a different coat pattern from her donor because of X-inactivation, a process that genes alone do not fix in advance.

title: Soldier
text: In 1996, a military programme selects orphaned infants and raises them to be ruthless, disciplined soldiers, culling those who fall short. In 2036, Sergeant Todd 3465, one of the original recruits, is about to be replaced by a new generation of genetically engineered soldiers, created by Colonel Mekum to be physically superior and devoid of emotion except aggression. In a test, the engineered soldier Caine 607 defeats three of the veterans, and Todd, presumed dead, is dumped on the waste-disposal planet Arcadia 234. He is taken in by a community of stranded colonists, who struggle with his rigid military conditioning and eventually expel him. When Mekum's new soldiers land on the planet for a training exercise and attack the colonists, Todd uses his experience and knowledge of the terrain to defeat them all, including Caine, and then takes over the troop ship with his old comrades to rescue the settlers. Genetic engineering is a secondary element. The film contrasts two kinds of manufactured soldier: Todd, an ordinary human shaped by brutal training from infancy, and the newer soldiers who have been genetically engineered for strength and aggression. The project's commander, Colonel Mekum, embodies the cold military-technical establishment, discarding the old soldiers as obsolete and treating the civilian colonists as acceptable targets. The story ultimately favours experience, loyalty and recovered humanity over engineered superiority, since Todd defeats the genetically designed troops. No geneticist is shown and the film says nothing about how the engineering is done; it borrows the idea mainly as a device for the action. Writer David Webb Peoples set the film in the same fictional universe as Blade Runner, which he co-wrote.

title: Species II
text: Three astronauts return from the first crewed mission to Mars, unaware that an alien substance from the soil samples has infected one of them, Commander Patrick Ross. On Earth, Ross has sex with several women, who undergo accelerated pregnancies and die giving birth to human-alien hybrids. Meanwhile, a military team led by Dr. Laura Baker has created Eve, a more docile clone of the alien-human hybrid Sil from the first film, to study the alien species. When the scientist Dr. Orinsky is killed, analysis reveals alien DNA similar to Eve's, and Baker brings back Press Lennox to hunt Ross. Eve's alien DNA is activated so she can track him telepathically. Baker discovers that astronaut Dennis Gamble was not infected because he carries the sickle-cell trait, and that the alien has no defence against human genetic diseases. Ross mates with Eve before the team kills him using Gamble's blood. In the final scene, Eve's womb begins to swell. Genetics underpins the film: human-alien hybridization, cloning and genetic disease. Government scientists have cloned the hybrid Sil to produce Eve, a "docile" version kept for study, and then switch on her alien DNA as a tracking tool, a gamble that backfires. The alien DNA spreads to humans and drives Ross to breed. The scientists are portrayed as working for the military, and Dr. Baker is ambivalent about the risks of her own creation. The resolution relies on human genetic variation: Gamble resists infection because he carries the sickle-cell trait, and his blood kills the hybrid. This loosely echoes the real case in which carrying one copy of the sickle-cell allele protects against severe malaria, an example of natural selection in humans, although the film's idea that a genetic disease could be lethal to an alien when injected is pure fantasy. The hybridization itself, with pregnancies lasting minutes, has no scientific basis.

title: Spiral
text: In this sequel to Ring, pathologist Mitsuo Andō, still grieving his drowned son, performs the autopsy of his friend and rival Ryūji Takayama and finds a coded message in the stomach. Reiko Asakawa and her son Yōichi are then found dead. With Takayama's student Mai Takano, Andō investigates the cursed videotape that kills its viewers a week later and the murdered psychic Sadako Yamamura. Tests show that the deaths are caused by a virus, and that the virus that killed Reiko's boss, Yoshino, differs from the one that killed Takayama and his son. Andō survives the curse, but Mai is found dead having apparently given birth, and a woman who looks like her turns out to be Sadako reborn through Mai's body. Andō learns that Reiko's diary now spreads the curse and that Takayama was helping Sadako. In exchange for his help, Sadako brings back Takayama and Andō's son. Genetics plays only a marginal role in this film. Its horror rests on a supernatural curse that behaves like an infectious agent: the videotape, and later a written diary, transmit a virus that kills within a week, and the virus changes as the curse spreads. Sadako uses the virus to be reborn through another woman's womb and returns, in her own words, as "perfectly dual-gendered", able to reproduce herself. These ideas evoke viral mutation and asexual reproduction, but the film does not develop them in genetic terms, and its scientist, a pathologist, investigates causes of death rather than heredity. The real content is the folklore of a vengeful spirit, here translated into a pseudo-medical vocabulary. Spiral was released in Japan alongside Ring in 1998 and was later replaced by Ring 2 as the sequel to Ring. It does not deal with genes, DNA or genetic research in any meaningful way, and its inclusion in a database on genetics is doubtful.

title: The Origin of Species
themes: genetic engineering eugenics engineered pathogens genetic disease
text: In this sequel to "Double Helix", Dr. Nodel, a scientist whose body has been altered so that he can communicate with aliens who once seeded Earth with their genetic material, boards their spaceship with his son Paul and six students, including Paul's girlfriend Hope. When Nodel touches a glowing post in the control room, he and Paul are consumed by light, and the students fear they have been led into a trap as the ship pulls them through the walls two by two. Hope reads Nodel's journal and touches the post herself; her body begins the same transformation, and a glowing entity speaks to her with the voices of Nodel and Paul. Eventually all the students are left suspended and unconscious in a black void. They wake to find that the ship has landed on a dead planet, and must wonder whether the aliens, who promised them a great experiment in hope, have betrayed them. Genetics provides the background of this two-part story. In "Double Helix", the geneticist Dr. Nodel studies introns, non-coding sections of genes that he believes hold the key to future evolution, and activates them in himself, starting a transformation that lets him communicate with the aliens who seeded humanity's DNA. "The Origin of Species" follows the consequences: the chosen humans are taken as a new seed population for an alien experiment, and genetic transformation becomes a form of selection. The episode concentrates on suspense aboard the ship rather than on science. The idea that introns contain a hidden evolutionary programme is fiction; introns are spliced out of RNA before translation, and although they play a part in regulating gene expression, they do not hold dormant plans for future humans. The notion that life on Earth was seeded by aliens is a long-standing science fiction theme without scientific support.

title: After the Truth
text: Peter Rohm, a young German lawyer, has long been planning a book about Josef Mengele, the Auschwitz doctor known as the "Angel of Death". He is taken to Argentina by a mysterious publisher and meets Mengele himself, now in his late eighties and terminally ill; the man who drowned in Brazil in 1979 was a relative. Mengele has decided to return to Germany and stand trial, and wants Rohm to defend him. Rohm accepts, to the horror of his colleagues and his wife. Mengele is arrested on arrival and tried. Survivors testify about his crimes; Mengele does not deny the facts but claims he acted for medical progress and by the standards of his time, and his eloquence begins to sway people. Rohm and his family face hostility, and he learns that his own mother, a nurse, took part in killings at a psychiatric clinic. In his final plea he declares Mengele guilty and says he should spend his remaining life in prison. The film is a fictional trial of Josef Mengele, the SS doctor who carried out experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz, including on twins, and selected prisoners for the gas chambers. Before the war Mengele had worked as assistant to the geneticist Otmar von Verschuer, studying the genetic factors behind traits such as cleft lip and palate, and at Auschwitz he conducted twin studies for the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Anthropology. The film's trial, however, deals with his crimes as a whole rather than with genetics specifically. Mengele is portrayed as an unrepentant, intelligent man who defends himself as a servant of medical progress, and the film examines how such arguments can persuade. Rohm's mother's role in killings at a psychiatric clinic links the story to the Nazi "euthanasia" of disabled people, a programme rooted in eugenic thinking. The scenario is hypothetical: the real Mengele died in Brazil in 1979, and his identity was confirmed by forensic examination of his remains and by DNA testing in 1992.

title: Bats
text: After a series of deaths in the small town of Gallup, Texas, the Centers for Disease Control calls in bat expert Dr. Sheila Casper and her assistant Jimmy. With Sheriff Emmett Kimsey, they learn from the scientist Dr. Alexander McCabe that the culprits are bats he has genetically modified to be more intelligent and omnivorous, supposedly to protect them from extinction. The bats, now numbering thousands, overrun the town and kill many people, including a CDC specialist. The National Guard evacuates Gallup and gives Casper 48 hours before it destroys the area. She plans to freeze the bats in their roost, an abandoned mine, so that they hibernate and die rather than scatter. During a siege at the school it emerges that McCabe deliberately designed the bats as the ultimate predator to kill humans; he walks outside thinking he can control them and is killed. Casper and Kimsey restart the coolant inside the mine, and the bats are sealed in and frozen. Genetic engineering is the origin of the monster in this creature feature. Dr. McCabe has altered bats to be smarter, more aggressive and omnivorous, and his experiment escapes into the wild as a swarm of thousands. His first explanation, saving bats from extinction, gives way to the truth: he built them as killing machines and never seriously considered the risk. Reviews describe McCabe as a government scientist working on a shadowy, unexplained project, and the military's response, a deadline to bomb the area, adds a note of official cover-up. The film presents the scientist as a reckless, ultimately insane figure destroyed by his creation, while the heroine is a field biologist whose knowledge of real bat behaviour, such as hibernation in cold, saves the day. The genetics is never explained and should be read as a plot device; no real genetic modification could produce such coordinated, intelligent hunting behaviour.

title: Deep Blue Sea
text: At Aquatica, a remote research facility at sea, Dr. Susan McAlester and Dr. Jim Whitlock study mako sharks in search of a cure for Alzheimer's disease, harvesting a protein complex from the sharks' brain tissue that reactivates dormant human brain cells. After a shark escapes and attacks a boat, the company sends executive Russell Franklin to inspect the facility. During a test that proves the treatment works, the largest shark bites off Whitlock's arm, and as a storm hits, a rescue helicopter crashes into the facility, which begins to flood. Susan admits that she and Jim genetically engineered the sharks to enlarge their brains, against protocol, to obtain more of the protein, making them far more intelligent. The sharks pick off the survivors as they climb towards the surface, and Carter, the shark wrangler, realises the animals have been flooding the facility to escape to the open sea. Susan sacrifices herself as bait, and the last shark is blown up. Genetic engineering is the trigger of this shark thriller. The researchers' goal is medical and sympathetic, a treatment for Alzheimer's disease, but Susan McAlester breaks the rules to reach it faster: she enlarges the sharks' brains genetically to get more tissue, and by doing so makes them intelligent enough to outwit their captors. The film follows the familiar pattern of the ambitious scientist whose shortcut unleashes disaster. It is somewhat more nuanced than most, since the treatment appears to work and Susan admits her responsibility, destroys her research and dies trying to save the others. The science is fanciful, and the film never explains how the sharks' brains were enlarged or how the protein would restore human brain cells. In reality Alzheimer's disease still has no cure, and available treatments offer only modest relief of symptoms.

title: Descent
themes: gene therapy human experimentation human enhancement eugenics
text: Dr. Arthur Zeller is a brilliant but shy researcher in a university anthropology department whom his co-workers ignore and a vagrant regularly bullies for money. He daydreams about unleashing the animal within himself and, after comparing DNA from a Homo erectus specimen with his own, begins a kind of gene therapy, injecting himself with genes for dominance taken from primitive primates. His personality changes: he becomes assertive, but also suffers lapses in which he reverts to the mind of a caveman, attacking his boss and killing and eating a dog. When his colleague Dr. Laura White does not return his affection, he secretly injects her with genes for submissiveness during a routine flu shot. She becomes ill, and Arthur, regaining control, confesses and asks for her help. Together they develop an experimental antidote, but when he admits what he did to her, he realises he has lost her for good. He flees with his syringes and injects himself with a massive dose of the ape genes before Laura can reach him. Gene therapy misused for behavioural modification is the subject of the episode. A frustrated anthropology researcher, convinced that modern medicine has weakened humanity, compares Homo erectus DNA with modern DNA and injects himself with "dominance genes" from primates, and then secretly injects a colleague with "submissiveness genes", a non-consensual experiment that the episode treats as a violation. Zeller is a variation on the Jekyll and Hyde story: a researcher who experiments on himself to escape his limitations and ends up destroyed by it. The premise rests on a simplified idea of genetic determinism, as if single genes for dominance or submissiveness existed and could reshape an adult's personality within days. In reality, behavioural traits are influenced by many genes with small effects as well as by environment, and gene therapy, first used successfully in 1990 to treat an inherited immune deficiency, aims to correct specific diseases.

title: E-I-E-I-(Annoyed Grunt)
alt: EIEI (Gesto de disgusto) The Simpsons, season 11, episode 5
text: Inspired by a Zorro film, Homer goes around Springfield slapping people with a glove and challenging them to duels to get his way, until a Southern colonel accepts. To escape the duel, the Simpsons flee to the farmhouse where Homer grew up. Homer tries farming, but nothing grows in the poor soil, so he asks Lenny for some plutonium. The crops grow, but because Homer had mixed tomato and tobacco seeds, a new plant appears: a tomato with brown, tobacco-flavoured flesh. He calls it "tomacco". It tastes terrible but is highly addictive, and it sells so well that executives from Laramie Cigarettes offer $150 million for the rights. Lisa protests, and Homer rejects the offer anyway, demanding $150 billion. Addicted animals from neighbouring farms then devour the crop. The last plant ends up with the executives, but their helicopter crashes and it is destroyed. Back home, Homer finally fights the duel and is shot in the arm. The episode satirises genetic modification and the tobacco industry. Homer creates a hybrid plant by accident, combining tomato and tobacco seeds and irradiating the field with plutonium, a parody of fears about radiation, mutation and "Frankenfood". The new crop is a commercial success precisely because it is addictive, and a tobacco company immediately tries to buy it. There are no scientists in the story; the experimenter is an ignorant amateur, and Lisa voices the ethical objection to profiting from addiction. Nature's editors listed the episode among the top ten science moments in The Simpsons. The idea has a real basis: tomatoes and tobacco both belong to the nightshade family, and a 1959 Scientific American article reported that nicotine could be found in tomato plants grafted onto tobacco. Inspired by the episode, an Oregon fan, Rob Baur, grew a grafted "tomacco" plant in 2003, and tests found nicotine in its leaves. Unlike Homer's crop, the real tomacco was made by grafting rather than by crossing or irradiation, and its fruit looked like an ordinary tomato.

title: Fantozzi 2000: The Cloning
text: On the eve of the third millennium, the Megaditta faces a crisis because its new employees no longer show proper subservience, so its executives use advanced biotechnology to bring back the most servile employee of all time, the late accountant Ugo Fantozzi. Revived, he is given the task of looking after the youngest son of the despotic director Balabam, who turns out to be the family's black sheep because he is kind and generous; Fantozzi escapes with him and other boys from a brutal boarding school that teaches abuse of power, and the boy is later flogged by his father. Fantozzi then plays the SuperEnalotto lottery with former colleagues; his wife Pina secretly fails to submit the ticket that would have won, and Fantozzi, believing himself rich, rents a castle and lives beyond his means with Signorina Silvani until his creditors arrive. Further misadventures follow with his granddaughter Uga, and at a countess's birthday party on New Year's Eve 2000. Cloning serves only as the comic device that justifies the return of Paolo Villaggio's character, who had died in the previous film of the series: the company brings him back through biotechnology because it needs a perfectly docile employee. The idea satirises corporate power, with managers who would rather recreate an obedient worker than deal with assertive young staff, but the film shows no scientists or laboratory and does not explore cloning or genetics further; after the opening, the episodes concern lotteries, family life and class humiliation. In real life a clone would be born as a baby and would share the original's genome, not his memories or personality, so the revival of an adult Fantozzi is pure fantasy. The genetics content of the film is minimal, limited to its title and premise.

title: One Piece
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement cloning human experimentation
text: Based on Eiichiro Oda's manga, this long-running anime follows Monkey D. Luffy, whose body became like rubber after he ate a Devil Fruit, and his crew, the Straw Hat Pirates, as they sail the Grand Line in search of the legendary treasure known as the One Piece. In the Whole Cake Island arc, the crew's cook, Sanji, is forced to return to his birth family, the Vinsmoke royals of the mercenary Germa Kingdom, ruled by his father, Vinsmoke Judge. Judge, a scientist, had altered his children before birth to make them superhuman soldiers. Sanji's brothers gained great strength and lost much of their capacity for emotion, and his sister Reiju cannot disobey their father, but Sanji was born an ordinary human, so Judge despised him, locked him away as a child and later let him leave on condition that he never revealed his origins. In the later Wano arc Sanji's dormant enhancements awaken while he keeps his emotions, and the Egghead arc takes the crew to the island of the scientist Vegapunk and his cloned soldiers. Genetics matters in two arcs of a vast adventure series. Vinsmoke Judge, a scientist specialised in engineering and genetics, once belonged to the rogue research group MADS alongside the great scientist Vegapunk. Together they discovered the "Lineage Factor", the series' equivalent of a hereditary blueprint, and Judge later used it to modify his unborn sons into super-soldiers and to build an army of cloned soldiers for Germa 66. He forced his wife Sora to undergo the procedure against her wishes; she secretly took a counter-drug, which is why Sanji alone was born a normal human, kind and capable of empathy. His sister Reiju was also modified and kept her emotions, but cannot disobey Judge. The story frames the emotionless brothers as the true cost of Judge's project, and when Sanji's enhancements later awaken he stays compassionate. The Egghead arc adds Vegapunk's cloned living weapons, the Pacifista and Seraphim, MADS's first human clone, Stussy, and the cruel experiments of the World Government elder Saturn. The science is fantasy, but the series presents eugenic enhancement as dehumanising and tied to militarism and dynastic ambition.

title: Splicers
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human enhancement human experimentation
text: A new fad sweeps the teenagers of Gotham: "splicing", offered by Dr. Abel Cuvier's Chimera Institute, which mixes animal DNA into people to give them traits such as cat eyes, claws or horns. Cuvier insists the procedure is safe and reversible, but District Attorney Sam Young is trying to ban it because it increases aggressive behaviour. When Batman (Terry McGinnis) investigates, Cuvier's spliced thugs capture him and Cuvier injects him with vampire bat DNA. While the spliced gang attacks Young and Barbara Gordon, Terry turns into a raging bat-like creature, until Bruce Wayne subdues him with an antidote. With the help of the dog Ace, Batman tracks Cuvier to a taxidermy studio. Cuvier injects himself with several animal strains to become a "true chimera"; Batman injects him with more, turning him into a monstrous creature that apparently dies in an explosion. Genetic engineering of humans is the subject of the episode. Splicing human and animal DNA is presented as a commercial cosmetic service for teenagers, a body-modification fashion compared on screen with tattoos, and the plot turns on its unforeseen side effects, especially increased aggression and loss of control. Dr. Cuvier is a classic mad scientist: a private entrepreneur who markets the procedure as safe and "utterly beautiful", orders the murder of the official trying to regulate him, and finally transforms himself into a monster. Bruce Wayne, by contrast, produces a cure. The genetics is pure comic-book fantasy: injecting animal DNA into an adult cannot rapidly rewrite the body's form, and real human gene therapy delivers specific genes to particular cells for medical purposes. The episode is nonetheless a clear parable about unregulated enhancement and consumer biotechnology aimed at the young.

title: The Shroud
text: Marie Wells and her husband Justin, unable to have a child, turn to the fertility clinic of the Tilford Institute, where Dr. Gail Cowlings implants what Marie believes is an ordinary IVF embryo. Marie does not know, but Justin does, that the nucleus of one of her eggs was replaced with DNA taken from the Shroud of Turin: the Reverend Doctor Thomas Tilford, a televangelist who worships both God and science, intends to bring about the Second Coming. When Marie learns the truth she is angry and doubts she is worthy to be the mother of Christ, until the toys she has bought for the baby begin to float around the room. Dr. Cowlings suspects that the DNA may instead come from an ancient man with telekinetic powers. Tilford confines the couple to the institute to take the child at birth, but they escape, and when he finds them after the birth Cowlings stops him; the family leaves for a new life, helped, in one account, by the baby's powers. Cloning from ancient DNA is the episode's premise. A televangelist's institute transfers genetic material from the Shroud of Turin into one of the eggs of a woman seeking fertility treatment, after removing its nucleus, and implants the embryo without her knowledge; remarks about "the others" imply earlier attempts. The episode's opening narration frames it as a clash between science and religious faith, and it portrays the scientists as servants of a zealot who wants to control the child's upbringing, with the mother's consent violated from the start. The scientist Dr. Cowlings introduces doubt: the shroud's DNA might belong not to Christ but to an ordinary man with unusual abilities, which the story leaves open. The idea draws on real controversies about the shroud, which radiocarbon dating places in the Middle Ages. Even genuine ancient DNA is usually degraded and fragmentary, and nuclear transfer requires an intact nucleus, so a clone could not be made from a cloth relic.

title: A Clone of My Own
text: Professor Farnsworth is lured to Mars University, apparently to lose his professorship, only to find a surprise party for his 150th birthday. Confronted with his own mortality, he announces his successor: not one of his employees but Cubert, a 12-year-old clone of himself. Cubert is unimpressed by science and mocks the professor's inventions, including the Planet Express ship's engines, which Farnsworth says he learned to build in a dream. A depressed Farnsworth confesses that he is really 160, the age at which the robots of the Sunset Squad take people away, and he is duly abducted to the Near-Death Star. The crew infiltrate it with Fry disguised as the professor and Cubert on his back as a hump, carrying a jar of Cubert's blood as a DNA sample, and rescue him. When the ship's engines are damaged, Cubert fixes them, having dreamed how, and decides to follow in Farnsworth's footsteps. Cloning is the premise of this comic episode, which introduces Cubert Farnsworth, the professor's clone and designated heir. The story plays with the popular notion that a clone is a younger copy who should inherit the original's identity and vocation: Cubert shares Farnsworth's DNA, which lets the crew pass Fry off as the professor using a sample of the boy's blood, yet he has his own opinions and initially rejects his "father's" career. By the end he also shares the professor's ability to dream up the ship's engines, a joke on the idea that genes carry knowledge. Farnsworth is the series' archetypal mad scientist, eccentric and self-absorbed, but here he is treated sympathetically as an old man afraid of death. A real clone would share the original's genome but would be a separate person, with no inherited memories or skills.

title: Batman Beyond: Return of the Joker
alt: Batman del futuro: El regreso del Joker
text: Decades in the future, the Joker, presumed dead for forty years, reappears in Gotham City at the head of a new gang, the Jokerz, who steal high-tech equipment. He shows that he knows the secrets of the elderly Bruce Wayne and his successor as Batman, Terry McGinnis. Commissioner Barbara Gordon reveals what really happened: the Joker and Harley Quinn kidnapped and tortured Robin, Tim Drake, turning him into a copy of the Joker, until Tim came to his senses and shot him. Terry suspects Tim, now an engineer with a family, and confronts him, only to see him turn into the Joker. The Joker explains that he had encoded himself into a stolen DNA microarray hidden behind Tim's ear, allowing him to take over Tim's body after death. Using the stolen equipment to control a military satellite, he plans to destroy Gotham. Terry defeats him by destroying the chip with the Joker's own joy buzzer, freeing Tim. Genetics plays a limited but decisive role, as the solution to the film's mystery. The Joker's return is explained by a piece of stolen biotechnology: a DNA microarray, implanted secretly in Tim Drake, that carries the Joker's genetic information and personality and gradually allows him to take over Tim's body. Genetics thus stands in for a kind of resurrection, and the twist turns a former hero into the villain's host. There are no geneticists in the film; the technology is used by a criminal, not by scientists. The story mixes genetics and psychology freely, implying that a person's character and memories could be stored with their DNA and imposed on another body. DNA microarrays are real laboratory tools, also called DNA chips, but they are used to measure the activity of many genes at once or to genotype regions of a genome, not to store or transfer a personality.

title: Brand X
text: Assistant Director Walter Skinner is protecting Dr. James Scobie, a former researcher for the Morley tobacco company who is about to testify against his former employer. Scobie develops a cough and is found dead with his face eaten away. Mulder and Scully learn that Morley has developed a "super-tobacco" containing a genetically engineered tobacco beetle whose eggs survive cigarette manufacture and are released in the smoke. Scobie and his colleague Dr. Peter Voss tested the cigarettes on four people, and only Darryl Weaver, a chain smoker, has survived. More victims die covered in beetles, and Mulder is exposed to Weaver's smoke and begins coughing up blood as the eggs hatch in his lungs. Voss tells Skinner about the tests, and Skinner tracks down Weaver and stops him. Scully realises that nicotine stopped the beetles from developing in Weaver and saves Mulder with it, leaving him with a craving for cigarettes. Genetic engineering is the premise of the episode, though it receives little explanation. A tobacco company has created a "super-tobacco" carrying a genetically engineered beetle whose eggs survive manufacturing and hatch inside smokers' lungs, and the company's scientists tested the product on human subjects before covering up the deaths. The writers, fans of the 1999 film The Insider, drew on the tobacco industry's corporate cover-ups, so the scientists are portrayed as employees of a company that places profit above safety, with one of them eventually coming clean. The genetic engineering is a horror device rather than a plausible technology, and the cure, nicotine, is an ironic twist rather than a scientific one.

title: CSI: Crime Scene Investigation
text: CSI: Crime Scene Investigation is a police procedural that ran on CBS for 15 seasons, from 2000 to 2015. It follows the crime scene investigators of the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, who solve murders and other crimes mainly through physical evidence rather than confessions or witnesses. The team is first led by Gil Grissom, a forensic entomologist, with blood-spatter analyst Catherine Willows as his second in command and investigators Warrick Brown, Nick Stokes and Sara Sidle; the laboratory technician Greg Sanders, the team's DNA specialist, later becomes a field investigator. Medical examiner Al Robbins and police captain Jim Brass complete the core cast, and in later seasons D.B. Russell and Julie Finlay take over the lab. Each episode typically follows one or two cases from the crime scene to the laboratory, mixing scientific deduction with the characters' personal lives. The series ended with a feature-length finale, "Immortality", and spawned several spin-offs and a revival, CSI: Vegas. Genetics appears as forensic science: DNA profiling of blood, saliva, hair and other traces is one of the team's routine tools for identifying victims and linking suspects to crime scenes, alongside fingerprints, toxicology, entomology and trace evidence. The scientists are the heroes of the series, portrayed as meticulous, sceptical and devoted to letting the evidence speak, and the lab staff, such as the DNA analyst Greg Sanders, are given full characters rather than serving as background. The series compresses forensic work considerably: results that take days or weeks in real laboratories often arrive within an episode. It has been credited with the so-called "CSI effect", the claim that crime dramas raise jurors' and victims' expectations about forensic evidence, particularly DNA testing. Early studies suggested the effect might be a myth, but later research found that television crime dramas do influence public and juror expectations, and prosecutors have reported pressure to present more forensic evidence in court.

title: Dark Angel
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement genetic discrimination human experimentation eugenics hybrids chimeras
text: In 2009, a group of genetically enhanced children, trained as soldiers and assassins, escape from Manticore, a secret U.S. government facility. Months later, terrorists detonate an electromagnetic pulse that throws the country into chaos. Ten years on, in a run-down Seattle, one of the escapees, X5-452, now calling herself Max Guevara, works as a bicycle messenger and burglar while searching for her "siblings" and evading Manticore's hunters, led by Colonel Lydecker. She helps the cyber-journalist Logan Cale, alias Eyes Only, fight corruption, and the two fall in love. In the second season Manticore is exposed and burned, and hundreds of transgenics, some with animal features, are released into a hostile world. Max learns that Manticore's founder, Sandeman, was a renegade from an ancient breeding cult that plans the extinction of ordinary humans and that he hid special sequences in her DNA. The series, created by James Cameron and Charles H. Eglee, ended after two seasons with the transgenics besieged in Terminal City. Genetic engineering drives the whole series. Max and her fellow X5s are transgenic supersoldiers designed and raised by a covert military programme, and later seasons add creatures with conspicuous animal DNA, such as the dog-like Joshua, and clones such as Alec, a copy of Max's brother Ben. Manticore embodies the state using genetics to make weapons. The second season moves the focus to discrimination: once the transgenics are freed, they are feared and hunted, and Max leads them to claim a place in society. It also adds a mythology about heredity, with a millennia-old cult that has bred its own advanced humans and Sandeman, the cult renegade who created Manticore and hid in Max's genome a message and, in the plans for an unmade third season, a genetic immunity meant to save ordinary humanity. Critics have compared Max to a postmodern Frankenstein's monster who blurs the boundary between human and monster; the science is not meant literally, but the show uses it to explore identity, family and who counts as human.

title: Mission: Impossible II
text: In Sydney, Dr. Vladimir Nekhorvich, a scientist at Biocyte Pharmaceuticals, warns IMF agent Ethan Hunt that his employer forced him to develop a biological weapon, the Chimera virus, so that it could profit from its cure, Bellerophon. Rogue IMF agent Sean Ambrose, disguised as Hunt, steals the Bellerophon samples and kills Nekhorvich. Hunt recruits the thief Nyah Nordoff-Hall, Ambrose's ex-girlfriend, to infiltrate his circle. Ambrose blackmails Biocyte's chief executive, planning to release Chimera, which kills within 20 hours unless Bellerophon is given in time, and then sell the cure in exchange for control of the company. Hunt breaks into Biocyte's laboratory to destroy the virus, but Nyah injects herself with the last sample to keep it from Ambrose, who releases her in Sydney to start an epidemic. Hunt recovers the Bellerophon, kills Ambrose in a fight on the beach, and his team gives Nyah the cure in time. Genetics plays a minor role. The plot device is an engineered pathogen: Chimera is a virus designed in a pharmaceutical laboratory by a scientist the film calls a bio-genetics researcher, together with its cure, so that the company can create a market for the treatment. The names come from Greek myth, in which the Chimera was a monster combining parts of different animals and Bellerophon the hero who killed it. Nekhorvich is a sympathetic scientist coerced by his employer, and the film's villains are a rogue agent and a corporation seeking profit from a pandemic, not the researchers themselves. The film gives no detail on how the virus was built, and its 20-hour window between infection and the point at which the cure no longer works is a dramatic convenience. Its premise of a company that profits from both the disease and the remedy reflects a recurring suspicion of the pharmaceutical industry in thrillers of the period.

title: Seeds of Destruction
alt: Las semillas de la destrucción The Outer Limits, season 6, episode 7
text: The biotechnology company Macroseed chooses the farming town of Hobson to test TX-40, a fast-growing genetically engineered corn that promises bigger harvests. The local veterinarian, Dr. Linda Andrews, grows suspicious when a farmer brings in a dead cat from his field with a tumour that sprouts a fifth leg. Aggressive tumours then appear in people, including teenagers and her own nephew. Her husband Rex and her lover Harold Zimmer, both Macroseed employees, insist the corn is safe and that her inquiries could ruin the town's new prosperity. Reading the company's test data, the town doctor explains that crops are modified either with a particle gun or with the tumour-inducing bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, and he and Linda notice that the safety tests used DNA only from middle-aged white men, while the victims all have high levels of growth hormone. TX-40 has crossed from the corn to milkweed and from there to people. Harold admits he knew, shoots the doctor and tries to kill Linda, but Rex stops him. Workers burn the crops, but a crow carries off a piece of contaminated plant. Genetically modified crops are the subject. The episode imagines an engineered corn whose trait escapes into a wild plant and then into animals and humans, causing tumours in those with high growth-hormone levels, and it ends on a warning that the contamination cannot be contained. It names real techniques of plant transformation, the particle gun and the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, and criticises safety testing done only on DNA from middle-aged white men, which misses the people at risk. The scientist-executives of Macroseed are driven by profit, conceal what they know and are ready to kill to protect the product, while the investigator is a local veterinarian. The episode aired amid public controversy over genetically modified crops, including the StarLink corn recall of 2000. Gene flow from crops to related plants is a real subject of study, but a transgene jumping from corn to an unrelated weed and then into people, where it causes tumours, has no basis in science. The episode is best read as an expression of the era's anxieties about agricultural biotechnology.

title: The 6th Day
text: In the near future, animal cloning is commonplace, but human cloning is banned by "Sixth Day" laws. Charter pilot Adam Gibson is hired by Michael Drucker, billionaire owner of the cloning company Replacement Technologies, and undergoes what seem to be routine tests. That day, his partner Hank takes his place on the flight, and Drucker and Hank are killed by an anti-cloning assassin. Believing Adam was killed too, Drucker's people clone him, and Adam comes home to find a copy of himself living with his family. Hunted by Drucker's security team, he learns from the company's chief scientist, Dr. Griffin Weir, that his DNA and memories were recorded during the tests, that Drucker himself is a clone, and that Weir has repeatedly cloned his own wife, who is dying of cystic fibrosis. Adam and his clone join forces, destroy the facility and save the family; the clone starts a new life in Argentina. Human cloning drives the whole plot. The film imagines a mature cloning industry built on pet cloning ("RePet") and a secret capacity to clone adult humans in hours, complete with their memories. Its scientist, Dr. Weir, is a sympathetic but compromised figure: he serves Drucker's illegal programme because he hopes to save his wife, whom he keeps recreating as she dies of cystic fibrosis. Drucker, the businessman, is the true villain: he uses cloning to cheat death and keep control of his fortune, and has his clones engineered with deliberately shortened lifespans as insurance against betrayal. The film raises questions about identity, legal personhood and ownership of clones, which have no legal rights in its world. The science is fictional: real cloning produces an embryo that must develop and grow like any other, so an adult copy with the original's memories is impossible. Pet cloning, however, has been offered as a service since the 2010s, so the film's opening premise is less far-fetched than it seemed in 2000.

title: The Crimson Rivers
alt: Les Rivières pourpres Los ríos de color púrpura
themes: eugenics heredity genetic disease human experimentation
text: In Guernon, an isolated university town in the French Alps, Superintendent Pierre Niémans investigates the brutal murder of a professor and librarian whose eyes have been removed. Elsewhere, Inspector Max Kerkerian looks into the desecration of the grave of Judith Hérault, a girl who died in 1982. The two cases converge. Niémans learns that the town's academic elite has spent generations trying to breed a race of superior intellect, and that inbreeding has left the faculty with serious hereditary disorders. To keep the programme going, doctors at the university hospital have been secretly swapping healthy babies from the village for the faculty's own. Judith was the identical twin of Fanny Ferreira, who was swapped as a baby; their mother faked Judith's death after the family was pursued. The detectives trace the murders to the twins and confront them on a mountain, where a gunfight triggers an avalanche. The mystery rests on a eugenic breeding programme. The founders of Guernon's university, intellectuals rather than geneticists, set out to create a "super-race" defined by intellect by marrying within their own closed community. The film shows the classic consequence: generations of inbreeding produce serious genetic disorders, as an ophthalmologist explains to Niémans. Rather than abandon the project, the faculty and the hospital doctors replace their affected children with healthy babies taken from local families, keeping one of a pair of twins with her birth family as a control. The programme thus survives on stolen children and ends in murder. Its organisers act out of elitism and the belief that they are improving the species, and the film presents them as secretive and ruthless. The genetic premise is sound: related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive variants, so their children more often inherit two copies and develop recessive disease.

title: The Other Me
text: Will Browning, a struggling high-school student, is threatened with being sent to a strict summer camp unless his grades improve. He orders a science kit for a school project, but the kit has been contaminated with a cloning formula belonging to two greedy scientists, and Will accidentally creates a copy of himself, whom he names Twoie. Twoie is more confident than Will and takes his place at school, where he becomes popular, makes peace with Will's rival, asks out the girl Will likes and draws Will's reclusive grandfather out of his shell. Will grows jealous, and Twoie decides to leave town after a school dance. Will then learns from the scientists that Twoie will weaken and die without a stabilising formula. He steals it, the scientists capture Will by mistake, and Twoie rescues him. The scientists are arrested, Will tells his family the truth, and they welcome Twoie into the household. This Disney Channel comedy, based on Mary C. Ryan's novel Me Two, uses cloning as a vehicle for a story about self-confidence. Will's clone appears as a teenager identical to him, and the differences in personality between the two boys make the point that identical genes do not mean identical people. The scientists who developed the cloning formula are cartoonish, greedy villains, and the dependence of the clone on a stabilising formula adds a note of fragility to artificial life. The ending, in which the family adopts the clone as a second son, treats him as a full person. Real cloning bears no resemblance to the film's: it cannot be done with a home science kit and does not produce a grown copy, but a new embryo that develops and ages normally. Genetics here is a playful premise rather than a subject the film examines.

title: What Lies Beneath
text: Claire Spencer, a former cellist, lives in a lakeside house in Vermont with her husband Norman, a research scientist at the local university. After her daughter leaves for college, Claire begins to experience strange events: doors open by themselves, the bathtub fills with water and she sees a woman's face reflected in it. She first suspects that her neighbour has murdered his wife, but the wife turns up alive. Claire then finds that the ghost is Madison Elizabeth Frank, a young woman who disappeared a year earlier, and she recovers the repressed memory that Norman had an affair with Madison, one of his students. Norman first claims that Madison killed herself, then confesses that he murdered her when she threatened to expose the affair, and tries to kill Claire by paralysing her with a drug and drowning her in the bath. Claire escapes, and in the lake Madison's body seems to drag Norman to his death. Genetics is only the professional background of the villain in this ghost story. Norman Spencer is described by reviewers as a brilliant geneticist who has taken a prestigious chair at the university where his late father taught, and he does laboratory research; one critic calls him a "brilliant (i.e. unstable) geneticist". His science plays no part in the plot apart from his access to laboratory chemicals: he paralyses Claire with an anaesthetic. The film draws on an old association between scientific brilliance and moral coldness. Norman is ambitious and outwardly charming, has an affair with a student and kills her to protect his career, and then tries to kill his wife. Nothing in the story concerns heredity, DNA or genetic research, so the title belongs in the database mainly as an example of how a scientist, and specifically a geneticist, is portrayed on screen.

title: X-Men
text: In a world where some people are born as mutants with superhuman powers, US Senator Robert Kelly campaigns for a Mutant Registration Act. The telepath Charles Xavier, who runs a school for young mutants, fears the response of his old friend Erik Lehnsherr, known as Magneto, a Holocaust survivor who can control magnetic fields. Rogue, a teenager whose touch absorbs other people's life force and powers, runs away from home and meets Logan, or Wolverine, a mutant with metal claws and accelerated healing. After the members of Magneto's Brotherhood attack them, both are taken to Xavier's school, home of the X-Men. Magneto has built a machine that generates radiation able to induce mutations in normal humans; tested on Senator Kelly, it eventually kills him. Magneto plans to use it on the world leaders gathered at a summit on Ellis Island, powering it through Rogue at the cost of her life, but the X-Men defeat the Brotherhood on the Statue of Liberty and destroy the machine, and Logan saves Rogue by transferring his healing power to her. Genetics is present as the premise rather than as science. Mutants are people born with mutations that give them extraordinary powers, usually emerging in adolescence; the plot is about how society treats them, from the registration law proposed by Senator Kelly to Magneto's plan to force mutation on world leaders with radiation. No geneticist appears: the leading characters are mutants themselves, and Magneto's machine is the only experiment in the story, one that kills its first human subject. The film works as an allegory of discrimination against minorities. It opens in Auschwitz, linking the registration of mutants with Nazi persecution, and director Bryan Singer described the mutants as outsiders whose difference appears at puberty, an allegory that actor Ian McKellen read as being about gay people. Real mutations do not produce abilities of this kind, and radiation causes random DNA damage rather than useful new traits.

title: Geneshaft
text: In the late 23rd century, genetic engineering defines human society. A totalitarian world government has kept peace for 200 years by controlling all births and designing each person's genes for their role in society; lifespan is limited to 45 years, family structures have been abolished and love and lust removed. Women outnumber men nine to one, since men are thought to carry irreducibly destructive tendencies, and each man is watched by an emotionless female "Register". Five years after a giant ring-shaped object appears near Earth and devastates a space station and much of the planet's surface, a crew of genetically engineered men and women aboard the spaceship Bilkis sets out to investigate the ring and the alien technology found on Ganymede. Fighting the ring's machines with the giant robot Shaft, the crew meet people and situations that lead them to doubt whether they are as superior as they believe, and how perfect their society really is. This anime series is built around a society organised entirely by genetic engineering, and it explores the consequences of that technology dominating human life. The state controls reproduction and designs every individual for a function, people are ranked by the quality of their DNA, and those of supposedly inferior gene types, such as the main character Mika, are openly mocked. Emotions and family ties are engineered away, and the sex ratio is set by policy on the belief that male genes carry aggression. Some characters are defined by their pride in their "perfect" DNA, while a rebel faction wants to restore humanity's natural order. The series is therefore a dystopia about eugenics and genetic determinism, in which the crew's journey leads them to question the system. The idea that complex traits such as leadership, personality or emotional life could be precisely designed into people goes far beyond real genetics, in which such traits depend on many genes and on environment.

title: Jurassic Park III
text: Palaeontologist Alan Grant is struggling to fund his research on the intelligence of Velociraptors when Paul and Amanda Kirby, apparently a wealthy couple, offer him money in exchange for guiding an aerial tour of Isla Sorna, the island where the company InGen bred its dinosaurs. Once there, the Kirbys force the plane to land; they are in fact a divorced couple searching for their son Eric, who went missing near the island while parasailing. After a Spinosaurus destroys their plane, the group crosses the island, chased by the Spinosaurus, by Pteranodons in a giant aviary and by a pack of Velociraptors. The raptors are pursuing them because Grant's assistant Billy has stolen two of their eggs, hoping to sell them to fund the excavation. They find Eric alive, return the eggs to the raptors, and are finally rescued by the US Navy and Marines, summoned by Grant's former colleague Ellie Sattler. Genetics is the background rather than the subject of this sequel. The dinosaurs on Isla Sorna were created by InGen using the franchise's premise of cloning dinosaurs from DNA preserved in blood-filled mosquitoes trapped in amber, filling the gaps with frog DNA. No geneticist appears on screen; the film's scientist is a palaeontologist who distrusts the whole project. In an early scene Grant tells his students that real scientists make real discoveries in the rocks, and that what John Hammond and InGen created were "genetically engineered theme park monsters, nothing more and nothing less". Consistent with research at the time, the film's Velociraptors were given feather-like quills. Cloning dinosaurs is not possible: claims of recovering dinosaur DNA were later attributed to contamination, and the oldest DNA ever recovered is about two million years old, far younger than the dinosaurs.

title: Lineage
alt: Linaje Star Trek: Voyager, season 7, episode 12
themes: genetic engineering gene therapy genetic discrimination hybrids chimeras genetic disease
text: B'Elanna Torres, Voyager's half-Klingon chief engineer, discovers that she is pregnant by her husband, Tom Paris. The Doctor finds that the seven-week-old fetus has a genetic defect that causes an abnormal curvature of the spine in Klingon females, the same condition B'Elanna had surgically corrected as a child, and proposes to fix it by genetic resequencing. When a holographic projection shows that her daughter will have Klingon forehead ridges, B'Elanna, haunted by memories of being teased as a child and of her human father leaving the family, asks the Doctor to remove the baby's Klingon traits as well. Tom and the Doctor object, and Captain Janeway treats it as a matter for the couple. The Doctor suddenly changes his mind and declares the procedure medically necessary; Icheb finds an error in his assessment, Seven discovers that his program has been tampered with, and Tom stops the operation in time. B'Elanna admits her fear that Tom will leave her, the alterations are undone, and she asks the Doctor to be the child's godfather. The episode is built around the difference between treating a disease and changing who a child will be. Correcting the inherited spinal defect is presented as uncontroversial medicine, but B'Elanna's wish to erase her daughter's Klingon features, so that she will not be rejected as she was, turns gene editing into a way of avoiding discrimination by changing the child rather than the society. Tom and the Doctor stand for acceptance of the child as she is, and the Doctor's integrity is tested when his program is secretly altered. B'Elanna's motives are shown with sympathy, rooted in childhood pain and fear of abandonment, and she finally accepts her daughter's heritage. The distinction between therapy and enhancement or cosmetic selection is central to real bioethical debates on germline editing, and the episode also touches on hybrid ancestry, since the child is a quarter Klingon.

title: Lion's Den
text: Peter Shotwell once dreamed of the Olympics but blew out his knee, while his best friend Jon went on to become an international athletics star. Peter is now the coach of the Lewisborough Lions, his old high school's wrestling team, which sits at the bottom of the league, and his son Morris, a member of the team, resents his failures. Jon offers him Nuriflex 500, a new performance-enhancing drug he says contains scientifically balanced nutrients. Under pressure from the principal and his own son, Peter agrees to a trial. The team soon rises to the top, but the drug has horrific side effects: the wrestlers become aggressive and their eyes and teeth turn animal-like, and they kill a rival coach who threatens to expose them. When Peter tries to take them off the drug, the team, including his son, kills him. Genetics plays a secondary role in this episode about doping in school sports. The drug Nuriflex 500 is said to be spliced with animal DNA, big cat DNA according to the episode summary on Wikipedia, and the Outer Limits fan wiki describes it as based on animal hormones; the young wrestlers gradually take on animal features and predatory behaviour. The story uses this as a Jekyll-and-Hyde metaphor for steroids and the pressure to win, and its moral concerns parents and coaches rather than scientists, who never appear: the drug comes through Jon, a former champion turned promoter. The idea that taking DNA in a pill transfers animal traits has no basis in biology, since ingested DNA is digested like any other food. The episode's real-life counterpart is the fear of gene doping in sport, the misuse of gene therapy to enhance performance, which the World Anti-Doping Agency added to its list of banned practices in 2003.

title: Mimic 2
text: Four years after the events of Mimic, three men are found mutilated in New York, their faces removed. Detective Klaski discovers that all of them knew Remi Panos, an entomologist teaching at an inner-city high school. Klaski first suspects Remi, until he sees the creature that has been stalking her: an intelligent mutant insect that can take the face of its last victim and wants to mate with her. Remi, Klaski and two students are trapped inside the school as the creature hunts them, while a special forces unit led by a man called Darksuit prepares to gas the building. Remi escapes, but the creature has killed Klaski and taken his form, and it follows her home. Remi decapitates it in her apartment, yet the creature is not dead, leaving her and a student wondering what to do next. Genetics appears here only as backstory. The creature belongs to the "Judas breed", the insect created by genetic engineering in the first film to wipe out disease-carrying cockroaches, which survived and evolved into a predator able to mimic human appearance. Mimic 2 itself focuses on a horror chase in a school and does not show the creation of the creatures, a geneticist or any laboratory work; its scientist character, Remi, is an entomologist and the creature's target, not its maker. The premise implicitly warns about the unintended consequences of releasing engineered organisms, but the film does not develop the idea. Its connection to genetics is weak, and it may not merit inclusion in the database.

title: Mutant X
themes: genetic engineering mutants human experimentation hybrids chimeras genetic discrimination
text: Mutant X follows a team of "new mutants", people with extraordinary powers who were used as test subjects in covert genetic experiments run by Genomex. Their leader, Adam Kane, was the chief bio-geneticist behind those experiments and formed Mutant X to atone for his mistakes; he uses a stolen database to find other new mutants, protect them and help them control their powers. The original team includes Jesse Kilmartin, who can change his body's density; Shalimar Fox, a "feline feral" with combined human and animal DNA; the empath Emma DeLauro; and Brennan Mulwray, who generates electricity. Their main enemy is Mason Eckhart, Genomex's former security chief, who heads the Genetic Security Agency and hunts new mutants to control them. Another adversary is Gabriel Ashlocke, the psychopathic "patient zero" of the experiments. The series ran for three seasons, from 2001 to 2004, and was cancelled abruptly, ending on a cliffhanger. Genetic engineering is the premise of the series: every new mutant owes his or her powers to the experiments of Genomex, described as covert and government-backed, and categories such as "feral", "molecular" or "elemental" mutants reflect the different kinds of genetic manipulation they received. Some carry recombined human and animal DNA, and the new mutants live with medical problems derived from the procedures; Jesse is said to be the only one to have outlived his "expiration date". The show offers two contrasting portraits of geneticists.
