Adam Kane is a repentant creator who turns his knowledge to caring for his creations, looking for treatments for their conditions; Eckhart and the Genetic Security Agency represent the institution that wants to keep them under control, and other scientists, such as a biogeneticist recruited to make a mind-controlling toxin, serve those aims. The series is action-adventure in the mould of X-Men, and its genetics is fantasy, but its theme of people harmed by secret medical experiments and then treated as a threat gives the show its moral frame.

title: No Ordinary Baby
text: Also known as After Amy, this television film follows Linda Sinclair, an ambitious reporter who gets the scoop on the birth of the first human clone. As the story breaks, a media and public furore develops around the pregnancy and the unborn child, and Dr. Amanda Gordon, the physician responsible for the cloning, sees her reputation and career put at risk. The film follows the consequences of the coverage for everyone involved, including the baby, and the reporter's growing ethical doubts about her role. It is based on "Carbon Copy: Meet the First Human Clone", a 1998 short story by Richard Kadrey published in Wired magazine. Human reproductive cloning is the subject of the film, approached through its social reception rather than its science. The story imagines the announcement of the first cloned human baby and focuses on the media frenzy, public outrage and professional backlash that follow, and on the damage they do to the doctor who performed the procedure and to the child. The scientist is a physician presented as the target of controversy rather than as a villain. Made in 2001, a few years after the cloning of Dolly the sheep, when claims of imminent human cloning were in the news, it reflects the debate of its time. Monkeys were first cloned by the Dolly method in 2018, but human reproductive cloning is prohibited in many countries, including Australia and Canada. Detailed plot information on this film is scarce, so this description relies on short synopses.

title: Replica
text: Zach and Nora Griffiths, scientists played by Peter Outerbridge and Sherilyn Fenn, run a biotech firm with a business partner that is close to producing cloned human organs. Nora has developed a "neuro-mapper" that can copy a mind into a cloned brain, and when their partner orders the program shut down she tests the untried device on herself and suffers a seizure. A year later she lies in a coma, which Zach blames on a drowning accident. Pressed to withdraw life support, he illegally clones her as an adult, with the reluctant help of a colleague, using the company's organ replicator, archived body scans and her stored memories. The clone, who believes she is Nora, grows jealous of the comatose original, and then Nora unexpectedly wakes up. Both women share the same memories and both claim Zach; the couple plan to erase the clone's memory, and the two Noras fight in the lab. Zach's solution is to clone himself: in the final scene the two couples share a skiing holiday and toast "to science". The episode is built around human reproductive cloning, used here to replace a loved one rather than to create a new person. The scientist is a grieving husband who misuses his company's technology and breaks the law for personal reasons, after his wife's own reckless self-experiment caused her coma, and the story turns on the consequences of treating a clone as a substitute: once the original wife wakes up, the copy has her own claim to the life she was given. In this way the episode raises the question, common in Outer Limits stories, of whether a duplicate is a person with her own rights, although its almost comic ending, in which the husband clones himself so that each Nora has a partner, sidesteps the dilemma. Its science is speculative: real cloning would produce a genetically identical embryo that would have to develop and grow up, not an adult double, and the episode instead assembles the body from old scans and supplies the mind by uploading recorded memories, which is not genetics at all.

title: Replicant
text: Edward "the Torch" Garrotte is a serial killer who murders mothers and sets them on fire. Seattle detective Jake Riley has hunted him for three years without success. Shortly after Jake retires, a secret government agency recruits him for a special project: it has cloned Garrotte from DNA found at a crime scene. The clone, the Replicant, has the body of a forty-year-old but the mind of a child, together with fragments of Garrotte's memories and a telepathic link to him. Jake must train him to track the killer down. Jake treats him roughly, but the Replicant sees Jake as family and gradually learns about the world. He refuses Garrotte's invitation to join him and discovers that he is not a killer. In the final fight in a hospital furnace room, Jake shoots Garrotte. The Replicant seems to die in an explosion, but weeks later Jake finds he is alive and leading a normal life. Cloning and the question of nature versus nurture are central to this action film. A government agency creates an adult clone of a serial killer from crime-scene DNA, hoping that his genetic identity will give him access to the murderer's memories and help catch him. The film plays on the fear that a clone of a killer will inherit his violence, but argues the opposite: brought up, however harshly, by a policeman who becomes his only family, the clone develops a gentle personality and rejects his original. A flashback shows that Garrotte's violence comes from childhood abuse, reinforcing the idea that environment shaped him. The scientists are faceless government operatives who use the clone as a tool. Real clones are born as babies and grow up normally; they cannot be produced as adults, and memories are not stored in DNA or shared telepathically between genetically identical people.

title: Tail Sting
text: A low-budget creature feature. After a scheduled flight is cancelled, a group of passengers boards a charter from Melbourne, Australia, to Los Angeles. In the hold is a cargo of genetically engineered scorpion hybrids that a team of scientists is taking to the United States to find funding for their research. A double-dealing scientist on the team, working for a rival company, sneaks into the hold to steal the samples, and turbulence smashes the jars. The scorpions, grown to giant size, attack passengers and crew, kill most of the flight crew and chew through vital wiring. The surviving passengers, led by the pilot and one of the scientists, must fight off the creatures and bring the crippled plane down safely, while the traitor tries to protect the scorpions so that he can sell them. Genetic engineering is little more than the pretext for the monsters. The scorpions are hybrids created by a research team, and one scientist explains that they were crossed with DNA from prehistoric giant scorpions, a choice reviewers note the film never justifies. Scientists appear in several roles: an older scientist who mostly delivers exposition, a female researcher who is one of the heroes, and a treacherous colleague who sells out to a rival corporation and endangers everyone to save the creatures. The film thus repeats the familiar pattern of the genetic monster unleashed by commercial greed rather than by research itself. Scientifically it is implausible: DNA from extinct arthropods has not been recovered, and giant body size in insects and scorpions is constrained by how they breathe and by their exoskeletons, not just by their genes.

title: The Clone
text: In the early 1980s, Jade, a young Muslim woman raised in Rio de Janeiro, moves to Fez, Morocco, to live with her strict uncle Ali after her mother's death. There she falls in love with Lucas Ferraz, a wealthy Brazilian visiting with his identical twin Diogo, their father Leônidas and the twins' godfather, the geneticist Augusto Albieri. Their romance defies her family and religion. When Diogo dies in a helicopter crash, Lucas abandons his plan to run away with Jade, who marries Said. The grieving Albieri secretly uses Lucas's cells to create the first human clone and implants the embryo in Deusa, a patient who believes she is receiving ordinary artificial insemination. Twenty years later, Lucas and Jade, both unhappily married, meet again, while the clone, Léo, has grown into the image of the young Lucas and falls for Jade. When the cloning is discovered, Leônidas and Deusa fight in court over Léo, who struggles to find his place in the world. Human cloning is one of the telenovela's main storylines, alongside a cross-cultural romance between Brazil and the Muslim world. The geneticist Augusto Albieri is a sympathetic but tragic figure: grief at the death of his godson, combined with the ambition to be the first to clone a human, leads him to create a clone in secret and to implant the embryo in a woman without her knowledge, a serious violation of consent. The story then explores the consequences for the clone himself, who shares Lucas's genome but not his life, and for the families who claim him, including a legal fight over parenthood. Writer Glória Perez said she was inspired by Dolly the sheep and wanted to contrast a Muslim world submissive to God with a West that installed geneticists as new creators of life. Human reproductive cloning remains unachieved and widely opposed, but the telenovela's central point holds: a clone would be a much younger genetic twin with a life of his own, as Léo is.

title: 28 Days Later
text: Animal rights activists break into a laboratory in Cambridge where chimpanzees are kept in an abnormally aggressive state. Despite a scientist's warning that the animals are infected with "rage", they free one, which attacks them; within seconds the infected become violent, and the virus spreads across Britain. Twenty-eight days later, Jim, a bicycle courier, wakes from a coma in a deserted London hospital. Rescued from the infected by the survivors Selena and Mark, he finds that his parents have killed themselves, and after Mark is infected, he and Selena join the taxi driver Frank and his daughter Hannah. A radio broadcast leads them to a military blockade near Manchester, where Frank is infected and shot. The soldiers who take in the others turn out to be planning to keep the women as sex slaves. Jim escapes, releases an infected soldier to attack the troops, and rescues Selena and Hannah; weeks later, the three wave a giant "HELLO" banner at a passing jet from a remote cottage, where the infected are dying of starvation. Genetics plays a minor role. The film's starting point is a pathogen kept in a research laboratory, where scientists hold chimpanzees infected with an aggression-inducing "rage" virus; its accidental release by activists who do not believe the scientists' warning causes the catastrophe. The film does not explain how the virus was created or what the research was for, and the scientists appear only briefly; the rest of the story deals with survival and with the violence of the survivors themselves, especially the soldiers. Rather than supernatural zombies, the infected were conceived as victims of a biological contagion: Danny Boyle drew on real diseases, especially Ebola and aspects of rabies, and on the British outbreaks of BSE and foot-and-mouth disease of the time. An abandoned ending showed the laboratory that created the virus. The rage virus is fictional, and its near-instant effect is a dramatic device.

title: Black Mask 2: City of Masks
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human enhancement human experimentation
text: Kan Fung, a former super-soldier who escaped from the organisation that gave him his abilities, fights crime in a futuristic city as Black Mask while looking for a geneticist who can cure him. A wrestling promoter's stars, Iguana, Chameleon, Snake, Wolf and others, turn out to have been injected with animal DNA by Dr. Moloch, which lets them transform into human-animal hybrids. After Iguana dies in a fight with Black Mask, the others seek revenge. Black Mask contacts the geneticist Dr. Marco Leung, but is himself injected with animal DNA and becomes a tiger hybrid until Leung finds a chemical that reverses the change. In the climax, his old enemy Lang, who has overpowered Moloch, plants a bomb capable of altering the DNA of everyone in the city. The hybrid wrestlers are killed one by one, the invisible Chameleon sacrificing herself to hand Black Mask the bomb, and he defeats Lang and defuses it. Leung finally rides off with Kan, implying she has cured him. Genetics is the source of the film's monsters and its central threat. The villain scientist, Dr. Moloch, injects wrestlers with animal DNA to improve their performance, and they gain the power to turn into human-animal hybrids, at the cost of losing control of their bodies. The climax revolves around a "DNA bomb" designed to mutate the population of a whole city. Scientists appear on both sides: Moloch works for profit and for a criminal organisation, while the geneticist Dr. Leung is the one who can undo the damage and cure the hero, so genetics is shown both as a weapon and as a cure. The genetics is pure comic-book fantasy. Real gene therapy modifies genes in some of a patient's cells to treat a disease, and its effects are limited to the cells it reaches; adding animal DNA to an adult cannot make a body take on another species' shape or abilities, let alone switch between forms at will.

title: Blade II
themes: eugenics genetic engineering engineered pathogens mutants human experimentation
text: In Prague, the half-vampire hunter Blade rescues his mentor Whistler, who had been turned into a vampire, and cures him. A pandemic is turning vampires into "Reapers", ravenous mutant creatures whose infectious bite transforms both vampires and humans, spread by the first carrier, Jared Nomak. The vampire overlord Eli Damaskinos proposes a truce, and Blade joins the Bloodpack, an elite vampire squad trained to kill him. They discover that Reapers are immune to most vampire weaknesses except ultraviolet light and destroy their nest, but most of the team die. Damaskinos then captures Blade and reveals that the Reapers are the result of his own attempts to engineer a stronger breed of vampire without its natural weaknesses; Nomak, the first Reaper, is his son, whom he regards as a failure. He plans to use Blade's blood to create vampires immune to sunlight. Blade escapes, Nomak kills his father, and Blade defeats Nomak. Genetics plays a background role. The Reapers are presented as the product of a vampire lord's experiments to breed a superior race free of vampires' weaknesses, a eugenic project that fails and produces an uncontrollable plague. Damaskinos is a ruthless creator who experiments on his own son and dismisses him as a failure, and his daughter Nyssa, who dissects a Reaper to study its anatomy, turns against him when she sees how he treats his children. Blade himself is a human–vampire hybrid whose blood Damaskinos wants in order to create vampires that can walk in daylight. The Reaper condition spreads like an infectious disease, so the film mixes ideas of engineering, mutation and contagion without explaining any of them in genetic terms. It is mainly an action-horror film, and its relevance to genetics is limited to this "engineered master race" motif.

title: Clone High
text: This animated sitcom is set in a high school in the fictional town of Exclamation, USA, populated by teenage clones of famous historical figures created in the 1980s. Officially the school is a military experiment run by the Secret Board of Shadowy Figures, which plans to harness the clones' talents for the US military, while the principal, mad scientist Cinnamon J. Scudworth, secretly wants to use them for a clone-themed amusement park. The show follows the clones of Abe Lincoln, Joan of Arc, Cleopatra, JFK and Gandhi through teenage crushes, exams and parties, centred on Abe's choice between the vain Cleopatra and Joan, who loves him. The first season (2002–2003) ended with the clones abducted on prom night. In the 2023 revival on HBO Max, they are unfrozen twenty years later and return to Clone High, where they meet a new generation of clones, including Harriet Tubman and Frida Kahlo. Human cloning is the comic premise of the series rather than its subject. Each clone has the genome of a historical figure, and much of the humour comes from the gap between the "clonefathers" and their teenage copies: Gandhi is a party animal, JFK a narcissistic womaniser, Abe Lincoln an insecure romantic. The characters' struggle to live up to, or rebel against, their genetic originals is a running joke about the limits of genetic determinism; personality, the show suggests, is not written in DNA. The scientists are cartoon villains: a government board that wants to use the clones as military assets and a principal who sees them as amusement-park attractions, a satire of the idea of breeding people for a purpose. The series is mainly a parody of teen dramas such as Dawson's Creek. Its Gandhi character provoked protests in India in 2003, and he was left out of the revival.

title: Jurassic Bark
text: At a museum exhibit, Fry is shocked to find a fossilised dog that he recognises as Seymour, the pet he had in the 20th century before he was frozen. After he protests outside the museum for three days, he is given the fossil. Professor Farnsworth explains that, because the dog fossilised unusually fast, a DNA sample can be used to produce a clone, and even to restore Seymour's personality and memories. Bender, jealous of the attention Fry gives the dog, throws the fossil into a pit of lava, then regrets it and dives in to recover it. As the cloning begins, the computer reports that Seymour died at the age of 15, twelve years after Fry was frozen. Believing the dog moved on and forgot him, Fry stops the process. A closing flashback shows that Seymour in fact spent the rest of his life waiting faithfully outside Panucci's Pizza for Fry to return. Cloning from ancient DNA is the device of the plot. The Professor proposes to recover DNA from a fossil and grow a new Seymour, and adds that the clone would also have the dog's personality and memories, which is the science-fiction part: a clone shares its donor's genes, not its experiences. The computer's ability to read Seymour's age at death from the sample is another comic liberty. The episode uses the idea not to explore science but to raise an emotional question, whether bringing back a lost companion would be for the dog's sake or Fry's. The Professor is the series' usual eccentric scientist, here a helpful one. Pets have been cloned in real life, but mammalian cloning requires intact, viable cell nuclei rather than DNA alone, so a fossil could not serve; the episode itself presents Seymour's rapid fossilisation as a special case.

title: Lilo & Stitch
text: On the planet Turo, the scientist Dr. Jumba Jookiba is convicted by the United Galactic Federation of illegal genetic experimentation. His creation, Experiment 626, an aggressive, almost indestructible creature built for destruction, is sentenced to exile but escapes and crash-lands on Kauaʻi, Hawaii, where it poses as a dog at an animal shelter. Lilo, a lonely girl being raised by her older sister Nani after their parents' death, adopts him and names him Stitch. Stitch's destructive behaviour costs Nani her job and strengthens the doubts of the social worker Cobra Bubbles about her ability to care for Lilo. Jumba and the agent Pleakley are sent to recapture him, and their fights destroy the family's house. When Captain Gantu captures Lilo, Stitch, who has learned from her the Hawaiian idea of ʻohana, or family, asks for help, and Jumba joins in the rescue. The Grand Councilwoman lets Stitch stay on Earth with Lilo, and Jumba and Pleakley join the family. Genetic engineering explains Stitch's existence and his nature. Jumba Jookiba is a stock mad scientist made comic: an alien geneticist convicted for illegal experiments who designed Experiment 626 as a weapon, with great strength, near-indestructibility and an urge to destroy. The film then sets up a contest between design and upbringing: Stitch was engineered to destroy, but Lilo's affection and the idea of ʻohana gradually change his behaviour, and by the end his creator, too, has become part of the family. The message is that a creature's genetic programming does not fix its destiny, a light-hearted version of the nature-versus-nurture debate. The film does not dwell on the science, and Stitch's abilities are pure fantasy. According to the filmmakers, the relationship of creator and creation was not part of the original concept: Stitch began as the leader of an intergalactic gang with Jumba as a former crony, and the two were recast as scientist and experiment after test screenings.

title: Minority Report
text: In 2054, Washington, D.C.'s experimental Precrime unit arrests murderers before they act, using the visions of three "precogs" who foresee homicides. Its chief, John Anderton, still grieving the abduction of his son, is himself predicted to kill a man he has never met, Leo Crow. On the run, he visits Dr. Iris Hineman, the geneticist whose research made Precrime possible. She tells him that the precogs' abilities arose in children born to mothers addicted to the drug neuroin, and that the precogs sometimes disagree: the dissenting vision, a "minority report", is deleted. Anderton kidnaps the strongest precog, Agatha, to search her memories, and uncovers a murder covered up by Precrime's director, Lamar Burgess: the killing of Agatha's own mother, Anne Lively, who had tried to reclaim her. Exposed, Burgess kills himself, Precrime is shut down and its prisoners are released. Genetics plays a modest but important role in the film's backstory. The precogs' clairvoyance is a side effect of damage caused in the womb by their mothers' addiction to neuroin, and Dr. Iris Hineman, a geneticist, studied these children and developed the research on which Precrime is based. She is portrayed as an ambiguous, reclusive figure living apart from the system her work made possible, and it is she who reveals that its supposed infallibility depends on deleting dissenting visions. The film is less about heredity than about determinism: whether a person can be punished for a predicted act and whether the future is fixed. In that sense it touches the same concerns raised by genetic prediction of behaviour and disease risk, though the film's mechanism is psychic rather than genetic. The precogs themselves are treated as tools of the state and are only freed, to live in anonymity, at the end.

title: Mobile Suit Gundam SEED
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination cloning
text: In the Cosmic Era, humanity is divided between Naturals and Coordinators, people genetically enhanced before birth. Persecuted on Earth, most Coordinators have emigrated to space colonies called the PLANTs, and the two sides are at war. When the PLANTs' forces, ZAFT, attack the neutral space colony Heliopolis to seize prototype mobile suits built for the Earth Alliance, Kira Yamato, a young Coordinator student, pilots one of them to protect his friends, and finds himself fighting his childhood friend Athrun Zala, now a ZAFT pilot. Kira joins the crew of the warship Archangel and later, with the singer Lacus Clyne and other defectors, forms a third force that tries to stop both sides from destroying each other. Along the way he learns that he is the "Ultimate Coordinator", the product of a secret research project, and that the masked ZAFT commander Rau Le Creuset is a clone. The 50-episode series aired in Japan in 2002–2003. Genetic enhancement is the foundation of the series' world. The war between Naturals and Coordinators is a conflict born of genetic inequality: Coordinators are engineered to be stronger and more intelligent, Naturals resent them, and the natural-human supremacist group Blue Cosmos campaigns, with the slogan "for the preservation of our blue and pure world", for their destruction, while radicals on the PLANTs plan genocide in return. Behind the story is GARM R&D, a research company on the Mendel colony. Its chief researcher, Dr. Ulen Hibiki, developed Kira as the Ultimate Coordinator, a foetus grown outside the womb with enhancements intended to surpass all other Coordinators; Kira was the only one to survive the process. Hibiki also cloned the wealthy Al Da Flaga, and the clone, Rau Le Creuset, has short telomeres that make him age rapidly, which feeds his hatred of humanity. The series uses these ideas to explore prejudice and the ethics of designing people; its sequel, Gundam SEED Destiny, extends them to a plan to assign everyone's role in life by their genes.

title: Repli-Kate
text: Max Fleming, a graduate student, has built a cloning machine for the egotistical Dr. Jonas, who takes all the credit. Kate Carson, a magazine reporter, comes to interview Max about the research and accidentally cuts herself, letting a few drops of her blood fall into a cloning sample. That night Max runs the machine and creates an adult replica of Kate, whom he calls Repli-Kate. She has none of Kate's knowledge, so Max and his roommate Henry set out to educate her as their ideal woman: beer-drinking, sports-loving and sexually forward. Max soon realises that the woman he really wants is the original Kate. Jonas learns of the clone, kidnaps both women and plans to present "his" cloning breakthrough to scientists from around the world, but Max and Henry rescue them with the help of a clone of Jonas. Max takes over the lab and becomes famous, Max ends up with Kate and Henry with Repli-Kate. Cloning is the comic premise of this National Lampoon sex comedy. A machine produces an instant adult copy of a woman from a few drops of blood, and the clone is a blank slate that two young men try to shape into their fantasy partner. The scientists are a credit-stealing professor and an awkward student inventor, played for laughs rather than as a comment on research. The film is not interested in the science, and its depiction of cloning is pure fantasy: real cloning, as with Dolly the sheep in 1996, requires nuclear transfer into an egg and a pregnancy, and produces a baby rather than an adult. The film's only link to real debates is the idea, also common in more serious works, that a clone shares the original's appearance but not her memories or personality.

title: Resident Evil
text: Beneath Raccoon City lies the Hive, a secret genetic research facility owned by the Umbrella Corporation. When a thief steals the genetically engineered T-virus and releases it inside, the facility's artificial intelligence, the Red Queen, seals the Hive and kills everyone in it. Alice wakes up with amnesia in a mansion above the facility and is taken down into the Hive by a team of Umbrella commandos, together with a police officer, Matt, and another amnesiac, Spence. Once they shut down the Red Queen, the infected staff rise as zombies, together with Lickers, creatures created through experiments with the virus. As the group fights its way out, Alice remembers that she was helping Matt's sister, an activist, to expose Umbrella's illegal experiments, and Spence turns out to be the thief. Only Alice and Matt survive, but Umbrella scientists take them; Matt is assigned to the Nemesis programme, and Alice later wakes up to find Raccoon City devastated. Genetic engineering appears as the activity of a ruthless corporation. The Umbrella Corporation runs a hidden underground laboratory where it develops the T-virus, a genetically engineered virus that reanimates the dead and that has been used to create monsters, as well as an antivirus to counter it. The research is illegal and secret, and the scientists remain faceless employees of the corporation: when the virus escapes, the company's response is to seal the laboratory with its staff inside and later to reopen it for study, while turning the survivors into new experimental subjects. The film reflects a common fear about biotechnology: that commercial research on dangerous pathogens, kept away from public scrutiny, could cause a catastrophe. The T-virus itself is fantasy, as no virus can bring the dead back to life.

title: Spider-Man
text: On a school trip to a Columbia University genetics laboratory, shy teenager Peter Parker is bitten by a genetically engineered spider. The next day he has spider-like abilities: strength, agility, heightened senses, the ability to cling to walls and organic webbing produced in his wrists. Meanwhile Norman Osborn, head of the company Oscorp and father of Peter's friend Harry, tests a performance-enhancing chemical on himself to win a military contract; it gives him superhuman strength but drives him insane. After Peter lets a thief escape and the same man kills his Uncle Ben, he becomes the masked crime-fighter Spider-Man and sells photos of himself to the Daily Bugle. Osborn, as the Green Goblin, kills Oscorp's board, deduces Peter's identity and targets the people he loves, finally forcing him to choose between saving Mary Jane and a cable car full of children. Peter saves both, and Osborn dies impaled by his own glider. Peter then hides his feelings for Mary Jane to protect her. Genetic engineering is the origin story. Peter gains his powers from the bite of a genetically modified spider exhibited in a university genetics laboratory, and the film presents the result as a lasting change to his body: overnight his strength and senses are enhanced and he begins to produce web from his own wrists. The film does not explain how a bite could do this, and it works purely as a superhero device. The villain's origin is chemical rather than genetic: Norman Osborn is an industrialist-scientist who tests an untried enhancer on himself under pressure to secure a military contract, and its side effects turn him into a murderous split personality. The two transformations offer a contrast familiar in the genre, between an accidental gift used responsibly and a reckless self-experiment in the service of corporate and military interests. In reality no animal bite can rewrite the genome of an adult's cells, and it is the film's moral, "with great power comes great responsibility", rather than its science that has endured.

title: Star Trek: Nemesis
text: After the Romulan Senate is wiped out by a weapon planted during a debate, the Reman rebel leader Shinzon seizes power. The Enterprise, carrying Captain Picard and his crew, recovers B-4, a prototype android resembling Data, and is sent to Romulus because Shinzon claims to want peace with the Federation. There Picard learns that Shinzon is his clone, created by the Romulans to replace him as a spy within Starfleet. The plan was abandoned and the child was sent to the mines of Remus to die, but he rose to lead the Remans and built the warship Scimitar, armed with thalaron radiation. Dr. Crusher discovers that Shinzon is dying because of the way he was cloned and that only a transfusion of Picard's blood can save him. Shinzon kidnaps Picard and plans to use his weapon against Earth. Picard kills Shinzon aboard the Scimitar, and Data sacrifices himself to destroy it. Cloning is the film's central device. Shinzon is a genetic copy of Picard grown by the Romulans for espionage, and the story uses him to explore nature against nurture: sharing Picard's genome, he was shaped by abandonment and slavery into a very different man, and much of the drama turns on whether Picard, in his place, would have become the same. The cloners themselves are an unseen Romulan intelligence programme that treats the boy as a disposable tool. A further plot point is that Shinzon's cloning was flawed, leaving him with a fatal degeneration that only Picard's blood can stop. In real terms, a clone is simply a delayed identical twin, and the film's attention to the role of upbringing reflects that well.

title: Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones
alt: Star Wars. Episodio II: El ataque de los clones
text: Ten years after the events of The Phantom Menace, the Galactic Republic is threatened by a Separatist movement led by Count Dooku. After two attempts on the life of Senator Padmé Amidala, Obi-Wan Kenobi follows the trail of the assassin's employer to the ocean planet Kamino, where he finds a clone army being produced for the Republic, supposedly ordered by a dead Jedi Master. Its genetic template is the bounty hunter Jango Fett, who also keeps an unaltered clone as his son, Boba. Obi-Wan follows Jango to Geonosis and discovers the Separatists' droid army, but is captured. Meanwhile Anakin Skywalker, guarding Padmé, falls in love with her and massacres the Tusken Raiders who killed his mother. When Obi-Wan, Anakin and Padmé are about to be executed, Yoda arrives with the clone troopers, beginning the Clone Wars, and Anakin and Padmé marry in secret. Cloning is the plot device that gives the film its title. On Kamino, the Kaminoans, a species of expert cloners, have produced an army of soldiers from the DNA of Jango Fett, a bounty hunter recruited by Count Dooku. The clones are genetically altered so that they age at twice the normal rate and are more obedient and easier to command, while Jango asked for one unaltered clone to raise as his son, Boba. The Kaminoans are presented as detached, courteous technicians who treat the clones as a product, and the army is later revealed to be part of the Sith plan to seize power: in the following film the clones turn on the Jedi. Real reproductive cloning produces a genetically identical twin that must develop at the normal pace and does not copy memories or skills; accelerated growth and engineered obedience are fiction.

title: Treehouse of Horror XIII
alt: La casa-árbol del terror XIII The Simpsons, season 14, episode 1
text: The fourteenth-season Halloween anthology of The Simpsons contains three segments. In "Send in the Clones", a parody of Multiplicity, Homer buys a cursed hammock that produces copies of anyone who lies in it; he uses his clones to do his chores, but they grow progressively dimmer, multiply into an army and overrun Springfield until the government lures them over a cliff with giant doughnuts, leaving Marge with a kinder clone. In "The Fright to Creep and Scare Harms", Lisa's campaign to ban guns leaves the town defenceless against undead outlaws led by Billy the Kid. In "The Island of Dr. Hibbert", a parody of The Island of Doctor Moreau, the family visit Dr. Hibbert's island resort, where he turns Marge into a panther and other residents of Springfield into human–animal hybrids; Homer, turned into a walrus, decides that he likes it. The connection with genetics is loose. Two of the three segments use themes associated with it, cloning and human–animal hybrids, but neither involves genetic science. Homer's clones come from a cursed magic hammock, and the joke about each copy being less intelligent than the last parodies the idea that copies degrade, not any real process. Dr. Hibbert's hybrids parody The Island of Doctor Moreau, and the episode does not explain how he transforms people. Hibbert is presented as a mad doctor whose victims end up enjoying their new animal lives. The episode is a comic pastiche of horror and science fiction conventions rather than a story about genetics, and its inclusion in a genetics database is marginal.

title: Accelerate
text: Lana Lang believes she is seeing the ghost of Emily Dinsmore, a childhood friend who drowned six years earlier, and who appears to her still ten years old. Clark discovers that Emily is real and that she seems to vanish and walk through walls because she can move at super-speed. Searching her father's house, Clark and Lana find a hidden laboratory with two more copies of Emily asleep in glass tanks. Lex learns that Emily's father, Pete Dinsmore, had been working on accelerating cell growth and could bring a rabbit embryo to adulthood in days. Emily is a clone whose growth was accelerated with green meteor rock, and her father warns that she has no moral conscience. Angry at Lana for not saving her years ago, Emily pushes her off the bridge where she died, and Clark rescues her. Lex discovers that his father, Lionel Luthor, is funding the cloning research, and Lionel takes Emily away to a new lab. Human cloning is at the centre of this episode. A grieving father uses his research on accelerated cell growth, boosted by kryptonite, to recreate his dead daughter as a ten-year-old clone, and keeps spare copies in tanks. The episode plays on the "replacement child" theme: the clone has the girl's appearance and childhood attachments, but lacks a moral conscience and turns violent. The scientist is driven by grief rather than ambition, but his work is financed by Lionel Luthor's LuthorCorp, which takes over the clone at the end; Lex accuses his father of continuing the secret Level Three projects he believed had been abandoned. Real cloning produces a genetically identical baby who must grow at a normal rate, so a clone could not be made at the age of the original or inherit her memories. Like many science-fiction clones, Emily also embodies the misconception that a copy will be a defective version of the person it replaces.

title: Blueprint
text: Iris Sellin, a celebrated concert pianist, learns that she has multiple sclerosis. Fearing that her talent will die with her, she persuades the reproductive medicine specialist Martin Fischer to clone her, and gives birth to Siri, her genetic copy and her daughter. When Siri is thirteen, Fischer makes the cloning public, and she learns what she is. The bond between them breaks, and for years mother and daughter make each other's lives miserable. Seeking to escape her mother's shadow, Siri moves to the Canadian wilderness, where she lives alone and works as a wildlife photographer. There she meets Greg, an architect, whose love helps her build a life of her own and ease the conflict with Iris. Franka Potente plays both Iris and Siri; the film is based on Charlotte Kerner's prize-winning young-adult novel. Human reproductive cloning is the premise, but the film is mainly a psychological drama about identity and a mother-daughter relationship. Iris has herself cloned to preserve her musical gift, treating her daughter as a copy rather than as a new person, and Siri struggles to find out whether anything in her is her own. Fischer, the doctor who performs the cloning, breaks the secret when Siri is thirteen, exposing her to stigma; at a Mother's Day concert, Siri wears a Star of David bearing the word "Klon" (clone), an image that recalls the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany. The German film magazine film-dienst noted that the ethics of gene technology serves mainly as a backdrop. The film's central idea fits genetics well: a clone is in effect a delayed identical twin, and twin studies show that sharing a genome does not mean sharing talents, personality or fate. No cloned human has ever been verified, and reproductive cloning is banned in many countries, including Germany under its Embryo Protection Act.

title: Code 46
themes: cloning genetic testing genetic discrimination engineered pathogens
text: In 2077, people live either "inside" in tightly controlled cities or "outside" in the desert as an underclass, and movement is regulated by "papeles", travel documents issued as insurance cover. William Geld, an investigator from Seattle, is sent to Shanghai to find who is forging papeles at the company that issues them. Helped by an engineered empathy virus, he identifies Maria Gonzalez as the forger, but he is drawn to her, blames someone else and begins an affair with her. When he returns, Maria has been taken to a clinic: she was pregnant, and the pregnancy was terminated as a breach of Code 46, which forbids reproduction between genetically related people. Her memory of him has been erased. William tests her DNA and discovers that she is a clone of his mother. He takes her to Jebel Ali, where they flee together, but they are caught after a car crash. William's memories are erased and he returns to his family, while Maria is exiled outside. Genetics shapes both the society and the love story. In this world, widespread use of in vitro fertilisation, embryo splitting and cloning means that people cannot know who they are related to, so the law called Code 46 forbids reproduction between any two people who share 25% or more of their genetic identity; violations are detected through genetic tests, pregnancies are terminated, memories erased, and viruses are used to make offenders physically averse to their partners. Genetic and health information is also used to decide who may live and travel inside the cities. William's discovery that Maria is a clone of his mother turns the affair into a form of incest. The film does not focus on scientists but on the state and corporate apparatus that applies genetics, and critics noted that it explains its biotechnology through opening text rather than exploring it. The 25% threshold corresponds to the relatedness between, for example, a grandparent and grandchild. As a clone of his mother, Maria would share about half of William's genome, as a mother does.

title: Hulk
themes: heredity genetic engineering mutants human enhancement
text: In the 1960s, David Banner, a government genetics researcher trying to improve human DNA, experiments on himself after his superior, Thaddeus Ross, forbids tests on humans. His son Bruce inherits his altered DNA. When Ross shuts down his research, David sabotages a gamma reactor and accidentally kills his wife; he is sent to a mental hospital, and Bruce is adopted and represses the memory. As an adult, Bruce works on regenerative "nanomeds" at Berkeley with Ross's daughter Betty. Shielding a colleague in an accident, he absorbs a massive dose of gamma radiation that merges with his altered DNA, and from then on rage turns him into the Hulk, a giant green creature. David, now a lab janitor, uses Bruce's DNA to mutate dogs that attack Betty. The military, now led by General Ross, and the corporate opportunist Talbot try to capture the Hulk. David gains the power to absorb energy and matter and fights his son until a bomb destroys him; Bruce is presumed dead. Ang Lee's film changes the Hulk's origin to make heredity central. Bruce's condition begins with his father's self-experimentation: David Banner, a researcher for the military, alters his own DNA in pursuit of human improvement, passes the change to his son, and the gamma accident decades later only activates what Bruce inherited. Much of the film is a family drama about what children inherit from their parents, biologically and emotionally, with Bruce's repressed childhood trauma acting as the trigger for each transformation. Scientists are shown at their worst through David, whose ambition turns to megalomania and who uses his son's DNA to create monstrous dogs, while military and corporate interests, represented by Ross and Talbot, want to exploit the Hulk for regenerating soldiers. The genetics is fictional, but the film touches on a real distinction: changes to a person's germline, unlike those to other body cells, can be passed to the next generation, which is why editing the genomes of human embryos is so tightly restricted today.

title: Lilith Needs a Favor
text: On a flight to Seattle, Frasier's ex-wife Lilith meets Albert, a pale, awkward fellow passenger, and tells him she is going to ask an old friend for a favour. In Seattle she asks Frasier to donate sperm so that she can have another child, appealing to their memories of raising their son Frederick. The two go to a sperm bank, where they talk the matter through and part on good terms. Meanwhile, Daphne takes her mother, Roz and Roz's daughter Alice to a theme park in Canada, leaving Niles with a set of photographs; he and Frasier puzzle over the last one, which Niles mistakes for a picture of Daphne until she reveals that it shows Martin. On the flight back to Boston, Lilith meets Albert again, learns that he is a divorced scientist, and the two discover that they have much in common. Genetics enters through the choice of a biological father. Lilith wants another child and turns to her former husband as a sperm donor, hoping in effect for another child like their son Frederick, a comic take on choosing a donor for his traits. The episode treats assisted reproduction, sperm banking and donor choice as ordinary parts of modern family planning, mining them for awkward humour rather than ethical debate. No scientist plays a role in the procedure, although Lilith's new acquaintance, Albert, turns out to be one. Its relevance to genetics is therefore light: it reflects the idea, common in real donor selection, that prospective parents look for desirable traits in a donor, though the heredity of complex traits such as intelligence or temperament is far less predictable than such choices assume.

title: Seeing Double
text: The pop group S Club are finishing a tour in Barcelona when their manager Alistair is abducted. The next day they see an S Club performing on television that they do not recognise: perfect copies of themselves, managed by Alistair. Arrested for running out on their hotel bill and for allegedly impersonating S Club, they escape and make their way to Los Angeles. Swapping places with some of their doubles, they discover that the clones have no belly buttons, live by strict rituals and are brainwashed at night. They learn that the clones were made by Victor Gaghan, a former genetics professor fired for illegal cloning experiments, who plans to take over the world through music, since celebrities attract more attention than politicians. At his Hollywood castle, Eagle Peak, the band find Gaghan's other cloned stars, from Elvis Presley to Madonna. Clones and originals join forces, Gaghan is arrested, and the clones end up standing in for the band when it wants a holiday. Cloning is the comic premise of this musical. The villain, Victor Gaghan, is a stock mad scientist, a disgraced genetics professor who clones pop stars from memorabilia he buys online, including their underwear, and uses the copies to pursue world domination through pop music. The clones are adults made to order with implanted, programmed memories and a telltale lack of belly buttons, and they have to learn simple pleasures for the first time once they rebel. The film plays the idea entirely for laughs, and its sympathy lies with the clones, who are treated as people in their own right and are freed rather than destroyed. Its science is pure fantasy: a real clone would start life as an embryo and would grow into a much younger twin, without the memories or skills of the original.

title: Similitude
text: During the Enterprise's mission against the Xindi, Chief Engineer Trip Tucker falls into a coma after an engine accident. Doctor Phlox proposes a controversial procedure: growing a "mimetic symbiote" from Tucker's blood to serve as a source of neural tissue. Captain Archer approves it for the sake of the mission. The symbiote, named Sim, ages from baby to adult in days, has a natural lifespan of about two weeks, and develops Tucker's memories and personality, including his love of engineering and his attraction to T'Pol. Sim learns that the transplant will kill him and that an experimental procedure might extend his life, which Phlox had kept quiet. He asks to live out his life, and Archer tells him he would rather Sim agree than be forced. Thinking of his sister, killed in the Xindi attack, Sim accepts the procedure. Tucker recovers, and the crew hold a funeral for Sim. The episode is an ethical drama about creating a person for spare parts. Sim is effectively a short-lived clone grown from Tucker's blood, and the story asks whether a being created to save someone else has a right to his own life. Phlox, the ship's doctor, is portrayed as caring, acting as Sim's father, but he withholds information about a possible way to extend Sim's life; Captain Archer puts the mission first and is willing to sacrifice Sim. Reviewers have singled out the episode as one of the most thought-provoking in the series for this dilemma. The science is invented: the clone ages to adulthood in days and inherits Tucker's memories, neither of which is possible with real cloning. The premise echoes real debates about creating embryos or "saviour siblings" as sources of tissue for others.

title: Borderland
text: In 2154, genetically enhanced humans known as Augments seize a Klingon Bird-of-Prey after killing its crew. Starfleet sends the Enterprise to stop them, and Captain Archer collects Dr. Arik Soong from prison, where he is serving a sentence for stealing the embryos from which the Augments were raised. Soong, who regards them as his children, promises to persuade them to stand down. In the Borderland, a lawless region between Klingon and Orion space, Orion slavers attack the Enterprise and capture several crew members, including T'Pol, and Archer needs Soong's help to rescue them from a slave market. Soong tries to escape during the rescue and then refuses to lead Archer to the Augments. Aboard the Klingon ship, Persis manipulates the Augment leader Raakin, who is killed by Malik. The Bird-of-Prey docks with the disabled Enterprise, Malik forces Archer to release Soong, and Soong announces that they will now go after the remaining Augment embryos. The episode opens a three-part arc about human genetic enhancement. The Augments were raised by Soong from embryos preserved from the time of the Eugenics Wars, the conflict that in Star Trek's history produced Khan Noonien Singh, and their strength and intelligence are matched by arrogance and violence. Soong is a brilliant but irresponsible geneticist who sees himself as their father, steals the embryos and refuses to accept that his project has gone wrong; later in the arc he tries to remove aggressive behaviour from the remaining embryos, and he ends it doubting that engineering humans is feasible. He is the ancestor of Noonien Soong, creator of the android Data. The arc reflects Star Trek's long-standing suspicion of human genetic enhancement, while letting Soong argue for its potential, and its "Augments" echo real concerns that enhancing traits could create a privileged class.

title: Cold Station 12
themes: eugenics human enhancement genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: In the middle episode of a three-part story, Captain Archer and his crew pursue Dr. Arik Soong and the Augments, genetically enhanced humans Soong raised from embryos stolen after the Eugenics Wars. On the planet Trialis IV they find the building where the young Augments were raised and capture Udar, nicknamed "Smike", an Augment cast out by his siblings because he lacks their enhanced abilities except for his hearing. Meanwhile Soong and the Augments seize a Denobulan medical ship and use it to enter Cold Station 12, a secret Starfleet medical facility that stores pathogens and 1,800 frozen augmented embryos. They take the staff hostage, including Dr. Lucas, a friend of Enterprise's Dr. Phlox. Tension grows between Soong and the ruthless Augment Malik, who tortures Lucas and threatens other scientists with deadly pathogens. Malik finally forces Lucas to give up the security codes. The Augments escape with the embryos, but not before Malik kills Smike, steals pathogens and sabotages the station's containment systems. The episode deals directly with human genetic enhancement and its legacy. Soong raised the Augments as his "children", and they themselves show the dangers his critics feared: they are stronger and smarter than ordinary humans but also arrogant and increasingly violent, and Malik's ruthlessness strains his relationship with Soong. Smike, born with the Augments' genome but without their abilities, shows that genetic design does not guarantee the intended result, and his rejection and murder by his siblings shows how they value people by their traits. Starfleet, for its part, keeps the embryos from the Eugenics Wars in storage instead of destroying them. The arc revives the genetically engineered Augments who appeared alongside Khan Noonian Singh in the original series and is a cautionary tale about eugenic ambitions. Its enhancements are fictional; nothing comparable can be engineered into human embryos.

title: Corn
text: Emily Rasmussen, a young woman who is pregnant and has dropped out of college, returns to the rural sheep ranch of her family to rebuild her life; the father of her child, a politician, refuses to help her for fear of scandal. She notices that the sheep are behaving strangely: they fight viciously, and even injure themselves on the fence wire, to reach a weed that grows from the neighbouring farm's corn. The neighbour has planted a new genetically engineered corn supplied by a large company. After a lamb is born with only two legs and the newborn baby of a friend who regularly eats lamb dies, Emily investigates and discovers that the corn is an experiment in genetic engineering. She tries to warn people about the contaminated meat, but few listen, and she ends up confronting the company testing the corn, her employers and her own family. The film is a cautionary drama about genetically modified crops. A biotechnology company tests a new corn variety in an ordinary farming community; the crop spreads an unexpected weed, the sheep that eat it become aggressive and addicted to it, and the effects appear to pass through the food chain to the people who eat the meat, causing birth defects and deaths. The scientists behind the corn appear only occasionally and grow worried as the problems emerge, while the company is portrayed as a powerful interest that local people are reluctant to challenge. Sources differ on the details of the modification: one synopsis describes a corn engineered to resist pesticides and grow with little water, while a review mentions a gene from a cold-water fish. The film was made on a very small budget and reviewers found its treatment of the theme thin. The harms it depicts are fictional: there is a scientific consensus that food from currently available GM crops poses no greater risk to health than conventional food, although each new crop must be assessed case by case.

title: Elfen Lied
themes: mutants human experimentation genetic discrimination nature nurture
text: This anime series, adapted from Lynn Okamoto's manga, follows the Diclonii, a newly mutated species that looks human apart from two small horns but has "vectors", invisible telekinetic arms that can cut through anything within reach. Lucy, a teenage Diclonius held in a secret research facility off the coast of Kamakura, escapes in a massacre but is wounded in the head and develops a second, childlike personality called Nyu, who can say little more than her name. She is taken in by two students, Kouta and his cousin Yuka, who know nothing of her past. The facility repeatedly tries to recapture her, sending a special assault team and other Diclonii, including Mariko, the daughter of one of its researchers. Flashbacks gradually reveal how Lucy was rejected by humans as a child, and that her meeting with Kouta, who has lost his childhood memories, is not a coincidence. The 13-episode anime ended while the manga was still running, so its ending differs from the manga's. Elfen Lied uses a mutation as the basis of its conflict between two species. The Diclonii are a new branch of humanity that could replace their parent species: a Diclonius's vectors can transmit a "vector virus" to human men, whose children are then born as Diclonii, so the mutation spreads by infection rather than ordinary inheritance. The scientists who run the research facility hold Diclonii captive, experiment on them and treat them as a threat to be contained, and they take drastic measures against the virus's spread: one researcher, Kurama, whose daughter Mariko was born a Diclonius after he was touched by a Diclonius's vectors, urges a colleague to be sterilised. A central question of the series is whether the Diclonii's violence is part of their genetic code or the result of abuse by humans, and the anime's director, Mamoru Kanbe, said he intended it to show how atrocities are shaped by the way people are treated. In the manga, the Diclonii are kept in a cave named after the Nazi Lebensborn programme. A virus that turns a man's future children into another species has no real counterpart.

title: Frankenfish
text: In the Louisiana bayou, a fisherman is killed by an unseen animal. Medical examiner Sam Rivers and biologist Mary Callahan go to investigate and reach a small community of houseboats and stilt houses, where residents say a strange boat washed upriver after a hurricane three months earlier. Sam and Mary find the boat with its crew dead in the hold and accidentally trigger a homing signal. That night, huge fish that can breathe air and move on land begin attacking the residents, killing several people and sinking their homes. Jeff, a wealthy hunter whose team was tracking the signal, arrives and explains that the fish are genetically engineered snakeheads. Sam and the survivors are forced to join his hunt; a third, much larger fish kills Jeff and his men. Sam kills it by luring it into the fan of his airboat, but the film ends with dozens of young fish attacking a survivor stuck in the mud. Genetic engineering explains the monsters but is barely explored. The fish are snakeheads modified to grow to the size of a man, and they escape when the boat carrying them is wrecked by a hurricane; the people responsible are never seen, and the only figure linked to them is a wealthy bounty hunter tracking the boat's signal. The film thus treats genetic modification as a commercial product released through negligence, with ordinary bayou residents paying the price. Its real inspiration was ecological rather than genetic: in 2002 a northern snakehead, an invasive East Asian fish that can breathe air and wriggle between bodies of water, was found in a pond in Crofton, Maryland, an incident that also inspired two other films. Real genetically engineered fish do exist; AquAdvantage salmon, which grow to market size faster thanks to an added growth hormone gene, became the first genetically engineered animal approved as food in the United States and Canada, but they are not larger at maturity and pose nothing like the film's threat.

title: Godsend
text: The day after his eighth birthday, Adam, the only son of Paul and Jessie Duncan, is killed by a car. Soon after, Dr. Richard Wells, a former professor of Jessie's, offers to clone the boy, an illegal procedure that requires the family to move and change identity. The new Adam grows up normally until he passes the age at which his predecessor died; then he begins to have nightmares and waking visions of a boy named Zachary, of a school on fire and of a woman killed with a hammer, and he becomes cruel and violent. Paul discovers that Zachary Clark was a disturbed boy who set fire to his school, killed his mother and died in a house fire, and that his father was a geneticist: Wells, living under a new name. Wells had mixed Zachary's DNA into Adam's clone in the hope of bringing his own son back. The family flees, but the ending suggests that Zachary has taken over. Godsend is a supernatural thriller built on human reproductive cloning, presented as a way to replace a dead child. Its geneticist, Richard Wells, works illegally and deceives the grieving parents: he secretly uses their son's cloning to resurrect his own dead son, whose fire-damaged DNA he mixes with Adam's. The film treats the clone as a kind of reincarnation in which personality, memories and even violent tendencies return with the DNA, and it raises the ethical questions of grief-driven cloning and of a doctor playing God with families. Biologically, a clone is a genetic copy, a later-born identical twin, not a copy of a person's mind or memories, and DNA from two individuals cannot simply be blended to bring one of them back. Mammalian cloning from an adult cell was achieved with Dolly the sheep in 1996, but human reproductive cloning has never been demonstrated.

title: ReGenesis
text: This Canadian series, which ran for four seasons from 2004 to 2008, follows the scientists of NorBAC, the North American Biotechnology Advisory Commission, a fictional agency based in Toronto that investigates scientific threats across North America, such as bioterrorism, mysterious diseases and sudden environmental changes. The team is led by David Sandström, a molecular biologist and the agency's chief scientist, and includes the geneticist and physician Carlos Serrano, the biochemist Bob Melnikov, virologists and bioinformaticians, together with the agency's executive directors, who handle its political pressures. Episodes combine scientific detective work with personal storylines. In the first season, for example, Sandström befriends Mick, a teenage boy who believes he is a clone: he was in fact a frozen embryo whose DNA his father, a doctor, manipulated to remove a cancer-causing gene, with unintended changes that left him ill. Genetics and biotechnology are the subject of the series, and its central characters are working scientists. NorBAC's cases range from bioterrorism and outbreaks of unknown diseases to embryo manipulation and mad cow disease, and the show often uses them to address social, political and ethical questions. The scientists are portrayed as skilled but fallible professionals who work for a public agency rather than for a corporation or a villain, and are as likely to solve a crisis as to be drawn into its ethics. The Mick storyline illustrates the show's approach: a father's attempt to correct a disease gene in an embryo has unintended effects elsewhere in the genome, a concern that still applies to real embryo editing. The series' scientific consultant was Aled Edwards, a Canadian molecular biologist and director of the Structural Genomics Consortium, and the first-season DVD included white papers by the Ontario Genomics Institute on the facts behind the fiction.

title: The Augments
text: Concluding a three-part story, Dr. Arik Soong and the "Augments", genetically enhanced humans he raised from embryos, escape Cold Station 12 with 1,800 frozen Augment embryos from the time of the Eugenics Wars and pathogen samples. Captain Archer pursues them into Klingon space in the Enterprise. Soong wants to hide in a remote region and raise the embryos, but Malik, the Augments' leader, plans to fire a pathogen-filled torpedo at a Klingon colony to start a war between the Klingons and Starfleet. When Soong tries to remove aggressive traits from the embryos, Malik mutinies; Soong escapes and helps Archer. The Enterprise destroys the torpedo, Malik scuttles his ship, killing the other Augments and the embryos, and Archer kills Malik when he tries to murder Soong. Back in custody, Soong begins to doubt that humans can be improved through genetic engineering and turns his thoughts to artificial life. Human genetic enhancement is the subject of the episode, which ends the Enterprise arc about the Augments, descendants of the engineered supermen of Star Trek's Eugenics Wars, and links the series to Khan in the original series. Dr. Arik Soong is an idealistic scientist who sees himself as the Augments' father and believes they represent the future, yet the episode shows his creations as arrogant, aggressive and willing to commit genocide. Soong's attempt to edit aggression out of the embryos provokes the mutiny, and his final conclusion is that genetic engineering of humans may be a dead end, and he turns instead to artificial life, foreshadowing the android Data. The episode repeats Star Trek's recurring message that enhancement brings ambition and violence along with superior abilities. Genetic enhancement of human traits, as opposed to the treatment of disease, remains hypothetical.

title: Affliction
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering engineered pathogens pandemic
text: As Enterprise returns to Earth and Trip Tucker transfers to the new starship Columbia, Doctor Phlox is kidnapped in San Francisco. Following clues that point to Rigelian attackers, Enterprise gives chase, while Lieutenant Reed is secretly given orders by an agent of a covert organisation he seems to know. Enterprise is attacked and boarded, and a captured intruder who looks human turns out to be a Klingon; saboteurs force the ship to flee at record speed to avoid a warp core breach. Meanwhile, Phlox is taken to a Klingon colony, where General K'Vagh and Doctor Antaak demand that he cure a plague. Examining a victim, Phlox finds that his DNA has been combined with that of genetically augmented humans: the Klingons had experimented with Augment DNA, but it mutated and spread as a plague. Given five days to stop the outbreak, Antaak proposes creating stable augmented Klingons, but Phlox refuses to help. The story continues in "Divergence". Genetic engineering drives the episode, the first part of a two-part story. The Klingon Empire, alarmed by the genetically enhanced human "Augments" seen earlier in the season, has tried to create its own super-soldiers using Augment DNA, and the experiment has turned into a plague. Phlox, a doctor kidnapped to fix the problem, refuses to help produce more augmented Klingons, while the Klingon scientist Antaak is a reluctant participant in a military programme. The plague's symptoms include the loss of the Klingons' forehead ridges, and the story was designed to explain in-universe why Klingons looked human in the original series of the 1960s and had ridges from the 1979 film onwards. Critics welcomed the link to the Augments. Scientifically, the idea of a virus spreading another species' engineered genes and reshaping the anatomy of adults is fantasy, although viral vectors are used in real gene therapy to deliver genes into cells.

title: Ben 10
text: Ten-year-old Ben Tennyson is spending his summer holidays travelling across the United States in a motorhome with his cousin Gwen and their grandfather Max. On their first night camping, Ben finds an alien pod containing the Omnitrix, a prototype device shaped like a watch that attaches itself to his wrist and lets him transform into a range of alien creatures, each with its own powers. As he learns to use it responsibly, the trio face a series of extraterrestrial and supernatural enemies, above all the alien warlord Vilgax, who wants the Omnitrix for himself. Other recurring villains include Dr. Animo, a scientist who mutates animals, and Kevin 11, a delinquent who absorbs energy and eventually turns into a permanent hybrid of Ben's alien forms. Genetics provides the series' central gadget. The Omnitrix contains the DNA of many alien species, and by using it Ben temporarily rewrites his body into one of those species, an idea that presents DNA as a code that fully determines an organism's form and abilities and can be swapped at will. The device can also scan new species, as happens by accident with the alien Zs'Skayr, so DNA acts almost as a collectable resource. The clearest scientist figure is the villain Dr. Animo, a veterinary scientist whose career ended when he was discovered carrying out twisted genetic experiments on animals, and who keeps creating mutant creatures to defeat Ben and rule the world. Kevin 11's transformation into an irreversible hybrid of Ben's aliens shows the risks of such power. The series is aimed at children and does not attempt realism: an adult body cannot be transformed by changing its DNA, since DNA directs development and cell function rather than reshaping an existing organism instantly.

title: Carl²
text: Carl², or Carl Squared, is a Canadian animated sitcom that ran for four seasons on Teletoon from 2005 to 2011. Carl Crashman is a lazy 14-year-old whose only talent is slacking. After a bad day, while complaining about his life online, he accidentally orders a clone from a spam e-mail, supplying his fingerprint, a yearbook photo and a scabby bandage. An online cloning company sends him an exact copy of himself in a box, whom he names C2. C2 looks, talks and walks like Carl, though with a higher-pitched voice, but he is ambitious, hard-working and charming. Carl uses him to slack off even more, but C2 often does the opposite of what Carl wants. Carl keeps the clone secret from everyone except his best friend, Jamie James, and the episodes follow the comic complications of sharing one identity. Cloning is the series' premise, played for comedy and aimed at children and young teenagers. The clone is ordered online from a company advertising through spam, made from a fingerprint and a scab, and delivered fully grown in a box, a parody of consumer biotechnology rather than a depiction of real science. The series explores identity through the contrast between two genetically identical boys with opposite personalities: the original is lazy, while the clone is diligent and likeable, implying that sharing a genome does not mean sharing a character. No scientists play a significant role. In reality a clone would be an embryo that develops and grows up like any child, making it a much younger identical twin rather than an instant double of the same age.

title: Divergence
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation
text: In this second part of a two-part story, Doctor Phlox is a prisoner at a Klingon colony, forced to work with the Klingon physician Antaak on a cure for a plague. The disease began as an attempt to create Klingon "Augments" using the DNA of genetically enhanced humans; the altered DNA mutated, spread as a virus and is killing its victims after stripping them of their cranial ridges. Meanwhile, Commander Tucker joins Enterprise from Columbia to purge the sabotage that keeps the ship at dangerous speed, and Captain Archer learns that Lieutenant Reed has been working for Section 31. As a Klingon admiral prepares to destroy the colony to contain the outbreak, Enterprise and Columbia arrive. Phlox infects Archer to obtain the human antibodies needed for the cure, and Antaak beams the virus onto the admiral's ship, forcing him to accept the cure. The Klingon High Council distributes it, but the cured keep their human-like appearance. The episode concludes an arc about the Augments, genetically enhanced humans in Star Trek's history. Klingon scientists tried to create their own super-soldiers by adding Augment DNA to Klingons, but the modified genome turned into a contagious virus that threatens the whole species. Phlox, who refuses to build "living weapons", works to switch off the virus rather than perfect the Augments, and the cure leaves the survivors with smooth foreheads. The episodes were written to explain why Klingons look human in the original 1960s series but have ridged foreheads in later productions. Scientists appear on both sides: Antaak, who blames himself for the outbreak, and Phlox, a doctor with firm ethics; the experiment itself was ordered by the military and tested on prisoners and on a unit of soldiers. A virus that spreads a genetic modification evokes real viral vectors used in gene therapy, but the idea that such changes could sweep through a population as an epidemic is fiction.

title: Doom
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation mutants human enhancement
text: Loosely based on the video game series. In 2046, the Union Aerospace Corporation (UAC) runs a research station on Mars, reached through the Ark, a portal discovered under the Nevada desert. After an attack on the facility, a squad of marines led by Sarge is sent to retrieve the company's research data, accompanied by the scientist Samantha Grimm, sister of the marine John "Reaper" Grimm. They find that the scientists had uncovered the remains of an ancient humanoid race with an artificial extra pair of chromosomes, the 24th, and had been injecting this "C24" into humans. Most of those injected turn into monsters, which spread through the station and through the Ark to Earth. Samantha suggests that C24 transforms people according to their nature. When Reaper is gravely wounded, she injects him with it: he gains superhuman abilities, kills the infected Sarge and carries his sister home. Genetics provides the film's horror premise. The UAC's anthropology and genetics research has found that an extinct Martian race was genetically enhanced with an artificial 24th chromosome pair, and the company has been testing this "Martian chromosome" on people, without regard for the consequences. Samantha Grimm explains the results in moralistic terms: C24 grants superhuman abilities to some but turns those with violent or psychotic tendencies into monsters, as she believes happened to the Martians. The scientists are mostly victims of their own experiments, while the corporation is the real culprit, valuing the data above the lives of its staff. Genetically, the premise does not hold up. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, so a 24th pair would be a new, artificial addition, and a single injection could not insert it into the trillions of cells of an adult body. Behaviour is shaped by many genes and the environment, not by a switch that sorts good people from bad.

title: Painkiller Jane
themes: engineered pathogens human enhancement genetic engineering human experimentation
text: During a mission in Chechnya, a special forces unit is exposed to a biochemical weapon and then executed by men in hazmat suits. Captain Jane Browning survives both the execution and the infection, and develops rapid healing, increased speed and strength, heightened senses and a photographic memory. Questioned by a psychiatrist, Dr. Graham Knight, and tested by the military, she escapes with the help of a thief, Nick Pierce, when her superior, Colonel Ian Watts, plans to move her to Alaska. Searching for answers, she learns that the virus she was exposed to was designed to alter people's DNA and enhance them, and that its creator, Peter Erfan, is the man who posed as Dr. Knight. Erfan calls her the "new Eve": her body altered the virus, which in turn changed her. He kidnaps her to use her for his project, but she escapes. In the final scene Erfan, who has apparently injected himself, meets Asian business partners to create an army of superhumans. The film's premise is a virus engineered to modify human DNA. The geneticist Peter Erfan creates it as a way of enhancing people, but it is used as a weapon and kills an entire special forces unit; only Jane survives, because something in her body changes the virus, which then gives her healing and other enhanced abilities. The scientist is a villain who conceals his identity, uses the military and plans to sell the enhancement to foreign business partners to build an army of superhumans, so genetic modification is shown as a weapon and a commodity rather than a medical advance. Using viruses to carry genes into human cells is a real technique in gene therapy, where modified viruses act as "vectors". In reality, however, they deliver genes to some cells to treat specific diseases, and the risks include immune reactions; nothing like the instant, body-wide transformation in the film is possible.

title: Prototype
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras evolution human enhancement
text: Investigating a gravitational disturbance near the planet P3X-584, SG-1 finds an underground laboratory containing a DNA manipulation device, records written in the language of the Ancients, and a man in a stasis pod. They bring him to Earth, where he calls himself Khalek and claims to have been a prisoner of a Goa'uld. By translating the laboratory's records, Daniel Jackson learns the truth: Khalek was created by the Goa'uld Anubis, who combined human and Goa'uld DNA, gave him the genetic memory of the Goa'uld and accelerated his evolution, but was defeated before finishing this "prototype". Khalek has superhuman abilities, including telekinesis, and is close to being able to ascend to a higher plane of existence. Daniel argues that he must be killed, but an oversight committee sends Richard Woolsey to ensure he is kept alive for study. Khalek escapes his confinement and SG-1 must stop him. Khalek is a product of genetic engineering by a villain. Anubis built him in a laboratory by combining human and Goa'uld DNA and artificially accelerating his evolution, producing a being with the inherited memories of the Goa'uld, the series' parasitic villains, who is close to ascension. The episode uses the series' concept of "genetic memory", inherited knowledge passed through DNA, which is fictional; real DNA does not store memories, and evolution is not a ladder that an individual can be pushed up. The scientist, Anubis, is absent and malicious, and the episode's dilemma is about what to do with his creation: whether a being made as a weapon can be held responsible, killed preventively, or kept for research. The oversight committee's wish to study him despite the danger adds the familiar temptation to exploit a dangerous discovery.

title: The Island
text: In 2019, Lincoln Six Echo and Jordan Two Delta live in a sealed compound whose residents believe that the outside world has been contaminated and that their only hope is to win a lottery to go to "the Island", the last uncontaminated place on Earth. Lincoln, troubled by dreams of things he has never experienced, discovers that the residents are clones of wealthy sponsors, and that the lottery winners are killed to harvest their organs or used as surrogate mothers. He escapes with Jordan, who has just been selected, pursued by mercenaries hired by Dr. Merrick, the scientist who runs the institute. In Los Angeles they meet Lincoln's sponsor, Tom Lincoln, who betrays them because he needs a new liver. Lincoln tricks the mercenaries into killing Tom and takes his identity. Learning that Merrick plans to exterminate the latest clone generations, Lincoln and Jordan return to the compound, kill Merrick and free the other clones. The Island is an action film about reproductive cloning used to supply spare parts. Rich clients pay the Merrick Institute to keep a clone of themselves as an insurance policy for organ transplants, or as a surrogate to bear their children. They are told that the clones are kept in a vegetative state, but Dr. Merrick has found that the organs only survive if the clones are conscious, so he raises them as people kept in ignorance. Merrick is the archetype of the scientist who has abandoned ethics for profit and power. The film raises the question of whether clones have the same rights as other people, and its answer is that they are fully human. It also uses a familiar fictional device: Lincoln inherits some of his sponsor's memories, attributed to a cloning defect, which has no basis in biology. The film's premise closely resembles Parts: The Clonus Horror (1979), whose creators sued for copyright infringement. Human reproductive cloning has not been achieved, and research on producing tissues for transplants focuses on therapeutic cloning and stem cells rather than whole cloned people.

title: Æon Flux
text: In 2011 a virus kills 99 percent of humanity. Four centuries later, the last five million people live in Bregna, a walled city-state ruled by a congress of scientists, where people regularly disappear and are plagued by nightmares.
