Æon Flux, an agent of the Monican rebels, is sent to kill the city's leader, Trevor Goodchild, after her sister Una is killed. She discovers that she is being manipulated by council members plotting a coup, and that every inhabitant of Bregna is a clone grown from recycled DNA, because the cure for the virus left humans infertile. Æon is the first clone in 400 years of Katherine, the original Trevor's wife. Trevor has been trying to reverse the infertility, and Una was pregnant as part of his experiments, but his brother Oren had the fertile women killed to keep the Goodchild clone dynasty in power. Æon turns against Oren and destroys the Relical, the airship storing the DNA, and its crash breaks open the city wall. Cloning is the hidden foundation of the society in which the film is set. After the cure for a pandemic left humanity infertile, Bregna's rulers sustain the population by cloning the dead from DNA stored in an airship, so that people are reborn again and again with fragments of their previous lives surfacing as nightmares. Genetics thus serves as a tool of political control: the Goodchild dynasty has ruled for four centuries through its own clones, and when nature begins to restore fertility, Oren kills the pregnant women to preserve its power. Trevor, the scientist-ruler, is more ambiguous, a well-meaning researcher trying to cure infertility within a system built on deception. The film ends with a rejection of endless cloning in favour of natural reproduction and mortality. As science, it is speculative: cloning produces a genetic copy, not a continuation of the same person, and the idea of inherited memories reflects the story's themes of identity rather than biology.

title: Black Sheep
text: Henry Oldfield, who grew up on a New Zealand sheep farm, developed a crippling fear of sheep after his older brother Angus played a cruel prank on him. Fifteen years later, he returns to sell his share of the farm to Angus, unaware that Angus has been running secret genetic experiments on the flock with the scientist Dr. Astrid Rush. Two environmental activists break into the lab and accidentally release a mutant lamb, which bites one of them and then other sheep. The bite spreads quickly: the docile flock becomes a horde of carnivorous killers, and bitten humans begin to turn into monstrous human-sheep hybrids. Angus presses on with a presentation of his new breed to international investors, who are devoured. Henry, the activist Experience and their friend Tucker discover that amniotic fluid from the mutant lambs reverses the transformation, destroy the flock and save the bitten humans, while Angus is eaten by his own sheep. Genetic engineering is the source of the horror in this comedy, which plays on New Zealand's sheep-farming identity. Angus, the farmer, wants to breed the perfect sheep and present it to investors, while the scientist Dr. Rush carries out the work in a farm laboratory; both are driven by ambition and commercial interest, and their creation goes disastrously wrong. The environmental activists, who want to expose the experiments, unwittingly trigger the outbreak, so the film satirises both biotech enthusiasm and protest culture. Genetics behaves here like a virus: a bite transmits the mutation and turns humans into sheep-hybrids, and the cure is amniotic fluid. None of this resembles real genetic modification: engineered changes are inherited by offspring but cannot be passed on by a bite, and the film makes no attempt at plausibility, using the premise for gore and satire.

title: Heroes
themes: mutants human enhancement engineered pathogens pandemic heredity
text: Heroes follows ordinary people around the world who discover that they have superhuman abilities and must work together to prevent catastrophic futures. In the first season, the geneticist Mohinder Suresh continues his late father's research into the biological source of the abilities, including a list of people who have them, while Noah Bennet works for "the Company", a secret organisation that tracks, controls and, if necessary, eliminates people with powers. The second season deals with the Company's research on the Shanti virus, whose strains affect both people with abilities and ordinary humans, and the threat of a global pandemic from a weaponised strain. In the third, Arthur Petrelli and his rival company Pinehearst seek a formula that would give ordinary people abilities, and Mohinder injects himself with an early version. The fourth season introduces a carnival whose leader gathers people with abilities to increase his own power. The series ran on NBC for four seasons, from 2006 to 2010. Genetics provides the scientific frame of the series. The abilities are treated as a biological phenomenon, and a research geneticist, Mohinder Suresh, is one of the main characters; he follows his father's work, studies the source of the powers and later develops a cure for a new strain of the Shanti virus using the blood of Claire, a girl who can regenerate. Scientists are shown in several roles: as independent researchers, as employees of the secretive Company, which studies and contains people with abilities and weaponises the Shanti virus, and as part of Pinehearst's project to create a formula that gives powers to anyone. Mohinder's self-experiment with an incomplete formula gives him strength but also makes his body mutate, a classic warning about scientists who test on themselves. Arthur Petrelli presents the formula as a way to improve the world, while it is pursued for power. Like most superhero fiction, the series uses the language of genes and evolution loosely; no real genetic variant confers anything like these abilities.

title: Idiocracy
text: In 2005 Joe Bauers, an army librarian chosen for being the most average man in the armed forces, and Rita, a prostitute, take part in a one-year military hibernation experiment that is forgotten when its officer is arrested. Over the next five centuries, the narrator explains, intelligent people choose not to have children while the least intelligent reproduce freely, and intelligence and civilisation decline. Joe and Rita wake in 2505 in an anti-intellectual, hyper-commercial America where crops are failing. Arrested for lacking a bar code tattoo, Joe takes an IQ test that reveals him as the most intelligent person alive, and President Camacho, a former wrestler, appoints him Secretary of the Interior. Joe finds that the crops are being irrigated with a sports drink, Brawndo, and replaces it with water; the economic collapse that follows leads to his death sentence, but when the crops sprout he is pardoned. He later becomes president and marries Rita. The film's premise is a satirical version of dysgenics, the idea that a population can deteriorate genetically when people with less desirable traits have more children. In the film, the most intelligent people choose not to have children while the least intelligent reproduce freely, and five hundred years later society is too dim to run its own technology. No scientists or genetic technologies are involved: the mechanism is simply who has children. The film is mainly a satire of anti-intellectualism, commercialism and consumerism, but its premise echoes the worries of nineteenth- and twentieth-century eugenicists about the 'wrong' people having children. The real evidence points the other way: genetic studies have found no sign of dysgenic effects in human populations, and intelligence test scores rose substantially across much of the world during the twentieth century, a trend known as the Flynn effect.

title: Kyle XY
themes: cloning human enhancement human experimentation nature nurture
text: Kyle XY is an American science fiction series broadcast on ABC Family from 2006 to 2009. A teenage boy wakes up naked in a forest near Seattle with no memory and no navel. He is taken in by a therapist, Nicole Trager, and her family, who name him Kyle. Kyle must learn everyday life from scratch but has extraordinary mental abilities. In the first season he searches for his origins and finds a link to Adam Baylin, a brilliant student who disappeared twenty years earlier. In the second season he learns that he was created by scientists in an experiment in artificial gestation at a facility called Zzyzx, and meets Jessi, a female counterpart created by a rival programme and controlled by the company Madacorp. The third season centres on the secret society Latnok, whose director, Michael Cassidy, killed Jessi's mother. In the series finale Kyle learns that Latnok plans to produce multiple clones of him and that Cassidy is his half-brother. Human cloning and artificial gestation are at the core of the series' mythology, though the show is mainly a family and teen drama. Kyle, codenamed "781227" or "XY", was cloned from the scientist Adam Baylin and grown at Zzyzx, Baylin's facility for experiments in artificial gestation; Jessi, "781228" or "XX", was cloned from Baylin's former girlfriend Sarah Emerson in a competing experiment. The scientists and organisations around them are mostly portrayed as treating the clones as assets: corporations and a secret society seek to control or copy Kyle, while Baylin is shown more sympathetically as his mentor. The series suggests that Kyle's abilities come from his engineered development, but it also stresses that his identity is shaped by the family that raises him. Real clones would be born as babies, not as teenagers without memories or navels, and cloning would not create superhuman mental powers.

title: Leroy & Stitch
text: After capturing and rehabilitating all of Jumba's alien experiments, Lilo, Stitch, Jumba and Pleakley are honoured by the Galactic Alliance; Jumba returns to his laboratory, Pleakley takes a teaching post and Stitch becomes captain of the Galactic Armada, leaving Lilo behind in Hawaii. Gantu frees the villain Dr. Hämsterviel from prison, and Hämsterviel forces Jumba to create a new experiment from Stitch's template: Leroy, a red near-twin of Stitch. Hämsterviel defeats Stitch, sends him, Jumba and Pleakley towards a black hole, and clones Leroy into an army to conquer the galaxy and destroy the other 624 experiments. Lilo, helped by Experiment 625, Reuben, and a reformed Gantu, rejoins her friends after they escape, and in the final battle at Aloha Stadium they disable the Leroys with a shutdown command Jumba secretly built in: Elvis Presley's version of "Aloha ʻOe". Genetic engineering is part of the premise of the whole Lilo & Stitch franchise: Stitch and the other experiments are artificial creatures designed by the alien mad scientist Jumba Jookiba, and this film's antagonists are a new engineered creature, Leroy, built from Stitch's template, and an army of his clones. The film treats these ideas as cartoon devices rather than science; Leroy is created under duress, and a song acts as a built-in kill switch. Jumba is a comic, ultimately benevolent scientist, coerced into working for the villain, and the story's message is that engineered beings can find a family and a place in the world. For younger audiences it presents genetic creation and cloning as tools of good or evil depending on who uses them. There is no attempt at scientific plausibility.

title: Michael
themes: human experimentation gene therapy hybrids chimeras
text: A man wakes up in the Atlantis infirmary with no memory and is told that he is Lieutenant Michael Kenmore, an expedition member rescued from the Wraith. Dr. Carson Beckett gives him regular injections, and he notices that people treat him with suspicion: he can read Wraith writing, Ronon attacks him, and he dreams of seeing himself as a Wraith. Only Teyla shows him friendship. Searching Beckett's office, he finds recordings showing that he was a captured Wraith, transformed into a human by Beckett's experimental retrovirus, which also erased his memories. Feeling betrayed, Michael argues that he has been changed for humans' benefit, not his own. He escapes, killing a guard, and is recaptured. While being moved to another planet for a stronger dose, he takes Teyla hostage and flees through the Stargate as his Wraith body returns. Sheppard and Ronon rescue Teyla, and Michael rejoins the Wraith. The episode centres on a genetic experiment on a sentient being. Dr. Beckett's retrovirus suppresses the Wraith's Iratus bug DNA so that their otherwise suppressed human traits are expressed, turning a Wraith into a human, with the side effect of wiping his memory. The Atlantis team, who are the protagonists, are shown in an uncomfortable light: they experiment on a prisoner without consent, invent a false identity for him and debate wiping his mind again when he learns the truth. Michael's question, whether he was "cured" for his own sake or for theirs, is the moral core of the episode, and Teyla and Beckett are shown doubting what they have done. The idea of reversing a species by switching off its non-human genes is fiction, though it loosely echoes real gene therapy using modified viruses to deliver genes. Michael later becomes a recurring villain who conducts his own genetic experiments.

title: X-Men: The Last Stand
text: Worthington Labs announces a "cure" for mutants: an injection that suppresses the X-gene responsible for their powers, made from the genome of a young mutant, Jimmy, who neutralises the powers of mutants near him. The cure attracts some mutants, such as Rogue, who cannot touch anyone without harming them, while Magneto warns that it will be used as a weapon and rebuilds his Brotherhood to destroy it. Meanwhile Jean Grey, believed dead, returns as the destructive Phoenix, kills Cyclops and Professor Xavier and joins Magneto. The cure is soon turned into a weapon, fired in darts. Magneto's army attacks Alcatraz, where the cure is produced, to kill Jimmy; the X-Men defend the island, Magneto is injected with the cure and loses his powers, and Wolverine is forced to kill Jean to stop her. In the aftermath, Rogue takes the cure, and Magneto shows a hint that his powers may be returning. The mutant cure is the film's central idea. In the X-Men world, mutants owe their powers to an X-gene, and Worthington Labs, founded by an industrialist whose son is a mutant, develops a treatment from Jimmy's genome that permanently suppresses it. The science is presented through Dr. Kavita Rao, a researcher at the company, and the film is ambivalent about the scientists' intentions: the cure is offered as voluntary, but it is soon used as a weapon, fired at mutants in darts. The story asks whether a genetic difference is a disease to be treated or an identity to be protected. Some mutants, such as Rogue, want the cure because their powers keep them from normal lives, while others, led by Magneto, see it as an attempt to eliminate their kind, and the film leaves Rogue's choice to take it as a legitimate personal decision. The ending suggests that the cure may not even be permanent. The X-gene itself is a fictional device of the comics, not a real gene.

title: I Am Legend
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic genetic engineering human experimentation
text: In 2009, a genetically engineered measles virus developed as a cure for cancer mutates, kills 90% of humanity and turns most survivors into Darkseekers, aggressive nocturnal creatures that cannot bear sunlight. Three years later, US Army virologist Robert Neville, who is immune, lives alone with his dog Sam in deserted Manhattan. He scavenges by day, broadcasts radio messages to find survivors and works in his home laboratory on a cure, testing it on rats and on a Darkseeker woman he captures. After Sam is bitten by infected dogs and he has to kill her, Neville recklessly attacks the Darkseekers and is rescued by two survivors, Anna and the boy Ethan. When the Darkseekers besiege his house, Neville finds that his latest treatment is curing the captured woman. In the theatrical ending he hands a sample of her blood to Anna, hides her and Ethan, and kills himself and the attackers with a grenade. In an alternate ending, Neville returns the woman to the Darkseekers and leaves for Vermont with Anna and Ethan. Genetic engineering causes the apocalypse. Dr. Alice Krippin, seen in a television interview at the start of the film, announces a cancer cure based on a genetically engineered measles virus; the modified virus mutates and becomes a lethal pandemic. The film thus contrasts two scientists: the researcher whose well-meaning medical innovation backfires on a global scale, and Neville, a military virologist who sacrifices everything to find a cure, experimenting on animals and on captured infected people. His work finally produces a cure. The premise draws on real research: viruses that selectively destroy cancer cells, known as oncolytic viruses, are an active field, measles virus has been tested in clinical trials, and a genetically modified herpes virus was approved in the United States in 2015 for melanoma. Nothing in this research suggests the risk of a virus turning into one that transforms people as shown, and experts consulted by Popular Mechanics questioned the film's depiction of the virus's mutation.

title: Ice Spiders
text: In a secret laboratory on a Utah mountain, Dr. April Sommers and other scientists are working for the army on a new breed of giant spiders. When the spiders escape, they kill most of the lab staff and head for the ski resort on the other side of the mountain, where a team of teenage skiers is training. Sommers teams up with Dash, a former Olympic skier who works at the resort, as the spiders kill hunters, a park ranger and guests at the lodge. Reading the experiment's records, Sommers realises that Professor Marks deliberately accelerated the spiders' growth, making them larger and stronger, insatiably hungry and resistant to the cold. With the help of an army captain, Dash lures the spiders into a snowboard half-pipe, where they are blown up with an avalanche cannon; Marks, who tried to protect them, is killed by the last one. The government then covers up the incident. Ice Spiders is a low-budget creature feature in which genetic experimentation by the military supplies the monsters. Dr. Sommers' original aim is to obtain large amounts of spider silk for new types of armour, a project that is presented as legitimate, but Professor Marks secretly pushes the experiment further, accelerating the spiders' growth to make them bigger and stronger. The result is a breed of giant, cold-resistant black widows that escape and kill, and the film follows the familiar pattern of an ambitious scientist working with the military who refuses to destroy his creation and is killed by it, while the government covers everything up. The biology is not explained. The film does start from a real line of research: spider silk is exceptionally strong, and because spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms, scientists have produced silk proteins in genetically modified organisms, such as goats that secrete them in their milk, with applications that include ballistic armour.

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
themes: cloning engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation
text: Five years after the T-virus escaped from Raccoon City, the infection has spread worldwide and turned most of the planet into desert. Alice, who has acquired telekinetic powers, wanders the wasteland and joins a convoy of survivors led by Claire Redfield, persuading them to head for a reportedly uninfected area in Alaska. In an underground Umbrella Corporation facility, Dr. Isaacs breeds clones of Alice, which die one after another in tests, and experiments on zombies to make them more intelligent and docile, creating faster and stronger "Super Undead". Against orders from his superior, Albert Wesker, he ambushes the convoy to recapture Alice and is bitten. The survivors escape by helicopter, while Alice enters the facility and learns from an artificial intelligence that her blood can cure the virus. Helped by one of her clones, she kills the mutated Isaacs and later warns Wesker that she and her clones are coming for him. The film combines two genetic motifs: a virus engineered by a corporation and human cloning. The T-virus has turned humanity into the undead, and Umbrella's scientists continue experimenting rather than containing the disaster. Dr. Isaacs, the chief scientist, works on dozens of clones of Alice and uses blood taken from them to create the "Super Undead"; he is ambitious, defies his superiors and ends up infected and mutated by his own work. The clones are treated as disposable: their bodies are dumped in a pit after each failed test, an image the film uses to underline the company's disregard for human life. Alice's immunity, which makes her blood a potential cure, echoes the real use of survivors' antibodies to develop treatments. The film draws on the Resident Evil video games, where the corporation's bioweapons research is a constant theme; scientific plausibility is not a concern.

title: Underdog
text: Dr. Simon Barsinister, a scientist whose proposal for genetic experiments has been rejected, sets out to prove his theory in a secret laboratory, assisted by his henchman Cad. Cad kidnaps a beagle that has been dismissed from the police bomb squad, but the dog escapes after a fire and exposure to the laboratory's chemicals alter his DNA, giving him super strength, speed, hearing, smell, the ability to fly and the power of speech. He is adopted by Dan Unger, a former police officer, and his teenage son Jack, who names him Shoeshine. Secretly, he becomes the caped hero Underdog. Unable to recreate the serum, Barsinister tries to obtain Underdog's DNA, turns his powers into "super pills" given to three German Shepherds, and plans to use a mind-control serum in a bomb to take over Capital City. Underdog rescues Molly and Polly, carries the bomb away before it explodes, and Barsinister is arrested and injected with an antidote. Genetic engineering is the source of the hero's powers and of the villain's ambitions. Barsinister is a classic frustrated scientist: his genetic research has been rejected by the establishment, and he turns to secret, unlicensed experiments to prove himself and then to seize power. The laboratory accident alters the dog's DNA, granting abilities from flight to speech, and his later plans, harvesting the hero's DNA and turning it into pills, treat genetics as a source of power to be bottled and distributed. The film is a family comedy based on the 1960s cartoon, and its science is pure fantasy: no change to DNA could give a dog flight or human speech, and real genetic modification of an adult animal would not take effect instantly. The story nevertheless follows the familiar pattern of the mad scientist undone by his own creation, with the dogs he mistreated finally turning against him.

title: Viyabari
text: Suryaprakash is an ambitious businessman who wants to become richer than Bill Gates. His obsession costs him his family and social life. Savithri, a college student researching him for a project, falls in love with him, and he marries her, though mostly because she is a good cook. Bothered by the demands of his family, Suryaprakash asks the scientist Stephen Raj to clone him, so that the clone can take care of things at home while he concentrates on his business. The clone soon realises that the problem lies not with the family but with Suryaprakash himself, and sets out to show him what his family is worth. After the death of his mother, Suryaprakash finally gives up his greed and comes to understand the value of his family. S. J. Suryah plays both the businessman and his clone in this Tamil comedy. Cloning is the comic premise. The businessman commissions a copy of himself as a way to delegate his family life, and the story turns on the contrast between the original and the clone, who turns out to be the better son and husband. As in many clone comedies, the copy is created as an adult with the original's appearance but a different character, which serves the moral of the film, that a person's choices and attention matter more than his identity. The scientist, Stephen Raj, plays a supporting role as the provider of the technology and is not the focus of the story. Real cloning creates a new embryo that would grow up as a younger, genetically identical twin, not an adult double. Genetics here is a narrative device for a family drama and comedy and is not explored.

title: Anaconda 3: Offspring
text: A giant anaconda captured in the Amazon is held at a genetic research facility in Romania owned by the company Wexel Hall, where scientists led by Dr. Amanda Hayes are developing a serum from the Blood Orchid, a plant recovered in Borneo. When the project's backer, the industrialist J.D. Murdoch, provokes the snake, it breaks free, kills many of the staff and releases a second, "queen" anaconda. Murdoch sends the hunter Stephen Hammett and his team after the snakes. As the hunters are killed one by one, Amanda admits that the queen is pregnant and will soon give birth to genetically altered offspring. Hammett turns out to be working for Murdoch, who wants a live baby snake. Amanda wounds him and blows up the factory where the queen gives birth, killing Hammett, the queen and her young. However, one of Murdoch's men finds a surviving baby snake and delivers it to him, while Amanda burns her research. Genetic research is the source of the threat, although the film is mainly a creature feature. The anacondas are kept for experiments at a corporate genetic research facility working on a serum derived from the Blood Orchid, and the danger is that the pregnant queen will give birth to more genetically "special" offspring. The scientists work for a wealthy industrialist who funds the research for profit and is willing to sacrifice everyone to obtain a live specimen; the lead researcher, Amanda, admits her responsibility only reluctantly and ends by destroying her own documentation, a gesture against the misuse of her work. The film thus repeats a familiar pattern of the genre: commercial genetic research, poor containment and an animal that turns on its creators. Its science is not developed beyond this premise. Real anacondas are among the largest snakes, but no genetic technique could produce animals of the size and abilities shown.

title: Clone
text: This six-part BBC Three comedy follows Dr. Victor Blenkinsop, an arrogant scientist hungry for scientific glory, who creates the world's first human clone for the military as a prototype super-soldier meant to replace Britain's army. The clone emerges from his birthing tube as an adult with the mind of a naive, clumsy and gentle child, more likely to hug than to shoot. To avoid his ruthless paymaster, Colonel Black of MI7, Victor flees with the clone, later named Albert after Einstein, and his loyal assistant Ian to a small village, where he poses as a travel writer. There he meets Rose Bourne, the landlady of the local pub, whose photographic memory and mathematical gifts suggest that a map of her brain could unlock the clone's dormant military "memory engrams". Victor manipulates Rose to scan her brain and builds a device to "fix" Albert, while Black closes in. The series ends on a cliffhanger. Human cloning is the premise, played for comedy. The series reworks Frankenstein, with Victor as a modern Dr. Frankenstein and Ian as his Igor, and adds a military motive: the clone is designed as a weapon for the state, and the scientist is driven by vanity and the wish to join the great names of science. Albert emerges as an adult equipped with implanted "memory engrams", but he behaves like an innocent child, so the comedy rests on the gap between the scientist's design and what he has actually created. The scientific side is fantastical: a real clone would be born as a baby and grow up normally, and memories or skills cannot be programmed into a cloned brain. The series is better understood as a satire of scientific ambition and military patronage than as a story about genetics.

title: Cyborg Soldier
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering human experimentation
text: I.S.A.A.C. (Intuitive Synthetic Autonomous Assault Commando), played by mixed martial artist Rich Franklin, is the first prototype of a secret military "human weapon" programme. A former death-row inmate, he has been genetically reconstructed and trained into a deadly assassin, with a regenerating body and enhanced intellect. After escaping, he takes deputy sheriff Lindsay Rearden hostage while on the run. Both are pursued by military agents led by the robotics engineer Simon Hart, who wants his creation back, and the two end up working together to expose the group behind the programme to create such super soldiers. The film was directed by John Stead and released in 2008. Genetic engineering, combined with other modifications, is how the military programme creates its soldier: I.S.A.A.C. is described as genetically reconstructed, physically regenerative and intellectually superior, a man redesigned as a weapon. The scientists behind him serve a secret military project, use a death-row inmate as raw material and pursue him when he escapes, so the film follows the familiar pattern of the super-soldier story, in which the creation turns against its makers and the hero's task is to expose those responsible. The available sources describe the method only in vague terms, and the film, despite its title, seems to treat genetic and cybernetic enhancement interchangeably. Real research on regeneration or on enhancing human performance is nowhere near producing a soldier of this kind.

title: Os Mutantes: Caminhos do Coração
alt: The Mutants: Ways of the Heart
themes: mutants genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human experimentation genetic discrimination
text: This Brazilian telenovela, broadcast by Record in 2008–2009, is the second part of a trilogy that began with Caminhos do Coração. In the first part, Dr. Júlia Zaccarias, a physician at the biotechnology company Progênese, had created genetically modified humans with superpowers in a secret laboratory on the island of Arraial. Now, having taken a rejuvenating elixir to escape prison, she runs the laboratory under the name Juli Di Trevi. The existence of the mutants becomes public, and men and women turned into vampires, werewolves, snakes, spiders and other creatures attack São Paulo, while a government department, DEPECOM, is divided between controlling the mutants and exterminating them. Maria, heiress to the Mayer fortune, founds the League of Good to protect peaceful mutants against the villains' league, which includes her twin sister Samira, raised in Júlia's laboratory. The story expands to include aliens, reptilians, vampires and a journey to the centre of the Earth. Genetic engineering is the origin of the mutants around whom the whole telenovela revolves. Dr. Júlia, a physician at the biotech company Progênese, created superpowered humans in secret experiments and kept some of them, such as Samira, in her laboratory from birth. She is a classic mad scientist: driven by her experiments, she has people murdered to protect them, takes an elixir of youth and allies herself with alien reptilians. The series uses the mutants to stage a debate about difference and persecution, in the manner of X-Men, a model for the first part of the trilogy: the public hunts the mutants, and a government department splits between those who want to imprison only the violent and those who want to exterminate them all. As the story progresses, genetics gives way to fantasy, with references to Dracula, The Island of Dr. Moreau and Jurassic Park, Brazilian folklore and science-fiction aliens. The science is not meant to be realistic.

title: Repo! The Genetic Opera
text: In 2056, after an epidemic of organ failures has killed most of humanity, the megacorporation GeneCo sells organ transplants on credit, and Repo Men hunt down clients who miss payments to "repossess" their organs. GeneCo's terminally ill founder, Rotti Largo, despises his three spoiled children and plans to leave his fortune to 17-year-old Shilo Wallace, daughter of his late former fiancée Marni. Shilo has supposedly inherited her mother's rare blood disease and is kept indoors by her father Nathan, who believes he killed Marni with a treatment he created; in fact Rotti poisoned it and blackmailed Nathan into becoming GeneCo's chief Repo Man. Shilo meets a grave robber who sells an addictive painkiller extracted from corpses, and Blind Mag, a singer whose GeneCo eyes will be repossessed when she resigns. At the opera, Mag gouges out her own eyes and is killed, Rotti reveals that Nathan has been poisoning Shilo's medicine to keep her at home, and shoots him. Shilo refuses the company and leaves. Despite its title, this rock opera is more about biotechnology and transplant medicine as business than about genetics in the strict sense. GeneCo turns the body into merchandise: organs and surgical enhancements are sold on credit, and debtors are killed to recover them, a satire of commercial medicine, debt and cosmetic surgery addiction. The corporation's scientists and surgeons serve power and profit, and its founder uses medicine to manipulate and kill. The genetic element lies mainly in Shilo's story: she believes she has inherited her mother's blood disease and is defined by it, until she discovers that her symptoms were caused by her father's "medicine". Her final song, "Genetic Emancipation", celebrates her decision that her parents' actions and her inheritance do not dictate her future, a rejection of genetic and family determinism.

title: The Doctor's Daughter
alt: La hija del Doctor Doctor Who, season 4, episode 6
text: The TARDIS takes the Doctor, Martha and Donna to the planet Messaline, where human soldiers force the Doctor's hand into a "progenation machine", which within moments produces a fully grown young woman from his tissue: his daughter, whom Donna names Jenny. Humans and the fish-like Hath are locked in a war, each side breeding new soldiers in the machines, and both are searching for "the Source", which the humans' General Cobb believes will let them wipe out the enemy. Donna works out from dated plaques that the colony ship landed only seven days ago: so many generations have been produced in a week that the war's origins have become myth. The Source turns out to be a terraforming device, and the Doctor releases it and declares the war over. Cobb tries to shoot the Doctor, and Jenny dies taking the bullet. After the Doctor leaves, Jenny revives and departs in a stolen rocket. Reproductive technology drives the story. The progenation machines take a tissue sample and generate a fully grown soldier within moments, so that each side can breed armies continuously. Jenny is genetically derived from the Doctor, and the episode is mostly about whether that makes her his daughter: he initially rejects her as a mere product of a machine, then comes to accept her as his child. Jenny is effectively a clone of the Doctor, and the episode turns on the difference between genetic origin and family ties. No scientists appear; the technology is used by soldiers who have forgotten why they fight. Producing an adult person from a tissue sample in moments is pure fantasy, but the episode raises the familiar question of whether shared genes make a family.

title: The Sky Crawlers
text: Mamoru Oshii's animated film, based on Hiroshi Mori's novels, is set in an alternate world at peace, where two private corporations, Rostock and Lautern, stage a real air war to give the public a sense of conflict. Their pilots are the Kildren, genetically engineered humans who remain adolescents and never age. Pilot Yūichi Kannami arrives at Area 262 to replace a pilot who has died, and grows close to the base commander, Suito Kusanagi, who is also a Kildren but has a daughter who passes as her younger sister. Kannami begins to sense that he has no real past, that new pilots resemble the dead, and that his memories may belong to his predecessor. Kusanagi admits that she killed that predecessor at his own request. Kannami dies challenging the Teacher, an invincible enemy ace and an adult, and a new pilot with Kannami's mannerisms arrives, continuing the cycle. Genetic engineering underpins the film's world but is never explained on screen. The Kildren are humans designed not to age, created to serve as disposable pilots in a staged war, and the film suggests that when they die they are replaced by new individuals carrying traces of their predecessors' memories and manner. Their arrested development is the core of the story: they live in an endless adolescence with no past and no future, unable to grow up, and the film treats their condition as a metaphor for repetition and stagnation. The engineers and corporations behind them remain invisible, which makes the system seem impersonal and inescapable. Scholarly readings have discussed the film's depiction of engineered adolescence and endless war as a critique of a society that sustains conflict as a commodity. Arrested ageing has no real genetic equivalent in humans, although researchers study the genetics of ageing in model organisms.

title: Tokyo Gore Police
text: In a dystopian Japan whose police force has been privatised, a mad scientist known as the Key Man has created a virus that turns humans into "Engineers", mutants whose wounds sprout grotesque biomechanical weapons. The police have formed a special squad of Engineer Hunters, who maintain order through sadistic violence and street executions. Ruka, a skilled hunter, is obsessed with finding the assassin who killed her father, a police officer, years before. The Key Man infects her by inserting a key-shaped tumour into her arm. Investigating, she learns that he is a scientist, Akino Miyama, whose father was the sniper hired to kill her father and was then murdered by the police commissioner, the real mastermind; Akino turned himself into the Key Man by injecting himself with the DNA of infamous criminals. Ruka kills Akino and, as her own body begins to mutate, takes revenge on the commissioner. A post-credits scene shows that the Key Man survived. Genetics serves as the pretext for the film's extreme body horror. The Key Man, a scientist driven by revenge, spreads a virus that rewrites the bodies of infected people, and he transforms himself by injecting the DNA of notorious criminals, as if criminality could be acquired by taking up their genes. The film treats this mutation as a way to criticise a violent, privatised police state: the Engineers are hunted and executed in public, and the authorities use the crisis to justify indiscriminate killings of anyone suspected of being infected. The scientist is portrayed both as a monster and as a victim of the corrupt system he attacks. The film, written and directed by Yoshihiro Nishimura, is deliberately excessive and makes no attempt at scientific credibility: injected DNA cannot transfer behaviour, and no virus could produce such transformations.

title: District 9
text: In 1982, a huge spaceship stops over Johannesburg, carrying a population of starving insect-like aliens. They are confined to a camp, District 9, which becomes a slum, and humans despise them as "prawns". Twenty-eight years later, the private military company Multinational United (MNU) is hired to evict them to a new camp, and the operation is led by Wikus van de Merwe, a mild bureaucrat. In an alien shack, Wikus is sprayed by a fluid that the alien Christopher Johnson had spent twenty years synthesising as fuel for their ship, and he begins to turn into an alien. MNU scientists discover that his hybrid DNA lets him operate the aliens' biologically locked weapons, and his own father-in-law orders his body harvested. Wikus escapes and allies with Christopher, who reaches the mothership with his son and promises to return to cure him. Wikus, now fully transformed, stays behind. Genetics is central to the second half of the film. Exposure to the alien fluid rewrites Wikus's body, and MNU's laboratory finds that his partly alien DNA allows him to use alien weapons, which only respond to alien biology. MNU has long been carrying out vivisections and other brutal experiments on the aliens in search of this capability, and its executives treat Wikus as a source of genetic material to be harvested. The scientists are portrayed as instruments of a corporate weapons programme, indifferent to the suffering of their subjects, human or alien, in a story that uses the aliens' treatment to evoke apartheid-era forced removals in South Africa, such as those of Cape Town's District Six. The biology is not meant to be plausible: there is no reason to expect life from another world to share our genetic code, and no fluid could rebuild an adult's whole body. The film's interest lies in its picture of biological research serving discrimination and profit.

title: Moon
text: Sam Bell is nearing the end of a three-year contract as the only worker at Sarang, a lunar base where the company Lunar Industries mines helium-3 for energy on Earth. With live communications apparently broken, his only company is the base's computer, GERTY, and recorded messages from his wife Tess. After a rover accident, Sam wakes up in the infirmary, goes out against orders, and finds an injured double of himself in the crashed rover. GERTY admits that both are clones of the original Sam Bell, given his implanted memories. The older Sam is already deteriorating, as earlier clones did at the end of their contracts, and the two find a vault of hundreds of sleeping clones and a jamming system that blocks contact with Earth. Calling home, the older Sam learns that Tess has died and that the original Sam lives on Earth with their teenage daughter. The dying clone stays behind while the newer one escapes to Earth, where he becomes a whistleblower. Cloning is the film's central twist and its moral subject. Lunar Industries uses clones of one employee, each given implanted memories of a wife and daughter and a three-year lifespan, to avoid the cost of training and sending new astronauts; at the end of each contract, the clone believes he is going home but is incinerated. No scientists appear: the cloning is a corporate cost-saving measure, managed remotely, and the only helper the clones have is the base's AI, GERTY. The film's focus is on identity: the two Sams share the same genes and memories but differ in age and temperament, and their humanity is never in doubt for the viewer. Its science is deliberately simplified. A real clone would start life as an embryo and would have to grow up, rather than emerge as an adult copy, and memories are not inherited or transferable with DNA. Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born in 1996.

title: My Sister's Keeper
text: When their young daughter Kate is diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukaemia and no one in the family is a genetic match, Sara and Brian Fitzgerald conceive Anna through in vitro fertilisation as a "saviour sister". From her umbilical cord blood onwards, Anna donates blood and stem cells to Kate, at the cost of repeated hospitalisations and painful procedures. When Kate, now fifteen, goes into kidney failure, eleven-year-old Anna hires the lawyer Campbell Alexander to sue her parents for medical emancipation rather than give up a kidney. The case divides the family: Sara, who gave up her legal career to fight for Kate, cross-examines her own daughter in court. Flashbacks show Kate's romance with another young cancer patient, Taylor, and his death. At the hearing, Anna's brother Jesse forces her to admit that she refused at Kate's request, because Kate knows she would not survive another operation and is ready to die. Kate dies peacefully, and Anna wins the case. The film is built around a real reproductive technology: the saviour sibling. Anna is conceived by IVF so that she will be a genetic match for her sister; in practice, several embryos are created and tested by preimplantation genetic diagnosis, and only one whose tissue type (HLA) matches the sick child is transferred. No scientist is a character; the genetics is in the background, and the drama is ethical and familial. It turns on the objection most often raised against the practice, that the child is conceived as a means to an end, and extends it to a question the procedure itself does not settle: who may decide what is done to the donor's body afterwards. The first saviour sibling selected this way, Adam Nash, was born in the United States in 2000, and the practice is regulated differently from country to country; Spain authorised it in a 2006 law. Jodi Picoult's novel, on which the film is based, has a different ending, in which Anna dies and her kidney saves Kate.

title: Night of Desirable Objects
text: In Lansdale, Pennsylvania, a construction worker is dragged into a tunnel under a cornfield by an unseen creature, one of several unexplained disappearances in the area. Still recovering from a car crash, Olivia Dunham returns to work while Walter believes she travelled to a parallel universe; she begins to develop unusually sharp hearing. At the scene, Walter finds a blue paralytic substance that he suspects comes from mutated DNA. The investigation leads to local resident Andre Hughes, who says he lost his wife and baby in childbirth and refuses to give a blood sample. When the bodies are exhumed, the baby's coffin is empty, and Hughes kills himself before he can be questioned. Walter discovers that Hughes's wife had a form of lupus that made her unable to carry a child, so Hughes genetically altered the baby to survive. The child has grown into a creature that feeds on people; it is killed when its tunnel collapses. Genetic modification of an unborn child drives the case in this Fringe episode. Andre Hughes, desperate for his child to survive a pregnancy his wife's lupus made impossible, altered the baby's DNA, and the boy became a burrowing predator that secretes a paralytic substance and feeds on people. Walter identifies the substance as a product of mutated DNA. Hughes is portrayed as a parent driven by love and grief rather than a cold scientist, and his experiment shows the series' recurring theme of well-meant science with monstrous consequences. The episode reflects real anxieties about germline modification and "designer babies", but grossly exaggerates its effects: no genetic change could turn a human infant into a creature with animal traits within a few years.

title: Pandorum
text: With Earth exhausted by overpopulation, the ship Elysium carries 60,000 colonists in hypersleep on a 123-year voyage to Tanis, an Earth-like planet. Corporal Bower and Lieutenant Payton wake with partial amnesia in a dark, apparently abandoned section of the ship. While Payton guides him by radio, Bower crawls through the ducts towards the reactor and meets other survivors, Nadia and Manh, as they evade cannibalistic humanoid hunters. A survivor, Leland, explains that years earlier a crew member, Gallo, went mad with "pandorum", a deep-space psychosis, after learning that Earth had been destroyed, and that the hunters descend from passengers changed by an enzyme meant to help them adapt to Tanis. "Payton" turns out to be an aged Gallo. Bower restarts the reactor and learns that 923 years have passed and that the ship lies on the ocean floor of Tanis. Bower and Nadia escape in a hypersleep pod, and the remaining 1,211 pods rise to the surface. Genetics provides the film's monsters. The hunters are the descendants of colonists exposed to a treatment, described as an enzyme, that was meant to help them adapt to the new planet; after centuries in the closed environment of the ship, it has driven an accelerated evolution that produced a cannibalistic, predatory form of human. The idea combines two themes: the hubris of engineering humans in advance for an unknown environment, and the fear that evolution, once accelerated, might not lead towards anything resembling progress. The scientists who designed the treatment never appear, and the horror lies in its unintended consequences rather than in a villainous researcher. As biology the premise is fanciful: evolution acts on populations through selection over many generations, and no single treatment could steer a population towards a new form in a few hundred years, let alone within a lifetime. The film treats the mutants mainly as a horror device in a story about isolation and madness.

title: Splice
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: Clive Nicoli and Elsa Kast, genetic engineers at the company N.E.R.D., splice animal DNA to create hybrids for medical use, including two large worm-like creatures, Fred and Ginger. When their employers forbid them to move on to a human-animal hybrid and order them to extract proteins for drug production instead, they secretly create one. The creature, Dren, grows rapidly and develops gills, wings and a stinger, and Elsa bonds with her as a mother. At a public presentation Fred and Ginger kill each other: Ginger had spontaneously changed sex. On Elsa's childhood farm, where they hide Dren, their relationship with her grows increasingly disturbed. Clive has sex with Dren and reveals that the human DNA came from Elsa herself. Dren apparently dies, returns as a male, kills Clive and two others, and rapes Elsa, who kills him. In the final scene, Elsa, pregnant, accepts payment from the company to carry the child to term. Genetic engineering is the film's subject. Clive and Elsa build hybrid organisms by combining DNA from different species, and they create Dren out of scientific ambition and, in Elsa's case, personal need: she secretly uses her own DNA, which makes Dren in effect her genetic daughter. Their employer, interested only in proteins it can patent, is equally reckless and ends by exploiting the outcome. The story plays on familiar fears about biotechnology: hybrids with unpredictable traits, unforeseen changes such as the creatures' sex reversal, and scientists who cross ethical limits and lose control of their work. Moving genes between species is routine in real laboratories; bacteria carrying the human insulin gene have produced insulin for decades. But, as a scientist reviewing the film for Discover noted, creating a viable creature that combines human and multiple animal genomes, as Splice shows, remains very far off.

title: The Day of the Triffids
text: In an alternative present-day Britain, triffids, large carnivorous plants able to move and to kill with a venomous sting, are farmed worldwide because their oil has become a clean fuel that ended climate change. Bill Masen, who works with triffids,, whose mother was killed by one of the plants, is in hospital with his eyes bandaged when a solar storm blinds more than 95% of the world's population. With the electric fences failing, the triffids escape and begin to hunt. Bill teams up with radio presenter Jo Playton and encounters groups of survivors, among them a religious colony led by Durrant and the brutal Torrence, who seeks to impose his rule. At Shirning House Bill finds his estranged father Dennis, who plans to genetically engineer a new triffid to neutralise the old ones, but the new plant attacks and kills him. Bill finally remembers a childhood trick, triffid poison applied to the eyes, which lets the group pass among the plants and reach a colony on the Isle of Wight. This two-part BBC adaptation of John Wyndham's 1951 novel uses biotechnology at two levels. The triffids themselves are an exploited resource, farmed industrially for their oil despite their danger, and the series hints at the human arrogance of relying on a creature that cannot be controlled. The main genetic element is Dennis Masen's plan to genetically engineer a new type of triffid that could neutralise the existing ones, a technological fix for a biological disaster; his son considers the idea absurd, and the experiment fails when the new plant kills its creator. The scientist is a lone, obsessive figure working outside any institution after the collapse of society. In the original novel the triffids' origin is uncertain, but Bill suspects they were bioengineered in the Soviet Union, and some editions link them to the theories of the Soviet agronomist Trofim Lysenko, a proponent of Lamarckism whose ideas were thoroughly discredited. In this version the triffids are instead tied to a story about energy and climate.

title: Unleashed
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic engineering animal experimentation
text: Animal rights activists break into a laboratory and unwittingly release a creature, which follows them and kills them. The Fringe team, Olivia Dunham, Charlie Francis, Phillip Broyles and the Bishops, find marks from several different animals on the bodies, and a team of animal control workers is later killed too. When Charlie is attacked, Walter concludes that the creature is a man-made chimera combining traits of several species, including a lizard, a bat and a wasp. He had once tried to create such an animal without success, and the team learns that the creature was based on the work of one of his peers. One of the dead activists was the son of a scientist who carries out animal testing and had broken into his father's laboratory. The chimera has injected larvae into Charlie, who has less than a day to live. Walter, feeling responsible, confronts the creature alone in the storm drains and kills it, and its blood is used to cure Charlie. The episode is built around a laboratory-made chimera, an animal assembled from the genetic traits of several species. Walter Bishop, the series' scientist, admits he once attempted the same thing, and the creature turns out to be based on a colleague's research, so the episode continues Fringe's theme of scientists facing the consequences of past experiments. It also touches on animal research: the creature is released by activists breaking into a testing lab run by the father of one of them. The monster is pure fiction: combining whole body plans from reptiles, mammals and insects is far beyond any real technique. In real biology, a chimera is a single organism made of cells with different genotypes, for example from the fusion of two embryos, and artificial chimeras are produced for research rather than to combine features into a new predator.

title: Conviction
text: Based on a true story. Kenny Waters is convicted of the 1980 murder of a neighbour in Ayer, Massachusetts, on circumstantial evidence, testimony from his ex-wife and ex-girlfriend, and a blood-type match, and is sentenced to life without parole. His sister Betty Anne, a mother of two convinced of his innocence, puts herself through school and law school to become his lawyer, at the cost of her marriage. Realising that the new technique of DNA testing could prove Kenny's innocence, she contacts Barry Scheck of the Innocence Project. After a long search, she finds the blood evidence that was believed to have been destroyed, and the DNA results show that the blood at the scene was not Kenny's. The prosecutor still resists, but the two key witnesses admit that a police officer pressured them into lying, and in 2001 Kenny is freed. DNA forensics is what resolves the case, although the film is a legal and family drama rather than a story about science. Kenny was convicted when only blood groups could be compared, a test that can exclude a suspect but cannot identify one. Betty Anne's realisation that DNA testing can match blood to a single person is the turning point, and the decisive scene is the discovery of the stored evidence, which shows the importance of preserving biological samples after a trial. No geneticists appear on screen; the laboratory work is off screen and the expert voice is Barry Scheck's, co-founder of the Innocence Project, which uses DNA testing to challenge wrongful convictions. The case is one of the many exonerations obtained this way in the United States. The real story went further than the film: in 2025, further DNA testing identified Joseph Leo Boudreau, who died in 2004, as the murderer.

title: El Clon
text: This Spanish-language remake of the Brazilian telenovela O Clone, co-produced by Telemundo, RTI Televisión and Globo, stars Mauricio Ochmann and Sandra Echeverría. Jade, a young woman of Arab descent, goes to live with her family in Morocco after her mother's death and falls in love with Lucas, the son of a wealthy Miami businessman, who is visiting the country. Cultural and religious barriers keep them apart, and Jade is married to Said. After Lucas's twin brother Diego dies in an accident, the scientist Augusto Albieri, devastated by the loss, secretly clones Lucas and implants the embryo in a woman, Dora, who gives birth to Daniel. Twenty years later, Lucas and Jade are drawn together again, and Daniel, the clone, now identical to the young Lucas, enters Jade's life, creating a love triangle between the man she loved and his younger double. Subplots deal with drug addiction and Islam. As in the Brazilian original, human cloning is one of the central storylines. The scientist Augusto Albieri clones a young man in secret out of grief for his dead twin brother, implanting the embryo in a woman, and twenty years later the clone, Daniel, grows up resentful and searching for the man he regards as a father. The geneticist is portrayed as a lonely, obsessive figure whose private grief overrides ethics and consent, and the story deals with the identity of a person who is a genetic copy of someone else but has a different upbringing and life. The telenovela uses cloning mainly to set up a melodramatic love triangle rather than to examine the science. Human reproductive cloning remains unachieved and widely opposed; a clone would, as here, be a genetic twin born decades later, not a copy of the original's mind.

title: Extraordinary Measures
text: John Crowley, a Portland advertising executive, and his wife Aileen have two children with Pompe disease, a genetic disorder that typically kills children before their tenth birthday. John contacts Robert Stonehill, a researcher at the University of Nebraska who has done innovative work towards an enzyme treatment. To raise money for the research and the required clinical trials, John devotes himself to the cause full-time and the two found a small biotech company, which they later sell to a larger firm, Zymagen, to finance development. There, Stonehill's temper, rivalry with other research teams and the company's profit motives repeatedly threaten the project and John's hope that his own children will be treated in time. The film is based on the true story of John and Aileen Crowley, as told in the journalist Geeta Anand's book The Cure, with names and some events changed. The film deals with a real inherited disease and with how treatments for rare genetic disorders are developed and paid for. Pompe disease, or glycogen storage disease type II, is an autosomal recessive condition in which a missing enzyme, acid alpha-glucosidase, lets glycogen build up in cells and damages muscle and nerve cells throughout the body. The treatment the characters pursue is enzyme replacement therapy, which supplies the missing protein rather than correcting the gene. The scientist, Stonehill, is a gruff idealist devoted to basic research, while the companies are shown as driven by money but essential to bringing a drug to patients. A review in The Scientist found the story told with remarkable accuracy, though it noted that the sick children appear healthier than real patients and that the film tends to dismiss basic research as idealistic. The real drug, Myozyme, was approved in 2006, and enzyme replacement has greatly improved the outlook for people with Pompe disease.

title: Never Let Me Go
text: In an alternative history, a medical breakthrough in the 1950s has extended life expectancy beyond 100 years. Kathy, Ruth and Tommy grow up at Hailsham, an English boarding school whose pupils are encouraged to stay healthy and make art, the best of which is chosen for "the Gallery" run by the mysterious Madame. A new teacher tells them that they exist to donate their organs and will die young; she is dismissed. As young adults living in the Cottages, they learn that they are clones and hear rumours that couples truly in love can obtain a deferral. Ruth takes Tommy from Kathy, who leaves to become a carer for donors. Years later, Ruth, weakened by donations, reunites the three, admits her betrayal and dies. Kathy and Tommy become a couple and seek a deferral, but Madame and the former headmistress tell them that deferrals never existed: the Gallery was meant to prove that clones have souls. Tommy dies after his fourth donation, and Kathy awaits her own. Human cloning is the foundation of the society shown, but the film is not interested in how it is done. The clones are created and raised to supply organs, and the medical progress that allows ordinary people to live beyond 100 depends on their early deaths, which the system calls "completing". The real question is whether clones are fully human: the art collected at Hailsham was meant to prove that they have souls, and the guardians argue for better treatment while accepting the donation system itself. There are no scientists on screen; the responsibility lies with an entire society that prefers not to look. Some reviewers missed a fuller explanation of the cloning and the logic of this parallel world, while others have compared the clones' fate to that of farmed animals. Like the novel by Kazuo Ishiguro on which it is based, the film presents genetic identity as irrelevant to personhood; real cloning of mammals from adult cells became possible only with Dolly the sheep in 1996.

title: Sharktopus
text: The US Navy hires the geneticist Nathan Sands and his daughter Nicole to create a new weapon: S-11, an intelligent shark with the tentacles of an octopus. The creature is controlled by electromagnetic pulses from a device attached to its head, but during a test it discards the device and heads for Mexican waters in search of food, killing the people it meets. Andy Flynn joins Nicole in the hunt for the creature. After a long rampage, Andy shoots S-11 with a device that allows Nicole to hack the chip in its brain; she overloads it, the chip explodes and the creature dies. The Syfy television film was directed by Declan O'Brien and produced by Roger Corman. Genetic engineering is the premise of this deliberately absurd monster film. The Sharktopus is a cross between a shark and an octopus made in a private laboratory under contract to the Navy, and its creator, Nathan Sands, is a scientist working for military clients who loses control of his creation and then tries to cover up the damage. His daughter Nicole, also a scientist, ends up destroying the animal. The film follows the standard pattern of the creature feature, in which a hybrid made as a weapon escapes and turns on people, and it makes no attempt at realism. Sharks and octopuses are only very distantly related, a vertebrate and a mollusc, and their bodies are built on entirely different plans, so a functional hybrid of the two is impossible; real transgenic animals carry at most a few genes from other species.

title: The Bishop Revival
text: Fifteen guests suffocate at a Jewish wedding, all of them from the groom's side, whose grandmother survived the Holocaust; Walter Bishop concludes that the poison targeted a shared genetic trait. When customers with brown eyes die the same way in a coffee shop, fingerprints identify the killer as Alfred Hoffman, a Nazi scientist who is somehow still alive at over 100. Walter realises that Hoffman probably worked with his own father, Robert Bishoff, a German scientist who defected to the United States in 1943, on a toxin that, released as a heated gas, can be keyed to any trait using the DNA of the target, especially of those outside the "master race". The team finds Hoffman's laboratory and learns that he plans to strike a convention promoting world equality. Walter disperses his own toxin, tailored to Hoffman, and kills him. Peter later recovers his grandfather's papers, which include a photograph of Bishoff and Hoffman together. The episode imagines a genetically targeted weapon: a toxin that kills only people who share a particular inherited trait, such as brown eyes or the ancestry of a Jewish family. The villain is a Nazi scientist still pursuing the racial goals of the Third Reich, which places the story in the history of Nazi racial science, while Walter learns that his own father was involved in the original research before defecting to the Allies. The ending complicates the portrayal of the scientist as hero, since Walter uses the same technique to tailor a poison to Hoffman's DNA and kill him. The episode also reveals that the seahorse seen in the series' promotional images is a genetically encoded signature created by Walter's father. A poison that selectively kills people according to their eye-colour genes or ancestry is fiction.

title: The Gardener of God
text: This Italian drama, written and directed by Liana Marabini, follows the life and work of Gregor Mendel, played by Christopher Lambert, presenting him as a monk devoted to both prayer and science. Set in the Austro-Hungarian Empire of the nineteenth century, the film shows Mendel's struggle against the taxes imposed on monasteries and his efforts to convince others of the importance of his discovery about heredity. Mendel wonders whether faith and science can be reconciled, and whether his findings will benefit humanity or prove dangerous, since they could be used for eugenic purposes. His benefactor and friend, Princess Hanna von Limburg, supports him. Finally he publishes his conclusions and travels to the Vatican to meet the Pope, who welcomes his work. The film is a biography of Gregor Mendel, the Augustinian friar whose experiments with pea plants established the basic laws of heredity and who is regarded as the founder of modern genetics. It portrays the scientist as a man of faith for whom research and religion are compatible, and it has him foresee that knowledge of heredity could be misused for eugenics. According to Wikipedia's article on Mendel, his work, published in 1866, attracted little attention in his lifetime and was only recognised after 1900, when Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently confirmed his findings. The film's ending, with Mendel's work welcomed in Rome, contrasts with this history of neglect. The film offers a rare screen portrait of a real geneticist, told from a Catholic perspective.

title: Womb
text: As children, Rebecca and Tommy swear eternal love, but Rebecca moves to Japan with her mother. Twelve years later she returns and they resume their relationship. Tommy, an activist against biotechnology companies that are opening a park of cloned animals, is killed by a car on the way to disrupt its opening. Unable to live without him, Rebecca decides to have him cloned and to carry the clone herself; Tommy's father gives her his son's cells, despite his wife's objections. She gives birth to a son, also called Tommy, and raises him. Other parents shun clones, whom they call "copies", and Rebecca moves with her son to an isolated house. As an adult, Tommy increasingly resembles the original. When he brings home a girlfriend and the original Tommy's mother appears, he demands the truth; Rebecca gives him his predecessor's laptop, and he rapes her. The next day he leaves, thanking her for the life he has had. Womb is an intimate drama about human reproductive cloning used to bring back a lost loved one. Cloning is available in its near-future world, but socially stigmatised, as shown by the prejudice against children known as "copies". No scientist appears on screen; the film concentrates on Rebecca's decision and its consequences rather than on the technology. Its central question is identity: the clone grows up to resemble the original physically and in temperament, but he is a different person with his own life, and Rebecca's attempt to recover her lover through her son produces an impossible, incestuous relationship. The film thus explores nature versus nurture and the ethics of creating a person to fulfil someone else's wishes. Biologically, a clone is a delayed identical twin that shares its genome but not its memories or experiences. Mammals have been cloned from adult cells since Dolly the sheep in 1996, but human reproductive cloning has never been achieved.

title: 7aum Arivu
text: The film opens with Bodhidharma, a Pallava prince skilled in martial arts and medicine, who travels to China, cures an epidemic and teaches the villagers medicine, hypnotism and the training that gave rise to Shaolin kung fu, before agreeing to die there. In the present day, the Chinese government sends the mercenary Dong Lee to Chennai to start "Operation Red", a biological war against India using the same virus Bodhidharma once cured. Meanwhile, Subha Srinivasan, a genetics student, believes Bodhidharma's abilities can be revived in a descendant whose DNA matches his, and finds a match in Aravind, a circus performer. Her professor rejects her idea and turns out to be secretly helping Lee for money. Lee hunts down Subha, Aravind and their friends and kills several of them. During the final fight, Aravind awakens Bodhidharma's powers, kills Lee and cures the disease with an ancient remedy. Genetics provides the premise for this Tamil science fiction action film. A genetics student believes that a historical figure's skills can be reawakened in a living descendant by matching their DNA, a version of the idea of "genetic memory", and the genetics professor is shown as a corrupt scientist who collaborates with a foreign bioweapons plot. The threat that drives the story is a biological attack with an ancient virus, the same strain Bodhidharma once cured, rather than an engineered one. The film links genetics with national pride, presenting ancient Indian knowledge as the answer to modern science. The notion that abilities or memories acquired by an ancestor can be inherited and reactivated through DNA has no scientific basis; learned skills are not encoded in the genome. Commentators compared the premise to the Assassin's Creed video games, and a critic in The Hindu noted that the telepathy and hypnotism were "comic book stuff". The film was also criticised for historical inaccuracies about Bodhidharma.

title: Contagion
text: Back in Minneapolis from Hong Kong, Beth Emhoff dies of an unknown disease, followed by her young son; her husband Mitch is immune. As the virus spreads worldwide, the film follows several interlinked stories. At the CDC, Dr. Ellis Cheever sends epidemiologist Dr. Erin Mears to trace Beth's contacts, and Mears herself is infected and dies. Dr. Ally Hextall finds that the new virus, MEV-1, combines genetic material from pig and bat viruses; when a researcher in San Francisco defies orders to destroy his samples and finds a way to grow it in cell culture, she develops a vaccine and tests it on herself. A WHO epidemiologist traces the outbreak to Macau and is kidnapped by an official who wants vaccines for his village, and a conspiracy blogger promotes a fake cure, while society breaks down until the vaccine is distributed by lottery. A final flashback reveals how the virus jumped from a bat to a pig and to Beth. Genetics appears as a tool of virology and public health rather than as a theme in itself. Scientists identify the new virus by its genetic material, showing that it is a recombinant of bat and pig viruses, model how its mutations increase transmission and use that knowledge to make a vaccine. The film portrays scientists and public health workers in an unusually positive and realistic light: they are competent, overworked and willing to take personal risks, as when Hextall tests the vaccine on herself, while the obstacles come from bureaucracy, fear, misinformation and inequality of access. Made with advice from the virologist W. Ian Lipkin and the epidemiologist Larry Brilliant, it was praised by scientists for its accuracy. The chain of infection from a bat colony disturbed by deforestation, through pigs, to humans echoes the Nipah virus, which emerged in Malaysia in the late 1990s, and the film even uses a Nipah protein model on screen. Its relevance was underlined in 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic brought it renewed popularity.

title: Hanna
themes: human enhancement genetic engineering nature nurture human experimentation
text: Fifteen-year-old Hanna lives in the forests of northern Finland with her father, Erik Heller, a former CIA operative who has trained her since early childhood as an assassin. When she declares herself ready, she activates a beacon that alerts the CIA, and Erik leaves for Berlin. Captured and taken to an underground base in Morocco, Hanna kills a double of the CIA officer Marissa Wiegler and escapes, travelling across Spain and Europe with a British family on holiday while Marissa and the hired killer Isaacs pursue her. In Berlin she learns that Erik is not her biological father: he had recruited pregnant women into a CIA programme in which their children's DNA was enhanced to create super-soldiers, and when the programme was shut down all its subjects except Hanna were killed. Erik is shot dead by Marissa, and Hanna tracks Marissa down and kills her. Genetic enhancement is the secret at the heart of the story, revealed late in the film. Hanna is the surviving product of a covert CIA project that modified the DNA of foetuses to create super-soldiers with "high intelligence, muscle mass, and no pity"; when the project was shut down, the agency eliminated its subjects. The scientists remain off screen, but the programme is shown as a cold state enterprise that treats people as disposable. Much of the film's interest lies in the tension between Hanna's engineered nature and her upbringing: Discover magazine's Kyle Munkittrick called her a "transhumanist hero" who is nevertheless a good-natured person, and said she symbolises the contest between genetics and environment, nature versus nurture. Engineering complex traits such as intelligence or empathy in human embryos remains beyond current science.

title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes
alt: El origen del planeta de los simios
themes: gene therapy animal experimentation engineered pathogens pandemic
text: In San Francisco, scientist Will Rodman is testing ALZ-112, a virus-based drug intended to cure Alzheimer's disease, on chimpanzees at the biotech company Gen-Sys. The drug greatly increases the intelligence of a female chimpanzee, but she is shot during a rampage and the project is closed. Will secretly takes home her newborn son, Caesar, who has inherited the drug's effects, and raises him as he grows into a highly intelligent ape. Will also treats his own father, who has Alzheimer's, and the drug restores his mind until his immune system fights it off. After Caesar attacks a neighbour to defend Will's father, he is sent to a brutal primate shelter, where he becomes the apes' leader. Gen-Sys develops a stronger gaseous version, ALZ-113, which proves lethal to humans. Caesar steals it, makes the other apes intelligent and leads them to freedom across the Golden Gate Bridge, while an infected man unknowingly spreads ALZ-113 around the world. The film's premise is a gene-therapy-like treatment that goes wrong. ALZ-112 is a virus-based drug designed to repair the brain in Alzheimer's disease; in apes it boosts intelligence, and its effects are passed from Bright Eyes to her son Caesar. Will Rodman is a sympathetic scientist, motivated by his father's illness, but he cuts corners by testing the drug on his father and raising Caesar at home, while his boss pushes the more powerful ALZ-113 into further trials despite the risks. The result is both the rise of intelligent apes and a pandemic lethal to humans, setting up the later films. The film raises questions about animal experimentation and corporate pressure on research. Modified viruses are in fact one of the main ways of delivering genes in real gene therapy, but no treatment can create human-level intelligence in apes, and Alzheimer's disease still has no cure.

title: The Skin I Live In
text: Robert Ledgard, a plastic surgeon in Toledo, has created an artificial skin resistant to burns and insect bites, which he calls "Gal" after his late wife, who was disfigured in a car crash and later took her own life. At a symposium he privately admits to having carried out illegal transgenic experiments on humans and is forbidden to continue. In his secluded estate he keeps a young woman, Vera, captive, helped by his housekeeper Marilia, who is secretly his mother. After Marilia's other son, Zeca, breaks in and rapes Vera, Ledgard kills him. Flashbacks reveal the past: six years earlier, Ledgard's fragile daughter Norma was assaulted at a wedding by a young man, Vicente, and later killed herself. Ledgard kidnapped Vicente and, over years of surgery and transgenesis, transformed him into a woman resembling his dead wife: Vera. Finally Vera kills Ledgard and Marilia, escapes, and returns to her mother's shop to say: "I am Vicente." Genetic engineering is the instrument of an obsessive revenge. Ledgard develops a transgenic artificial skin, presented at a medical symposium as a potential treatment for burns, but he has crossed the ethical line by testing his methods on humans, and when the scientific establishment forbids him to continue, he carries on in secret in his own clinic. The film portrays him as a brilliant, respected surgeon who uses his skill to imprison and remake another human being without consent, combining transgenesis with surgery to change Vicente's sex and appearance into a copy of his dead wife. Science here serves personal grief, control and punishment, and the film raises questions about bodily autonomy and identity, since Vera's body is transformed but Vicente's sense of who he is survives. Almodóvar described it as "a horror story without screams or frights". The transgenic skin and the transformation shown in the film are fictional.

title: X-Men: First Class
text: In 1944, at Auschwitz, the Nazi officer Klaus Schmidt sees the young Erik Lehnsherr bend a metal gate with his mind and kills his mother to make his power appear. In 1962, Erik, now a hunter of Nazis, is tracking Schmidt, who calls himself Sebastian Shaw and leads the mutant Hellfire Club. CIA officer Moira MacTaggert enlists the telepath Charles Xavier, a new Oxford graduate, and his adoptive sister Raven, a shapeshifter. Charles saves Erik, and with the CIA they recruit young mutants, including the scientist Hank McCoy. Shaw plans to provoke a nuclear war through the Cuban Missile Crisis, so that mutants can inherit the earth. Hank develops a "cure" for mutant appearance from Raven's DNA, but it turns him into the blue-furred Beast. The mutants stop the war and Erik kills Shaw, but Charles is paralysed and Erik, now Magneto, leaves with Raven and others to lead mutants separately. Genetics underlies the film's premise rather than its plot. In the X-Men universe, mutants are humans born with a genetic mutation, later called the X-gene, that gives them special powers.
