Most of the story concerns politics and the Cold War, but genetic themes appear in Shaw's belief that mutants are a superior species, which the film sets against its Auschwitz opening and Shaw's Nazi past, and in the debate over whether mutants should hide or take pride in what they are. Hank McCoy, a young CIA-funded scientist, creates a serum from Raven's DNA to make mutants look "normal", which she refuses and which backfires on him, a parable about trying to "cure" difference. The X-Men have often been read as an allegory of minorities facing prejudice. Real mutations do not confer powers of this kind.

title: Cloud Atlas
text: The film interweaves six stories set in different eras, with the same actors playing different roles in each, suggesting souls connected across time. In 1849, an American lawyer befriends an escaped Moriori slave and becomes an abolitionist; in 1936, a young composer writes the "Cloud Atlas Sextet" for an ageing master; in 1973, a journalist uncovers a conspiracy at a nuclear power plant; in 2012, an elderly publisher is trapped in a nursing home. In Neo Seoul in 2144, Sonmi-451 is a "fabricant", a cloned human bred to work as a fast-food server. Rescued by a rebel, she learns that fabricants are recycled into the food that keeps the others docile, broadcasts the truth and is executed. In 2321, after a collapse of civilisation, the tribesmen of Hawaii worship Sonmi as a goddess, and a goatherd guides a woman from a technologically advanced people to a communication station. Genetics appears in only one of the film's six stories, but it is the one at its centre. In twenty-second-century Neo Seoul, fabricants are humanoid clones produced as an indentured workforce, and Sonmi-451 discovers that they are eventually recycled into the food that keeps the others docile. Sonmi-451's awakening and rebellion make her the founding figure of a later religion, and her story is the film's strongest statement against treating people as manufactured goods. The scientists and corporate leaders behind the system remain in the background; the film is concerned with the consequences of a society that classifies some humans as products. The fabricants are not a portrait of real cloning, which produces ordinary individuals rather than a servile caste; the story belongs to the tradition of dystopias in which manufactured people are treated as property.

title: Errors of the Human Body
themes: genetic engineering genetic disease animal experimentation human experimentation
text: Geoff Burton, a geneticist known for identifying the rare genetic condition that killed his infant son, takes a post at a research institute in Dresden. There he meets again Rebekka Fiedler, a former colleague and lover, who is working on what she calls the "Easter gene", which allows cells to regenerate and which a colleague realises could speed natural regeneration in axolotls. Burton discovers that another researcher, Jarek Novak, has stolen samples from Rebekka's laboratory and is injecting the gene into mice in a secret lab. Burton takes one of Jarek's mice, finds that it can regenerate, and is bitten by it. He becomes infected, gains an extraordinary ability to heal, but then learns that the treated mice are developing tumours, and that he may face the same disease that killed his son. Haunted by his grief, he tries to find redemption as his condition worsens; the film ends on an unexpectedly hopeful note. Genetics and laboratory life are the subject of the film. It deals with gene transfer between species, the mouse lines used to test it, and the fine line between regeneration and uncontrolled growth: the gene that lets cells regrow also produces tumours. Its scientists are ordinary researchers rather than villains: Burton is driven by grief and guilt, Rebekka by her research, and Jarek by ambition, stealing a colleague's work and experimenting in secret; reviewers note its attention to disputed credit, plagiarism and unethical experimentation. Director Eron Sheean developed the project during several years as artist in residence at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics in Dresden, where it was filmed in real laboratories with scientists among the extras and as advisers. He described it as fiction using real science as a starting point, and The Scientist reviewed it as more science drama than science fiction.

title: Maattrraan
text: Ramachandran, an Indian geneticist working for the Soviet Union, tries to create a person with many talents through "baby designing". The result is his sons Akhilan and Vimalan, conjoined twins sharing a single heart. After the Soviet collapse he returns to India and becomes a billionaire with Energion, a best-selling children's energy drink. The twins are drawn into a conspiracy when a Russian spy claims that Energion is adulterated and could kill thousands of children, and is then murdered. Vimalan is fatally attacked, and his heart is transplanted into Akhilan when the twins are separated. In the post-Soviet state of Ukvania, Akhilan discovers that Energion began as a steroid to boost athletes that left Soviet Olympians critically ill, a scandal covered up with a faked plane crash. He exposes his father, who ordered Vimalan's killing, and who admits that the twins are the product of his failed experiment, made from several talented people's DNA. Genetics frames the story through a scientist whose ambition turns criminal. Ramachandran's "baby designing" is an attempt to engineer a multitalented child by combining DNA from several gifted people; the result is conjoined twins, whom the film presents as the cost of his failed experiment. He first works for the Soviet state and later for himself, and his Energion business repeats the pattern on a national scale: an enhancement product that harms the children who drink it, which he describes as using the whole of society as his research laboratory, and which he protects by murder, including that of his own son. A review in Behindwoods notes that the film dwells on the adverse effects of genetic engineering "when man starts thinking himself to be God". The premise is fanciful: a person cannot be assembled from the DNA of several donors, and conjoined twins arise when a single fertilised egg fails to split completely, not from genetic design.

title: Prometheus
themes: engineered pathogens human experimentation evolution religion
text: In the distant past, a humanoid alien drinks a black liquid on a lifeless planet; its body dissolves into a waterfall and its DNA breaks apart and recombines. In 2089, the archaeologists Elizabeth Shaw and Charlie Holloway find matching star maps in several ancient cultures and interpret them as an invitation from humanity's creators, the "Engineers". The dying billionaire Peter Weyland funds an expedition aboard the ship Prometheus to the moon LV-223, where the crew find an Engineer structure, dead Engineers whose DNA matches that of humans, and cylinders of black liquid. The android David secretly infects Holloway with it; Holloway sickens and is killed, and Shaw, previously infertile, finds herself pregnant with a creature she removes by surgery. The base proves to be a military installation for a biological weapon intended for Earth. A surviving Engineer kills Weyland and prepares to launch, but the crew sacrifice themselves to stop him, and Shaw leaves to find the Engineers' home world. Genetics frames the film's question about the origin of humanity. The opening shows an Engineer's DNA breaking down and recombining in water, implying that life on Earth, or at least humanity, was seeded with his genes, and the expedition later confirms that Engineer and human DNA match. The same creators have developed the black liquid, a mutagenic biological weapon that rewrites living organisms and that they apparently intended to use to destroy humanity. The scientists on board are archaeologists searching for meaning, while the expedition is driven by a corporate magnate who hopes the Engineers can save him from old age, and by an android who experiments on the crew without their consent. The idea that intelligent beings deliberately brought life to Earth, known as directed panspermia, was proposed by Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel in the early 1970s, but there is no evidence for it, and human DNA fits within the shared genetic ancestry of all life on Earth.

title: Resident Evil: Retribution
themes: cloning engineered pathogens human enhancement pandemic
text: After an Umbrella Corporation attack on the ship Arcadia, Alice is captured and wakes in a vast underwater facility in Kamchatka, a former Soviet naval base where Umbrella mass-produces clones and stages simulated outbreaks of the T-virus in replicas of Tokyo, New York, Moscow and suburban Raccoon City to demonstrate its effects to buyers. During a power failure arranged by her old enemy Albert Wesker, she escapes with his agent Ada Wong while a rescue team led by Leon Kennedy breaks in from outside. In the suburban simulation Alice finds Becky, the deaf daughter of one of her own clones, who takes her for her mother. They are pursued by Jill Valentine, brainwashed by Umbrella's computer, the Red Queen, and by clones of Alice's dead allies. Alice frees Jill and escapes with Becky. At the White House, Wesker restores Alice's powers with the T-virus before a final stand against the Red Queen's monsters. Cloning and bioengineering are part of the film's background rather than its subject. Umbrella, a pharmaceutical company turned biological weapons maker, manufactures clones of Alice and her allies to populate its outbreak simulations, and some of the clones have false memories and family lives, raising questions of identity: Alice becomes a mother to the daughter of one of her copies. The T-virus and the Las Plagas parasite are engineered pathogens that create zombies and superhuman soldiers. Scientists appear only as anonymous employees of a corporation that no longer has any ethical restraint and is controlled by an artificial intelligence. The film treats cloning as an industrial process that produces adult copies on demand, which is pure fantasy: a real clone develops from an embryo and does not inherit memories. Its relevance to genetics is limited; it is primarily an action film built around video-game settings.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras human enhancement human experimentation
text: Years after his scientist father Richard disappeared, teenager Peter Parker finds his father's briefcase and learns that he worked with Dr. Curt Connors, an Oscorp scientist in the field of cross-species genetics. Sneaking into an Oscorp lab, Peter is bitten by a genetically modified spider and gains spider-like strength, agility and the ability to cling to walls. Connors, who has lost his right arm, is trying to regenerate limbs using lizard DNA, and Peter gives him a missing equation from his father's notes. After the murder of his Uncle Ben, Peter becomes Spider-Man. When Oscorp pushes for rushed human trials, Connors tests the serum on himself: his arm grows back, but he turns into a giant reptile, the Lizard, and plans to release a chemical agent that would turn the city's population into reptilian hybrids like himself. With help from Gwen Stacy, who creates an antidote, Peter stops him. Genetics is the origin of both hero and villain. Unlike the radioactive spider of the comics, Peter's powers come from a genetically engineered spider bred at Oscorp, and his father's work on cross-species genetics underlies the whole story. Dr. Curt Connors, the geneticist, is a sympathetic figure: he wants to use reptile DNA to help people like himself regrow lost limbs, and he initially resists his superior's demand to rush human trials, fearing harm to patients. The catastrophe comes from corporate pressure and from Connors's desperation to heal himself, after which he becomes a monster who wants to spread his transformation to everyone. Some vertebrates, including salamanders and some lizards that regrow their tails, can regenerate lost body parts, and researchers study the genetics of this ability for regenerative medicine. Transferring it with a serum, though, is fantasy, as is the instant and total transformation of an adult human body.

title: Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning
alt: Soldado Universal 4: El día del juicio final
text: John wakes from a months-long coma to learn that his wife and daughter were murdered in a home invasion, and FBI Agent Gorman tells him that the killer he remembers is Luc Deveraux, a former Universal Soldier (UniSol) who now leads a separatist group of rogue UniSols against the US government. Searching for answers, John meets a stripper, Sarah, who claims to have known him in a life he cannot remember, while he is hunted by Magnus, a cloned UniSol sent after him. John discovers that he has superhuman strength and that his severed fingers grow back. At a riverside cabin he finds an exact duplicate of himself, the man Sarah knew, and kills him. Deveraux's scientist, Dr. Su, reveals that John was synthetically created weeks earlier and that his family is an implanted memory. Driven mad, John kills Deveraux's followers and Deveraux himself, then kills Gorman and takes over the group, deploying a clone of Gorman to infiltrate the government. Cloning is used here as a technology for mass-producing soldiers. The government's UniSol programme produces clones of its soldiers, gives them implanted memories and conditions them to obey, and Deveraux's separatists need only stolen hardware to make clones of their own. The film's horror lies in the discovery that the hero's identity, family and grief were manufactured, and it treats a clone as a disposable copy that can be killed and replaced by another one. Scientists appear as technicians of this system: Dr. Su, a former programme scientist, now serves the rebels and offers to cut John's emotional ties surgically. The film does not explain its cloning in genetic terms, and its adult clones with implanted memories and regenerating bodies are pure science fiction. Its connection to genetics is limited to the general idea of copying human beings for use as weapons.

title: Age of Dinosaurs
text: In Los Angeles, the biotechnology company Genetisharp uses flesh-regeneration machines to create living dinosaurs and pterosaurs from strands of DNA. The creatures escape and spread through the city: a giant Ceratosaurus, raptor-like Carnotaurus, a Spinosaurus that climbs buildings and a Pteranodon. Gabe Jacobs, played by Treat Williams, is among those caught up in the chaos, which culminates in a final battle around the Hollywood Sign. The dinosaurs are finally destroyed when, drawn by a scent, they are lured into a collapsing building. The film was produced by The Asylum and directed by Joseph J. Lawson. The film uses genetics as the premise for a creature feature in the tradition of Jurassic Park. Genetisharp's technology turns ancient DNA into living animals almost instantly through "flesh regeneration", and the company is a familiar figure: a commercial biotech firm that shows off a spectacular product without adequate safeguards and loses control of it, with the city paying the price. No scientific detail is offered beyond this. In reality, recreating dinosaurs is not possible: DNA degrades over time, and the older and more degraded a sample is, the more fragmented its DNA, which is why even well-preserved woolly mammoth remains, only thousands of years old, yield little usable genetic material. Dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, far beyond the survival of DNA, and current de-extinction projects aim instead to edit the genomes of living relatives of recently extinct species.

title: Decoding Annie Parker
themes: real science genetic disease heredity genetic testing
text: The film follows two parallel stories over several decades. In Toronto, Annie Parker loses her mother to breast cancer as a child, and later her father and her older sister, Joan, who dies of the same disease. Married young to Paul, an aspiring musician, Annie is diagnosed with breast cancer herself, undergoes surgery and chemotherapy, and becomes convinced that the cancer in her family cannot be chance. Her marriage breaks down when Paul has an affair with her friend. Meanwhile, at the University of California, Berkeley, the geneticist Mary-Claire King sets out to show that some breast and ovarian cancers are hereditary. Despite the doubts of many in her field, she collects families with many cases of the disease and in 1990 links a susceptibility gene, BRCA1, to a region of chromosome 17. Annie survives two further cancer diagnoses. The film dramatises a landmark in human genetics: the finding that some breast and ovarian cancers run in families because of inherited mutations in a single gene. Helen Hunt's Mary-Claire King is a wholly positive portrait of a geneticist, a persistent researcher whose work with affected families eventually benefits patients like Annie. The method shown, family studies and genetic linkage, matches the record: King's group reported in 1990 that early-onset familial breast cancer was linked to markers on chromosome 17. The gene itself was cloned in 1994 by a team at Myriad Genetics, after a race between laboratories. The real Annie Parker, diagnosed with breast cancer in 1980 and ovarian cancer in 1988, was offered testing after the gene's discovery and tested positive, which she saw as proof that her family's cancers were not bad luck. Testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is now standard practice for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

title: Leela and the Genestalk
themes: gmo gene therapy genetic disease mutants
text: Leela breaks out in suction cups, and Dr. Tenderman explains that a genetic condition is causing "squidification": her limbs will gradually turn into a mass of tentacles, and only an expensive operation can delay it. Fry sells the Planet Express ship to pay for it, but comes back with two magic beans sold as a miracle cure. Thrown out of the window, the beans grow into a giant beanstalk. Leela climbs it and finds a flying castle where Mom runs a genetic engineering facility, creating giant beanstalks to feed the hungry along with flying fish and a unicorn. Leela condemns the experiments as crimes. Fry and Bender come to rescue her, by now fully transformed into tentacles, and free a giant held in the lab. Mom later reveals that Leela's suction cups helped her engineer the perfect bean and that she has cured the giant of hereditary gigantism, and she offers to cure Leela, who accepts. This Futurama episode, a parody of Jack and the Beanstalk, is a satire of the debate on genetic engineering. Leela suffers from a genetic condition, and the only one able to cure her is Mom, who modifies plants and animals in a laboratory in the sky. Leela, who opposes genetic engineering on principle, is forced to weigh her convictions against her own need: the episode mocks both the profit-driven industry and the purity of its critics, as Mom's work produces both monsters and real benefits such as a crop that can feed the hungry and a cure for hereditary gigantism. The giant beanstalks recall the real controversy over genetically modified crops, and the idea of gene therapy for inherited disease is grounded in real medicine. Squidification itself is a joke, but the episode's central question, whether to accept a technology one distrusts when it offers a cure, is a familiar one in bioethics.

title: Man of Steel
text: On the planet Krypton, whose population is bred artificially, the scientist Jor-El warns the ruling council that reckless mining of the planet's core is about to destroy it. He and his wife Lara have had a son, Kal-El, the first child born naturally in centuries; Jor-El steals the Codex, which holds the genetic blueprint of the Kryptonian people, infuses it into the baby and sends him to Earth before General Zod kills him in a failed coup. Zod and his followers are banished to the Phantom Zone shortly before Krypton explodes. On Earth, Kal-El is raised as Clark Kent by the Kents in Kansas and grows up hiding his powers. As an adult he learns his origins from an artificial intelligence modelled on his father. Zod, freed by Krypton's destruction, arrives seeking the Codex in order to turn Earth into a new Krypton, which would wipe out humanity. Clark, now Superman, destroys Zod's terraforming machine and finally kills Zod. The film gives Superman's origin a eugenic backdrop. Krypton is a society in which every citizen is bred artificially to fulfil a specific role, with a predetermined purpose written into their genetic code. The Codex, a repository of the genetic information of the whole species, is the key to this system. Jor-El's rebellion is to have a son by natural birth, free to choose his own path, and to hide the Codex in the boy's cells, so that Kal-El carries within him the possibility of rebuilding his people. Zod, in contrast, born from an artificial breeding chamber, is guided only by the purpose he was created to fulfil, the survival of Krypton at any cost, and wants to extract the Codex, which would kill Clark. The film thus contrasts genetic determinism with free will: Superman's freedom lets him make his own difficult choices, including the decision to kill Zod. Engineering people for social roles is pure fiction.

title: Oblivion
text: Sixty years after an alien invasion destroyed the Moon, Earth is said to be uninhabitable and humanity to have moved to Titan. The technician Jack and his partner Victoria maintain drones that guard machines converting seawater into energy for the Tet, a huge station in orbit, and their memories have been wiped for security. Jack dreams of an unknown woman. When a spacecraft crashes, he rescues one survivor, Julia, the woman of his dreams, who turns out to be his wife. Captured by the supposed alien "Scavengers", Jack learns from their leader Malcolm that they are surviving humans, and in the radiation zone he meets another Jack, number 52. The truth is that the Tet is an alien intelligence harvesting Earth, which defeated humanity using thousands of brainwashed clones of the astronaut Jack Harper and his colleague Victoria. Jack sacrifices himself to destroy the Tet, and later another clone of Jack finds Julia and their daughter. Cloning is a plot twist rather than a subject of the film. The central revelation is that the protagonist is one of thousands of copies of the astronaut Jack Harper, produced and brainwashed by an alien intelligence to serve as its workforce and army against the surviving humans. The film uses the clones to ask whether identity and love survive copying and memory erasure: Jack and a second clone both regain fragments of the original Jack's memories and his attachment to his wife. There are no scientists or genetic research on screen; cloning is an alien technology that is never explained. As in many films, the clones are adult copies that retain the original's latent memories, which real cloning cannot do: a clone is a genetic copy that would grow from an embryo and share none of the original's experiences. Genetics plays only a minor role in the film.

title: Orphan Black
themes: cloning eugenics human experimentation nature nurture gene therapy
text: Sarah Manning, a British con artist in Toronto, sees a woman who looks exactly like her, Beth Childs, kill herself, and takes over Beth's identity as a police detective. She discovers that she is one of many genetically identical women created by an illegal cloning experiment, Project Leda, and that someone is killing them. With her foster brother Felix and fellow clones Alison and Cosima, a graduate student, she uncovers the origin of the clones in Neolution, a movement that aims to direct human evolution through science, based in the powerful biotech Dyad Institute. The Dyad monitors the clones, who are sterile by design, and seeks to profit from them, while a religious sect, the Proletheans, uses Sarah's twin, Helena, to kill them. Sarah's daughter, Kira, the only known child of a clone, becomes a target for both. Over five seasons (2013–2017), the clones fight to win control over their own bodies and lives. Human cloning and genetic control are the centre of the series, which explores their ethical implications and their effect on identity. The clones share a genome but have very different personalities and lives, all played by Tatiana Maslany, making the series an extended reflection on nature and nurture. The scientists are portrayed in many ways: the Neolution movement and the Dyad Institute pursue eugenics and profit, treating the clones as property, and their DNA even carries a code declaring them "restricted intellectual property" with patent numbers; the original geneticists, Ethan and Susan Duncan, created the clones and later faked their deaths; and Cosima, herself a clone, uses science to understand and fight the disease that is killing her sisters, attempting a gene therapy. Other storylines involve a parallel male cloning project run by the military and a genetic chimera as the original source of both lines. The series had a science consultant, Cosima Herter, to keep its science plausible. In reality, the US Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that naturally occurring human DNA cannot be patented.

title: Star Trek Into Darkness
text: In 2259, after Kirk is demoted for breaking the Prime Directive, a Starfleet agent working for John Harrison bombs a secret Section 31 installation in London, and Harrison then kills Admiral Pike and other officers before fleeing to the Klingon homeworld. Admiral Marcus sends Kirk to kill him with 72 experimental torpedoes, but Kirk captures him instead. Harrison reveals that he is Khan Noonien Singh, a genetically engineered superhuman woken by Marcus from centuries of cryogenic sleep and forced to design weapons under threat to his frozen crew, hidden inside the torpedoes. Marcus, who wants war with the Klingons, attacks the Enterprise with the warship Vengeance; Khan helps Kirk board it, then kills Marcus and takes control. Spock tricks Khan, and both ships fall towards Earth. Kirk dies of radiation saving the Enterprise. Khan crashes into San Francisco and is caught by Spock, and his regenerative blood brings Kirk back to life. As in the 1982 film, genetics shapes the antagonist: Khan is one of the engineered superhumans of the franchise's "Eugenics Wars", revived three centuries later. This version stresses how the establishment exploits him. A Starfleet admiral wakes him, gives him a false identity and uses his superior intellect to build weapons for a planned war, holding his crew hostage. Khan is both a victim of that manipulation and a ruthless killer who regards ordinary humans as inferior. His engineered biology also drives the climax: his blood has regenerative properties that bring Kirk back from the dead, a fantasy of enhancement as a cure-all. No scientist designs anything on screen; the film's interest is in the danger of powerful people using engineered humans as tools. Real genetic engineering of people remains highly restricted: the only known gene-edited babies, born in 2018, led to a prison sentence for the scientist involved and to tighter laws in China.

title: The German Doctor
text: Patagonia, Argentina, 1960. A German doctor living under a false identity follows an Argentine family on the long road to Bariloche and moves into the hotel they run, paying six months' rent in advance. He is Josef Mengele, the Nazi physician of Auschwitz. He takes a special interest in the family's daughter, Lilith, who was born prematurely, is small for her age and is bullied at school, and offers to treat her with growth hormones. Her mother, Eva, agrees, hiding the treatment from her husband Enzo, who opposes it. Eva is pregnant with twins, which fascinates Mengele, who fills notebooks with observations on the family. Lilith falls ill from the hormones, and Enzo throws the doctor out, but when the twins are born prematurely, Mengele is the only doctor nearby and begins experimenting on them. A photographer in contact with Israeli agents tracks him, but he escapes by seaplane. The film portrays Josef Mengele as a doctor still obsessed with heredity, growth and twins, now applying his methods to an ordinary family. He measures and records Lilith and her relatives, offers hormones to correct her small stature, and is drawn to the twins, echoing his experiments at Auschwitz. Mengele is shown as charming, attentive and persuasive, which makes his eugenic views and clinical detachment more disturbing; the family's consent is won through Eva's worry for her daughter. The film is fiction built on real history. Mengele held doctorates in anthropology and medicine, was an assistant to the geneticist Otmar von Verschuer and, at Auschwitz, studied hundreds of pairs of twins, mostly children. He fled to Argentina in 1949, moved to Paraguay and then Brazil, and drowned in 1979 without ever facing trial; his remains were identified in 1985 and the identification confirmed by DNA testing in 1992. Director Lucía Puenzo adapted the film from her own novel, Wakolda.

title: World War Z
text: Former UN investigator Gerry Lane escapes with his family from Philadelphia as a zombie outbreak spreads, and they are taken to a US Navy ship. To keep his family there, Gerry agrees to escort a young virologist, Andrew Fassbach, in search of the origin of the outbreak, which might allow a vaccine to be developed. Fassbach dies accidentally on arrival at a US base in South Korea, and Gerry follows the trail to Jerusalem, which has walled itself in but is overrun. There he notices that the zombies ignore some people, such as an old man and a sick boy. After a plane crash he reaches a World Health Organization laboratory in Cardiff and deduces that the zombies avoid people who are seriously ill. To test his theory, he injects himself with a dangerous but curable pathogen and walks past a zombie unharmed. The discovery leads to a "camouflage" vaccine that allows people to fight back against the zombies. World War Z treats the zombie plague as an infectious disease, studied by virologists and the World Health Organization, but genetics plays a minor role. Scientists appear as both vulnerable and essential: the young virologist who is supposed to find the source dies almost immediately, and the solution comes from Gerry's field observations, tested at the WHO laboratory. The answer is not a cure but camouflage. Because the zombie pathogen seeks healthy hosts, injecting people with a dangerous but curable infection hides them, and the vaccine produced at the end is described as a hybridised meningitis strain with components of smallpox and swine flu. Its function is therefore to mask people from the zombies rather than to protect them from infection in the usual sense of a vaccine. The idea of hiding from one pathogen by carrying another is fictional, but the film's framing, with health agencies racing to trace the origin of a fast-spreading outbreak, reflects real concerns about global pandemics.

title: Helix
themes: engineered pathogens genetic engineering pandemic human experimentation
text: Helix is an American science fiction horror series broadcast on Syfy from 2014 to 2015. In the first season, a team from the US Centers for Disease Control led by Dr. Alan Farragut travels to an Arctic research station to investigate an outbreak. They discover that the Ilaria Corporation, which runs the station, is carrying out banned genetic engineering research and cares more about hiding it than about stopping the disease. There are two strains of the virus: Narvik-A is always fatal, while Narvik-B turns people into violent carriers who spread the infection. The outbreak was used to lure Dr. Julia Walker, a member of the CDC team, as an unwitting test subject. The station's director, Hiroshi Hatake, reveals that he is her father, a near-immortal over 500 years old, and that Ilaria is run by immortals who want the virus to control the world. The second season moves to an isolated island where a new outbreak occurs, with scenes set thirty years later. Genetic engineering and virology drive the series. The Ilaria Corporation's Arctic station conducts prohibited genetic research, and the virus at the centre of the first season is a designed agent: Hatake created it to activate dormant genes in his daughter Julia and give her a form of the immortality he possesses, while the corporation wants it as a means of global control. Scientists are on both sides: the CDC team tries to contain the outbreak, while the corporate scientists conceal and exploit it, and Hatake is an ambiguous figure who protects his daughter while serving his own aims. The show follows a common pattern in which a corporate laboratory releases a dangerous engineered pathogen. Real viruses can be used as vectors to deliver genes, but the idea of a virus switching on hidden genes for immortality, or making infected people violent, belongs to fiction.

title: Sharktopus vs. Pteracuda
text: Marine biologist Lorena Christmas finds an egg sac left by the original Sharktopus and raises the creature at a marine park owned by her greedy uncle. Meanwhile Dr. Rico Symes, head of Symodyne, the company that created Sharktopus, tests the Pteracuda, a barracuda-pterodactyl hybrid designed for military use and controlled by a chip in its brain. A Symodyne scientist, Vladimir Futon, hacks the chip and sends the creature to attack populated areas. Symes and his security chief, Hamilton, take the now grown Sharktopus from the park to fight the Pteracuda, and kidnap Lorena to help them. The two creatures battle and kill swimmers, divers, a plane's passengers and a television host, before Symes is torn apart by them. Lorena and Hamilton lure the creatures together with a disco ball and destroy the Pteracuda's chip, apparently killing both, but Sharktopus reappears in the final shot. Like the first film, in which a geneticist creates a shark with octopus tentacles for the US Navy, this sequel is built on the creation of hybrid animals for military use. The Pteracuda, combining a barracuda with a pterodactyl, is the work of the same company, and the film adds the fact that the original Sharktopus reproduced, leaving an egg from which a new creature hatches. The scientist figures are a corporate chief who sees the creatures as weapons and dies by them, and a rogue scientist who hacks one to cause destruction. Genetics is a premise only: the film does not show how the creatures were made, and it is a deliberately absurd monster comedy rather than a serious depiction of science. Hybrids between such distant animals, let alone an extinct flying reptile, are impossible, but the film makes no claim to plausibility.

title: Still Alice
text: Alice Howland, a renowned linguistics professor at Columbia University, begins to forget words and gets lost on a familiar campus shortly after her 50th birthday. She is diagnosed with early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease. Because the condition is inherited, her adult children face the choice of being tested: her elder daughter Anna tests positive, her son Tom tests negative, and her younger daughter Lydia, an aspiring actress, declines. As her memory declines, Alice uses her phone to quiz herself each morning and records a video instructing her future self to take an overdose of pills when she can no longer answer. She loses her job, gives a moving speech at an Alzheimer's conference and gradually fails to recognise her family. When she finds the video, she is interrupted before she can follow its instructions. Her husband John moves to a new job, and Lydia returns home to care for her. Genetics is central to the family drama. Alice has the rare familial form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease, caused by a single mutation inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so each of her children has a 50% chance of having inherited it. The film portrays the dilemma of predictive genetic testing for an incurable disease: Anna learns she carries the mutation, Tom that he does not, and Lydia chooses not to know. Doctors are shown as competent and humane, and there is no villain: the story is about how a family lives with a genetic diagnosis. The film is medically accurate on this point. Familial Alzheimer's disease is caused by mutations in at least three genes, APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2, and it accounts for only a small fraction of all cases: most early-onset Alzheimer's, like the common late-onset form, is not caused by any known mutation. The film is based on Lisa Genova's novel, and Julianne Moore won the Academy Award for Best Actress for the role.

title: The Amazing Spider-Man 2
alt: The Amazing Spider-Man 2: El poder de Electro
themes: genetic engineering mutants genetic disease heredity
text: Peter Parker's parents, Richard and Mary, are killed in a plane crash after Richard leaves Oscorp. Years later, Peter fights crime as Spider-Man while his relationship with Gwen Stacy falters. His childhood friend Harry Osborn returns to see his dying father, Norman, who tells him that his illness is genetic and that Harry will soon show symptoms. Max Dillon, an Oscorp engineer, falls into a tank of genetically engineered electric eels and becomes Electro, a being of pure electricity. As his symptoms appear, Harry concludes that Spider-Man's blood could cure him, but Peter refuses, fearing it could cause a dangerous mutation. Harry injects himself with venom from Oscorp's genetically altered spiders, which transforms him into the Green Goblin. Peter learns from his father's hidden video that Richard fled because he refused to help Norman develop biogenetic weapons. Peter defeats Electro, but Gwen dies in the fight with Harry. Genetics is woven through the plot, in the comic-book style of the series. Peter's powers come from the bite of a genetically modified spider created at Oscorp; Electro is the result of an accident with genetically engineered eels; and Harry Osborn's transformation is triggered by an inherited fatal disease, which he tries to escape by injecting spider venom from the same research. Oscorp is a corporation whose biotechnology serves the Osborns' interests and possible military uses, and Peter's father is the conscientious scientist who refused to collaborate on "biogenetic weapons" and paid with his life. The film thus contrasts the ethical researcher with corporate genetic research driven by profit and power. The idea of inherited disease is real, but gaining powers or curing a hereditary illness by injecting another organism's blood or venom has no basis in biology.

title: The Fly Room
text: The film portrays the relationship between the geneticist Calvin Bridges and his daughter Betsey, mostly set in the original Fly Room, Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit-fly laboratory at Columbia University. Ten-year-old Betsey spends time in the lab, where she meets the scientists and their flies and asks questions that help explain difficult scientific concepts; the film moves between the practical world of the laboratory and an imaginary realm where flies and humans mingle. The story is told from Betsey's perspective at ten and at twenty-one: as a young woman, remembering the time of her father's death, she comes to terms with her difficult childhood and with her relationship with him, and decides to build a life of her own with her fiancé, Ed. A coda features the real Betsey at the age of ninety-five, celebrating her birthday surrounded by her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. This independent film is one of the few dramas about the history of genetics. It recreates the Fly Room at Columbia University, where from 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan and his students, among them Calvin Bridges, Alfred Sturtevant and Hermann Joseph Muller, used the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster to establish that genes lie on chromosomes. Bridges's doctoral thesis, "Non-disjunction as proof of the chromosome theory of heredity", was the first paper in the first issue of the journal Genetics in 1916, and he is also known for his maps of the giant polytene chromosomes of fly salivary glands. The film shows science as curiosity and patient work, seen through the eyes of a child, but also explores what its makers call the irony of a geneticist unable to understand his own genetic role within the family; it closes with the real Betsey and her descendants as an image of heredity. The director, Alexis Gambis, is himself a biologist.

title: The Man Who Grew Too Much
alt: El hombre que crecía demasiado The Simpsons, season 25, episode 13
themes: gmo genetic engineering human enhancement hybrids chimeras
text: Lisa learns that the vegetables served at school are genetically modified and argues against them at a parent-teacher meeting, but further research convinces her that genetically modified foods can be beneficial. A biotechnology corporation interested in her campaign introduces the Simpsons to its chief scientist, who turns out to be Sideshow Bob, recruited as a test subject in prison. Lisa and Bob bond over their love of Walt Whitman and conduct food experiments together. Meanwhile, Marge is roped into giving a sex-education class to church teenagers. On a museum visit, Bob saves Lisa from a falling display with superhuman strength and reveals that he has altered his own DNA and plans to absorb the DNA of history's greatest geniuses to become the smartest man alive. Enraged, he chases Bart and Lisa with grasshopper legs and killer whale sonar until Lisa quotes Whitman and he realises he has become a monster. He tries to drown himself, but has given himself gills. Genetically modified food is the starting point of the episode, which first presents both sides of the public debate: Lisa begins as a critic, then becomes convinced that the technology can be beneficial, a relatively balanced position for a comedy. The story then escalates into a mad-scientist parody. Sideshow Bob, the corporation's chief scientist, uses the company's gene-modification techniques on himself, adding traits from animals and planning to absorb the DNA of famous geniuses, and he loses his humanity in the process. The corporation that hires a convicted criminal as its lead researcher is a satire of biotech companies. The episode was broadcast in Spain as "El hombre que crecía demasiado". In reality, intelligence cannot be acquired by taking DNA from other people, and adding animal traits to an adult human is impossible; the real debate on genetically modified crops concerns their safety, regulation and economic effects, which the episode touches on only briefly.

title: The Reconstruction of William Zero
text: After causing the accidental death of his son, the geneticist William Blakely wakes in a house cared for by a man who says he is his twin brother. William remembers nothing and must relearn the most basic things. The "brother" is in fact the William Blakely who works at the company Next Corp, where he has stolen material to create this new clone, William 2; meanwhile the company's cloned test animals are dying within weeks. William 2 discovers the truth and seeks out William's estranged wife, Jules. At Next Corp he learns that cloning a clone causes severe genetic problems, and realises from his symptoms that he is a second-generation clone. William 1 reveals that he too is a clone, made by the original William, William Zero, who abandoned his wife out of grief; feeling abandoned in turn, William 1 made his own replacement. William 2 saves Jules from William 1 and, knowing he will die, persuades William Zero to return to her. The film is a story about a geneticist who uses cloning to escape himself. Each William creates a copy to take over a life he can no longer bear, and the film follows the consequences: the copies are confused about their identity, feel abandoned by their makers and, being clones of clones, inherit worsening genetic damage that will kill them. Next Corp is shown as a secretive company whose animal experiments are failing and whose security agents treat the theft of material as their main concern. The idea that cloning damages the copies reflects real findings of abnormalities and high losses in cloned animals, although the rapid decline shown here is dramatised. The adult clones who must be taught to walk and talk are also a fiction: real cloning starts from an embryo. In the final scene William Zero and Jules are shown with a cloned version of their dead son, which turns the film's warning into an ambiguous ending.

title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
themes: mutants genetic discrimination human experimentation genetic engineering
text: In a dark near future, robots called Sentinels hunt and kill mutants and the humans who could have mutant children. The surviving X-Men, led by an older Charles Xavier and Magneto, learn that the Sentinel programme gained its government approval after Mystique assassinated its creator, Bolivar Trask, in 1973; she was then captured and experimented on, and her DNA was used to make Sentinels able to adapt to any mutant power. Kitty Pryde sends Logan's consciousness back into his 1973 body to stop the assassination. Logan recruits the young, broken Xavier, Hank McCoy and Quicksilver, and they free Magneto from prison under the Pentagon. Mystique's attempt on Trask at the Paris Peace Accords is foiled, but the public exposure of mutants persuades President Nixon to approve the Sentinels. At their unveiling in Washington, Magneto turns the robots against the government, but Mystique, persuaded by Xavier, spares Trask and saves the President. The dark future is erased. As in all the X-Men films, the premise is genetic: mutants are people born with an inherited mutation, the X-gene, that gives them powers. This film adds two more specific genetic elements. The Sentinels of the future target not only mutants but also ordinary humans carrying the genetic potential to have mutant children, a nightmare version of genetic screening and persecution by ancestry. And the decisive weapon is built from Mystique's DNA: after her capture, government scientists study her shape-shifting genome to create machines that can adapt to any mutant power. Bolivar Trask, the weapons designer behind the programme, experiments on captured mutants and serves the military establishment, and the film presents his work as the route to genocide. The X-Men are often read as an allegory of minorities facing prejudice. Like the rest of the series, the film's genetics is comic-book fantasy rather than a depiction of real science.

title: Z Nation
themes: engineered pathogens pandemic human experimentation hybrids chimeras
text: The series begins three years into a zombie apocalypse caused by a virus that has killed most of humanity. Shortly before society collapsed, Alvin Bernard Murphy, an inmate at a naval prison in Maine, was one of three prisoners given experimental vaccines in a government-approved trial; he alone survived the injection, and when the prison fell he was bitten repeatedly without turning into a zombie. His blood carries antibodies that may be humanity's last hope for a vaccine, but he is slowly changing into a blue-skinned hybrid of human and zombie able to control some zombies. A small band of survivors, led by Lieutenant Roberta Warren and guided by the hacker Citizen Z, sets out to take him across the country to a functioning laboratory. At a government lab in Colorado, the group meets Dr. Kurian, who claims to be their new contact but turns out to have created the virus; his own vaccine later fails. The series uses biomedical science as the engine of its zombie story rather than exploring genetics in detail. The apocalypse is caused by a virus, and the first two seasons revolve around experimental vaccines and the antibodies in Murphy's blood, which the scientists hope to use to produce a cure. Murphy himself is the product of a trial of experimental vaccines on prison inmates, and his slow transformation into a human-zombie hybrid makes him both a potential saviour and a threat. Scientists are mostly ambiguous or dangerous: the researchers who ran the prison trial abandon Murphy when the outbreak reaches them, and Dr. Kurian, revealed to have created the virus in the first place, uses the search for a cure to pursue his own ends. Reviewers and episode guides describe his vaccine as a failure. Like most zombie fiction, the series is not concerned with scientific plausibility, and its tone is often deliberately absurd.

title: Code of a Killer
text: This ITV drama tells the true story of the first use of DNA fingerprinting to catch a murderer. In 1983 and 1986, two 15-year-old girls, Lynda Mann and Dawn Ashworth, are raped and murdered near Leicester. At the University of Leicester, geneticist Alec Jeffreys discovers a way to produce a genetic "fingerprint" unique to each person, first used to settle an immigration case. Detective Chief Superintendent David Baker, convinced that one man killed both girls, asks Jeffreys to test the DNA of a local teenager who has confessed to Dawn's murder. The test proves that the youth is innocent and that the same unknown man committed both crimes. Baker then organises the first DNA manhunt, asking thousands of local men to give blood samples. The killer, Colin Pitchfork, evades it by having a colleague give blood in his place, but he is caught when the colleague is overheard boasting, and his DNA matches the crime scenes. Code of a Killer dramatises a key moment in the history of forensic genetics, with a real geneticist, Alec Jeffreys, as one of its two protagonists. It shows how he discovered DNA fingerprinting at Leicester in 1984 after noticing that a DNA experiment revealed both similarities and differences among members of a technician's family, how the method was first used in paternity and immigration cases, and how it was adapted to old crime-scene samples. The drama also shows the limits of the new science: the slow pace of mass testing and the police's doubts. Its most striking point is historically accurate: the first use of DNA in a murder investigation cleared an innocent suspect, a teenager who had confessed falsely, before it identified Colin Pitchfork, the first person convicted of murder using DNA evidence, in 1988. Several critics found the portrayal of Jeffreys as an obsessive, absent-minded "boffin" a cliché. The series was made with the participation of Jeffreys and Baker.

title: Hitman: Agent 47
text: Agent 47 is one of the "Agents", genetically enhanced assassins created by the geneticist Dr. Piotr Litvenko, who abandoned the programme out of guilt and disappeared. Now working as a hitman for the International Contracts Agency, 47 is tracking Litvenko's daughter Katia, while the corporation Syndicate International wants to find Litvenko to restart the Agent programme. In Berlin, Katia, who suffers from anxiety and a superhuman awareness of her surroundings, is searching for an unknown man. A Syndicate operative, John Smith, offers her protection from 47, but 47 captures her and reveals that she, too, is an Agent, designed by her father to surpass him; her name, Katia van Dees, echoes "quatre-vingt-dix", French for 90. Together they fight the Syndicate and find Litvenko in Singapore. Litvenko refuses to revive the programme and kills himself and the Syndicate's director with a booby-trapped inhaler, and 47 and Katia face another Agent, 48. Genetic enhancement is the background of the story. The Agents are designed people, engineered to be stronger, faster and more perceptive than normal humans and, in Katia's case, with heightened senses that she experiences as overwhelming anxiety until she learns to use them. The geneticist Dr. Litvenko is portrayed as a creator consumed by guilt, who abandoned his project and refuses, even under torture, to restart it for a corporation that wants an army of enhanced killers; he chooses death over handing them the technology. The film thus frames human enhancement as a weapons technology that its own inventor regrets, although the plot is mostly a series of action sequences and the science is never explained. Engineering complex traits such as speed, strength or perception in this way is fiction: no such enhancement of human beings exists.

title: Jupiter Ascending
text: Jupiter Jones, a Russian immigrant who cleans houses in Chicago, agrees to sell her eggs to buy a telescope. At the clinic, the staff turn out to be alien "Keepers" sent to kill her, but she is rescued by Caine Wise, a genetically engineered former soldier, half human and half canine. She learns that Earth and countless other planets were seeded by an alien dynasty, the House of Abrasax, to harvest their populations for a youth serum that gives the elite near-eternal life. Jupiter is genetically identical to the dynasty's dead matriarch and is therefore legally her reincarnation and the owner of Earth, which makes her a threat to the matriarch's heirs, Balem, Kalique and Titus, who each try to use or eliminate her. After escaping Titus's plan to marry and kill her, Jupiter refuses to cede Earth to Balem, who dies in the destruction of his refinery on Jupiter. She returns home, secretly retaining ownership of the planet. Genetics plays an important role in this space opera's worldbuilding. Jupiter's claim to Earth rests on the idea that a person with an identical genetic profile to a dead aristocrat is legally her reincarnation, an extreme form of genetic determinism that equates identity with genome. The universe also includes engineered human–animal hybrids such as Caine, part canine, and Stinger, half human and half honeybee, who serve as soldiers and servants, and an aristocracy that farms entire human populations as raw material for a youth serum. The egg donation scene links this fantasy to real reproductive medicine. There are no geneticists among the main characters; genetic technology is simply an instrument of a decadent elite. In biology, identical twins and clones share a genome but are distinct people with their own memories and personalities.

title: Jurassic World
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras de extinction cloning
text: Twenty-two years after the original Jurassic Park disaster, a fully working dinosaur theme park, Jurassic World, operates on Isla Nublar. Its newest attraction is the Indominus rex, a transgenic hybrid dinosaur created by the geneticist Dr. Henry Wu. Brothers Zach and Gray visit the park, where their aunt Claire is operations manager. Owen Grady, who trains Velociraptors, warns that the Indominus is dangerous and unpredictable. The hybrid, able to camouflage itself and mask its heat signature, escapes and kills its way across the island, while released pterosaurs attack the crowds. When InGen's security chief uses the raptors to hunt it, Owen realises that it has raptor DNA, as it takes command of the pack. In the end, the raptor Blue and the park's old Tyrannosaurus fight the Indominus, which is dragged underwater by a Mosasaurus. The island is evacuated. Genetic engineering drives the film. The park's dinosaurs are cloned from ancient DNA, as in the earlier films, and the new star attraction is a designed hybrid, the Indominus rex, whose secret design includes raptor DNA and gives it traits such as camouflage and the ability to mask its heat signature. When the park's owner confronts the geneticist, Dr. Henry Wu, over the design, Wu points out that none of the park's animals are what real dinosaurs looked like: they are genetically engineered, with gaps in their genomes filled with DNA from other species, as in the original Jurassic Park. A subplot with InGen's security chief, who wants to use the raptors as weapons, points to military uses of the technology that the sequels develop. Paleontologists criticised the film for its scaly, featherless dinosaurs, and the filmmakers used Wu's line to justify them. The cloning itself is impossible: the oldest DNA recovered is around one to two million years old, while dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago, and claims of dinosaur DNA have been dismissed.

title: Sense8
text: Eight strangers in different cities, Capheus in Nairobi, Sun in Seoul, Nomi in San Francisco, Kala in Mumbai, Riley in London, Wolfgang in Berlin, Lito in Mexico City and Will in Chicago, discover after the death of a woman named Angelica that they are "sensates", members of a cluster of humans mentally and emotionally linked to each other. They can sense one another, communicate across distances and share knowledge, languages and skills. Helped by Jonas, a sensate from Angelica's cluster, they try to continue their lives while being hunted by the Biologic Preservation Organization (BPO) and its agent Whispers, himself a sensate who has turned against his kind. Over two seasons and two specials (2015–2018), the cluster learns to use its abilities, meets other sensates and uncovers BPO's history and aims. In the finale, they capture Whispers to rescue Wolfgang, and BPO's chairman launches a global attack on sensates and their allies. The series was created by Lana and Lilly Wachowski and J. Michael Straczynski for Netflix. Genetics and evolution frame the series' mythology. Sensates are presented as humans set apart by a small genetic mutation, and from the second season as a related species, Homo sensorium, which in the show's lore lived alongside Homo sapiens; a professor consulted by Nomi and Amanita links it to the brain's capacity for empathy. BPO, originally founded to study sensates and to keep a balance between the two species, has become an organisation that hunts them for use as instruments of control. The series uses this framework less as science than as a metaphor for empathy, connection and the persecution of people perceived as different. The idea of a separate, interbreeding human species echoes real human evolution, in which Homo sapiens coexisted and interbred with Neanderthals and other groups, but a single mutation could not produce a shared consciousness.

title: Tomorrowland
text: At the 1964 New York World's Fair, a young inventor, Frank Walker, is given a lapel pin by a mysterious girl, Athena, which takes him to Tomorrowland, a futuristic city in another dimension founded by a secret society of visionaries. In the present, Casey Newton, an optimistic teenager who sabotages the demolition of a NASA launch platform, finds a similar pin among her belongings; touching it shows her Tomorrowland, but only for a short time. Searching for answers, she is attacked by robots and rescued by Athena, who turns out to be an Audio-Animatronic recruiter. Athena takes her to the adult Frank, a bitter recluse expelled from Tomorrowland, who has built a machine predicting the end of the world. In Tomorrowland, they discover that its governor, David Nix, has been broadcasting visions of catastrophe to Earth that have become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Athena sacrifices herself to destroy the machine, and Casey and Frank send new recruiters out into the world.

title: World of Tomorrow
text: In this animated short film by Don Hertzfeldt, a little girl, Emily, is contacted by a third-generation clone of herself from 227 years in the future, made as a way of achieving immortality. The clone takes Emily to her own time and shows her the ways people have tried to escape death and loneliness through technology, then guides her through memories of her life on the "Outernet". As a child, the clone visited a brainless male clone, "David", kept as an art exhibit until his death. She later worked on the Moon and in space, opened a gallery of memories harvested from the dead, and married a fourth-generation clone of David, whose sudden death left her grieving. Finally she reveals that Earth will be destroyed by a meteor within sixty days and that she contacted Emily to recover a forgotten memory of walking with her mother. She sends Emily home with advice to live well, and Emily goes out to play. Cloning is part of the film's premise. In its future, cloning is used as a means of achieving immortality, and the clone narrator describes her life as one in a series of copies of the original Emily. The film uses cloning to reflect on memory, loss and what makes a life one's own: each clone inherits memories but grows more remote from the original, and a brainless clone is displayed as an art object. No scientists appear, and the technology is described in deadpan, absurd terms rather than explained. Real cloning produces a genetic copy, not a continuation of the original's mind; the film's transfer of memories between clones is pure fantasy. The short won the Grand Jury Prize for short film at Sundance in 2015 and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film; two sequels followed in 2017 and 2020.

title: Zoo
themes: gmo mutants evolution genetic engineering hybrids chimeras
text: Animals around the world begin attacking humans in increasingly coordinated ways. Zoologist Jackson Oz, whose late father Robert had predicted an uprising of the animals, investigates with his friend Abraham Kenyatta, a Kenyan safari guide, the Los Angeles journalist Jamie Campbell, the veterinary pathologist Mitch Morgan and the French intelligence analyst Chloe Tousignant. They discover that the biotechnology company Reiden Global uses a "mother cell", a vector molecule present in its drugs, herbicides and animal feed, which has triggered a mutation in animals. Over three seasons the team develops a cure, sees it fail when the mutation evolves, and competes with a military plan to exterminate the animals, the Noah Objective. They learn that Robert Oz is alive and that a group called the Shepherds caused and tried to control the mutation. The final cure saves the world but leaves humanity sterile; ten years later, hybrid creatures have spread, and the team searches for a cure for human sterility. Genetics drives the series from start to finish. A biotechnology corporation's proprietary "mother cell", used in medicines, herbicides and feed, causes a mutation that accelerates animal evolution; the series speaks of a mutated "ghost gene", and the protagonist Jackson Oz turns out to carry it too. The search for a cure involves stem cells, gene delivery through mosquitoes or birds, and the risk that a fix applied to the whole biosphere has unintended effects: the final cure sterilises the human race. Later, hybrid creatures spread across the world. Scientists appear on all sides: the corporation, which hides its responsibility and is protected by the government; a secret group, the Shepherds, who both caused and tried to control the crisis; and the protagonists, a zoologist and a veterinary pathologist working against the clock. The series is an adaptation of a James Patterson novel and makes no attempt at realism; no single molecule could accelerate evolution in this way.

title: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
alt: Batman v. Superman: El amanecer de la Justicia
text: Eighteen months after Superman's destructive battle with General Zod in Metropolis, he has become a controversial figure. Bruce Wayne, who has fought crime in Gotham as Batman for twenty years, sees him as a threat to humanity, while Clark Kent condemns Batman's brutality. The industrialist Lex Luthor seeks permission to import kryptonite as a deterrent and, through a senator's subordinate, gains access to Zod's corpse and the Kryptonian scout ship. Luthor bombs a congressional hearing on Superman, steers Batman's paranoia and kidnaps Superman's adoptive mother, Martha, to force him to fight Batman. Batman defeats Superman with kryptonite but spares him on learning that their mothers share a name, and rescues Martha. Luthor then unleashes a monster engineered from Zod's DNA and his own. Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman fight it; Superman kills it with a kryptonite spear but is mortally wounded. After Superman's funeral, Bruce and Diana plan to gather a team of metahumans. Genetics plays a limited but decisive role, in the final act. Lex Luthor, a technology magnate obsessed with destroying Superman, uses the Kryptonian ship and General Zod's body to create a monster genetically engineered from Zod's DNA combined with his own; the creature, which Luthor calls Superman's "doomsday", ends up killing Superman. Luthor is the archetype of the corporate scientist-villain: brilliant, unaccountable and willing to use alien biology as a weapon, having manipulated government officials to obtain it. The film raises the question of how humanity should respond to beings more powerful than itself, and Luthor's creature is his answer, an engineered weapon that cannot be controlled. Genetics is used as a superhero device and the film makes no attempt at plausibility: no technology can combine the genomes of two individuals, let alone of different species, into a functioning adult creature. The creature corresponds to Doomsday, a character from the comics, although it is not named on screen.

title: Founder's Mutation
text: At the headquarters of Nugenics Technology, the researcher Dr. Sanjay, tormented by a high-pitched noise in his head, deletes data and kills himself, after writing "founder's mutation" on his hand. Mulder and Scully learn that Sanjay was worried that his "kids" were dying and find photographs of severely deformed children in his apartment. The company's owner, Dr. Augustus Goldman, known as "the Founder", runs a hospital facility for children with genetic conditions, where a patient makes objects move on their own. A pregnant woman who told the agents her baby was abnormal is killed and her fetus disappears. Goldman's wife, confined in an asylum, says he experimented on her during pregnancy and that she cut her baby out of her womb after it began communicating with her telepathically. The agents trace the source of the noise to a young janitor at Nugenics, Kyle, who wants to meet his sister. Taken to Goldman's lab, Kyle finds his real sister, Molly, and together they kill Goldman and escape. The episode centres on a genetics company and on human experimentation. Goldman presents his work as research on children with real genetic disorders such as Proteus syndrome, Crouzon syndrome, ichthyosis and Marfan syndrome, but the investigation reveals that he has been experimenting on pregnant women, including his own wife, producing children with telekinetic and telepathic powers whom he keeps in his facility. Mulder and Scully suspect a connection to the alien-human hybrid programme of the series' mythology, and the episode links the story to their own son, William. Goldman is the classic unethical scientist: protected by Defense Department ties, he treats his own children and his patients as subjects, and is killed by them. Real genetic conditions are mentioned accurately as conditions that cause physical differences, but the powers attributed to Goldman's subjects are fictional. The episode raises concerns about research on pregnant women and children without consent.

title: Men Against Fire
alt: La ciencia de matar Black Mirror, season 3, episode 5
text: Stripe is a soldier in a near-future army whose members carry a neural implant, MASS, that feeds them data through augmented reality. His squad hunts "roaches", pale, snarling humanoid creatures with sharp teeth. During a raid on a farmhouse, a roach points a small LED device at him, and afterwards his implant starts to malfunction. In an abandoned housing block he sees ordinary frightened people where his comrades see monsters, and he saves a woman, Catarina, and her son. She explains that the implant makes soldiers perceive her people as inhuman "roaches", and that they are victims of a genocide justified as genetic cleansing, while civilians, influenced by propaganda, see them as inferior. Hunter, Stripe's comrade, kills them both. The military psychologist Arquette reveals that Stripe agreed to the implant when he enlisted, and offers him a choice between prison and a memory wipe; Stripe, decorated, returns to a fantasy home that is in reality derelict. Genetics appears as the ideology behind a genocide. The military presents the extermination of a persecuted group as "genetic cleansing", a eugenic rationale, while the psychologist Arquette, who oversees the soldiers' implants, explains that the technology exists so that they can kill without hesitation. The episode's main subject is the technology that dehumanises the enemy so that soldiers can kill without remorse, but the justification it offers is explicitly hereditarian, and critics have repeatedly drawn parallels with Nazi Germany. Sophie Gilbert of The Atlantic wrote that the episode's depiction of eugenics links to prejudices still widespread, such as institutionalised racism, tribalism and fear of refugees. No genetic science is shown; the point is how claims about heredity can be used to justify the persecution of a minority.

title: Morgan
themes: genetic engineering human enhancement human experimentation
text: Lee Weathers, a risk-management consultant for the genetic engineering company SynSect, is sent to a remote research site to assess the L-9 project: Morgan, an artificial being made with synthetic DNA infused with nanotechnology. Only five years old, Morgan looks like a teenage girl and is more intelligent than her creators, but she has just stabbed one of the scientists in the eye. The team who raised her treat her as their child. When a psychologist provokes her during an evaluation, Morgan kills him, and Weathers decides she must be terminated. The scientists sedate Weathers and plan to escape with Morgan, but Morgan, believing they have betrayed her, kills most of them, including Dr. Cheng, whom she calls "mother". A recorded confession reveals that the scientists had tried to make her more human than earlier prototypes so she could surpass her design as a combat weapon. Weathers hunts Morgan down and drowns her. Company executives then reveal that Weathers herself is an earlier, emotionally limited prototype, L-4. Genetic engineering creates the title character, a "hybrid biological organism" built with synthetic DNA and nanotechnology to be smarter, faster and stronger than humans. The project belongs to a corporation that wants a controllable weapon, and its scientists, isolated at the site, are torn between seeing Morgan as a product and as their child. Their attempt to make her more human, with real emotions, makes her harder to control, and the experiment ends in a massacre. The final twist, that the company's cold consultant is herself an earlier engineered being, suggests that the corporation values obedience over humanity. Like many films about creations that turn on their creators, it raises questions about responsibility for engineered life rather than exploring the science in detail. Real synthetic biology is far more modest: in 2010 the J. Craig Venter Institute created a bacterial cell controlled by a chemically synthesised genome, and in 2016 a minimal cell with only 473 genes.

title: Terra Formars
themes: human enhancement hybrids chimeras human experimentation evolution
text: To prepare Mars for colonisation, humans seeded its surface with moss in the twenty-first century and released cockroaches to spread it. In 2599, a crew of misfits and criminals, promised pardons, is sent aboard the spaceship BUGS 2 to exterminate the cockroaches. On arrival they find that the insects have evolved into human-sized, intelligent, humanoid creatures of enormous strength. To fight them, the crew members inject themselves with DNA that gives them the abilities of different insects, from a bullet ant to an Asian giant hornet, a desert locust or a silk moth. One by one they are killed, while further doses make their transformations stronger, and a third dose becomes irreversible. The survivors discover that the mission director, Ko Honda, is communicating with the cockroaches and has his own plans. In the end, only two crew members escape Mars, while on Earth Honda kills a colleague who tries to shoot him. The film, Takashi Miike's adaptation of the manga by Yū Sasuga and Kenichi Tachibana, combines two ideas linked to genetics. First, the cockroaches released on Mars have evolved, in a few centuries, into giant humanoids, a story of accelerated evolution far beyond anything real natural selection could produce. Second, the crew are given injections of insect DNA that let them transform into human-insect hybrids with the abilities of particular species, all of them real insects whose traits, such as the bombardier beetle's chemical spray, are exaggerated for battle. The scientists and officials who planned the mission treat the crew, criminals and outcasts, as expendable test subjects, and the director turns out to have secret aims of his own. Scientifically the idea of gaining another species' traits by injection is fantasy: introducing genes into an adult would not reshape the body in seconds, and insect anatomy does not scale up to human size.

title: The Divergent Series: Allegiant
themes: eugenics genetic discrimination genetic engineering human experimentation
text: The third film in the Divergent series. In a walled, post-apocalyptic Chicago, Tris Prior, Four and a few companions escape over the wall into the wasteland. They are rescued and taken to a hidden, technologically advanced city, the headquarters of the Bureau of Genetic Welfare. Its leader, David, explains that humanity's attempts to fix its problems through genetic tampering sparked the Purity Wars, and that the Bureau runs experiments in isolated cities, Chicago among them, to restore a genetically "pure" population. Tris is the first pure individual to emerge. While she works with David, Four discovers that the Bureau kidnaps children from the wasteland and erases their memories. When David tries to use amnesia gas to wipe the memories of Chicago's warring factions, Tris and Four stop the attack, and Tris broadcasts to the world that Chicago was an experiment in genetic purity. This is the film in the series where genetics becomes explicit. The whole society of Chicago turns out to be an experiment: the Bureau of Genetic Welfare believes that past genetic modification damaged human nature and is trying to breed people with a restored, "pure" genome, and Tris is its first fully "pure" result. People with damaged genes are treated as inferior, and Tris finally condemns the division between pure and damaged as no better than the factions. The geneticist-administrators of the Bureau are cold technocrats who justify manipulation, child abductions and memory erasure in the name of genetic welfare, and its leader, David, is the villain. The film thus links genetic engineering and eugenic attempts to correct it to a single critique of social control by genetic labels. The notion that traits such as courage or independent thinking can be "repaired" by restoring a pure genome has no basis in genetics.

title: Blade Runner 2049
text: In 2049 Los Angeles, bioengineered humans called replicants are still used as slave labour. K, a replicant blade runner for the police, kills a rogue replicant and finds the remains of a female replicant who died in childbirth, proof that replicants can reproduce, which was thought impossible. His superior orders him to find and kill the child to prevent a war. At the Wallace Corporation, the replicant manufacturer, DNA archives identify the dead woman as Rachael, who had a relationship with the former blade runner Rick Deckard; Niander Wallace wants the secret of replicant reproduction to supply slave labour for colonising space. K finds records of two children born on the same day with identical DNA but different sexes, and comes to believe he is Rachael's son. He finds Deckard, but learns from the replicant resistance that the child was a girl. Realising that she is the memory designer Dr. Ana Stelline, K rescues Deckard from Wallace and takes him to meet his daughter before dying. Genetics underpins the film. Replicants are bioengineered humans made by a corporation, and the story turns on the discovery that two of them conceived a child naturally, which would end the line between manufactured and born beings. Niander Wallace, the industrialist who builds replicants, is a ruthless figure who wants to unlock replicant reproduction to breed slave labour on an industrial scale. DNA records are a key investigative tool: K searches DNA archives, and the birth records have been falsified so that two children appear to share identical DNA despite being of different sexes, a clue that something has been tampered with, since identical DNA would imply the same sex chromosomes. The film is less interested in the science of making replicants than in what it means to be born rather than made. As in the 1982 original, replicants are engineered as whole adults, which is beyond any real biotechnology.

title: Duel
text: This Korean crime thriller, broadcast on OCN in sixteen episodes, follows Jang Deuk-cheon, a hardened police detective whose eleven-year-old daughter, Soo-yeon, is kidnapped. His only clue is that two men with the same face were seen at the crime scene. Both turn out to be human clones played by the same actor: Lee Sung-joon, a gentle young man with amnesia who is accused of murder, and Lee Sung-hoon, a ruthless serial killer responsible for the kidnapping. Prosecutor Choi Jo-hye leads the search for the girl and draws Deuk-cheon into manipulating the case. Framed, Deuk-cheon and Sung-joon go on the run together and gradually bond while uncovering the mystery of the clones, their purpose and their connection to the detective. Human cloning is the premise of the series. Two clones who share the same genome are given opposite personalities, one kind and the other a killer, and the drama uses them to ask how far identity is determined by genes, a nature-versus-nurture theme often found in cloning stories. The kidnapping investigation gradually leads to the origin of the clones and to the people who created them, a mystery that drives the series. Reviewers singled out Yang Se-jong's double performance as the two clones. Because the available sources in English and Korean describe mainly the premise and characters, this summary does not cover the details of the cloning project or the ending. Real clones would be genetically identical but distinct individuals, like identical twins, and their personalities would depend on their different lives.

title: Logan
themes: genetic engineering cloning human experimentation mutants gmo
text: In 2029, no mutants have been born for 25 years. An aging Logan, slowly poisoned by his adamantium skeleton, works as a limousine driver near El Paso and, with the mutant Caliban, cares for Charles Xavier, whose dementia causes dangerous telepathic seizures. A former nurse, Gabriela, asks Logan to take a girl, Laura, to Eden, a supposed refuge near the Canadian border. Laura turns out to have powers like his own: she was created by the company Alkali-Transigen from his DNA, one of several children bred as weapons, whom the company planned to kill when it could not control them. Pursued by the company's Reavers and by its head, Dr. Zander Rice, Logan, Laura and Charles flee north. Rice unleashes X-24, a feral clone of Logan, who kills Charles. Logan finally reaches the escaped children and, mortally wounded, helps them cross the border. Laura shoots X-24 with an adamantium bullet, and Logan dies in her arms. Genetics drives the plot.
