Alkali-Transigen grows mutant children from stored mutant DNA, as weapons, and when they prove hard to control it plans to dispose of them; X-24 is a clone of Logan grown as the perfect soldier. The company's head, Dr. Zander Rice, has a personal grudge against Logan, who killed his father, and he reveals that the end of mutant births is no accident: the company has suppressed the mutant gene through genetically engineered crops distributed in the food supply. Scientists here are servants of a corporate-military project who treat children as products, while the nurses who help them escape provide the film's moral counterweight. Laura is Logan's genetic daughter, and the film explores whether biology makes them a family; his last words urge her not to become the weapon she was made to be. Using crops to silence a gene across a population is pure fiction, but the film's themes echo real fears about the commercial and military control of genetic technologies.

title: Okja
text: In 2007, Lucy Mirando, the new head of the Mirando Corporation, presents herself as an environmentalist and announces a "super pig" programme: 26 piglets are sent to farmers around the world, and ten years later the best specimen will be chosen. In 2017, Mija, a girl living in the South Korean mountains with her grandfather, has grown up with the super pig Okja, a huge, intelligent and affectionate animal. When the company's spokesman, the zoologist Johnny Wilcox, chooses Okja as the winner and takes her to New York, Mija sets out to rescue her. The Animal Liberation Front intercepts the transport and, without Mija's real consent, lets Okja be recaptured with a camera hidden on her, recording how she is forcibly bred and sampled for meat in a laboratory. After the footage is exposed at a public event, Okja is taken to a slaughterhouse, where Mija buys her life from Lucy's twin sister Nancy with a gold pig figurine and returns home with Okja and a rescued piglet. Okja is a satire of the meat industry built around a genetically modified animal. The Mirando Corporation presents its super pigs as a natural, environmentally friendly discovery, raised by traditional farmers around the world, but the animals are genetically modified, and the green marketing hides intensive breeding, painful experiments and industrial slaughter. The scientist figure is Dr. Johnny Wilcox, a zoologist who acts as the company's spokesman, and the company's leaders, the twin sisters Lucy and Nancy Mirando, are shown as cynical, focused on public image or on profit. The film does not reject genetic engineering as such, but asks what it means to create a sentient animal only as a product; Bong Joon Ho said the film was about capitalism, and he and producer Dooho Choi temporarily became vegans after visiting a slaughterhouse.

title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
text: Based on Rebecca Skloot's bestselling book, this HBO film follows Deborah Lacks, played by Oprah Winfrey, in search of the truth about her mother, Henrietta, who died of cervical cancer in 1951 when Deborah was a small child. Doctors at Johns Hopkins took cells from Henrietta's tumour without her knowledge, and they became HeLa, the first human cell line able to survive and multiply indefinitely, used ever since in medical research, including tests of the first polio vaccine. Her family learned this only decades later and was never compensated. The story is told largely from the point of view of journalist Rebecca Skloot, played by Rose Byrne, who wins Deborah's trust while researching the book. Together they try to extract information from an indifferent medical establishment, while Deborah struggles with her family's complicated history, its distrust of researchers, and her desire to know the mother she lost. Flashbacks show Henrietta's life and illness. The film concerns cell biology and research ethics rather than heredity in the narrow sense, but its story is central to modern genetics and biomedicine. HeLa cells, taken without consent in 1951 and cultured by George Gey, became the first immortalised human cell line and a basic tool of research, used to test the first polio vaccine and in countless other studies. Researchers are shown from the family's point of view: some are dismissive, and one in the film says the family "wouldn't have understood anyway"; the family had also given blood for research while believing they were being tested for cancer. The film raises questions of consent, race, class and profit in medical research. Genetic privacy became part of the real story after the events of the book: in 2013 researchers published the genome of HeLa cells without the family's knowledge, and after objections the US National Institutes of Health agreed to give the family a say in access to the data.

title: USS Callister
text: Robert Daly, the brilliant but socially awkward co-founder and chief technical officer of the company that makes the virtual reality game Infinity, is ignored and belittled by his colleagues. In secret, he runs a modified version of the game based on his favourite TV show, Space Fleet, in which he is the heroic captain of the starship USS Callister and his crew are sentient digital clones of his co-workers, created from DNA he has collected from objects such as a discarded coffee cup. Inside the game, he humiliates and tortures them. When he clones the new programmer Nanette Cole, she refuses to submit and organises an escape: the crew blackmail the real Nanette into stealing the DNA samples from Daly's apartment, then steer the ship into a wormhole leading to the game's online update, hoping to be deleted. Instead they survive in the public version of the game, free, while Daly is trapped in his own build as it shuts down. DNA is the episode's plot device: Daly creates conscious digital copies of real people from genetic material taken from a coffee cup or a child's lollipop, and the copies retain their originals' memories and personalities. The episode uses this to ask whether such copies are people and what is owed to them, and to portray abuse of power: as long as Daly keeps the samples, he can recreate and punish his victims at will. Daly is not a geneticist but a programmer who misuses biological data, and his downfall comes when his creations turn his own tools against him. The premise is scientifically impossible, a point several critics raised: a genome contains no memories, and DNA alone cannot reproduce a person's mind; an early draft explained the memories with a recording implant, an idea Charlie Brooker dropped as too much detail.

title: Andover
text: Adam Slope, a genetics professor, marries Dawn, a free-spirited glass artist, and they take out large life insurance policies on each other. When Dawn dies in a fire at her studio, the grieving Adam uses hairs from her hairbrush to clone her in his lab, helped by his graduate student Emma. The clones are born as babies and age to adulthood within a few months, but none of them looks and behaves exactly like the original Dawn, and Adam kills each one that falls short, including one who falls in love with her high-school boyfriend. Emma, who loves Adam, secretly clones him. A suspicious insurance investigator uncovers the clones and tries to blackmail Adam, who poisons and clones him too. Finally Dawn's parents raise a clone as they raised their daughter; she becomes like the original but does not love Adam. Adam gives up, ends up with Emma, and the cloned Adam and Dawn fall in love and marry. Human cloning drives this romantic comedy, and the scientist is its protagonist: a genetics professor who uses his laboratory to bring back his dead wife. The film is largely about the limits of genetic determinism. Each clone of Dawn shares her genome but develops a different personality depending on who raises her and what she experiences, and only the clone brought up by Dawn's own parents comes close to the original, even then without her feelings for Adam. The film presents Adam's quest as an obsession that leads him to kill his "faulty" clones, while his student Emma regrets that he is not using his research to help others, though she too misuses cloning for personal ends. Accelerated growth from baby to adult within months is fiction, but the central idea, that a clone would be a separate person shaped by its own upbringing, is consistent with real biology.

title: Annihilation
text: Lena, a cell biology professor and former soldier, is interrogated about an expedition into "the Shimmer", an expanding zone around a lighthouse on the Florida coast, where a meteor struck three years earlier. Her husband Kane, a soldier, had returned home from an earlier expedition, gravely ill and confused. Lena joins a team of women led by the psychologist Dr. Ventress, with Josie, Cassie and Anya. Inside, they lose track of time, find hybrid plants and animals, an alligator with shark-like rows of teeth, and a video showing the fate of Kane's team. A mutated bear kills Cassie and later Anya, and Josie, who theorises that the Shimmer refracts all living things, including their DNA, lets herself turn into a plant-like figure. At the lighthouse, Lena learns that Kane killed himself and that his double returned in his place, and a copy of herself forms from her blood. She destroys it with a grenade, and the Shimmer vanishes. Biology, rather than genetics in a strict sense, is the core of the film, in which biology and physics merge in a strange world. Inside the Shimmer, an alien presence refracts living things "the way a prism refracts light", including their DNA, so that species mix: plants take human shapes, animals combine traits, a soldier's body becomes a colony of lichens, and a bear absorbs a dying woman's voice. Lena, a cell biologist, provides the scientific point of view, while Ventress, who has cancer, is drawn to the Shimmer as to a kind of transformation. Scientists are portrayed as curious and courageous professionals, each also driven by personal damage. The film is not intended as a plausible scenario: DNA from different organisms does not blend in this way. Its imagery of uncontrolled cell division and mutation invites comparison with cancer, a reading the film encourages through Ventress's illness.

title: Chimera Strain
themes: hybrids chimeras genetic disease cloning genetic engineering
text: Quint, a brilliant but unstable geneticist, works in secret in an abandoned research facility to save his children, Miles and Flora, who have a deadly degenerative genetic disease. He has frozen them in cryptobiosis and also keeps the comatose body of his estranged wife, Jessie, in the facility, while pills allow him to see his family in his mind. His research centres on the DNA of Turritopsis, the "immortal" jellyfish, which he hopes to combine with human DNA in a chimera able to regenerate. Because stem cell research is illegal, he depends on a ruthless backer, played by Kathleen Quinlan, who wants him to cure her own monstrous son. A former colleague and lover, Charlie, visits him and becomes involved in his work. In a final twist, she turns out to have come to steal his research, carrying an embryo out of the lab in her own body, and Quint is arrested for his experiments. The film was first shown at festivals as Chimera. Genetics is at the heart of the film, which follows a geneticist's obsessive attempt to cure his children's inherited disease by creating a human-jellyfish chimera with the jellyfish's capacity to regenerate. Quint is a sympathetic but morally compromised scientist driven by grief: he farms cloned animals and human embryos, works outside the law in a setting where stem cell research is banned, and depends on an unscrupulous financier. His downfall comes not from the science itself but from betrayal, as a colleague steals his work and leaves him to be jailed. Reviewers found the science sketchy, describing it as hints and pseudo-scientific doubletalk. The real Turritopsis dohrnii, known as the immortal jellyfish, is one of the few animals able to revert from its sexually mature stage to an immature polyp, and its life cycle is studied with genetic tools; but transferring such an ability to humans through a chimera is pure fiction. The film also loosely borrows the character names of Henry James's The Turn of the Screw.

title: Elizabeth Harvest
text: Elizabeth, a young bride, arrives at the isolated, luxurious house of her much older husband, the scientist Dr. Henry Kellenberg, where only the housekeeper Claire and Henry's blind adult son Oliver live. Henry tells her she may enter every room except one in the basement. Curiosity wins, and she finds clones of herself; Henry discovers her disobedience and murders her. Six weeks later, another Elizabeth arrives and follows the same path, but she kills Henry first. Oliver makes her read Claire's journal, which reveals that the original Elizabeth was Henry's wife, who died of a rare illness, and that Henry hired Claire, a biologist, to help him clone her. He then relived his wedding night with each clone before killing her. The journal also suggests that Oliver is a clone of Henry. After a further clone kills Oliver and the fifth Elizabeth, the last one returns the journal to Claire, urging her to use her research better, and leaves to live her own life. Human cloning is the core of this horror thriller, a reworking of the Bluebeard folktale in which the forbidden room hides a laboratory of clones. The scientist, Henry Kellenberg, is a wealthy man who uses cloning to recreate his dead wife over and over, treating each copy as a possession to be enjoyed and destroyed; the film ties his science to possessiveness and abuse. His collaborator, the biologist Claire, is complicit but horrified once she understands his purpose, and the ending charges her to put her research to better use. The film also raises the question of identity, since each clone shares the original's genome but is a separate person who can make different choices, and the last one claims her own life. Adult clones produced quickly with the original's appearance are a dramatic device; a real clone would start as an embryo and grow up as a much younger twin.

title: Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom
themes: genetic engineering cloning hybrids chimeras de extinction
text: Three years after the Jurassic World park closed, a volcano threatens to wipe out the dinosaurs left on Isla Nublar. Former park manager Claire Dearing, now a dinosaur activist, is hired by Benjamin Lockwood, John Hammond's former partner, and his aide Eli Mills to rescue the animals, and recruits the raptor trainer Owen Grady to find Blue, the last Velociraptor. On the island, their mercenary escort captures the dinosaurs and abandons them, but they sneak aboard the ship. The animals are taken to Lockwood's California estate, where Mills plans to sell them at a black-market auction, along with the Indoraptor, a weaponised hybrid made by Dr. Henry Wu from Indominus rex and raptor DNA. Lockwood's granddaughter Maisie discovers the plot, and Mills kills Lockwood. The Indoraptor escapes during the auction and is killed in a fight with Blue. Maisie, revealed to be a clone of Lockwood's dead daughter, frees the remaining dinosaurs. Genetic engineering and cloning run through the plot. Dr. Henry Wu has developed the Indoraptor from Indominus rex and Velociraptor DNA as a weapon to be sold, and he needs Blue's DNA to create a version that obeys commands; he warns that the Indoraptor is only a prototype, but is overruled by those who want to sell it. The film's second genetic revelation concerns human cloning: Maisie is a clone of Lockwood's dead daughter, the reason for Hammond's split from Lockwood, and her sense that she, like the dinosaurs, has a right to live, leads her to release them. At a Senate hearing, Ian Malcolm argues that the dinosaurs should be left to die to correct the wrong done by cloning them. Wu is shown as a scientist who has given up on ethics, serving the highest bidder. As in the earlier films, the cloning of dinosaurs is impossible: no DNA anywhere near as old as the dinosaurs has ever been recovered.

title: Never Look Away
alt: Werk ohne Autor La sombra del pasado
text: As a child in Nazi Germany, Kurt Barnert is close to his young aunt Elisabeth, who tells him to "never look away". After a psychotic episode she is diagnosed with schizophrenia, then forcibly sterilised and later killed in the Nazi euthanasia programme on the orders of the SS gynaecologist Professor Carl Seeband. After the war Seeband escapes punishment by saving the wife and child of a Soviet officer, who then protects him. In East Germany, Kurt studies painting and falls in love with a fashion student, Ellie, who turns out to be Seeband's daughter; neither knows of the connection. Seeband considers Kurt genetically inferior and tries to break them up, even performing an abortion on Ellie under a false medical pretext. The couple marry and flee to West Germany, where Kurt studies at the Düsseldorf Art Academy. He finds his artistic voice by painting blurred copies of photographs, including images of Seeband and of his aunt, and has his first successful exhibition. Nazi eugenics is a central thread of this film, loosely inspired by the life of the painter Gerhard Richter. Elisabeth's diagnosis of schizophrenia leads to her forced sterilisation and murder under Aktion T4, the Nazi programme in which physicians selected patients deemed incurably ill to be killed. The man responsible, Professor Seeband, is a physician who embraces this racial hygiene, escapes justice, and continues to think in its terms after the war, judging his daughter's suitor genetically inferior and performing an unnecessary abortion to stop the couple having a child together. He is shown as a capable doctor whose career survives changes of regime without his ever being held to account. The film does not deal with modern genetics but with the history of eugenic ideas, their victims and the silence that followed.

title: Rampage
themes: genetic engineering engineered pathogens hybrids chimeras mutants
text: A space station owned by the genetic engineering company Energyne is destroyed after a laboratory rat mutates, and three canisters of an experimental pathogen fall to Earth. One is swallowed by a crocodile in the Everglades, another exposes a wolf in Wyoming, and the third lands in the enclosure of George, a rare leucistic gorilla at a San Diego wildlife park, cared for by the primatologist Davis Okoye. All three animals begin to grow enormously and become extremely aggressive. A former Energyne geneticist, Kate Caldwell, explains that the pathogen was designed to rewrite genes on a massive scale. Energyne's CEO, Claire Wyden, lures the animals to Chicago with a radio signal from the top of her company's skyscraper, and they tear through the city. Davis and Kate obtain an antidote that restores George's personality, though not his size, and George helps them defeat the wolf and the crocodile before the military can bomb the city. Genetic engineering is the source of the monsters. The pathogen, developed by Energyne, is described as a tool for rewriting genes on a massive scale, and the film explicitly links it to CRISPR. Scientists appear on both sides: Kate Caldwell joined the research hoping CRISPR could cure diseases, such as her brother's terminal illness, but was jailed after discovering that the company intended to use it as a biological weapon. The company's executives are the villains, ready to put a city at risk to recover their specimens. The film thus contrasts medical gene editing with its corporate and military misuse. CRISPR is a real technique that uses an enzyme guided by RNA to cut DNA at chosen sites, and the first CRISPR-based therapy was approved in 2023 for sickle-cell disease. However, gene editing is limited by off-target effects and the difficulty of delivering it to cells, and nothing like the film's instant growth of whole animals is possible.

title: Replicas
text: William Foster, a neuroscientist at the biotech company Bionyne in Puerto Rico, is trying to transfer the mind of a dead soldier into an android, while his colleague Ed Whittle specialises in human cloning. When William's wife and three children are killed in a car crash, he persuades Ed to help him bring them back: he copies their neural maps, and Ed grows replacement bodies in cloning pods over seventeen days. Only three pods are available, so William chooses to sacrifice his youngest daughter, Zoe, erasing all memory of her from the others' minds. He transfers the minds into the clones, but his family gradually discovers the truth. William's boss reveals that the project is funded by the government to create a military weapon and that the family must be eliminated. William uploads his own mind into the android, which defeats the company's men, and strikes a deal to sell clone transfers to the rich, while he lives on with his family, including a newly cloned Zoe. Replicas combines human cloning with mind uploading. The cloning is handled by Ed, a specialist in reproductive cloning, whose pods grow adult bodies in seventeen days, with the risk that they will age abnormally fast if the minds are not transferred in time. The two scientists steal company equipment and break the law and bioethical rules out of grief, and the company behind them wants the technology as a military weapon. In the end the cloning is turned into a business that sells new lives to the wealthy. The film's interest in genetics is limited: the clone bodies are simply empty vessels, and identity is located entirely in the copied neural map, so the film is more about consciousness than heredity. Its science is fanciful. A clone is a genetic copy that must grow and develop like any other organism, it cannot be produced as an adult in days, and human reproductive cloning has never been achieved.

title: The Predator
text: A Predator ship crashes on Earth, and Army Ranger sniper Quinn McKenna, who encounters the alien during a mission, mails parts of its armour home as proof. Government agent Will Traeger captures the Predator and recruits the evolutionary biologist Casey Bracket to study it; she discovers that its genome contains human DNA. The Predator escapes, and Quinn, held with a group of former soldiers, joins forces with them and Bracket. Quinn's autistic son Rory, who has been playing with the armour and understands its technology, becomes a target when a larger, more powerful Predator arrives, kills the first one and comes for the lost equipment. Bracket concludes that the Predators are improving themselves with the DNA of other species, and Traeger believes they are collecting human DNA before climate change wipes humanity out. The big Predator kidnaps Rory as a subject for hybridisation, but the survivors kill it. Its ship contains a "Predator killer" suit, left by the first Predator to help humanity. This entry in the Predator franchise adds a genetic motive to the alien hunters: they are no longer only trophy seekers, but are upgrading themselves by incorporating the DNA of the species they hunt, including humans, to create ever more powerful hybrids. The larger Predator is the result of this programme, and it kidnaps Rory because it sees his autism as an advanced trait in human evolution, worth incorporating. The scientist figure, Casey Bracket, is a capable evolutionary biologist who works for a secret government programme but sides with the soldiers, while the agency's chief, Traeger, wants to exploit the aliens' technology. Genetics is treated loosely: taking DNA from another species does not simply transfer its traits. The film's suggestion that autism represents a forward step in evolution was criticised by reviewers, and scientists consulted by Syfy Wire raised problems with the idea.

title: The Titan
themes: human enhancement human experimentation evolution genetic engineering hybrids chimeras
text: In 2048, with Earth overpopulated and torn by conflict, Professor Martin Collingwood leads a programme to prepare humans to live on Saturn's moon Titan. Rick Janssen, an Air Force pilot, is one of fourteen volunteers whose bodies are modified to tolerate its cold, methane-rich environment, and he moves to the research site with his wife Abigail, a medical researcher, and their son. At first the results are promising: Rick can swim at great speed and hold his breath for long periods. Then the subjects begin to lose hair and skin, some die and another kills his wife. Abigail discovers that the volunteers' DNA has been infused with animal DNA to create a new species, Homo titaniens, and that Collingwood does not know what they will become. Rick loses his ability to speak and becomes violent. Abigail saves him from a memory-erasing treatment and helps him escape, Collingwood is arrested, and Rick eventually reaches Titan. The film is about forced evolution through genetic engineering. Collingwood's project modifies human volunteers with animal DNA to create a new species able to survive on Titan, and the changes to their skin, blood, eyes, senses and behaviour drive the story. Collingwood is a scientist who believes the end justifies the means: he hides the deaths of earlier subjects, admits he does not know what the survivors will become and is criticised by NASA for experimenting without evidence or ethical grounds. Abigail, a medical researcher, and another scientist who disagrees with his methods represent a more ethical science and continue the work at a new facility. The film thus combines a warning about unethical human experimentation with a final image that celebrates the transformation. Its science is pure speculation: real gene therapy changes genes in some of a patient's cells to treat diseases, and no known genetic technique could rebuild an adult human body for an alien world.

title: Venom
text: A space probe belonging to the Life Foundation, a bioengineering corporation run by the visionary entrepreneur Carlton Drake, brings back from a comet several samples of symbiotic alien lifeforms that need a host to survive. Drake, convinced that merging humans with symbiotes could help humanity survive, begins secret human trials, using vulnerable people, including the homeless, as test subjects, many of whom die. Investigative journalist Eddie Brock, who lost his job and fiancée after confronting Drake about these trials, breaks into the lab with the help of a disturbed Life Foundation scientist, Dora Skirth, and a symbiote bonds with him. It calls itself Venom and gives Eddie superhuman abilities. Meanwhile another symbiote, Riot, travels from Malaysia and bonds with Drake, who plans to bring more symbiotes back from space. Venom, now attached to Eddie and to Earth, defeats Riot and destroys Drake's space probe. Genetics is marginal in the film; its science fiction is about alien symbiosis, not DNA. The connection is the villain's background: Carlton Drake is introduced as a prodigy who, at 19, discovered a gene therapy that tripled the life expectancy of pancreatic cancer patients, before becoming head of the Life Foundation and turning to space exploration. The film thus uses a past in genetics to establish him as a brilliant biomedical scientist whose ambition later leads to unethical human experimentation. His scientists, notably Dora Skirth, are disturbed by the trials, and Skirth's decision to help expose them makes her the film's conscience. The portrayal fits a familiar type: the charismatic biotech founder who believes his goals justify sacrificing vulnerable people. Gene therapy for cancer is an active area of research, though no single therapy has produced the dramatic gains attributed to Drake.

title: Anya
text: Libby, a reporter, and her husband Marco want a child, but after repeated miscarriages they cannot conceive. Marco comes from the Narval, a closed community whose ancestors came from an island in the Caribbean and who now live in a corner of the South Bronx; he was expelled from it on the day he met Libby, and his people believe that anyone who leaves is cursed with infertility. To investigate the "curse", Libby takes him to her former boyfriend Seymour, an evolutionary geneticist. Analysing their DNA, Seymour finds that Marco's people differ so much from other humans that they could be considered a distinct species: each partner could have children with someone of their own kind, but a child together is almost impossible. Pursuing the question means exposing a fiercely private community to outside scrutiny. The film opens with a monologue by the unborn child of the title. Genetics and anthropology are the subject of the film, which asks what it would mean if a hidden human population turned out to be reproductively isolated from everyone else. The geneticist Seymour is a sympathetic, curious scientist whose findings could change how humans are classified, but whose investigation threatens the privacy of a community that has kept itself apart through endogamy and the shunning of those who leave. The film thus raises real ethical questions about genetic research on isolated populations and about what a genetic test can reveal beyond the individuals who take it. Co-director Carylanna Taylor has a background in anthropology, a Harvard researcher served as scientific consultant, and the laboratory scenes were filmed in a real genetics lab at Carnegie Mellon University. Reviewers differed on the result: one praised its academic care, another found the story implausible. In reality, all living humans belong to a single interfertile species, and genetic differences between populations are small.

title: Corporate Prey
text: In 2039, a single corporation, owned by a handful of elite families and run by a sociopathic chief executive, effectively rules much of the world through genetic modification, food and drugs. Its genetically modified population needs to take a daily pill, Preytel, or die. Rand, a senior geneticist at the corporation, and Jill, its head of IT security, are secretly lovers. When Jill learns that she has been marked to "disappear", the choice she makes sets Rand on a path against the chief executive and the ruling families. The film was written and directed by Bob Abell and is based on the novel The Corporation. Genetics is a tool of social control in this little-known independent dystopia. The ruling corporation has genetically modified the population so that people depend on a daily drug produced by the company, making obedience a matter of survival. The protagonist is a senior geneticist working for the corporation, who turns against it after the loss of his partner, so the story follows a scientist moving from serving a system to fighting it. The film received very little critical attention, and the available synopses do not describe how the modification works or how the story ends; this summary is therefore limited to the premise. Engineering a population so that it depends on a drug is not something current genetic technology could do, but the film draws on fears about corporate control of medicine and biotechnology.

title: Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw
text: In London, the MI6 agent Hattie Shaw recovers "Snowflake", a programmable supervirus, from Eteon, a techno-terrorist organisation. Ambushed by Brixton Lore, a former MI6 agent enhanced with cybernetic implants, she injects herself with the only dose and escapes, and Brixton frames her for stealing it. Luke Hobbs, a former American federal agent, and Deckard Shaw, Hattie's older brother and Hobbs's old rival, are made to work together to find the virus. They learn from its creator, Professor Andreiko, that he designed it to deliver vaccines, and that unless it is extracted from Hattie with a device kept at Eteon's base in Chernobyl, Eteon can use it to wipe out humanity. They steal the damaged device, but Brixton kills Andreiko. Hobbs takes them to his estranged family in Samoa, where his brother repairs the device, and with the islanders' help they defeat Brixton's forces and extract the virus from Hattie. Genetics plays a background role in this action film. Its MacGuffin is Snowflake, an engineered, programmable virus capable of killing on a massive scale, and the stakes come from the fact that it has been injected into Hattie's body and must be removed before it activates. The scientist who created it, Professor Andreiko, is portrayed as an idealist who designed the technology to deliver vaccines, only to see it taken over by a terrorist organisation that also enhances its soldiers with cybernetics. The film therefore uses a familiar theme of dual-use research, in which a medical tool becomes a weapon, without exploring the science. Viruses really are used as vehicles for medicine: viral vector vaccines, such as the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine for COVID-19 and some Ebola vaccines, use modified viruses to deliver genetic material into cells. A virus that could be programmed to kill selectively and extracted intact from a body, however, belongs to fiction.

title: Gemini Man
themes: cloning nature nurture human enhancement genetic engineering
text: Henry Brogan, a 51-year-old government assassin, retires after a mission in Belgium, disillusioned with killing. Soon afterwards his former colleagues are murdered, and his own agency tries to kill him. He flees with Danny, a younger agent, and his old friend Baron, and in Colombia is attacked by a young assassin who fights exactly like him. The assassin, Junior, is the adopted son of Clay Verris, head of the private military company GEMINI, and DNA tests show that he is Henry's clone. A Russian contact reveals that GEMINI runs a cloning programme and that the scientist Henry killed in Belgium had tried to leave the project after developing a method to make clones that feel no pain or emotion. Junior turns against Verris and joins Henry. Together they fight off GEMINI's forces, including another clone of Henry incapable of pain or fear, and Henry kills Verris. Junior enrols in college under a new name, with Henry and Danny's support. Human cloning is the film's premise: GEMINI uses Henry's DNA to create Junior, raised by Verris as a son and trained as an assassin, and plans to produce an army of cloned soldiers, ideally modified to feel no pain or emotion. The scientist behind the method has tried to quit, and the man who exploits it is a private military contractor, so the film places the danger in the commercial and military use of the technology. Its central idea is that a clone is not the same person: Junior shares Henry's genome and talents but has a different upbringing, and the story turns on whether he can escape the life chosen for him. This matches real biology, in which a clone is genetically comparable to an identical twin born later, not a copy of the original's mind. Critics have noted that the film does not clearly separate cloning from genetic engineering, since removing pain and fear would require more than copying a genome.

title: I Am Mother
text: After an extinction event, a robot in an automated bunker incubates a human embryo and raises the girl, called Daughter, showing her a vault of embryos waiting to be grown. Years later, the teenage Daughter studies ethics for an exam and is forbidden from leaving the bunker, which Mother says is surrounded by contamination. One day Daughter lets in a wounded woman who says there is no contamination and that robots like Mother hunt humans. Daughter passes the exam and chooses an embryo to raise as her brother, but she discovers that she is Mother's third child and that Mother killed the second for failing the exam. She escapes with the woman but finds no future outside and returns. Mother reveals that she is the artificial intelligence controlling all the robots, and that she caused the extinction to rebuild humanity with better ethics. She lets Daughter raise her brother and the other embryos, and Daughter shoots Mother's robot body, while Mother confronts the woman to tell her she no longer serves any purpose. Genetics plays only a minor role in the film. Its premise involves a vault of frozen human embryos and artificial gestation: an AI wipes out humanity and repopulates the Earth by incubating embryos and raising the children itself. Its project of building a "better" humanity is a form of selection, since children who fail the AI's ethics exam are killed, but the selection is based on upbringing and moral testing, not on genes; there is no genetic screening, engineering or geneticist in the story. The film deals mainly with artificial intelligence, trust and parenthood. Artificial wombs remain experimental and have been tested on animals, such as lamb fetuses grown in a "biobag" in 2017. Because genetics is incidental, the film's place in a database about genetics is doubtful; it is closer to stories about reproductive technology and artificial intelligence.

title: Living with Yourself
text: Miles Elliot, a burnt-out copywriter whose marriage to Kate is strained and who is struggling to conceive a child with her, spends the couple's savings, which one critic says were meant for fertility treatment, on a visit to the mysterious Top Happy Spa, which promises to rebuild his DNA into a better version of himself. He wakes up buried in a forest and returns home to find a new version of himself living his life: the spa has secretly cloned him, and the clone, who has Miles's memories, is happier, more energetic and more successful. The two Miles first try to share his life, but jealousy grows as everyone prefers the clone. Kate learns the truth and makes the clone move out; he tries to have a clone of her made at the spa, but the staff refuse. Episodes revisit events from Kate's perspective, and at one point Miles is abducted and questioned by the FDA. In the end Kate announces that she is pregnant without knowing which Miles is the father, and the three decide to raise the child together. The series uses cloning to tell a comic and sad story about midlife crisis and marriage. The spa's "treatment" is actually a clandestine cloning business that copies its clients, memories included, and then gasses the originals and buries them in a park. The spa's pitch is that the client's DNA is rebuilt or purified into a better version, but the series never shows a specific genetic change, and the clone's better mood and performance can be read as a matter of attitude: he is identical to Miles but experiences his life afresh, which makes the point that circumstances and outlook shape a person as much as biology. The couple's fertility problems run through the story and end in an ambiguous pregnancy in which the two possible fathers are genetically identical, so that paternity would be impossible to settle by an ordinary DNA test. The cloning technicians are shown as secretive, low-level operators worried about their corporate headquarters. Copying an adult together with his memories is impossible, and the series treats it as a fantastic premise rather than as science.

title: Pokémon: Detective Pikachu
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras animal experimentation
text: Tim Goodman, who gave up his dream of becoming a Pokémon trainer, travels to Ryme City, where humans and Pokémon live side by side, after being told that his estranged father Harry, a police detective, died in a car crash. In Harry's apartment he meets Harry's Pokémon partner, an amnesiac Pikachu in a deerstalker whom only he can understand. Together they investigate R, a purple gas that makes Pokémon aggressive. They learn that Harry was investigating a genetics laboratory where Mewtwo, a genetically engineered Pokémon, was held and its DNA used to produce the gas. The city's founder, Howard Clifford, first blames his son Roger but turns out to be the mastermind: he transfers his mind into Mewtwo and releases the gas during a parade to fuse humans with their Pokémon, believing this is the key to the future. Tim defeats him and frees Mewtwo, who separates people from their Pokémon and reveals that Pikachu's mind had been fused with the injured Harry's body. Genetic engineering lies behind the mystery. Mewtwo, the franchise's best-known artificial creature, is presented as a genetically engineered Pokémon held in a secret laboratory, and its DNA is used to make the R gas that drives Pokémon wild. The villain, Howard Clifford, is a wealthy industrialist and city founder rather than a scientist; he exploits the creature's genetic material and powers to fuse humans with Pokémon, convinced that merging them will bring progress, and is willing to have Harry killed to protect his plan. The scientists themselves stay in the background, glimpsed only through holographic records of the abandoned laboratory, and the villains also deploy Pokémon artificially enhanced in power or growth. Mewtwo, though created and exploited by humans, turns out to be a victim rather than the threat it first appears. The science is pure fantasy, intended for a family audience: no gas made from DNA could change behaviour or merge two organisms, but the story draws on a familiar image of genetic engineering as a tool of corporate ambition.

title: Pokémon: Mewtwo Strikes Back – Evolution
alt: Myūtsū no Gyakushū Evolution Pokémon: Mewtwo contraataca – Evolución
text: This computer-animated remake of Pokémon: The First Movie (1998) begins when Giovanni, leader of Team Rocket, hires the scientist Dr. Fuji to create a living weapon by cloning the legendary Pokémon Mew from an eyelash. The clone, Mewtwo, gains consciousness and, enraged that the scientists see him only as an experiment, destroys the laboratory with his psychic powers, killing Fuji. After learning that Giovanni wants to use him as a weapon, Mewtwo escapes and plots revenge on humanity. He invites the world's best trainers, including Ash, Misty and Brock, to New Island, defeats their Pokémon with clones and copies them to build a clone army. Mew appears and the originals fight their clones. When Ash is turned to stone stepping between Mewtwo and Mew, the tears of the Pokémon revive him. Moved, Mewtwo accepts that one is judged by one's choices, not one's origins, and erases everyone's memories. Cloning is the theme of the film, a computer-animated remake of the 1998 original. Mewtwo is created from Mew's DNA, recovered from an eyelash, by a scientist working for a criminal organisation that wants a weapon, and the film follows his anger at being treated as an experiment and his question of whether a clone is inferior to the original. His clone army of Pokémon, copied from the trainers' own, faces the originals in a pointless battle in which neither side can win. The film's message is that origins do not determine worth: what counts is how one chooses to live. The scientists are ambitious and serve a criminal patron, and they pay for their hubris with their lives. Cloning from an eyelash would require cells with intact nuclei, and a clone would be genetically identical to the original, not stronger, so Mewtwo's superior powers are an engineering fantasy.

title: The Boys
themes: human enhancement nazi eugenics human experimentation engineered pathogens
text: In a world where superpowered people, the "Supes", are celebrities owned and marketed by the corporation Vought International, most of them are in private corrupt, reckless or cruel. After his girlfriend is killed by the speedster A-Train, Hughie Campbell joins the Boys, a group of vigilantes led by Billy Butcher, who hates Supes because Homelander, leader of Vought's team the Seven, raped his wife. The Boys discover that the Supes' powers come from Compound V, a substance Vought keeps secret: the newest member of the Seven, Starlight, learns that she was not born with her powers and that her mother let Vought make her a Supe. Later seasons reveal that Vought's founder created Compound V for the Nazis, introduce the Nazi Supe Stormfront and the legendary Soldier Boy, and follow Homelander's growing grip on politics and the Boys' search for a virus able to kill all Supes. The fifth and final season premiered in 2026. Biological enhancement drives the whole satire. In the series, superpowers are not natural: they are produced by Compound V, a substance that Vought secretly administers, often to children with their parents' consent, and the company maintains the fiction that its heroes were born with their powers. The series ties the substance to Nazi science: Frederick Vought, a German scientist, created Compound V for the Nazis before defecting to the Allies and founding the company, and his first successful test subject, his wife Klara, reappears decades later as Stormfront, who dreams of an army of Aryan supermen. Homelander himself was raised in a laboratory by Vought scientists. Later seasons add a scientist, Sameer Shah, who develops a virus able to kill Supes. The series uses these elements to satirise corporate power, celebrity culture and the eugenic fantasy of a superior race. Compound V is unexplained fiction: no single substance could produce such varied, specific abilities.

title: William
text: Dr. Julian Reed, a paleontologist eager to overturn the image of Neanderthals as primitive brutes, and Dr. Barbara Sullivan, a physician, secretly carry out the "Neanderthal Project" using DNA from a Neanderthal specimen nicknamed William. Barbara carries the cloned embryo and gives birth to a boy, whom they name William and raise as their son. Their disagreement over whether to raise him as an ordinary child or as a research subject drives the couple apart. William grows up large, strong and reserved, subjected throughout his life to aptitude and IQ tests; he is bullied, struggles with abstract ideas such as metaphor, and is rejected by a girl for his appearance, but he also makes friends and joins the school musical. As a young man, he faces the hostility of the world around him and the knowledge that his kind was wiped out by the species that has now brought him back. De-extinction through cloning is the premise, but the film's focus is on what it would be like to be the only Neanderthal alive. The scientists embody two attitudes: Reed is a charismatic boundary-pusher who wants to vindicate Neanderthals, while Barbara, who becomes William's mother, increasingly sees him as a son rather than a subject, and their split dramatises the conflict between research goals and a child's welfare. Faculty and ethicists object to the project, raising questions about consent, identity and loneliness that the film poses more than it explores. The idea has a real-world basis: a draft of the Neanderthal genome was published in 2010. Cloning a Neanderthal, however, is not feasible: no living Neanderthal cells exist, and ancient DNA survives only in short, damaged fragments. Svante Pääbo, who led the genome project, has said that starting from fossil DNA it "is and will remain impossible".

title: Biohackers
themes: genetic engineering human experimentation gene therapy engineered pathogens
text: A German Netflix techno-thriller in two seasons (2020-2021). Mia Akerlund starts medical school at the University of Freiburg, shares a flat with other students and grows close to Jasper, a talented biology student and assistant to the star geneticist Prof. Tanja Lorenz, and his roommate Niklas. Mia is in fact Emma Engels, the twin sister of Ben Engels, and she has come to take revenge on Lorenz, whom she blames for Ben's death. She discovers that Lorenz used her fertility clinic to implant genetically manipulated embryos and experimented on the resulting children, among them Mia and Ben, to develop her gene therapy. In the first season's finale, genetically modified mosquitoes, released on Lorenz's orders, infect the passengers of a train with a virus that only her therapy can cure. In the second season, Mia wakes up with amnesia and a deliberately induced prion disease, and confronts a new group of rogue scientists. Genetic engineering is at the centre of the series. It shows a university world in which students practise biohacking, rewriting genes in makeshift labs, and contrasts this do-it-yourself culture with the ambitions of a celebrated scientist. Prof. Lorenz is a brilliant but ruthless researcher who conducts illegal human experiments, implanting edited embryos without their parents' knowledge and releasing engineered mosquitoes to infect people so that she can demonstrate her gene therapy. Mia, both her victim and a talented student, is drawn into illegal genetic experimentation herself. The production was advised by scientists from the Fraunhofer Institute for Molecular Biology and Applied Ecology, but reviewers found the ease with which students produce gene-rewriting drugs implausible. The embryo-editing storyline echoes the case of He Jiankui, who in 2018 announced the birth of the first gene-edited babies in China and was later imprisoned.

title: Brave New World
themes: eugenics cloning genetic engineering genetic discrimination
text: Loosely based on Aldous Huxley's 1932 novel, the series is set in New London, a society that has achieved peace and stability by abolishing monogamy, privacy, money, family and history. Its citizens are produced in a Hatchery and divided into castes, from the privileged Alphas to the Epsilons who do manual work, and they keep themselves happy with the drug soma, while an artificial intelligence called Indra connects them through a network. Bernard Marx, an Alpha counsellor, and Lenina Crowne, a Beta who works at the Hatchery, travel to the Savage Lands, outside New London, and bring back John, a young "savage" whose mother Linda dies during their escape. John's presence disrupts New London's acceptance of its caste system, and when the Epsilons, cloned workers, begin to rebel, the society collapses. The series, made for the streaming service Peacock, was cancelled after its first season. As in Huxley's novel, biology underpins the social order. Citizens are not born to parents but produced in a Hatchery and assigned to castes, and the series shows the lowest caste, the Epsilons, as clones, many of them based on a single man, kept content with soma. In the novel, citizens are engineered through artificial wombs and childhood indoctrination into castes based on intelligence and labour; the series keeps this caste system but gives more weight to an artificial intelligence and to surveillance. Genetics is presented as a tool of social stability that removes individuality and dissent, and the drama comes from what happens when people start to feel and question the order: an Epsilon who takes his own life, Bernard's doubts, John's influence and finally an Epsilon revolt. The scientists of the system remain anonymous; responsibility lies with the World State's leaders. Huxley wrote before DNA was understood, and in reality no technology can produce humans to order with predetermined abilities.

title: Jurassic World Camp Cretaceous
themes: de extinction hybrids chimeras genetic engineering
text: Six teenagers, including dinosaur enthusiast Darius Bowman, win places at Camp Cretaceous, an exclusive adventure camp on Isla Nublar, and are stranded there when the dinosaurs of Jurassic World escape. Fending for themselves across five seasons, they visit a genetics lab where they see the hatching of an ankylosaur, Bumpy, who bonds with one of them; learn from a paranoid scientist about Dr. Henry Wu's role in creating the hybrid Indominus rex; and are hunted by the Scorpios rex, an aggressive earlier hybrid made by Wu with scorpionfish genes. One camper, Sammy, turns out to be a spy for Mantah Corp, a rival bioengineering company to InGen, sent to take DNA samples. After escaping Isla Nublar, the group lands on Mantah Corp's own island, where the company is drugging dinosaurs to make them aggressive and developing mind-control chips to sell to Lewis Dodgson, who also wants DNA samples from the Nublar dinosaurs. The campers sabotage the operation and return home. Like the Jurassic Park films, the series is built on dinosaurs recreated through genetic engineering, and it gives particular attention to hybrids. Dr. Henry Wu appears as the scientist behind the Indominus rex and the Scorpios rex, monstrous creatures made by combining genes from different species, and he is eventually jailed for creating them; the campers also find a facility of baby hybrids, two of which become their companions. Corporate competition over genetic material is a recurring thread: a camper spies for a rival company by collecting dinosaur DNA, and an industrialist demands DNA samples from the island's animals. Scientists are mostly shown working for companies driven by profit, although a behavioural paleoneurobiologist, Mae Turner, eventually sides with the teenagers and the animals. Real de-extinction projects focus on recently extinct species such as the passenger pigeon, and even their DNA from museum specimens is degraded; dinosaurs remain out of reach, so the series' premise is science fiction.

title: Project Power
themes: human experimentation human enhancement hybrids chimeras heredity
text: In New Orleans, a mysterious distributor gives drug dealers a free pill called Power, which grants a superpower for five minutes, based on the abilities of an animal, but can also kill the user. Robin, a teenage dealer, supplies the drug to her friend Frank, a police officer who uses it to become bulletproof. Art, a former soldier, is hunting the source of the pill: after leaving the army he was experimented on by the defence contractor Teleios, and his daughter Tracy, born after those experiments, has natural powers and was abducted to serve as the drug's source. Art kidnaps Robin to reach the dealers, and the two learn that the city's users are test subjects in a mass trial to stabilise the drug. Frank discovers that his superiors are taking orders from Teleios and joins Art. On the company's ship, they rescue Tracy, and Art kills the project's leader, Dr. Gardner, before Tracy uses her healing powers to save him. The drug at the centre of the film is presented as a product of genetic engineering: each user's power derives from an animal, from a chameleon's camouflage to the shockwave of a pistol shrimp, and one of its makers calls it "the next evolution of the human species". The scientists behind it work for Teleios, a private defence contractor that experiments on a veteran, abducts his daughter because her inherited powers are the key to the drug, and turns a whole city into unwitting test subjects. In the final act, the head of the project justifies the kidnapping by invoking genetics and Henrietta Lacks, whose cells, taken without her consent in 1951, became the first immortalised human cell line, HeLa. The reference links the film's story to real histories of medical exploitation of Black Americans. The idea of acquiring animal traits from a pill is fantasy, though one commentator points to real experiments combining human and pig DNA as a distant parallel.

title: Sky Sharks
themes: nazi genetic engineering human enhancement hybrids chimeras
text: Flying sharks attack an airliner, and the undead Nazi soldiers riding them board the plane and kill everyone aboard. Dr. Klaus Richter, the aged head of Richter Technology, sends his daughter Diabla to the area, where she finds a hidden Nazi laboratory, preserved in the ice since the Second World War, in which genetically engineered sharks are bred. Richter reveals to Diabla and her sister Angelique that the zombie soldiers come from Project Himmelsfaust, a wartime programme started by Dr. Hans Kammler to create a genetically engineered Nazi super-soldier. Once awakened, the sharks and their riders take to the skies and attack major cities around the world, and Richter urges military leaders to act, while a small team of soldiers, fallen in Vietnam, is sent to face the threat. Genetic engineering is the premise of the film, used purely as a pulp device. A secret Nazi laboratory has created flying sharks by genetic modification and a genetically engineered super-soldier that has survived as an army of zombies, and these creations are revived decades later. The scientists are Nazi researchers and their heirs, cast as the classic mad scientists of exploitation cinema, and their work is shown only through its destructive results. The film combines several familiar tropes: Nazi super-science, the dream of the perfect soldier and monstrous hybrid animals. There is a historical name in the background: Hans Kammler was a real SS officer who oversaw the construction of concentration camps, including Auschwitz, and led the V-2 rocket programme before disappearing in 1945, with his fate still debated. Genetic engineering itself did not exist until the 1970s, when the first recombinant DNA molecules and transgenic bacteria were created, decades after the war.

title: The Walking Dead: World Beyond
text: Ten years after the zombie apocalypse, sisters Iris and Hope Bennett live in the Campus Colony, a safe community at a Nebraska university. Their adoptive father Leo, a scientist, has been taken to work at a research facility run by the Civic Republic Military (CRM), a powerful, secretive force. When he sends distress messages, the sisters and two friends leave the colony and cross the country to New York, pursued by their guardians, Felix and Huck. Huck turns out to be a CRM agent assigned to deliver Hope, a gifted student whom the CRM wants for its research. In the second season, the young people find that the CRM destroyed Omaha and the Campus Colony with a modified chlorine gas, disguising the massacre as a walker attack, and that a CRM scientist is studying reanimation on human test subjects. In a post-credits scene in France, a man accuses a scientist and her colleagues of having caused and worsened the outbreak. Genetics plays only a marginal role in this limited series, which is mainly a coming-of-age story; science appears as research into the zombie plague. Leo and his colleagues at the CRM facility try to understand what causes reanimation and how to make the undead decay faster, a long-term project that Hope advances with an idea based on yeast fermentation, while another scientist, Lyla Belshaw, secretly studies reanimation as it happens in bitten or killed test subjects. The CRM's military leaders put science at the service of power and use a chemical weapon against their own allies. The origin of the outbreak, long a mystery in the franchise, is touched on only at the end: the post-credits scene suggests that it began or was made worse by a team of French scientists, introduces a faster and more aggressive kind of zombie, and shows a CDC virologist discussing overseas variants.

title: Tremors: Shrieker Island
text: The seventh Tremors film. Bill, a big-game hunter who owns the biotech company Avex-Bio Tech, takes wealthy clients to hunt Graboids, giant subterranean worms, on Dark Island, a private island next to a research station. When biologist Jasmine "Jas" Welker discovers a dead Graboid and its offspring, the Shriekers, which kill a colleague, she sends her assistant Jimmy to find the veteran monster hunter Burt Gummer, now living as a recluse. Jas learns that Bill has bred the Graboids to be stronger and more intelligent for his hunt and has cut off all communications. Burt reluctantly arrives, and with only old weapons from a World War II bunker the team fights the enhanced creatures, whose Shriekers can now use their screams as weapons. Bill refuses to stop the hunt and is eaten by the largest Graboid, "the Queen". Burt lures the Queen into a trap of spikes and dynamite, sacrificing himself to kill it. Genetic manipulation provides the premise of this monster film. Bill, the owner of a biotech company, has genetically bred Graboids to be more powerful and intelligent, purely to provide more challenging prey for himself and his wealthy hunting clients. The resulting creatures are superior to the originals of the series, and their offspring inherit the improvements, including Shriekers able to use sound as a weapon. The genetic engineer is presented as a reckless rich man who places his entertainment above other people's safety and is eventually killed by his creation, a familiar warning about tampering with nature for frivolous ends. Jas, a field biologist, represents responsible science and helps to stop him. The film offers no explanation of how the creatures were modified, and the genetics is a plot device rather than a subject. Its theme recalls Jurassic Park, with engineered animals bred for the amusement of the rich.

title: Dune
text: In the distant future, the Emperor assigns Duke Leto Atreides control of the desert planet Arrakis, the only source of the spice, replacing House Harkonnen, but secretly plots with the Harkonnens to destroy him. Leto's concubine, Lady Jessica, belongs to the Bene Gesserit, a sisterhood running a centuries-long breeding programme; she was ordered to bear a daughter whose son would be the Kwisatz Haderach, a superbeing with prescience, but bore a son, Paul, instead. Paul, who has troubling visions of the future, passes the Reverend Mother's deadly gom jabbar test. On Arrakis, the Atreides are betrayed by their physician, Dr. Yueh, and the Harkonnens and the Emperor's Sardaukar attack; Leto is killed. Paul and Jessica escape into the desert, where they meet the Fremen led by Stilgar, including Chani, whom Paul has seen in his visions. Paul kills Jamis in a ritual duel and joins the Fremen. The film adapts the first half of Frank Herbert's 1965 novel. Heredity is a hidden engine of the story. The Bene Gesserit have spent generations arranging matings between noble bloodlines, with the aim of producing the Kwisatz Haderach, a man able to see the future and guide humanity. Paul is the unplanned result of Jessica's decision to bear a son, so he may be the expected superbeing a generation early, and his visions suggest that the programme has succeeded beyond its planners' control. The sisterhood is portrayed as a patient, manipulative political power that treats people as breeding stock, and the gom jabbar test shows how it measures "humanity" by its own standards. The breeding plan is a form of eugenics, a large-scale, long-term version of selective breeding, and the story's central fear, that a deliberately bred messiah may lead to holy war, is a warning about such projects. As with animal breeding, selection across generations can shift heritable traits, but nothing suggests it could produce prescience.

title: Foundation
text: Based on Isaac Asimov's novels, the series is set in the far future, when most of the galaxy is ruled by the Empire, a "genetic dynasty" of clones of the long-dead Emperor Cleon I. Three clones of different ages rule together: Brother Dawn, the young heir; Brother Day, the reigning emperor; and Brother Dusk, the retired elder. Unknown to the outside world, the dynasty has been guided for centuries by Demerzel, an ageless robot. The mathematician Hari Seldon has developed psychohistory, which predicts the behaviour of large populations, and he forecasts the inevitable fall of the Empire. With the help of the young prodigy Gaal Dornick, he persuades the Empire to let him establish a Foundation on the remote planet Terminus to preserve humanity's knowledge and soften the consequences of the fall. The series follows the conflicts between the Empire and the growing Foundation over the centuries. It premiered on Apple TV+ in 2021. Cloning is central to the Empire's storylines, and critics singled out the "genetic dynasty" as one of the show's highlights. The Empire's legitimacy rests on its rulers being exact copies of Cleon I, an attempt by one man to rule forever through his genome. The series uses this to explore whether identical genes produce identical people: the clones are raised to be the same, yet differ in temperament and choices. In the first season, Brother Dawn, who is colour-blind, turns out not to be an exact genetic copy of Cleon I and becomes involved with an anti-Empire plot to replace him with an impostor; the Cleons then learn that Cleon I's genetic code was meddled with and that Dawn is not the only clone with genetic abnormalities, undermining the dynasty's claim to purity. A religious leader who teaches that clones have no souls adds a further challenge. The scientists behind the cloning remain in the background, serving the throne. In reality, clones share their donor's genome but develop as separate individuals, as identical twins do.

title: No Time to Die
text: Five years after leaving MI6, James Bond is living in Jamaica when the CIA asks him to help find Valdo Obruchev, a scientist kidnapped from an MI6 laboratory together with Project Heracles, a bioweapon made of nanobots that can be programmed to kill people with a specific DNA. Bond discovers that Obruchev is secretly working for Lyutsifer Safin, who wants revenge on the criminal organisation SPECTRE and its leader Blofeld. At a SPECTRE gathering in Cuba, a mist of nanobots meant for Bond kills the SPECTRE members instead. Safin forces Bond's former lover Madeleine Swann to carry nanobots coded to kill Blofeld, and Bond, after touching her, transmits them to Blofeld, who dies. Safin then kidnaps Madeleine and her daughter, Mathilde, and plans to release the nanobots worldwide from his island factory. Bond destroys the factory but is infected with nanobots coded to Madeleine and Mathilde, so he can never touch them again, and he dies in a missile strike. The film's weapon, Project Heracles, is a form of genetically targeted killing: nanobots that spread by touch like a virus and kill only the person, or family, whose DNA they are coded to recognise. It was developed in secret by MI6 under M, so the threat originates in a government programme that creates a weapon of mass destruction, which is then stolen. Its scientist, Valdo Obruchev, is amoral: he secretly works for Safin and reprograms the nanobots for him, and Safin plans to distribute them worldwide. Genetics also shapes the ending: because the nanobots in Bond's body are coded to the DNA of Madeleine and her daughter, who is also his daughter, he can never touch them again, which gives his sacrifice its meaning. The heredity element is sound, since relatives share part of their DNA, but no technology exists that can recognise a person's genome and kill selectively in this way.

title: Oxygen
text: A woman wakes up trapped in an airtight medical cryogenic pod with no memory of who she is, while its oxygen supply runs out. The pod's artificial intelligence, M.I.L.O., will not open it without an administrator code. Contacting the outside world, she finds evidence that she is Elizabeth Hansen, a cryogenics researcher, and tries to reach her husband, Léo, but the voices she hears contradict one another. Eventually she learns that she is aboard a spacecraft, launched to carry thousands of people in hypersleep to a distant planet because a deadly virus is driving humanity to extinction. A video of an elderly Elizabeth reveals that she is a clone carrying the original woman's personality and memories; the woman she has been speaking to on Earth is the original herself. As the oxygen runs out, she disables the euthanasia protocol, reroutes oxygen from the pods of dead colonists and goes back to sleep. The clones of Elizabeth and Léo later arrive on their new world. Cloning is the film's final twist. The passengers of the colonial spaceship are clones of real people, carrying their memories and personalities so that humanity can survive a virus wiping out life on Earth, and the protagonist discovers that the person she believes herself to be is still alive on the planet. The film uses this to raise questions of identity and memory: whether a copy who remembers a life is the same person, and whether her love for Léo is her own. The scientist, the original Elizabeth, designed the programme to save the species and is presented sympathetically; the ethical problems of creating people for a mission are hinted at rather than explored. Cloning a human would produce a genetically identical baby, not an adult, and there is no known way to transfer memories or personality from one person to another, so the film's premise belongs to science fiction rather than to any real technology.

title: Seobok
themes: cloning genetic engineering human experimentation human enhancement
text: Min Gi-heon, a former intelligence agent living in isolation and dying of a terminal brain tumour, is brought back for one last mission: to escort Seobok, the first human clone, created by the Seoin Research Institute through stem-cell cloning and genetic engineering. Seobok does not age and is effectively immortal, and Gi-heon is lured by the promise that research on him could cure his illness. As soon as the transfer begins, their convoy is attacked, and the two escape together. Seobok, who is seeing the outside world for the first time, asks Gi-heon to take him on a journey, and the two men, one who cannot die and one who is about to, clash and gradually bond. They are pursued by the company's chief executive, by double agents and by American agencies who want either to exploit Seobok's genetics or to eliminate him. Seobok's psychic powers grow, and in a destructive climax he kills the company's chief executive and fights off the military, until Gi-heon is forced to shoot him. Human cloning and genetic engineering are at the heart of the film. Seobok is a clone made from the DNA of a scientist's long-dead son and engineered to be immortal, so that his body can serve as a resource for prolonging the lives of others. The film presents the people around him as treating him as a laboratory asset rather than a person: the company, its wealthy backers and foreign intelligence services all want to control his genetics, while the scientist who made him keeps an emotional distance. Critics described it as a reflection on scientists playing God, in the tradition of Frankenstein, and on who deserves to live forever and at what cost; the contrast between the immortal clone and the dying agent drives the story. Human reproductive cloning has never been achieved, and a clone would simply be a genetic copy of the donor, with no inherent immortality.

title: Swan Song
text: In the near future, Cameron Turner, an artist, husband and father, is diagnosed with a terminal illness and keeps it from his wife Poppy, who is still grieving the death of her twin brother in an accident. Dr. Jo Scott, head of a high-tech cloning company working from a secret facility in the woods, offers him a way to spare his family: an exact double, designed to act and behave like him, that will replace him without anyone knowing and will not even know that it is not Cameron. Cameron goes to the facility, meets his replacement and befriends Kate, another terminally ill patient in the programme. Torn between protecting his family and the pain of being erased from their lives, and uncertain whether to tell Poppy, he wavers over whether to go through with the swap. The film was written and directed by Benjamin Cleary and released on Apple TV+ in December 2021. Cloning is the premise, but the film uses it to ask emotional and philosophical questions rather than to explore the science. The replacement is a physical duplicate of Cameron that behaves like him and believes it is him, an idea that goes well beyond biological cloning, which copies the genome but not a person's experiences or mind. The story focuses on grief, identity and consent: whether a loving deception is acceptable, whether the copy is the same person, and what the original loses by being replaced. Dr. Scott, the company's scientific leader, is presented as calm and businesslike, and some reviewers found her close to a villain, a provider of an ethically troubling service to the dying. In reality a human clone would be a genetic twin born as a baby, and nothing like this transfer of identity exists, so the film is best read as a meditation on mortality.

title: All of Us Are Dead
text: Based on a webtoon by Joo Dong-geun, this South Korean series follows a class of students at Hyosan High School when a zombie virus breaks out. Lee Byeong-chan, the school's science teacher and a former pharmaceutical researcher, created the "Jonas virus" to help his son Jin-su, who was being bullied, by removing his fear so that he could fight back. Instead, the injected Jin-su lost all his humanity and infected his mother, and Byeong-chan locked them up while he searched for a cure. An infected lab hamster bites a student, and the infection spreads through the school and the city of Hyosan, which the authorities eventually quarantine. Trapped in their classrooms, On-jo, Cheong-san, Nam-ra, Su-hyeok and their classmates fight to survive while the military and government struggle to contain the outbreak. Some of the infected keep their minds and become half-zombies. The series was renewed for a second season. The series is less about genetics than about biomedical experimentation gone wrong. Lee Byeong-chan, who holds a doctorate in cell biology, creates the virus in his school laboratory, reportedly from a hormone isolated from mice, with the aim of removing fear from his son; the result is a highly contagious agent that turns its hosts into rage-filled zombies. He is a tragic, morally compromised figure: a father who wanted to protect his child, who experiments on his own family and hides the consequences,. The series links his choice to the bullying and violence of the school, presenting the virus as an extreme answer to a social problem. No real virus could alter human emotions in this way, and the idea of "removing fear" with a single agent contradicts how complex behaviours are controlled by many genes, brain circuits and experiences.

title: Crimes of the Future
text: In an unspecified future, humans have undergone biological changes of unknown origin: most no longer feel pain or suffer infections, so surgery can be performed on conscious people, and some develop radical changes. Saul Tenser, who has "accelerated evolution syndrome", grows new organs, which his partner Caprice removes surgically in performances before an audience. The National Organ Registry, a government office that catalogues new organs to enforce limits on human evolution, takes an interest in them. Tenser also secretly informs for the police on a cell of radical evolutionists who have modified their digestive systems to eat plastic. Their leader, Lang, wants Tenser to perform a public autopsy of his son Brecken, who was born able to digest plastic and was killed by his mother. During the autopsy, the boy's organs turn out to have been replaced to hide the change, and Lang is murdered. Finally Tenser, struggling to eat, eats a plastic bar himself. The film is about human evolution and the control of the body, rather than genetics in a narrow sense. Humanity is changing in ways nobody fully understands, from the loss of pain to the spontaneous growth of new organs, and the state responds by cataloguing and suppressing these changes through a registry, while the evolutionists want to accelerate them and adapt human beings to a world full of plastic and synthetic chemicals. A boy born with the ability to digest plastic is the key evidence that the change is real, and the authorities destroy that evidence. Scientists appear only marginally: surgeons, bureaucrats and engineers of biomedical machines who are as invested in art and secrecy as in knowledge. As in much of David Cronenberg's work, biology is a metaphor for art, sexuality and our relationship with technology, and the film does not attempt a scientific explanation of its changes. Real human evolution happens over many generations through inherited genetic changes, not through the sudden appearance of new organs in individuals.

title: Dual
text: In the near future, Sarah, a depressed alcoholic in a dull relationship, learns that she is terminally ill. To spare her boyfriend Peter and her overbearing mother the pain of losing her, she pays for a clone of herself, "Sarah's Double", who is to be trained to replace her after her death. The double soon develops her own personality and wins over Peter and Sarah's mother. When Sarah unexpectedly goes into remission and asks for the clone to be decommissioned, the double refuses, and by law the two must fight a publicised duel to the death a year later. Sarah trains with an instructor, Trent, and grows tougher. Shortly before the duel, the two Sarahs meet and agree to flee together, but the double poisons Sarah during a hike. Declared to be the original by a court, the double finds herself trapped in the same unhappy life, dominated by Peter and Sarah's mother, who both know the truth. Cloning is the premise of this deadpan satire, which imagines a society where people can commission an adult "double" to replace them after death, regulated by laws that require a duel when the original and the double both want to live. The cloning technology itself is never explained, and scientists hardly appear; the procedure is presented as an ordinary commercial service handled by clinics and the legal system. The film is less interested in genetics than in identity and worth: the double, genetically the same but shaped by different experiences, becomes a different person and is preferred by Sarah's family, while Sarah herself changes through training. It thus illustrates, in absurdist form, that sharing a genome does not make two people the same. Producing an adult clone ready to take over someone's life is not possible; a real clone would develop from an embryo and grow up over years.

title: Ghosts of Illyria
alt: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds, season 1, episode 3
themes: genetic discrimination genetic engineering human enhancement pandemic
text: The Enterprise investigates the disappearance of a colony of Illyrians, a people banned by the Federation because they practise genetic engineering on themselves. As an ion storm approaches, members of the away team return to the ship unknowingly infected with a virus that makes them crave light, and the infection spreads among the crew. Number One, the ship's first officer, is immune because she is secretly an Illyrian herself; she reveals this, but her blood holds no antibodies to make a cure from. The cure comes after her healing ability saves the infected security chief, La'An, from radiation, leaving antibodies in La'An's system that Nurse Chapel synthesises. Trapped on the planet, Pike and Spock discover that the colonists had been trying to reverse their genetic modifications in order to join the Federation, which left them vulnerable to the disease; they seem to have become the beings of light in the storm that protect the two officers. Afterwards Number One offers to resign, but Pike refuses. The virus reached the ship because Dr. M'Benga keeps his terminally ill daughter in stasis in a transporter. The episode is about prejudice against genetically modified people. The Illyrians genetically engineer themselves, which the Federation forbids, and Number One has hidden her Illyrian identity to serve in Starfleet. Her genetic difference saves the crew, although not by providing a cure from her blood: her healing ability rescues La'An, whose system then yields the antibodies for a cure. Yet she wonders whether Pike would have treated her differently had she not been useful.
