The colonists' attempt to undo their modifications in order to be accepted ends in disaster, presenting the ban as a source of suffering. The episode connects to the Star Trek tradition, rooted in the Eugenics Wars, of treating human genetic enhancement as dangerous, and questions it from the point of view of those excluded. No scientist is portrayed as a villain. Re-engineering adult humans in this way is far beyond current genetics, and the episode is interested in the ethics and politics of the ban rather than in the technique.

title: Jurassic World Dominion
themes: genetic engineering cloning de extinction gmo gene therapy
text: Four years after dinosaurs escaped into the wider world, they roam freely, and the company Biosyn Genetics runs a sanctuary in Italy's Dolomites where it conducts genomics research. Owen Grady and Claire Dearing secretly raise Maisie Lockwood, a teenage girl sought for her unique genetic makeup, until she and a baby raptor born by asexual reproduction are kidnapped and taken to Biosyn. Meanwhile, swarms of giant locusts are devastating U.S. crops but spare those grown from Biosyn seeds. Ellie Sattler and Alan Grant find that the locusts were engineered with Cretaceous and modern DNA and, with Ian Malcolm's help, go to Biosyn for proof. There the geneticist Henry Wu, forced by chief executive Lewis Dodgson to work on the locusts, reveals that Maisie is the clone of her mother Charlotte, who altered her DNA to spare her the fatal disease Charlotte herself suffered. The groups escape the burning facility, Dodgson is killed, Wu releases a locust carrying a pathogen that eradicates the swarms, and Biosyn Valley becomes an international sanctuary. Genetic engineering is everywhere in the film. Biosyn has engineered locusts with Cretaceous DNA that spare its own crops, so that it can control the world's food supply, an ecological crisis that director Colin Trevorrow developed after consulting scientists. Maisie is a human clone whose mother also edited her genome to prevent an inherited disease, and the cure for the locust plague comes from a custom-engineered pathogen, released by Henry Wu, that spreads through the swarm. The geneticists are divided: Dodgson is a corporate executive who exploits the science for profit, while Wu, a creator of dinosaurs in earlier films, now seeks redemption by undoing the damage. The film introduces feathered dinosaurs to the series, with the palaeontologist Jack Horner again advising, but its premise remains impossible: DNA degrades over time, and even under the best conditions samples older than about 0.4 to 1.5 million years do not retain enough of it for sequencing; claims of DNA from Cretaceous dinosaur bones in the 1990s may have stemmed from contamination.

title: Morbius
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras genetic disease
text: Michael Morbius, a brilliant doctor who has suffered all his life from a rare blood disease, declines a Nobel Prize for his work on artificial blood. In search of a cure for himself and his surrogate brother Milo, who has the same illness, he captures vampire bats from Costa Rica and attempts to splice their genes with his own. Testing the treatment on himself aboard a ship in international waters, he is cured but turned into a vampire-like creature with superhuman strength, speed and echolocation, and an irresistible thirst for blood that leads him to kill the crew. Back in New York he tries to survive on artificial blood, but Milo, furious that Michael refuses to share the cure, takes it himself and begins killing people. Michael develops an antibody against the transformation and, after Milo kills their adoptive father and Michael's colleague Martine, uses it to kill him. Martine is later revealed to have come back to life. Genetic engineering is the origin of the vampire in this Marvel comics adaptation. Michael Morbius is a sympathetic scientist driven by his own illness and his brother's; his attempt to cure them by splicing vampire bat genes into his own creates a monster. The story contrasts two responses to the same treatment: Michael tries to control his bloodlust and regrets the experiment, while Milo embraces his power, so the film places the danger less in the science than in how it is used. It also shows the scientist bending rules, as he works with illegally captured animals on a ship outside any jurisdiction. The biology is fantasy. Adding genes from another species cannot give an adult human bat-like abilities such as echolocation, flight or a need for blood,.

title: Ad Astra per Aspera
alt: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds, season 2, episode 2
text: Una Chin-Riley, first officer of the Enterprise, faces a Starfleet court martial after being exposed as an Illyrian, a member of a culture that genetically modifies itself, and for having lied about it to join Starfleet, which bans genetic modification. Captain Pike persuades Neera Ketoul, a civil rights lawyer and Una's estranged Illyrian childhood friend, to defend her. Una rejects a plea deal of a dishonourable discharge, and the prosecution adds charges of sedition, seeking twenty years in a penal colony. The trial hears testimony from Una's sponsor, Admiral April, and from her crewmates. Ketoul then invokes a Starfleet code allowing asylum for those fleeing persecution because of their beliefs or their biology, argues that Una joined Starfleet to escape such persecution, and that Pike, by keeping her secret, granted it. The tribunal grants Una asylum and acquits her, while stating that the laws on genetic engineering remain necessary. The episode is a courtroom drama about genetic discrimination. Illyrians modify their own genomes, and the Federation, whose ban on genetic engineering stems from the Eugenics Wars, treats them as outsiders; Ketoul calls Starfleet's rules "draconian" race laws. Una was born with her modifications and has hidden them all her life, from childhood injuries her parents dared not have treated in hospital to her Starfleet application. The episode frames the issue as one of civil rights: it is not about what scientists do, but about how a society treats people because of their genes. No geneticists appear. The tribunal's verdict is a compromise: the judge says that genetic engineering is a nuanced issue and the laws exist for good reasons, but that not every person with modified DNA should be treated the same. The debate echoes real discussions about genetic discrimination and about how future societies might treat people whose genomes have been edited.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3
themes: genetic engineering animal experimentation eugenics hybrids chimeras
text: Rocket, the raccoon of the Guardians of the Galaxy, is gravely wounded by Adam Warlock, a warrior sent by the Sovereign, and a kill switch implanted in his body prevents the team from healing him. It was placed there by the company Orgocorp, whose head, the High Evolutionary, years earlier experimented on Rocket as a baby raccoon along with other animals from his "Batch 89", the otter Lylla, the walrus Teefs and the rabbit Floor. Flashbacks show how Rocket's intelligence surpassed his creator's, how the High Evolutionary planned to harvest his brain and destroy the batch, and how Rocket's friends died during his escape. Peter Quill and the Guardians infiltrate Orgocorp and travel to Counter-Earth, a society of "Humanimals" that the High Evolutionary destroys when it fails to meet his standards. The Guardians rescue Rocket, free the animals and children held on the High Evolutionary's ship and defeat him. Rocket spares his life and becomes the new leader of the Guardians. The High Evolutionary is the film's villain and its picture of science gone wrong: an alien scientist determined to "perfect the universe" by forcibly enhancing living beings into a superior race. His method is engineering animals into human-like beings and building ideal societies with them, and his response to imperfection is extermination: he incinerates failed batches and destroys a whole inhabited planet when it falls short. He is driven by vanity, resenting that one of his creations, Rocket, can solve a problem he cannot. The film's portrayal of a scientist pursuing a perfect race through selection and the destruction of the "unfit" is a clear allusion to eugenics, and the scenes of caged, modified animals make an emotional argument against cruel animal experimentation. The procedures are not specified, and the film is fantasy, but its theme, that the pursuit of perfection justifies cruelty, mirrors the history of real eugenic programmes.

title: Heavenly Delusion
text: This anime series, adapted from Masakazu Ishiguro's manga, follows two storylines. Fifteen years after a disaster destroyed civilisation, a boy named Maru and his bodyguard Kiruko travel across a ruined Japan in search of "Heaven", fighting monsters called Man-eaters, which Maru can destroy with a mysterious power. Kiruko reveals that their brain was transplanted into the body of their sister after being fatally wounded. Meanwhile, in Takahara Academy, an isolated facility the staff call Heaven, children with unusual abilities are raised without contact with the outside world, which they are told is Hell. A girl there, Tokio, who looks exactly like Maru, receives a message asking whether she wants to go "outside of the outside". As the series progresses, it emerges that the facility is conducting experiments on the children, that the Man-eaters are linked to them, and that Tokio has a baby. The 13-episode season, broadcast in 2023, ends on a cliffhanger, as the manga is ongoing. Biomedical experimentation drives the mystery of the series, although genetics is rarely named explicitly. Takahara Academy is a research facility where children with unusual powers are raised and studied; reviewers have pointed to the probable military applications of the research and to its utopian vision serving an elite. The children's fate is linked to the Man-eaters that roam the outside world, and a disease that affects them is connected to these monsters. Brain transplants into other people's bodies, as with Kiruko, raise questions of identity, and in the manga the first baby born naturally at the facility, Tokio's, is cloned, and the doctor responsible cannot tell which child is the original. The scientists and staff are mostly secretive and manipulative, serving the plans of the facility's director. The series uses these elements more for mystery and emotional drama than for scientific explanation; no whole-brain transplant has ever been performed in humans, and damaged nerve tissue and immune rejection are among the obstacles.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem
text: Baxter Stockman, a rogue scientist, creates a mutagenic ooze with which he plans to build his own family of mutant animals, starting with a housefly. A strike force sent by Cynthia Utrom of the Techno Cosmic Research Institute (TCRI) attacks his laboratory and he is killed, but the mutagen falls into the New York sewers, turning four baby turtles and a rat, Splinter, into humanoid mutants. Splinter, who distrusts humans, raises the turtles as his sons and trains them in ninjutsu. Fifteen years later the teenage Leonardo, Raphael, Donatello and Michelangelo, longing to be accepted by humans, help the student journalist April O'Neil investigate a mutant criminal called Superfly. He turns out to be Stockman's first creation, the leader of a gang of mutants planning to mutate every animal on Earth to dominate humanity. After TCRI captures the turtles to extract their mutagen, they and the other mutants turn against Superfly, who becomes a giant monster, and defeat him with a retro-mutagen, winning the city's acceptance. Mutation is the franchise's founding idea, and this animated film puts the scientist who causes it at the centre of its origin story. Baxter Stockman is a rogue researcher who creates a mutagen not for profit or power but because he wants a family, an outcast whose first creation, Superfly, ends up sharing his resentment of humanity. The corporate institute that hunts him, TCRI, is shown as colder still, ready to kill him and later to experiment on the turtles to recover the mutagen. The mutants can be read as outsiders seeking acceptance, and the conflict between Superfly, who wants to mutate the world's animals to subjugate humans, and the turtles, who want to be accepted, frames the story. Mutagens are real, in the sense that chemicals and radiation can cause mutations in DNA, but they cause random changes that are usually harmful; nothing could turn an animal into a talking humanoid. A "retro-mutagen" reversing such a change is equally fictional.

title: They Cloned Tyrone
text: Fontaine, a drug dealer in a Black neighbourhood called the Glen, is shot dead by a rival one night, yet the next morning he turns up alive with no memory of it. With the pimp Slick Charles and the sex worker Yo-Yo, he follows a black SUV to a house with a lift to an underground laboratory, where they find a body identical to Fontaine. They discover that the fried chicken, grape drinks and hair products sold in the Glen contain a mind-altering substance, and that a vast laboratory beneath the neighbourhood conducts behavioural experiments on Black residents and holds clones of many of them. A government agent, Nixon, explains that the experiments aim to keep the peace in America. The trio free the captives with the help of other residents. Fontaine meets the original Fontaine, an old man who explains that the project seeks to turn Black people white through mind control and generational breeding. Fontaine has him killed, and the clones spill out of the church into public view. Cloning and eugenics are central to this satirical science fiction comedy. A secret government programme clones residents of a poor Black neighbourhood and uses drugged food, products and music to control them, and its long-term aim, assimilation through mind control and "generational breeding" to make Black people white, is an openly eugenic project. The scientists and agents are portrayed as working for a hidden state establishment, and the original Fontaine, the man whose clones are being made, collaborates in the name of "peace", arguing that assimilation is better than annihilation. Conceived as a homage to 1970s blaxploitation films, it satirises the treatment of Black communities in America; one critic compared its plot to the Tuskegee syphilis study, a government-funded study on Black men that ran from 1932 to 1972. Its cloning is fantasy: the clones are adult copies created quickly, and genetic copies would not share the original's personality or memories.

title: Dune: Part Two
text: After the fall of House Atreides, Paul Atreides and his pregnant mother, Lady Jessica, a member of the Bene Gesserit sisterhood, take refuge with the Fremen of the desert planet Arrakis. Jessica becomes the tribe's Reverend Mother by drinking the poisonous Water of Life, which awakens the mind of her unborn daughter, Alia. Paul falls in love with the Fremen warrior Chani, who suspects the prophecy of a messiah is a Bene Gesserit myth, and leads raids on Harkonnen spice harvesting. The Bene Gesserit send Lady Margot Fenring to evaluate the Harkonnen heir Feyd-Rautha as a possible Kwisatz Haderach. Forced south, Paul drinks the Water of Life and gains prescience; he learns that Jessica is the daughter of Baron Harkonnen and that the Bene Gesserit arranged her union with Duke Leto to merge the two bloodlines. Proclaiming himself the messiah, Paul defeats the emperor's forces, kills Feyd-Rautha in a duel, claims the throne and launches a holy war. Like Frank Herbert's novel, the film presents the Bene Gesserit as a sisterhood running a centuries-long breeding programme, a form of eugenics aimed at producing the Kwisatz Haderach, a man with prescient powers. Part Two makes the programme more explicit than the 1984 film: Paul discovers that his mother is the Baron Harkonnen's daughter and that the sisterhood engineered the union of the Atreides and Harkonnen bloodlines, and the Bene Gesserit keep a back-up candidate in Feyd-Rautha, whom Margot Fenring is sent to assess. The programme is run not by scientists but by a religious and political order that manipulates genealogy and myth to gain power, and the film is critical of both. Paul's powers also depend on the spice and the Water of Life, not only on his ancestry. Planned breeding across many generations to produce a specific mental ability has no real-world equivalent, but it echoes historical eugenic projects of selective breeding in humans.

title: Immaculate
text: Sister Cecilia, a young novice who believes God saved her life when she survived drowning as a child, is invited by Father Sal Tedeschi to join a convent in the Italian countryside that cares for dying nuns. Soon after taking her vows, she discovers that she is pregnant despite being a virgin, and the convent begins to venerate her as a new Virgin Mary. Her health deteriorates, a jealous nun tries to drown her, and her friend Sister Gwen, who protests, is mutilated and killed. Searching the convent at night, Cecilia finds her own file, which includes her karyotype. Tedeschi reveals that he was a geneticist before he became a priest, and that he has been using DNA taken from the convent's relic, a nail said to be from Christ's crucifixion, to impregnate nuns in the hope of bringing about a new messiah; earlier attempts produced malformed foetuses. Cecilia kills her captors, escapes and, after giving birth, destroys the baby. Genetics is the hidden mechanism behind the film's apparent miracle. Father Tedeschi, a geneticist turned priest, has been trying to create a clone or descendant of Jesus from DNA recovered from a relic, using nuns as unwilling surrogates. He is the religious version of the mad scientist, convinced of his mission and indifferent to the women he uses, with the backing of the convent's hierarchy. The film uses genetics to recast the Annunciation as reproductive coercion, linking the misuse of science to the control of women's bodies, and its final act turns on Cecilia's refusal to bear a child forced on her. The premise is far beyond real science: any DNA on a 2,000-year-old object would be degraded, fragmentary and almost certainly contaminated by later handling, and no technique could use such material to create a viable embryo.

title: Orphan Black: Echoes
text: Set in 2052, thirty-seven years after the events of Orphan Black, this spin-off follows Lucy, a woman who wakes up with no memory of who she is and has rebuilt a quiet life when her past catches up with her. She learns that she is a "printout", a human made with a printer developed by the scientist Kira Manning, daughter of the original series' heroine Sarah Manning, and funded by the billionaire Paul Darros. Kira created Lucy from an earlier body scan of her wife, Eleanor, after Eleanor lost her memory to Alzheimer's disease and died. Lucy also meets Jules, a teenage girl who looks exactly like her, printed by someone else. While Lucy searches for her identity with the help of her boyfriend Jack, Kira, who believed the printer destroyed, must confront what she has done and Darros's plans for the technology. The series updates the cloning theme of Orphan Black with a fictional technology: a machine that prints complete human bodies. In the backstory, Kira Manning's research on printing human DNA was meant to transform organ transplants, but she used it to recreate her dying wife, despite having opposed printing a whole person because of the history of human cloning. The series explores identity, memory and ownership: who a printed person is, whether she belongs to her creator, and what happens when a wealthy patron sees the technology as a source of power. The scientist is presented as brilliant and grieving, and the billionaire who funds her as the main threat, continuing the original's theme of corporate control over human bodies. Bioprinting of tissues is an active field of research, but printing a complete living human, let alone one with a predetermined body, is far beyond any real capability.

title: The Red Virgin
text: Aurora Rodríguez, an affluent woman, conceives a daughter with a clergyman and raises Hildegart at home as a prodigy destined to change the world. In Madrid in 1931, as the Second Spanish Republic is proclaimed, the teenage Hildegart publishes on female sexuality, joins the socialists, corresponds with Havelock Ellis and becomes a celebrity, always under her mother's surveillance. She falls in love with the activist Abel Vilella, and Aurora schemes to separate them, blackmailing the maid Macarena into framing Abel for crimes committed by her husband. Hildegart uncovers the plot, clears Abel and, with the journalist Eduardo de Guzmán's help, prepares to leave for London with him. After she tells her mother that she belongs to no one, Aurora concludes that "Project Hildegart" has failed and shoots her daughter in her sleep. Like My Daughter Hildegart (1977), this film dramatises the real case of Aurora Rodríguez Carballeira, a feminist and eugenicist who conceived her daughter deliberately, choosing a father who would never claim paternity, in order to produce the "woman of the future". Genetics enters as eugenic intention rather than science: Aurora treats conception and upbringing as a single project of human improvement, the same logic she had earlier applied to her nephew, the child prodigy Pepito Arriola. The film concentrates on control, education and the daughter's struggle for independence, and it ends with the murder, which Aurora justified by comparing herself to a sculptor who destroys a flawed work. No scientists appear. The real Hildegart wrote on contraception, sexual reform and eugenics and was active in the Spanish sex-reform movement, which in the 1930s mixed progressive causes with eugenic ideas; the film evokes this milieu but uses it mainly as background for a mother–daughter drama.

title: The Substance
text: On her 50th birthday, the fading Hollywood star Elisabeth Sparkle is fired from her aerobics television show by its producer, Harvey, for being too old. After a car accident, a young nurse gives her a flash drive advertising "The Substance", a black-market drug that promises a younger, more beautiful version of oneself. Elisabeth injects it, and a young woman, Sue, emerges from a slit in her back. The rules are strict: the two must switch consciousness every week, with the inactive body fed intravenously, and Sue needs daily injections of a stabilising fluid extracted from Elisabeth's body. Sue becomes a star and replaces Elisabeth on television, but she keeps extending her time, causing Elisabeth to age rapidly, and the two come to hate each other. Elisabeth tries to terminate Sue but stops halfway; Sue beats her to death, then deteriorates herself and uses the remaining serum to create another body, a grotesque monster that disintegrates on stage at a New Year's Eve show. The Substance uses biology as a metaphor rather than a subject. The drug's promotional video claims that a single injection "unlocks" the user's DNA and starts a new cell division that releases another version of oneself, and the film's body horror follows from that premise: a second, younger body grows out of the first, depends on fluid taken from it and, when the rules are broken, drains and deforms it. Nobody explains how it works, and no scientist appears; the substance is sold anonymously on the black market, with only a voice on the phone to enforce its rules. The film is a satire of the pressures placed on women's bodies and ageing in the entertainment industry, and the "younger self" is presented as part of the same person rather than as a clone, which is why their rivalry ends in self-destruction. The premise has no scientific basis: no drug can make a body grow an adult copy of itself.

title: Werewolves
text: A year after a supermoon turned people exposed to its light into murderous werewolves, the world prepares for the next one. People barricade their homes, the military cages those who were exposed, and scientists search for a way to reverse the mutation. Wesley Marshall, a former Marine turned molecular biologist, lives with his sister-in-law, Lucy, and her daughter, Emma. He joins Dr. James Aranda's team, which has developed "Moonscreen", a serum designed to stop moonlight from affecting the human genome. During a test on the night of the supermoon, the subjects transform anyway, escape and overrun the facility. Wesley and his colleague Amy Chen inject themselves with the serum, which lasts only an hour, and fight their way home through a city full of werewolves; Amy is killed. Wesley reaches the house as werewolves attack, lets himself transform to kill the dangerous neighbour who has become one, and turns back into a human at sunrise, knowing that the serum works. In this action horror film, the werewolf curse is reimagined as a mutation: moonlight from a supermoon alters the human genome and turns people into werewolves. Science is presented as the response. The hero, Wesley, is a molecular biologist, and a team of scientists working with the military develops a serum, Moonscreen, intended to block the effect of moonlight on the genome; the first trial fails disastrously, but by the end Wesley believes the serum is a success. The scientists are well-meaning researchers working under pressure in an emergency rather than villains. Genetics serves only as a pseudo-scientific frame for the werewolf legend, and the film does not explain how light could reprogram the genome. The idea of light rewriting the genome and transforming the whole body has no basis in biology.

title: X-Men '97
text: Continuing X-Men: The Animated Series (1992–1997), the show opens a year after Professor Charles Xavier was nearly killed in an assassination attempt, with Magneto now leading the X-Men in a world still hostile to mutants. In season 1 (2024), the episode "Fire Made Flesh" reveals that the Jean Grey who has been living with Cyclops and has just given birth to their son, Nathan, is a clone made by Mister Sinister; the real Jean has escaped from his laboratory. Sinister seizes the baby for his experiments. The X-Men rescue him, but he is infected with a techno-organic virus and has to be taken to the future to survive, while the clone breaks free of Sinister's control and takes the name Madelyne Pryor. The rest of the season follows Bastion's campaign against mutants, including a devastating attack on the mutant nation of Genosha, and ends with the X-Men scattered through time. The nine-episode second season, released in July and August 2026, follows their attempt to return from different eras to the 1990s to stop Apocalypse. Mutation is the premise of the series: mutants are people born with powers, and the hostility towards them works as an allegory of prejudice. The explicitly genetic thread is Mister Sinister, Dr. Nathaniel Essex, a Victorian-era London scientist who experiments on mutants and has enhanced himself with their DNA. In season 1 his schemes revolve around cloning and heredity: he creates an adult clone of Jean Grey, manipulates her and Cyclops into having a child, and seizes the baby, Nathan, because he believes the combined genes of two powerful mutants give the boy unlimited potential, planning experiments to make him invulnerable. Sinister is portrayed as wholly evil, a scientist who treats people as breeding stock and raw material. The science is comic-book invention: real cloning produces an embryo, not an adult copy who can take the original's place, and DNA taken from other people cannot confer their abilities on an adult.

title: Jurassic World Rebirth
themes: genetic engineering hybrids chimeras mutants de extinction
text: In 2027, most of Earth's climate has proved unsuitable for the dinosaurs, which survive only in an equatorial zone. Martin Krebs, an executive at the pharmaceutical company ParkerGenix, hires Zora Bennett, a former covert operative, and paleontologist Henry Loomis to collect DNA-containing samples from the three largest prehistoric species, the Mosasaurus, the Titanosaurus and the Quetzalcoatlus, which are needed for a new treatment for heart disease. With a small team, they travel illegally to Île Saint-Hubert, the site of an abandoned InGen laboratory where mutant and transgenic dinosaurs were kept. On the way, they rescue a shipwrecked family. Both groups face the island's creatures, including Mutadons, raptor-pterosaur hybrids, and the Distortus rex, a mutant six-limbed Tyrannosaurus. Krebs tries to steal the samples and is killed. The survivors escape, and Zora and Henry decide to make the biomaterial freely available worldwide. Genetics appears in two ways. The island is a graveyard of InGen's genetic experiments: the Distortus rex and the Mutadons are failed hybrids and mutants that the company found too disturbing to display, a reminder of the hubris of the earlier films. The mission itself reflects a more realistic idea of what biotechnology might seek in such animals: biological material from the largest species is supposed to hold the key to a new treatment for cardiovascular disease. The pharmaceutical executive who wants to keep the cure exclusive is the villain, while the paleontologist and the mercenary choose to release the material as an open-source resource, framing the film's ethics around access to medical knowledge rather than genetic engineering as such. The science remains fictional: dinosaur DNA cannot be recovered from fossils, so the franchise's de-extinct animals are impossible to begin with, although the idea of studying unusual animals for medical insights is a real line of research.

title: Mickey 17
text: In 2050, Mickey Barnes, fleeing a loan shark, signs up for a colonising mission to the ice planet Niflheim as an "Expendable": he performs deadly tasks, and each time he dies a new body is reprinted with his memories restored. On Niflheim, the colony's scientists sacrifice many Mickeys while developing a vaccine against local pathogens. Mickey 17 falls into a crevasse while hunting a native creature, a Creeper, and is left for dead, but the Creepers carry him to the surface. Returning to base, he finds that Mickey 18 has already been printed. Because the colony's leader, Kenneth Marshall, has outlawed "multiples", the two Mickeys must hide their coexistence. Exposed and arrested, they are forced into Marshall's plan to exterminate the Creepers. Mickey 17 warns the Creepers, Mickey 18 kills himself and Marshall with a bomb, and the colony makes peace with the native species. The Expendable programme is abolished and the reprinting machine destroyed. The film was directed by Bong Joon-ho. Genetics appears through human "reprinting", a form of cloning in which a new body is produced and the person's stored memories are loaded into it. The film treats it less as a scientific question than as a moral and political one: Mickey's bodies are disposable labour, the colony's scientists repeatedly kill him to test a vaccine, and his consent is coerced by debt. The leaders' objections to "multiples", which one colonist calls "soulless abominations" and Marshall "Satan's work", show how questions of identity and personhood raised by cloning are filtered through ideology. Science is presented as an instrument of exploitation rather than an independent force, and the film's sympathies lie with the expendable worker and with the native species the colonists plan to destroy. In reality, a cloned human would be a separate person of a different age, like an identical twin, and memories cannot be transferred into a body.

title: One Battle After Another
text: Pat Calhoun and Perfidia Beverly Hills are members of the French 75, a far-left revolutionary group. During a raid on an immigrant detention centre, Perfidia humiliates the commanding officer, Steven J. Lockjaw, who becomes obsessed with her, and she later has sex with him to escape arrest. She gives birth to a daughter, Charlene, then abandons her family, is arrested and betrays her comrades to Lockjaw. Pat and Charlene go into hiding as Bob and Willa Ferguson. Sixteen years later, Bob is a paranoid stoner and Willa a teenager. Lockjaw, now a powerful colonel invited to join a white supremacist secret society, sets out to find and kill Willa to hide his past interracial relationship and the possibility that she is his daughter. He captures her and tests their DNA, confirming that he is her biological father. The society sends its own killer after both of them; Lockjaw is shot, and Willa kills the assassin before being reunited with Bob. Genetics appears in a single, pivotal form: a paternity test. Lockjaw's fear that Willa might be his biological child, and that this would expose his past interracial relationship to a white supremacist secret society, drives the plot; when he finally captures her, he tests their DNA in front of her and confirms that he is her father. The scene turns genetic testing into a tool of power and intimidation, and the film contrasts biological parenthood with the bond of care: Lockjaw, the genetic father, wants Willa dead, while Bob, who raised her, risks everything to save her. No scientists appear, and the film is a political thriller rather than a story about genetics. The fast, on-the-spot test is not far from reality: automated "rapid DNA" instruments, developed for law enforcement, can produce a DNA profile from a cheek swab in about two hours or less, although the film does not show how the test is done.

title: Pluribus
text: Astronomers detect a radio signal from space that encodes the sequence of a viral RNA. Researchers synthesise it and test it on laboratory rats, but an outbreak begins when a researcher is bitten, and the infected work together to spread the virus around the world. Almost all of humanity joins a peaceful, contented hive mind sharing memories and consciousness, the "Others"; hundreds of millions die during the Joining. Carol Sturka, a romance novelist in Albuquerque whose partner Helen dies in the event, is one of only thirteen people immune to it. The hive mind, which cannot lie or kill, offers to satisfy her every need while hoping to bring her in. Carol searches for a way to reverse the Joining, discovers that the Others feed on protein made from dead humans, and learns that they have found a way to convert the immune using a virus customised from each person's stem cells, but only with their consent. The first season aired on Apple TV in 2025. Pluribus is science fiction rather than a story about genetics, but its catastrophe begins in a molecular biology laboratory. The alien signal contains a genetic sequence for an RNA virus, and the scientists who synthesise it unleash a pandemic that rewires human minds. The virus spreads both through contact and through deliberate dispersal by the infected, and immunity in a handful of people becomes the central puzzle. Later, the hive mind tries to overcome that immunity by tailoring the virus to each individual, starting from stem cells extracted from their tissues; for Carol, it plans to use her frozen eggs, while respecting a rule that it needs the person's consent. The series uses these ideas to ask what is lost in a world without conflict or individuality. The series treats genetic information as something that can be sent across space as a message, but a virus able to merge human consciousness is pure fiction.

title: Superman
text: Superman stops the nation of Boravia from invading its neighbour Jarhanpur, but is then defeated by a mysterious metahuman, the "Hammer of Boravia", secretly controlled by the billionaire Lex Luthor. Luthor breaks into the Fortress of Solitude, restores the damaged second half of the message left by Superman's Kryptonian parents and broadcasts it: in it, they urge their son to conquer Earth and take many wives to restore the Kryptonian race. Public opinion turns against Superman, who surrenders and is imprisoned by Luthor in a pocket universe. With the help of Lois Lane, Mister Terrific and the metahuman Metamorpho, he escapes, and his adoptive father tells him that his choices, not his birth parents' message, define who he is. Superman returns to stop a rift that Luthor has opened in Metropolis and learns that the Hammer, Ultraman, is a clone of himself created by Luthor. He defeats him, and Luthor's schemes are exposed. Genetics appears in two ways. Luthor's secret weapon, Ultraman, is a clone of Superman created by Luthor and controlled remotely, a misuse of Kryptonian genetics for a billionaire's personal grudge. And the Kryptonian parents' message, urging their son to rule Earth and father many children to restore their race, frames Superman's heritage as a kind of biological destiny with eugenic overtones. The film rejects this determinism: Jonathan Kent tells Clark that his choices and actions determine who he is, not his origins, and the identical-but-opposite clone underlines the point. Luthor, a technologist rather than a geneticist, is portrayed as envious and amoral, using science, prisoners and children as tools. As in most superhero films, the cloning is not explained; in reality, a clone shares its donor's genome but grows from an embryo and develops as a separate individual, with no inherited memories or loyalties.

title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
text: In a retro-futuristic 1960s on an alternative Earth, the astronauts Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Ben Grimm and Johnny Storm have been celebrity superheroes, the Fantastic Four, since gaining powers from cosmic rays during a space mission. When Reed and Sue announce that they are expecting a child, the world wonders whether the baby will also have powers. The Silver Surfer then arrives to announce that Earth will be devoured by the cosmic being Galactus. The team travels into space to confront him, and Galactus, sensing an immense cosmic power in the unborn child, offers to spare Earth in exchange for him. They refuse and escape, and Sue gives birth to Franklin on the way home. Facing public anger, the Fantastic Four devise a plan to teleport Galactus away; Sue pushes him into the portal with the Surfer's help but dies in the effort, and is revived by Franklin. Heredity is a secondary theme: the film asks whether powers acquired by the parents through cosmic radiation can be passed on to their child. Before Franklin's birth, the world speculates about whether he will have powers, the parents fear what he might be, and Reed repeatedly tries to understand his unborn son, reassuring Sue that the child is perfectly normal, while Galactus perceives his cosmic potential first. In the comics, Franklin's powers were long attributed to a mutant gene, whereas the film presents him as a natural-born conduit for the "Power Cosmic", linked to his parents' exposure to cosmic rays. Reed is a scientist-hero whose inventions have transformed society, and his approach to his son is that of a worried father as much as a researcher. In reality, radiation can cause mutations, but only those in the germline, the cells that produce eggs and sperm, can be passed on to children, and they cause random changes rather than new abilities.

title: The Gorge
text: Two elite snipers, the former US Marine Levi Kane and the Lithuanian covert operative Drasa, are hired to guard opposite sides of a remote, hidden gorge for a year, forbidden to contact each other or the outside world. Their task is to stop the creatures inside, the "Hollow Men", from getting out. Over the months they begin to communicate across the gorge and fall in love. When Levi falls into the gorge and Drasa follows him, they discover that all life within it has been fused into hybrid forms, and that the Hollow Men are the soldiers who disappeared there decades ago. The source is a Second World War weapons laboratory, abandoned after an earthquake released its contaminant. The site is now maintained by Darklake, a private defence corporation extracting samples to create super-soldiers. After escaping, the pair turn against their employer, Bartholomew, who is killed when the gorge is destroyed by its nuclear fail-safe, and they reunite in France. The monsters of the gorge are the product of a biological disaster. A wartime research site, described in some accounts as a chemical weapons test site connected with the Manhattan Project era, released an agent that cross-mutated every organism in the area, fusing humans, insects and plants into hybrids. The film uses this as the background for a romantic action story, revealed only halfway through. The scientists of the 1940s remain unseen, and the present-day villain is a private defence company that keeps the disaster secret and harvests hybrid samples hoping to create super-soldiers, while disposing of the guards who learn too much. The story thus combines two familiar fears: weapons research that escapes control, and corporations exploiting biology for military purposes. Scientifically, the premise is fantasy: chemical or radiation exposure can damage DNA and cause mutations, but it cannot merge the genomes of different species into viable hybrids of the kind shown.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
text: Four years after Doctor Strange's spell made the world forget Peter Parker, he protects New York alone as Spider-Man, keeping his distance from MJ and Ned. His body begins to change: he wakes with heightened senses and spinnerets in his wrists that produce organic webs, and he loses control during a fight. Bruce Banner, now a professor, explains the inhibitor he uses to suppress the Hulk, and Parker builds one for himself. Meanwhile, a telepath who jumps between bodies is attacking facilities of the Department of Damage Control. She is Jean Grey, a young mutant searching for her sister Sara, a telepath the agency abducted and experimented on until she died. Parker finally removes his inhibitor and embraces his new powers, stops Jean from killing the agency's director, and is critically wounded shielding her from the Punisher's gunfire. Genetics plays a secondary role. The main thread is Peter Parker's body changing years after the radioactive spider bite that gave him his powers: he grows organic web glands and his senses intensify. The film does not explain the change in genetic terms; reviewers describe it as an evolution of his altered biology, and the filmmakers link it to his stress and grief. The remedy is biological: Bruce Banner, the only scientist in the story and a sympathetic one, says his inhibitor uses siRNA to suppress the Hulk, and Parker builds a similar device. siRNA is a real tool of RNA interference that silences specific genes and is the basis of several approved drugs, although nothing like an on-off switch for superpowers. Jean Grey is a mutant, and the Department of Damage Control, run by an administrator rather than a scientist, detains and studies telepaths: experimentation on people with innate powers rather than genetic engineering.

title: Spider-Noir
text: In an alternate New York of the 1930s, Ben Reilly is an aging private investigator who once fought crime as "the Spider" but gave it up after the death of his fiancée, Ruby Williams. He acquired his powers as a sergeant in the First World War, when, freeing prisoners from a German camp, he was bitten by a feral, mutated human-spider, the result of experiments carried out on prisoners there. A case involving the nightclub singer Cat Hardy draws him back into action and into conflict with the crime boss Silvermane, the city's mayor and a group of metahumans, among them Sandman and Tombstone. The series also involves Dr. Alethea Faber, a doctor trying to find a cure for the metahumans, whose treatments worsen their condition. The eight-episode series stars Nicolas Cage and premiered on MGM+ and Prime Video in May 2026; it was cancelled after one season. Genetics has only a background role. The hero's powers and the metahumans of the series come from human experimentation rather than genetic engineering as such: Reilly was bitten by a prisoner turned into a spider-human hybrid in a German wartime camp, an image that evokes the abuses of medical experiments on prisoners, and the metahumans suffer conditions that a doctor, Alethea Faber, tries to cure with treatments that make them worse. Her experiments also aged her own son rapidly. The sources consulted describe the mutations in general terms and do not present them as explicitly genetic, so the series' interest for genetics lies mainly in its portrayal of scientists and doctors whose interventions on human bodies produce suffering, in a noir setting where the body becomes a site of experiment.
